To throw into confusion or commotion by contention or discord; to entangle in a broil or quarrel; to make confused; to distract; to involve in difficulties by dissension or strife. The royal house embroiled in civil war.

Want of relish; dislike (of the palate or of the mind); distaste; a slight degree of disgust; as, a disrelish for some kinds of food. Men love to hear of their power, but have an extreme disrelish to be told of their duty.
To give up, the will, courage, or spirit; to be thoroughly disheartened; to lose all courage; to become dispirited or depressed; to take an unhopeful view. I should despair, or at least despond.
To annul in part; to repeal partly; to restrict; to limit the action of; -- said of a law. By several contrary customs, .

To corrupt or undermine in morals; to destroy or lessen the effect of moral principles on; to render corrupt or untrustworthy in morals, in discipline, in courage, spirit, etc.; to weaken in spirit or efficiency. The demoralizing example of profligate power an
To cry down; to censure as faulty, mean, or worthless; to clamor against; to blame clamorously; to discredit; to disparage. For small errors they whole plays decry.
A musical instrument used by the ancients. It is supposed to have been similar to the modern kettle drum, though perhaps smaller.
A device consisting of a short rope with flat hooks at each end, for hoisting casks or barrels by the ends of the staves.
To shrink; to start back; to draw back, from lack of courage or resolution; to flinch; to quail. Blench not at thy chosen lot.
The act of aspirating; the pronunciation of a letter with a full or strong emission of breath; an aspirated sound. If aspiration be defined to be an impetus of breathing.

An instrument which shows the direction of the wind; a wind vane; a weathercock; -- usually applied to a contrivance consisting of a vane above, connected in the building with a dial or index with pointers to show the changes of the wind.

To shrink back with shuddering from; to regard with horror or detestation; to feel excessive repugnance toward; to detest to extremity; to loathe. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.

A tract of soft wet land, commonly covered partially or wholly with water; a fen; a swamp; a morass. [Written also marish.] Marsh asphodel (Bot.), a plant (Nartheeium ossifragum) with linear equitant leaves, and a raceme of small white flowers; -- called also
A wasting of flesh without fever or apparent disease; a kind of consumption; atrophy; phthisis. Pining atrophy, Marasmus, and wide-wasting pestilence.
The lateral movement of a ship to the leeward of her course; drift.
A genus of large percoid fishes, of which one species (Lates Niloticus) inhabits the Nile, and another (L. calcarifer
The protection of the interior walls of a fortification from an enfilading fire, as by covering them, or by a high parapet on the exposed side.
A genus of coniferous trees, properly called Fir, as the balsam fir and the silver fir. The spruces are sometimes also referred to this genus.
Worthy of consideration, borne in mind, or attended to. It is considerable, that some urns have had inscriptions on them expressing that the lamps were burning.
An extensive division of Crustacea, having a dorsal shield or carapec
A division of Arachnida including those spiders which have four lungs, or pulmonary sacs. It includes the bird spiders (Mygale) and the trapdoor spiders.
A division of brachiopods including those which have a calcareous shell furnished with a hinge and hinge teeth. Terebratula and Spirifer are examples.

One in control of the stage during the production of a play. He directs the stage hands, property man, etc., has charge of all details behind the curtain, except the acting, and has a general oversight of the actors.
A Lenten dish, composed of eggs boiled hard, chopped, and seasoned with butter, salt, and pepper. Halliwell.

An engine, usually an internal-combustion engine of a certain type (the radial type) having several cylinders arranged radially like the spokes of a complete wheel. The semiradial engine has radiating cylinders on only one side of the crank shaft.
An order of marine Bryozoa, having a bilobed lophophore and an axial cord. The genus Rhabdopleura is the type.
A suborder of serpents including those that have permanently erect grooved poison fangs, with ordinary teeth behind them in the jaws. It includes the cobras, the asps, and the sea snakes.
A plant that has many, or more than two, cotyledons in the seed. -- Pol`y*cot`y*led"on*ous, a.
A genus of ctenophores having an ovate body and two long plumose tentacles.
A division of ganoid fishes including those that have large external bony plates and a cartilaginous skeleton.
A group of wading birds having the toes webbed, as the avocet.
A perennial plant of the genus Saururus (S. cernuus), growing in marshes, and having white flowers crowded in a slender terminal spike, somewhat resembling in form a lizard's tail; whence the name.
An order of sponges, having simple siliceous spicules and keratose fibers; -- called also Keratosilicoidea.

A glass tube provided with platinum electrodes, and containing some gas under very low tension, which becomes luminous when an electrical discharge is passed through it; -- so called from the name of a noted maker in germany. It is called also Plücker tube, fr
An order of sponges having a fibrous skeleton, including the commercial sponges.
A division of amphibians having suctorial disks on the toes, as the tree frogs.
The anterior portion of any one of the Arachnida and higher Crustacea, consisting of the united head and thorax.
A group of Annelida remarkable for having no external segments or distinct ventral nerve ganglions.
To disrobe; to undress; to take off the robes.
To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked. I.
To unite again; to join after separation or variance. Shak.
To trouble; to disturb; to annoy; to harass with petty vexations. We are pestered with mice and rats.
To cause to become an object; to cause to assume the character of an object; to render objective. J.
To become corporeal; to assume the qualities of a material body. See Embody.
To lay snares for rabbits. Huloet.
To fix by the root; to fix fast; to implant deep. Shak.
To hide under a false semblance or seeming; to feign (something) not to be what it really is; to put an untrue appearance upon; to disguise; to mask. Dissemble all your griefs and discontents.
To reduce from the privileges of a forest to the state of common ground; to exempt from forest laws. By charter 9 Henry III.
An incrustation over a sore, wound, vesicle, or pustule, formed by the drying up of the discharge from the diseased part.
That which is laid, staked, or pledged, as between two parties, upon the event of a contest or any contingent issue; the act of giving such a pledge; a wager. "Having made his bets." Goldsmith.
A distinctive mark, token, sign, or cognizance, worn on the person; as, the badge of a society; the badge of a policeman. "Tax gatherers, recognized by their official badges.
In mammals, a fluid excretion from the kidneys; in birds and reptiles, a solid or semisolid excretion.
One who, or that which, transforms. Specif.
The act of one who, or that which, sprinkles. Baptism may well enough be performed by sprinkling or effusion of water.
One who produces, brings forth, or generates.
Specifically, the disease known as the plague; hence, any contagious or infectious epidemic disease that is virulent and devastating. The pestilence That walketh in darkness.
A thin skin or film.
Serving to ornament; characterized by ornament; beautifying; embellishing. Some think it most ornamental to wear their bracelets on their wrists; others, about their ankles.
A name sometimes applied to the process of annealing metals.
A thin plate or scale; a laying over another; -- said of thin plates or platelike substances, as of bone or minerals.
The act of inflecting, or the state of being inflected.

An excrescent appendage, as, a wart or tumor; anything growing out unnaturally from anything else; a preternatural or morbid development; hence, a troublesome superfluity; an incumbrance; as, an excrescence on the body, or on a plant. "Excrescences of joy." Je
The staff for holding a bunch of flax, tow, or wool, from which the thread is drawn in spinning by hand. I will the distaff hold; come thou and spin.
The act of digressing or deviating, esp. from the main subject of a discourse; hence, a part of a discourse deviating from its main design or subject.

The act of declaring, or publicly announcing; explicit asserting; undisguised token of a ground or side taken on any subject; proclamation; exposition; as, the declaration of an opinion; a declaration of war, etc.
The act of deceiving or misleading. South.
Common possession or enjoyment; participation; as, a community of goods. The original community of all things.
p. pr.

The act of baptizing; the application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ. This is performed by immersion, sprinkling, or pouring.

(a) The whole mass of aëriform fluid surrounding the earth; -- applied also to the gaseous envelope of any celestial orb, or other body; as, the atmosphere of Mars. (b) Any gaseous envelope or medium.
A person invested with full power to transact any business; especially, an ambassador or envoy to a foreign court, with full power to negotiate a treaty, or to transact other business.
The act of lengthening in space or in time; extension; protraction. Bacon.
Having no wings; not able to ascend or fly. Wingless bird (Zoöl.), the apteryx.
Serving to effect reversal, as of motion; capable of being reversed. Reversing engine, a steam engine having a reversing gear by means of which it can be made to run in either direction at will.
Filled, covered, or sprinkled with dust; clouded with dust; as, a dusty table; also, reducing to dust. And all our yesterdays have lighted fools The way to dusty death.
Watchful; vigilant; active in vigilance.
A very large marine mammal (Trichecus rosmarus) of the Seal family, native of the Arctic Ocean. The male has long and powerful tusks descending from the upper jaw.
A rare white earthy substance, consisting of the oxide of thorium; -- formerly called also thorina.
A rope used for tying or hobbling the legs of a horse or cow. [Prov.
To smile in an affected or conceited manner; to smile with affected complaisance; to simper.

Any one of numerous species of oscinine birds of the family Laniidæ, having a strong hooked bill, toothed at the tip. Most shrikes are insectivorous, but the common European gray shrike (Lanius excubitor), the great northern shrike (L.
To mark or cut the edge or border of into segments of circles, like the edge or surface of a scallop shell. See Scallop, n., 2.
To hold in thought; to account; to estimate; to hold; to think; to reckon. Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight Job xviii.

Any one of several species of venomous American snakes belonging to the genera Crotalus and Caudisona, or Sistrurus. They have a series of horny interlocking joints at the end of the tail which make a sharp ratting sound when shaken.

One skilled in making poetry; one who has a particular genius for metrical composition; the author of a poem; an imaginative thinker or writer. The poet's eye, in a fine frenzy rolling, Doth glance from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven.
A plant common in Europe (Paris quadrifolia); herb Paris; truelove. It has been used as a narcotic.
An imaginary monster, or hideous giant of fairy tales, who lived on human beings; hence, any frightful giant; a cruel monster. His schoolroom must have resembled an ogre's den.

Insurrection against constituted authority, particularly military or naval authority; concerted revolt against the rules of discipline or the lawful commands of a superior officer; hence, generally, forcible resistance to rightful authority; insubordination. I
An oxide containing one atom of oxygen in each molecule; as, barium monoxide.
A basic compound containing one amido group; as, methyl amine is a monamine.
An elongated pod, consisting, like the legume, of two valves, but divided transversely into small cells, each containing a single seed.

The state, or condition, of belonging to a definite place, or of being contained within definite limits. It is thought that the soul and angels are devoid of quantity and dimension, and that they have nothing to do with grosser locality.

A similarity of crystalline form between substances of similar composition, as between the sulphates of barium (BaSO4) and strontium (SrSO4). It is sometimes extended to include similarity of form between substances of unlike composition, which is more properl
A very thin, slight, transparent stuff, generally of silk; also, any fabric resembling silk gauze; as, wire gauze; cotton gauze. Gauze dresser, one employed in stiffening gauze.
To protect, as a line of troops, against an onset of cavalry, by opposing bayonets raised obliquely forward. Wilhelm.
That which is fed out to cattle horses, and sheep, as hay, cornstalks, vegetables, etc.
To influence, or attempt to influence, by whispered insinuations or private talk. "No longer was he earwigged by the Lord Cravens." Lord Campbell.
A wave of the voice embracing both a rise and fall or a fall and a rise on the same a syllable. Walker.
To inflict pain upon, by means of stripes, or in any other manner, for the purpose of punishment or reformation; to punish, as with stripes. How fine my master is!
A pointed instrument, as a joiner's awl, a brad awl, a needle, or a small ship stick.
A salt containing two parts of chromic acid to one of the other ingredients; as, potassium bichromate; -- called also dichromate.
The pin or spindle on which a wheel revolves, or which revolves with a wheel.

A fruit allied to the plum, of an orange color, oval shape, and delicious taste; also, the tree (Prunus Armeniaca of Linnæus) which bears this fruit. By cultivation it has been introduced throughout the temperate zone.

A stone imagined by some to be of impenetrable hardness; a name given to the diamond and other substance of extreme hardness; but in modern minerology it has no technical signification. It is now a rhetorical or poetical name for the embodiment of impenetrable
To reduce to a common measure. Sir T.
Fitted to represent; exhibiting a similitude.
Note: [Usually construed with to.]
The form of the possessive case of the personal pronoun you.
a. & vb.
pl. of Child.
Carried; conveyed; supported; defrayed. See Bear, v.
A substance or device that has its conductivity altered in some way by electric waves, as a coherer.
A kind of cartilage with a fibrous matrix and approaching fibrous connective tissue in structure. -- Fi`bro*car`ti*lag"i*nous, a.
A group of Pulmonifera having the eyes at the base of the tentacles, including the common pond snails.
Consisting of three united; multiplied by three; threefold; as, a triple knot; a triple tie. By thy triple shape as thou art seen.

The external part of a thing; the part, end, or side which forms the surface; that which appears, or is manifest; that which is superficial; the exterior. There may be great need of an outside where there is little or nothing within.
of Lie, to tell a falsehood.
One with whom marriage is designed; one who is betrothed; an affianced lover. If it were not that I might appear to disparage his intended, .
Any matter used to produce heat by burning; that which feeds fire; combustible matter used for fires, as wood, coal, peat, etc.
The act of flexing or bending; a turning or curving; flexion; hence, obsequious bowing or bending. Will it give place to flexure and low bending Shak.
That which is fixed or attached to something as a permanent appendage; as, the fixtures of a pump; the fixtures of a farm or of a dwelling, that is, the articles which a tenant may not take away.
Anything used in fitting up; especially (pl.),
A man whose business is to extinguish fires in towns; a member of a fire company.
The act or process of completing or perfecting; the final work upon or ornamentation of a thing.
The act of one who calls; a crying aloud, esp. in order to summon, or to attact the attention of, some one.

Note: In trigonometrical surveying, it is customary to reckon the azimuth of a line from the south point of the horizon around by the west from 0º to 360º. Azimuth circle, or Vertical circle, one of the great circles of the sphere intersecting each other in th
Separately, in regard to space or company; in a state of separation as to place; aside. Others apart sat on a hill retired.
The commoner kind of frankincense, or that obtained from the Norway spruce, the long-leaved pine, and other conifers.
pl. of Stratum.

The external covering or coat, as of flesh, fruit, trees, etc.; skin; hide; bark; peel; shell. Thou canst not touch the freedom of my mind With all thy charms, although this corporal rind Thou hast immanacled.
The act of respiring or breathing again, or catching one's breath.
Intoxicated.
The part of an anchor which fastens in the ground; a flook. See Anchor.
The act of explaining, expounding, or interpreting; the act of clearing from obscurity and making intelligible; as, the explanation of a passage in Scripture, or of a contract or treaty.
The act of setting apart or consecrating to a divine Being, or to a sacred use, often with religious solemnities; solemn appropriation; as, the dedication of Solomon's temple.
A hundred; as, a century of sonnets; an aggregate of a hundred things. [Archaic.] And on it said a century of prayers.
A tough, white, aromatic resin, or gum, obtained from different species of the Laurus family, esp. from Cinnamomum camphara (the Laurus camphara of Linnæus.).
Lower in place, with something directly over or on; under; underneath; hence, at the foot of. "Beneath the mount." Ex.

A name given to a numerous family of brass wind instruments with valves, invented by Antoine Joseph Sax (known as Adolphe Sax), of Belgium and Paris, and much used in military bands and in orchestras.
To loose; to unfix; to unbind; to untie.
To line with boards or panelwork, or as if with panelwork; as, to wainscot a hall. Music soundeth better in chambers wainscoted than hanged.
To prove to be true or correct; to establish the truth of; to confirm; to substantiate. This is verified by a number of examples.
To open, as what is rolled or convolved; as, to unroll cloth; to unroll a banner.
To deprive of nerve, force, or strength; to weaken; to enfeeble; as, to unnerve the arm. Unequal match'd, .
To unfasten, as what is locked; as, to unlock a door or a chest.
To untwist; as, to unlay a rope.
To take from the hinges; as, to unhinge a door.
To deprive or divest or a frock; specifically, to deprive of priestly character or privilege; as, to unfrock a priest.
To cause to move backward and forward, or up and down, in undulations or waves; to cause to vibrate. Breath vocalized, that is, vibrated and undulated.
To take out of dock; as, to undock a ship.
To remove the turns of (a rope or cable) from the bits; as, to unbit a cable. Totten.
To remove a band from; to set free from shackles or fastenings; to unite; to unfasten; to loose; as, unbind your fillets; to unbind a prisoner's arms; to unbind a load.
To write over again, or in the same words; to copy; as, to transcribe Livy or Tacitus; to transcribe a letter.
To dry and brown by the heat of a fire; as, to toast bread.

To drink spirituous or strong liquors habitually; to indulge in the frequent and improper used of spirituous liquors; especially, to drink frequently in small quantities, but without absolute drunkeness. Few of those who were summoned left their homes, and tho
To wander on foot; to ramble idly or leisurely; to rove. These mothers stroll to beg sustenance for their helpless infants.
To weaken, as a joint, ligament, or muscle, by sudden and excessive exertion, as by wrenching; to overstrain, or stretch injuriously, but without luxation; as, to sprain one's ankle.
To deposit in a place of hiding; to hide; to conceal; as, to secrete stolen goods; to secrete one's self.
To play rudely and boisterously; to leap and frisk about in play.
To restore carbon to; as, to recarbonize iron in converting it into steel.
To offer for consideration; to exhibit; to propose; as, to propound a question; to propound an argument. Shak.
To feed, esp. to feed on growing grass; to supply grass as food for; as, the farmer pastures fifty oxen; the land will pasture forty cows.
To face down; to outstare. To outlook conquest, and to win renown.
To manage ill or improperly; as, to mismanage public affairs.
To give a wrong direction to; as, to misdirect a passenger, or a letter; to misdirect one's energies. Shenstone.
To delay; to loiter; to remain or wait long; to be slow or reluctant in parting or moving; to be slow in deciding; to be in suspense; to hesitate. Nor cast one longing, lingering look behind.
To water; to wet; to moisten with running or dropping water; to bedew.
To write or insert between lines already written or printed, as for correction or addition; to write or print something between the lines of; as, to interline a page or a book. Swift.
To bring in; to introduce; to usher in. The independent orator inducting himself without further ceremony into the pulpit.
To sacrifice; to offer in sacrifice; to kill, as a sacrificial victim. Worshipers, who not only immolate to them [the deities] the lives of men, but .
To make an idol of; to pay idolatrous worship to; as, to idolize the sacred bull in Egypt.
To strip; to lay waste; as, the Northmen came several times and harried the land. To harry this beautiful region.
To apply smoke to; to expose to smoke or vapor; to purify, or free from infection, by the use of smoke or vapors.
To lay as in a bed; to lay in surrounding matter; to bed; as, to embed a thing in clay, mortar, or sand.
To prevent by fear; hence, to hinder or prevent from action by fear of consequences, or difficulty, risk, etc. Addison.

To determine the future condition or application of; to set apart by design for a future use or purpose; to fix, as by destiny or by an authoritative decree; to doom; to ordain or preordain; to appoint; -- often with the remoter object preceded by to or for. W

To move slowly by drawing the body along the ground, as a worm; to move slowly on hands and kness; to creep. A worm finds what it searches after only by feeling, as it crawls from one thing to another.
To make acknowledgment or avowal in a matter pertaining to one's self; to acknowledge, own, or admit, as a crime, a fault, a debt. And there confess Humbly our faults, and pardon beg.
To reduce to minute particles, or to a fine powder; to pulverize; to triturate; to grind; as, to comminute chalk or bones; to comminute food with the teeth. Pennant.
To grow together; to unite by growth into one body; as, the parts separated by a wound coalesce.
To haul up by the brails; -- used with up; as, to brail up a sail.
To affect with blight; to blast; to prevent the growth and fertility of. [This vapor] blasts vegetables, blights corn and fruit, and is sometimes injurious even to man.
To express deep sorrow for, as by wailing; to lament; to wail over. Hath widowed and unchilded many a one, Which to this hour bewail the injury.
To sever the head from; to take off the head of.
To value; to make a valuation or official estimate of for the purpose of taxation.
To cover with asphalt; as, to asphalt a roof; asphalted streets.
To join or unite to; to lie contiguous to; to be in contact with; to attach; to append. Corrections .

To destroy the self-possession of; to confuse or confound, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to put to shame; to disconcert; to discomfit. Abashed, the devil stood, And felt how awful goodness is.
p. p.

Any one of numerous species of ciliated Infusoria belonging to Vorticella and many other genera of the family Vorticellidæ. They have a more or less bell-shaped body with a circle of vibrating cilia around the oral disk.
Any one of numerous species of handsomely colored butterflies belonging to Vanessa and allied genera. Many of these species have the edges of the wings irregularly scalloped.
To build over or upon another structure; to erect upon a foundation. This is the only proper basis on which to superstruct first innocency and then virtue.
A roc. [Obs.
Any fresh-water air-breathing mollusk belonging to Planorbis and other allied genera, having shells of a discoidal form.
imp. & p.
Dedicated; set apart; devoted; consecrated. "Dedicate to nothing temporal." Shak.
Having a general resemblance to lilies or to liliaceous plants.
Given to jokes and jesting; containing a joke, or abounding in jokes; merry; sportive; humorous. To quit their austerity and be jocose and pleasant with an adversary.

Having half of the similar parts of a crystals, instead of all; consisting of half the planes which full symmetry would require, as when a cube has planes only on half of its eight solid angles, or one plane out of a pair on each of its edges; or as in the cas
A fungicidal mixture composed of blue vitriol, lime, and water. The formula in common use is: blue vitriol, 6 lbs.; lime, 4 lbs.; water, 35 -- 50 gallons.

An improvised stockade; especially, one made of thorn bushes, etc. [Written also zareeba, and zeriba.] [Egypt] "Ah," he moralizes, "what wonderful instinct on the part of this little creature to surround itself with a zareba like the troops after Osman Digma."
Any one of certain plants whose soft, downy leaves have been used for dressing wounds, as the kidney vetch, and several species of the labiate genus Stachys.
To wind, or wrap; especially, to wind a rope round, as a mast or yard made of two or more pieces, at the place where it has been fished or scarfed, in order to strengthen it.
To reel, sway, or move from side to side; to move with a wagging motion; to waddle. Why do you go nodding and waggling so L'Estrange.
Any one of numerous species of limpet-shaped pulmonate gastropods of the genus Siphonaria. They cling to rocks between high and low water marks and have both lunglike organs and gills.
Any species of bee which has on the hind legs a brush of hairs used for collecting pollen, as the hive bees and bumblebees.

A white crystalline substance having a bitter taste, extracted from the buds of levant wormseed and used as an anthelmintic. It occassions a peculiar temporary color blindness, causing objects to appear as if seen through a yellow glass.
To feel pain, sorrow, or regret, for what one has done or omitted to do. First she relents With pity; of that pity then repents.
A man who has charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper; one who waits at the door to receive messages. Shak.
To apply to a moral purpose; to explain in a moral sense; to draw a moral from. This fable is moralized in a common proverb.
The operation of crushing a stone in the bladder with an instrument called lithotriptor or lithotrite; lithotrity.
A supposed new metallic element. It is said to have been discovered in pyrites, and some other minerals, and to be of a silver-white color, and malleable.
One crowned with laurel; a poet laureate. "A learned laureate." Cleveland.
To cut in; to furrow; to make trenches in or upon. It was this very sword intrenched it.
A light, with a powerful reflector, placed at the head of a locomotive, or in front of it, to throw light on the track at night, or in going through a dark tunnel.
to look intently; to stare angrily or with a scowl. Thackeray.

A frame from which is suspended the rope with which criminals are executed by hanging, usually consisting of two upright posts and a crossbeam on the top; also, a like frame for suspending anything. So they hanged Haman on the gallows.
To make foolish by drink; to cause to become intoxicated. [Colloq.] I am too fuddled to take care to observe your orders.
A word formerly used (as finis is now) at the conclusion of a book to indicate the end.
A clumsy craft, having one mast with a long sail, used for trading purposes on the coasts of Coromandel and Ceylon. [Written also dhony, doney, and done.]

A rare metallic substance usually associated with the metal cerium; -- hence its name. It was formerly supposed to be an element, but has since been found to consist of two simpler elementary substances, neodymium and praseodymium.
To explode with a sudden report; as, niter detonates with sulphur.
The act of leaving with an intention not to reclaim or resume; an utter forsaking abandonment. Cession or dereliction, actual or tacit, of other powers.
A form of the voltaic battery having large plates, used for producing rapid and powerful combustion.
To take form or position, as the parts of a complex structure; to agree with a pattern. Known by the name of uniformity; Where pyramids to pyramids relate And the whole fabric doth configurate.
One of the same country, and having like interests and feeling. The distrust with which they felt themselves to be regarded by their compatriots in America.
A mineral, found in crystals, of a yellow to green or brown color, and consisting of aluminia and glucina. It is very hard, and is often used as a gem.
To exhibit mental activity; to have the brain in action.

To combine wtih carbon or a carbon compound; -- said esp. of a process for conferring a higher degree of illuminating power on combustible gases by mingling them with a vapor of valatile hydrocarbons.

The peepul tree; esp., the very ancient tree standing at Anurajahpoora in Ceylon, grown from a slip of the tree under which Gautama is said to have received the heavenly light and so to have become Buddha. The sacred bo tree of the Buddhists (Ficus religiosa),
A case or box placed near the helmsman, containing the compass of a ship, and a light to show it at night. Totten.

Native sulphate of barium, a mineral occurring in transparent, colorless, white to yellow crystals (generally tabular), also in granular form, and in compact massive forms resembling marble. It has a high specific gravity, and hence is often called heavy spar.
To writhe with agony; to suffer violent anguish. To smart and agonize at every pore.
The act of accusing or charging with a crime or with a lighter offense. We come not by the way of accusation To taint that honor every good tongue blesses.

A short scale made to slide along the divisions of a graduated instrument, as the limb of a sextant, or the scale of a barometer, for indicating parts of divisions. It is so graduated that a certain convenient number of its divisions are just equal to a certai
The act or operation of opening a vein for letting blood; bloodletting; phlebotomy.
The power or capacity of enduring; the act of enduring; endurance. Diogenes, one frosty morning, came into the market place,shaking, to show his tolerance.
A small particle of fire or ignited substance which is emitted by a body in combustion. Man is born unto trouble, as hte sparks fly upward.
Milk sickness.
The denial of one's self; forbearing to gratify one's own desires; self-sacrifice.
The beat of the drum to call soldiers to arms.
Quitch grass.

The ordinary language of men in speaking or writing; language not cast in poetical measure or rhythm; -- contradistinguished from verse, or metrical composition. I speak in prose, and let him rymes make.
A portable case for holding loose papers, prints, drawings, etc.
The act or practice of opening a vein for letting blood, in the treatment of disease; venesection; bloodletting.
A fiend or incubus formerly supposed to cause trouble in sleep.
A receptacle in which anything is stored, especially military stores, as ammunition, arms, provisions, etc. "Armories and magazines." Milton.
The practices of a knave; petty villainy; fraud; trickery; a knavish action. This is flat knavery, to take upon you another man's name.
The central or topmost stone of an arch. This in some styles is made different in size from the other voussoirs, or projects, or is decorated with carving.

The act of inspiring or breathing in; breath; specif. (Physiol.), the drawing of air into the lungs, accomplished in mammals by elevation of the chest walls and flattening of the diaphragm; -- the opposite of expiration.
The gathering of a crop of any kind; the ingathering of the crops; also, the season of gathering grain and fruits, late summer or early autumn. Seedtime and harvest .
A narrow passage of water; as, the Gut of Canso.
A simultaneous discharge of firearms.

A pair of pinchers, or tongs; an instrument for grasping, holding firmly, or exerting traction upon, bodies which it would be inconvenient or impracticable to seize with the fingers, especially one for delicate operations, as those of watchmakers, surgeons, ac

A copy of anything made, either so as to be deceptive or so as to give every part and detail of the original; an exact copy or likeness. Facsimile telegraph, a telegraphic apparatus reproducing messages in autograph.
Remaining unwithered through the winter, or retaining unwithered leaves until the leaves of the next year are expanded, as pines cedars, hemlocks, and the like.
Any organ or part of the body (as the kidneys, skin, etc.,) which serves to carry off excrementitious or waste matter.
The act of expelling or throwing off; (Physiol.)
The root of the box tree, of which hafts for daggers were made. Gerarde (1597).
The state of being deficient; inadequacy; want; failure; imperfection; shortcoming; defect. "A deficiencyof blood." Arbuthnot.
A bird belonging to Cuculus, Coccyzus, and several allied genera, of many species.
A pipe, canal, channel, or passage for conveying water or fluid. All the conduits of my blood froze up.
A ship's carpenter. [Cant.]
A vessel used by soldiers for carrying water, liquor, or other drink. [Written also cantine..]
The larva of two species of geometrid moths which are very injurious to fruit and shade trees by eating, and often entirely destroying, the foliage. Other similar larvæ are also called cankerworms.
The act of deliberating, or of weighing and examining the reasons for and against a choice or measure; careful consideration; mature reflection. Choosing the fairest way with a calm deliberation.
Adjusted to something else according to a proportion; proportional. Longfellow.
Having a common measure; capable of being exactly measured by the same number, quantity, or measure. -- Com*men"su*ra*ble*ness, n.
A dress of strong materials for restraining maniacs or those who are violently delirious. It has long sleeves, which are closed at the ends, confining the hands, and may be tied behind the back.
A band in the same position as the bend sinister, but only half as broad as the latter.
To act or work in a clumsy, awkward manner.
A net or snare; any thread, web, or string spread for taking prey; -- usually in the plural. As a Numidian lion, when first caught, Endures the toil that holds him.
The powder or other combustible used to communicate fire to a charge of gunpowder, as in a firearm.
The double cyanide of ferrous and ferric iron, a dark blue amorphous substance having a coppery luster, used in dyeing, calico printing, etc. Cf.
An order of gastropod Mollusca having a heart with two auricles and one ventricle. The shell may be either spiral or shieldlike.
A division of beetles having the fifth tarsal joint minute and obscure, so that there appear to be but four joints. -- Pseu`do*te*tram"er*al, a.

Not commensurable; having no common measure or standard of comparison; as, quantities are incommensurable when no third quantity can be found that is an aliquot part of both; the side and diagonal of a square are incommensurable with each other; the diameter a
A division of Mollusca having slender, cirriform appendages near the mouth; the Scaphopoda.
That which disinfects; an agent for removing the causes of infection, as chlorine.
A small bundle, as of straw or other like substance. In a small basket, on a wisp of hay.
An aboriginal war club.
To laugh with the tongue striking against the root of the upper teeth; to laugh with restraint, or without much noise; to giggle. A group of tittering pages ran before.

To place or arrange in a compact mass; to put in its proper place, or in a suitable place; to pack; as, to stowbags, bales, or casks in a ship's hold; to stow hay in a mow; to stow sheaves. Some stow their oars, or stop the leaky sides.

Divination by the assistance, or supposed assistance, of evil spirits, or the power of commanding evil spirits; magic; necromancy; witchcraft; enchantment. Adder's wisdom I have learned, To fence my ear against thy sorceries.
A fibrous material obtained by "deviling," or tearing into fibers, refuse woolen goods, old stockings, rags, druggets, etc. See Mungo.
To rend asunder by force; to split; to cleave; as, to rive timber for rails or shingles. I shall ryve him through the sides twain.
To make a noise; to pop; also, to break wind.
To crack; to make a sharp, abrupt noise to chink. [Obs.
To engage in mock combat on horseback, as two knights in the lists; to tilt. [Written also just.] For the whole army to joust and tourney.
To mix together; to intermingle. In yonder spring of roses, intermixed With myrtle, find what to redress till noon.
A kind of spear or harpoon. See Fishgig.
A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; a fort; a castle; a stronghold; a place of defense or security.

To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart or withdraw from; to leave; as, false friends and flatterers forsake us in adversity. If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments.

To enter by gradual steps or by stealth into the possessions or rights of another; to trespass; to intrude; to trench; -- commonly with on or upon; as, to encroach on a neighbor; to encroach on the highway. No sense, faculty, or member must encroach upon or in

To separate from fellowship or union; to disunite; to disjoin; as, to dissociate the particles of a concrete substance. Before Wyclif's death in 1384, John of Gaunt had openly dissociated himself from the reformer.
To spy out or discover by the eye, as objects distant or obscure; to espy; to recognize; to discern; to discover. And the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel.
To translate from secret characters or ciphers into intelligible terms; as, to decipher a letter written in secret characters.
To murder by suffocation, or so as to produce few marks of violence, for the purpose of obtaining a body to be sold for dissection.
To prepare, as food, by cooking in a dry heat, either in an oven or under coals, or on heated stone or metal; as, to bake bread, meat, apples.
Of or pertaining to walking; having the faculty of walking; formed or fitted for walking; as, an ambulatory animal.
To render worthless by admixture; to adulterate; to damage; to pervert; as, to sophisticate wine. Howell.
A board, or piece of wood or metal, having one edge perfectly straight, -- used to ascertain whether a line is straight or a surface even, and for drawing straight lines.

The act or process of assimilating or bringing to a resemblance, likeness, or identity; also, the state of being so assimilated; as, the assimilation of one sound to another. To aspire to an assimilation with God.
The act of relinquishing.
The act of aggrandizing, or the state of being aggrandized or exalted in power, rank, honor, or wealth; exaltation; enlargement; as, the emperor seeks only the aggrandizement of his own family.
To subject to disassimilation.
Of or pertaining to Rome, or the Roman people; like or characteristic of Rome, the Roman people, or things done by Romans; as, Roman fortitude; a Roman aqueduct; Roman art.
Being within any limits, inclosure, or substance; inside; internal; inner; -- opposed to exterior, or superficial; as, the interior apartments of a house; the interior surface of a hollow ball.
A covering or garment; some part of clothing or dress; specifically (Eccl.), any priestly garment. "Royal vestiment." Chaucer.
Having the color mark ings ill defined, as if rubbed; as, the smeared dagger moth (Apatela oblinita).
Inferior in bulk, degree, importance, etc.; less; smaller; of little account; as, minor divisions of a body.
Guiding; directing; controlling; foremost; as, a leading motive; a leading man; a leading example. -- Lead"ing*ly, adv.
Consisting of, or resembling, grains; as, a granular substance. Granular limestone, crystalline limestone, or marble, having a granular structure.
Pertaining to the foundation or basis; serving for the foundation. Hence: Essential, as an element, principle, or law; important; original; elementary; as, a fundamental truth; a fundamental axiom.
Having celebrity; distinguished; renowned. Celebrated for the politeness of his manners.
Furnished with branches; shooting our branches; extending in a branch or branches. Shaded with branching palm.

A form of balance in which the body to be weighed is suspended from the shorter arm of a lever, which turns on a fulcrum, and a counterpoise is caused to slide upon the longer arm to produce equilibrium, its place upon this arm (which is notched or graduated)

A supposition; a proposition or principle which is supposed or taken for granted, in order to draw a conclusion or inference for proof of the point in question; something not proved, but assumed for the purpose of argument, or to account for a fact or an occur
The bubbles caused in fluids or liquors by fermentation or agitation; spume; foam; esp., a spume of saliva caused by disease or nervous excitement.
Which (of two); which one (of two); -- used interrogatively and relatively. [Archaic] Now choose yourself whether that you liketh.
To regard with reverential respect; to honor with mingled respect and awe; to reverence; to revere; as, we venerate parents and elders. And seemed to venerate the sacred shade.

(a) Consisting of, or containing, vessels as an essential part of a structure; full of vessels; specifically (Bot.), pertaining to, or containing, special ducts, or tubes, for the circulation of sap. (b) Operating by means of, or made up of an arrangement of,
Having value or worth; possessing qualities which are useful and esteemed; precious; costly; as, a valuable horse; valuable land; a valuable cargo.

To untwist; to separate, as that which is twined or twisted; to disentangle; to untie. It requires a long and powerful counter sympathy in a nation to untwine the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old.
To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex; esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like; as, to unsex a woman.
To read the riddle of; to solve or explain; as, to unriddle an enigma or a mystery. Macaulay.
To strip of harness; to loose from harness or gear; as, to unharness horses or oxen. Cowper.
To loose from a furled state; to unfold; to expand; to open or spread; as, to unfurl sails; to unfurl a flag.
To touch lightly, or play with; to tweedle; to twirl; as, to twiddle one's thumbs; to twiddle a watch key. [Written also twidle.] Thackeray.

To posper by industry, economy, and good management of property; to increase in goods and estate; as, a farmer thrives by good husbandry. Diligence and humility is the way to thrive in the riches of the understanding, as well as in gold.
Exhausted; worn out; having lost energy or motive force. Now thou seest me Spent, overpowered, despairing of success.
To sprinkle; to moisten by sprinkling; as, to sparge paper.
To look backward; hence, to affect or concern what is past. It may be useful to retrospect to an early period.
To pay back; to give in return, as payment, reward, or punishment; to requite; as, to retribute one for his kindness; to retribute just punishment to a criminal. [Obs.
To fund again or anew; to replace (a fund or loan) by a new fund; as, to refund a railroad loan.

To give fresh life to; to reanimate; to revive; especially, to refresh after wearying toil or anxiety; to relieve; to cheer; to divert; to amuse; to gratify. Painters, when they work on white grounds, place before them colors mixed with blue and green, to recr
To build again, as something which has been demolished; to construct anew; as, to rebuild a house, a wall, a wharf, or a city.
To admit again; to give entrance or access to again. Whose ear is ever open, and his eye Gracious to readmit the suppliant.
To search thoroughly; to search every place or part of; as, to ransack a house. To ransack every corner of their .

Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an organic acid which is produced in the distillation of wood, in the fermentation of various organic substances, as glycerin, calcium lactate, etc., and is obtained as a colorless liquid having a sharp, pungent odo
A fine powder, as of sandarac, or cuttlefish bone, -- formerly used to prevent ink from spreading on manuscript.

Of or pertaining to phosphorus; resembling or containing phosphorus; specifically, designating those compounds in which phosphorus has a lower valence as contrasted with phosphoric compounds; as, phosphorous acid, H3PO3.
To coat with parget; to plaster, as walls, or the interior of flues; as, to parget the outside of their houses. Sir T.
To value excessively; to rate at too high a price. "To overvalue human power." Holyday.
To lie over or upon; specifically, to suffocate by lying upon; as, to overlie an infant. Quain.
To tell, rehearse, or recite, as a story; to relate the particulars of; to go through with in detail, as an incident or transaction; to give an account of.
To convert into money; to adopt as current money; as, to monetize silver.
To address or petition by a memorial; to present a memorial to; as, to memorialize the legislature. T.
To grind or crush with, or as with, the teeth and prepare for swallowing and digestion; to chew; as, to masticate food.

To scatter or set here and there among other things; to insert at intervals; as, to intersperse pictures in a book. There, interspersed in lawns and op'ning glades, Thin trees arise that shun each other's shades.
To insert a leaf or leaves in; to bind with blank leaves inserted between the others; as, to interleave a book.
To strike together, as in anger or pain; as, to gnash the teeth.
The act or art of setting glass; the art of covering with a vitreous or glasslike substance, or of polishing or rendering glossy.
To convert into a fossil; to petrify; as, to fossilize bones or wood.
To discharge through pores or incisions, as moisture or other liquid matter; to give out. Our forests exude turpentine in .
To make equal; to cause to correspond, or be like, in amount or degree as compared; as, to equalize accounts, burdens, or taxes. One poor moment can suffice To equalize the lofty and the low.
To draw along as a current does; as, water entrained by steam.
To remove from one country or State to another, for the purpose of residence; to migrate from home. Forced to emigrate in a body to America.

To wash or strain out so as to purify; as, to elutriate the blood as it passes through the lungs; to strain off or decant, as a powder which is separated from heavier particles by being drawn off with water; to cleanse, as by washing.
Any thick liquid or pasty preparation, as of opium for medicinal purposes, of grease for a lubricant, etc.
To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair; as, to deteriorate the mind. Whately.
To remove obstructions or impediments in; to clear from anything that hinders the passage of fluids; as, to deobstruct the pores or lacteals. Arbuthnot.
To pay or discharge; to serve in payment of; to provide for, as a charge, debt, expenses, costs, etc. For the discharge of his expenses, and defraying his cost, he allowed him .
A debt; an entry on the debtor (Dr.) side of an account; -- mostly used adjectively; as, the debit side of an account.
A city of Syria. Damascus blade, a sword or scimiter, made chiefly at Damascus, having a variegated appearance of watering, and proverbial for excellence.
To make a countermine or counterplot; to plot secretly. 'Tis hard for man to countermine with God.
To overwhelm by argument; to refute conclusively; to prove or show to be false or defective; to overcome; to silence.
To sprout; to put forth buds; to shoot forth, as a branch. Gayly to bourgeon and broadly to grow.
To attack with bombards or with artillery; especially, to throw shells, hot shot, etc., at or into. Next, she means to bombard Naples.
To indicate by signs, as future events; to be the omen of; to portend to presage; to foreshow. A raven that bodes nothing but mischief.
To take vengeance for; to exact satisfaction for by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or evil on a wrongdoer. He will avenge the blood of his servants.
To explain or criticize by notes; as, to annotate the works of Bacon.
To make acid; to convert into an acid; as, to acidify sugar.
That part of the human body which is immediately below the ribs or thorax; the small part of the body between the thorax and hips. Chaucer.
Receiving pay; compensated; hired; as, a paid attorney.
One who compiles; esp., one who makes books by compilation.
Having two toes in front and two behind, as the trogons and woodpeckers.
Having the anterior limbs or hands adapted for flight, as the bats and pterodactyls.
The hut used by the nomadic Indian tribes of the arid regions of the west and southwest United States, typically elliptical in form, with a rough frame covered with reed mats or grass or brushwood.
A rope or halter made of flexible twigs, or withes, as of birch. [Scot.]
To utter a whoop, or loud cry, as eagerness, enthusiasm, or enjoyment; to cry out; to shout; to halloo; to utter a war whoop; to hoot, as an owl. Each whooping with a merry shout.

The act of willing or choosing; the act of forming a purpose; the exercise of the will. Volition is the actual exercise of the power the mind has to order the consideration of any idea, or the forbearing to consider it.
To cry out with vehemence; to exclaim; to bawl; to clamor. Cowper.

Having the power of acting or of invisible efficacy without the agency of the material or sensible part; potential; energizing. Heat and cold have a virtual transition, without communication of substance.
A small instrument with four strings, played with a bow; a fiddle.
Having thickset tufts of parallel hairs, bristles, or branches.
Of or pertaining to the smallpox; having pits, or sunken impressions, like those of the smallpox; variolar; variolic.
To cause to forget, or to lose from memory, or to disbelieve what has been taught. Experience will unteach us.
Having only one adductor muscle, and one muscular impression on each valve, as the oyster; monomyarian.
Having three sorts of flowers on the same or on different plants, some of the flowers being staminate, others pistillate, and others both staminate and pistillate; belonging to the order Trioecia.
A series of three dramas which, although each of them is in one sense complete, have a close mutual relation, and form one historical and poetical picture. Shakespeare's " Henry VI." is an example.

The principle of key in music; the character which a composition has by virtue of the key in which it is written, or through the family relationship of all its tones and chords to the keynote, or tonic, of the whole. The predominance of the tonic as the link w

A kind of sledge made of pliable board, turned up at one or both ends, used for coasting down hills or prepared inclined planes; also, a sleigh or sledge, to be drawn by dogs, or by hand, over soft and deep snow. [Written also tobogan, and tarbogan.]
An old name for the finest and most costly kind of velvet, having a fine, thick pile. I have served Prince Florizel and in my time wore three-pile.

An ancient ascription of praise (containing the word "Holy" -- in its Latin form, "Sanctus" -- thrice repeated), used in the Mass of the Roman Catholic Church and before the prayer of consecration in the communion service of the Church of England and the Prote
An instrument consisting of a fine, sharp hook attached to a handle, and used mainly for taking up arteries, and the like.
Having the posterior tarsal scales, or scutella, rectangular and arranged in regular rows; -- said of certain birds.
A lining made of brick, stone, or other hard material, as for a well. [Written also steaning.]
Having the mandibles large and palmate, or branched somewhat like the antlers of a stag; -- said of certain beetles.
Filled with, or showing, spite; having a desire to vex, annoy, or injure; malignant; malicious; as, a spiteful person or act. Shak.

Provided with a shroud or shrouds. Shrouded gear (Mach.), a cogwheel or pinion having flanges which form closed ends to the spaces between the teeth and thus strengthen the teeth by tying them together.
Covered with bristles; having or bearing a seta or setæ; setiferous; as, setigerous glands; a setigerous segment of an annelid; specifically (Bot.), tipped with a bristle.
To have a strong sexual impulse at the reproductive period; -- said of deer, cattle, etc.

Of a reddish brown color, or (by some called) a red gray; of the color composed of blue, red, and yellow in equal strength, but unequal proportions, namely, two parts of red to one each of blue and yellow; also, of a yellowish brown color. The morn, in russet
A musical instrument formerly in use, consisting of several sticks bound together, but separated by beads, and played with a stick with a ball at its end. Moore (Encyc.
Having the nature or habit of a rhizome or rootstock.
To clothe again; to cover, as with a robe; to robe. Her, nathless, .

Belonging to the reptiles. Reptilian age (Geol.), that part of geological time comprising the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods, and distinguished as that era in which the class of reptiles attained its highest expansion; -- called also the Secondary
Having a rank smell or taste, from chemical change or decomposition; musty; as, rancid oil or butter.
A group of Protozoa having both flagella and pseudopodia.
Having the nature or appearance of a radix or root.
Fourfold; as, to make quadruple restitution; a quadruple alliance. Quadruple time (Mus.), that in which each measure is divided into four equal parts.
A galley with four banks of oars or rowers.
An order of Arachnoidea having the palpi terminated by large claws, as in the scorpions, but destitute of a caudal sting; the false scorpions. Called also Pseudoscorpii, and Pseudoscorpionina.
Terminated abruptly, or as it bitten off. Premorse root or leaves (Bot.), such as have an abrupt, ragged, and irregular termination, as if bitten off short.
A confection made of nut kernels, usually of almonds, roasted in boiling sugar until brown and crisp.
A genus of bitter herbs or shrubs having eight stamens and a two-celled ovary (as the Seneca snakeroot, the flowering wintergreen, etc.); milkwort.
An Oriental dish consisting of rice boiled with mutton, fat, or butter. [Written also pilau.]
Having the ovary free, but the petals and stamens borne on the calyx; -- said of flower such as that of the cherry or peach.
A picture, or combination of pictures, consisting of a centerpiece and double folding doors or wings, as for an altarpiece.
Having feet resembling hands, or with the first toe opposable, as the opossums and monkeys.
A drink made of orange juice and water, corresponding to lemonade; orange sherbet.
Mosslike; resembling moss.

A frozen dessert of a frothy texture, made of sweetened and flavored whipped cream, sometimes with the addition of egg yolks and gelatin. Mousse differs from ice cream in being beaten before -- not during -- the freezing process.
Having the sexes united in one individual, as when male and female flowers grow upon the same individual plant; hermaphrodite; -- opposed to Ant: dioecious.
Having a single heart, as fishes and amphibians. -- n.
Furnished with a medulla or marrow, or with a medullary sheath; as, a medullated nerve fiber.
A severe beating with a stick, cudgel, or the fist.

The art or process of making a kind of hard, stereotypeplate, by pressing into a mold, taken from a page of type or other matter, a composition of gum shell-lac and sand of a fine quality, together with a little tar and linseed oil, all in a heated state.

A valve gear, consisting of two eccentrics with their rods, giving motion to a slide valve by an adjustable connecting bar, called the link, in such a way that the motion of the engine can be reversed, or the cut-off varied, at will; -- used very generally in
The third canonical book of the Old Testament, containing the laws and regulations relating to the priests and Levites among the Hebrews, or the body of the ceremonial law.
Having the left hand or arm stronger and more dexterous than the right; using the left hand and arm with more dexterity than the right.
Having thin, transparent, reticulated wings; as, the lace- winged flies.
Having the shape or appearance of a julus or catkin.

Having similar proportions, similar relations, or similar differences of composition; -- said specifically of groups or series which differ by a constant difference; as, ethane, ethylene, an acetylene, or their analogous compounds, form an isologous series.

to, or containing, iodine; specif., denoting those compounds in which it has a relatively high valence; as, iodic acid. Iodic acid, a monobasic acid, consisting of iodine with three parts of oxygen and one of hydrogen.
Having an involucre, as umbels, heads, etc. Martyn.
Inserted below the pistil or pistils; -- said of sepals, petals, and stamens; having the sepals, petals, and stamens inserted below the pistil; -- said of a flower or a plant. Gray.
Having the maxilla, or lower jaw, longer than the upper, as in the skimmer.
Furnished with a horn or horns; furnished with a hornlike process or appendage; as, horned cattle; having some part shaped like a horn. The horned moon with one bright star Within the nether tip.
Having the tail nearly or quite symmetrical, the vertebral column terminating near its base; -- opposed to heterocercal.
A Hebrew measure of liquids, containing three quarts, one pint, one gill, English measure. W.
Having the teeth differentiated into incisors, canines, and molars, as in man; -- opposed to homodont.
A dish made of portions of the head, or head and feet, of swine, cut up fine, seasoned, and pressed into a cheeselike mass.
A sweetmeat of boiled brown sugar or molasses made with almonds, and flavored with orange or lemon juice, etc. Thackeray.

A Scotch pudding made of the heart, liver, lights, etc., of a sheep or lamb, minced with suet, onions, oatmeal, etc., highly seasoned, and boiled in the stomach of the same animal; minced head and pluck. [Written also haggiss, haggess, and haggies.]
Having the limbs on, or directed toward, the ventral or hemal side, as in vertebrates; -- opposed to neuropodous.
An abnormal condition of certain animals, in which one side has the external characters of the male, and the other those of the female.
A four-wheeled pleasure carriage with two inside seats, calash top, and seats for driver and footman.
A mixture composed of unfermented grape juice, brandy, sugar, etc., for adulteration of wines. [Written also jerupigia.]

Destructive to germs; -- applied to any agent which has a destructive action upon living germs, particularly bacteria, or bacterial germs, which are considered the cause of many infectious diseases. -- n.
A stone composed of sand or grit; -- so called because it is easily cut or wrought.
A taste beforehand; enjoyment in advance; anticipation.
Feathered; furnished with feathers or wings; able to fly. Hfledge with wings.
Containing faults, blemishes, or defects; imperfect; not fit for the use intended. Created once So goodly and erect, though faulty since.
A fabrik made of silk and wool or hair. Simmonds.

An argument consisting of only two propositions, an antecedent and consequent deduced from it; a syllogism with one premise omitted; as, We are dependent; therefore we should be humble. Here the major proposition is suppressed.
To fence or fortify with stakes; to surround with a line of stakes for defense; to impale. All that dwell near enemies empale villages, to save themselves from surprise.
A method of determining the presence or absence of life in an animal organism with a current of electricity, by noting the presence or absence of muscular contraction.
To disentangle; to free from perplexity; to extricate from confusion. Vaillant has disembroiled a history that was lost to the world before his time.
Containing two carbon residues, or two carboxyl or radicals; as, oxalic acid is a dicarbonic acid.
Having a single, distinct, diagonal cleavage; -- said of crystals. Mohs.

Given up or forsaken by the natural owner or guardian; left and abandoned; as, derelict lands. The affections which these exposed or derelict children bear to their mothers, have no grounds of nature or assiduity but civility and opinion.

A dog with a docked tail; formerly, the dog of a person not qualified to course, which, by the forest laws, must have its tail cut short, partly as a mark, and partly from a notion that the tail is necessary to a dog in running; hence, a dog not fit for sporti
Eating away; having the power of gradually wearing, changing, or destroying the texture or substance of a body; as, the corrosive action of an acid. "Corrosive liquors." Grew.

Pertaining to, derived from, or having certain characteristics of, citric and aconitic acids. Citraconic acid (Chem.), a white, crystalline, deliquescent substance, C3H4(CO2H)2, obtained by distillation of citric acid.
A cloth with a cotton wart, and a woof of very fine wool, or wool and silk.
A forest composed of stunted trees and thorny bushes, found in areas of small rainfall in Brazil.
Byssuslike; consisting of fine fibers or threads, as some very delicate filamentous algæ.

Pertaining to, or derived from, butter. Butyric acid, C3H7.CO2H, an acid found in butter; an oily, limpid fluid, having the smell of rancid butter, and an acrid taste, with a sweetish aftertaste, like that of ether.
A burner consisting of two or more concentric Argand burners (the inner rising above the outer) and a central tube by which oxygen gas or common air is supplied.
Having two little bags, sacs, or pouches.
An expression consisting of two terms connected by the sign plus (+) or minus (-); as, a+b, or 7-3.
A zitherlike musical instrument, provided with dampers which, when depressed, deaden some strings, leaving free others that form a chord.
Not furnished with shields or beds for the spores, as the thallus of certain lichens.

A lamp with a circular hollow wick and glass chimney which allow a current of air both inside and outside of the flame. Argand burner, a burner for an Argand lamp, or a gas burner in which the principle of that lamp is applied.
Having the number of floral organs unequal, as four petals and six stamens.
Having to stomach, or distinct digestive canal, as the tapeworm.
Containing seeds or stones of grapes, or grains like them.

A long, hollow vessel, generally for holding water or other liquid, especially one formed by excavating a log longitudinally on one side; a long tray; also, a wooden channel for conveying water, as to a mill wheel.

Any sail extended on a stay.

An Alkali element, occurring abundantly but always combined, as in the chloride, sulphate, carbonate, or silicate, in the minerals sylvite, kainite, orthoclase, muscovite, etc. Atomic weight 39.0.

Any one of numerous species of longwinged sea birds belonging to the family Procellaridæ. The small petrels, or Mother Carey's chickens, belong to Oceanites, Oceanodroma, Procellaria, and several allied genera.
The fleshy pome, or fruit, of a rosaceous tree (Pyrus communis), cultivated in many varieties in temperate climates; also, the tree which bears this fruit. See Pear family, below.
(Chem.) A salt of palmic acid; a ricinoleate. [Obsoles.]
The state of being an owner; the right to own; exclusive right of possession; legal or just claim or title; proprietorship.
The act of obstructing, or state of being obstructed.
The quality or state of being noble; superiority of mind or of character; commanding excellence; eminence. Though she hated Amphialus, yet the nobility of her courage prevailed over it.
Substance or quality of temperament; spirit, esp. as regards honor, courage, fortitude, ardor, etc.; disposition; -- usually in a good sense.
(a) The bone of either the upper or the under jaw. (b) The bone, or principal bone, of the upper jaw, the bone of the lower jaw being the mandible.
Within the sides of; in the interior; contained within; as, inside a house, book, bottle, etc.
A large, northern, marine flatfish (Hippoglossus vulgaris), of the family Pleuronectidæ. It often grows very large, weighing more than three hundred pounds.
Any species of marine fishes of the genus Trichiurus; esp., T. lepterus of Europe and America.

The quality of being good in any of its various senses; excellence; virtue; kindness; benevolence; as, the goodness of timber, of a soil, of food; goodness of character, of disposition, of conduct, etc.
One who forms; a maker; a creator.

A young pig, or a litter of pigs.
One exempted or freed from duty; one not subject.
A quoit; a circular plate of some heavy material intended to be pitched or hurled as a trial of strength and skill. (b) The exercise with the discus.
A flattish or convex flower cluster, of the centrifugal or determinate type, differing from a corymb chiefly in the order of the opening of the blossoms.
A creeping plant, and its fruit, of several species of the genus Cucumis, esp. Cucumis sativus, the unripe fruit of which is eaten either fresh or picked.
The act of contemning or despising; the feeling with which one regards that which is esteement mean, vile, or worthless; disdain; scorn. Criminal contempt of public feeling.
Apprehension by the understanding; perception; observation. Within the cognizance and lying under the control of their divine Governor.
from Cleave.

Literally, leaf green; a green granular matter formed in the cells of the leaves (and other parts exposed to light) of plants, to which they owe their green color, and through which all ordinary assimilation of plant food takes place. Similar chlorophyll granu
A rare metallic element, occurring in the minerals cerite, allanite, monazite, etc. Symbol Ce.
An herbaceous or woody stem which bears leaves, and may bear flowers.
An elementary substance; a metal which combined with oxygen forms lime. It is of a pale yellow color, tenacious, and malleable.
Calcium carbonate, or carbonate of lime. It is rhombohedral in its crystallization, and thus distinguished from aragonite.
A blot or spot, as of color or of ink; especially a large or irregular spot. Also Fig.; as, a moral blotch.

Governing or controlling influence; domination; power. An undisputed ascendency.
One of a class of strongly basic substances derived from ammonia by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by a basic atom or radical.
The tie or obligation, implied or expressed, which a subject owes to his sovereign or government; the duty of fidelity to one's king, government, or state.
An albuminoid substance which occurs in minute grains ("protein granules") in maturing seeds and tubers; -- supposed to be a modification of protoplasm.
The act of digging or breaking up, as with a pick.
The act of piercing with a drill.

The act or state of growing worse, or the state of having become worse; decline; degradation; debasement; degeneracy; deterioration. Our degeneration and apostasy.
A rare element of the boron group, sometimes associated with yttrium or other related elements, as in euxenite and gadolinite. Symbol Yb; provisional atomic weight 173.2.
A plant which keeps its leaves green through the winter.
Wanting physical strength. Specifically: -- (a) Deficient in strength of body; feeble; infirm; sickly; debilitated; enfeebled; exhausted.
A saclike envelope of certain fungi, which bursts open as the plant develops.

The unit of electro-motive force; -- defined by the International Electrical Congress in 1893 and by United States Statute as, that electro-motive force which steadily applied to a conductor whose resistance is one ohm will produce a current of one ampère. It

Not easily wielded or carried; unmanageable; bulky; ponderous. "A fat, unwieldy body of fifty-eight years old." Clarendon.
A fabulous animal with one horn; the monoceros; -- often represented in heraldry as a supporter.
One who, or that which, sets type; a compositor; a machine for setting type.
The root of a plant which penetrates the earth directly downward to a considerable depth without dividing.
A lover of mistress.
Of or pertaining to the superficies, or surface; lying on the surface; shallow; not deep; as, a superficial color; a superficial covering; superficial measure or contents; superficial tillage.

A massive variety of talc, of a grayish green or brown color. It forms extensive beds, and is quarried for fireplaces and for coarse utensils.
One who sports; a sportsman. As this gentleman and I have been old fellow sporters, I have a frienship for him.
Of or pertaining to a siren; bewitching, like a siren; fascinating; alluring; as, a siren song.
A genus of transparent, tubular, free-swimming oceanic tunicates found abundantly in all the warmer latitudes. See Illustration in Appendix.
A salt of salicylic acid.
Having rotted; putrid; decayed; as, a rotten apple; rotten meat. Hence: (a) Offensive to the smell; fetid; disgusting.
A rare element of the light platinum group. It is found in platinum ores, and obtained free as a white inert metal which it is very difficult to fuse.
The estimation in which one is held; character in public opinion; the character attributed to a person, thing, or action; repute. The best evidence of reputation is a man's whole life.
Obstinate in disobedience; contumacious; stubborn; unmanageable; as, a refractory child; a refractory beast. Raging appetites that are Most disobedient and refractory.

The quality or state of being quiet; freedom from noise, agitation, disturbance, or excitement; stillness; tranquillity; calmness. I would have peace and quietness.

The act driving forward or away; the act or process of propelling; as, steam propulsion.
The act or process of populating; multiplication of inhabitants.
The form or constitution of the civil government of a nation or state; the framework or organization by which the various departments of government are combined into a systematic whole. Blackstone.
A small instrument of ivory, wood, metal, or quill, used in playing upon the lyre and other stringed instruments.

Turned aside; hence, specifically, turned away from the right; willfully erring; wicked; perverted. The only righteous in a word perverse.
The connective tissue sheath which surrounds a bundle of nerve fibers. See Epineurium, and Neurilemma.
A line of ancestors; descent; lineage; genealogy; a register or record of a line of ancestors. Alterations of surnames .
Of, pertaining to, or affecting, a part only; not general or universal; not total or entire; as, a partial eclipse of the moon. "Partial dissolutions of the earth." T.
A pyramidal form of inflorescence, in which the cluster is loosely branched below and gradually simpler toward the end.
A paroxysm of extreme pain or anguish; a sudden and transitory agony; a throe; as, the pangs of death.
A bursting forth.
A common name of the yellowish green mineral chrysolite, esp. the variety found in eruptive rocks.
A special structure found in the mouth of most mollusks, except bivalves. It consists of several muscles and a cartilage which supports a chitinous radula, or lingual ribbon, armed with teeth.

Not engaged on either side; not taking part with or assisting either of two or more contending parties; neuter; indifferent. The heart can not possibly remain neutral, but constantly takes part one way or the other.

Subject to death; destined to die; as, man is mortal.
The chief magistrate of a city or borough; the chief officer of a municipal corporation. In some American cities there is a city court of which the major is chief judge.
A large species of American grass of the genus Zea (Z. Mays), widely cultivated as a forage and food plant; Indian corn.

The act or process of locating.
A considerable collection of books kept for use, and not as merchandise; as, a private library; a public library.

The inner bark of plants, lying next to the wood. It usually contains a large proportion of woody, fibrous cells, and is, therefore, the part from which the fiber of the plant is obtained, as that of hemp, etc.

A sirupy variety of sugar, rarely obtained crystallized, occurring widely in honey, ripe fruits, etc., and hence called also fruit sugar. It is called levulose, because it rotates the plane of polarization to the left.
A surgical instrument of various forms, commonly sharp-pointed and two-edged, used in venesection, and in opening abscesses, etc.

A frame usually portable, of wood, metal, or rope, for ascent and descent, consisting of two side pieces to which are fastened cross strips or rounds forming steps. Some the engines play, And some, more bold, mount ladders to the fire.

A hair of a horse, especially one from the mane or tail; the hairs of the mane or tail taken collectively; a fabric or tuft made of such hairs. Horsehair worm (Zoöl.), the hair worm or gordius.
A genus of composite plants, with shining, commonly white or yellow, or sometimes reddish, radiated involucres, which are often called "everlasting flowers."

The pavement or floor of brick, stone, or metal in a chimney, on which a fire is made; the floor of a fireplace; also, a corresponding part of a stove. There was a fire on the hearth burning before him.
The sucking proboscis of various insects. See Lepidoptera, and Diptera.
A trade requiring skill of hand; manual occupation; handcraft. Addison.
A female guardian. I have placed a trusty, watchful guardianess.
Great; large; bulky; fat; of huge size; excessively large. "A gross fat man." Shak.
A plant of the genus Lithospermum (L. arvense), anciently used, because of its stony pericarp, in the cure of gravel.

A collection of glosses or explanations of words and passages of a work or author; a partial dictionary of a work, an author, a dialect, art, or science, explaining archaic, technical, or other uncommon words.
Excited with merriment; manifesting sportiveness or delight; inspiring delight; livery; merry. Belinda smiled, and all the world was gay.

A genus of vascular, cryptogamic, herbaceous plants; -- also called horsetails.

The act of deviating; a wandering from the way; variation from the common way, from an established rule, etc.; departure, as from the right course or the path of duty.

A woman who has had no carnal knowledge of man; a maid.
An embryonic insect which has twice cast its skin previous to hatching from the egg.
