To warrant; to guarantee.
To make a victim of, esp. by deception; to dupe; to cheat.
To divest of clothes; to strip.

To vex by bringing to notice, or reminding of, a fault, defect, misfortune, or the like; to revile; to reproach; to upbraid; to taunt; as, he twitted his friend of falsehood. This these scoffers twitted the Christian with.
To hang or move, as something loose and heavy; to sway; to swing. [Prov.
To overpower and crush; to subdue; to put down; to quell. Every rebellion, when it is suppressed, doth make the subject weaker, and the prince stronger.
To speak hastily and confusedly; to sputter. [Colloq.] Carleton.
To unite, as two ropes, or parts of a rope, by a particular manner of interweaving the strands, -- the union being between two ends, or between an end and the body of a rope.
A place of deep mud or mire; a hole full of mire. Chaucer.
imp. of Sling.
To cut off; to abrogate; to annul. The blessed Jesus .
To drive or beat back; to repulse. Who him, recount'ring fierce, as hawk in flight, Perforce rebutted back.
To direct the course of, as of a ship, where navigation is dangerous.
To impose penance; to punish. "Some penanced lady elf." Keats.
To inclose in a park, or as in a park. How are we parked, and bounded in a pale.

A tenet or proposition contrary to received opinion; an assertion or sentiment seemingly contradictory, or opposed to common sense; that which in appearance or terms is absurd, but yet may be true in fact. A gloss there is to color that paradox, and make it ap
To come between, or to be between, persons or things; -- followed by between; as, the Mediterranean intervenes between Europe and Africa.
To infuse new life or spirit into; to animate; to encourage; to invigorate. The courage of Agamemnon is inspirited by the love of empire and ambition.

To creep on the earth, or with the face to the ground; to lie prone, or move uneasily with the body prostrate on the earth; to lie fiat on one's belly, expressive of abjectness; to crawl. To creep and grovel on the ground.
To advance or gain upon; -- said of a vessel that gains upon another when sailing closehauled.

A complete assortment of printing type of one size, including a due proportion of all the letters in the alphabet, large and small, points, accents, and whatever else is necessary for printing with that variety of types; a fount.
To render more violent or bitter; to irriate; to exasperate; to imbitter, as passions or disease. Broughman.
To take out the entrails of; to disembowel; to gut.
A figure in which a harts or indelicate word or expression is softened; a way of describing an offensive thing by an inoffensive expression; a mild name for something disagreeable.
To pierce, scour, or rake with shot in the direction of the length of, as a work, or a line of troops. Campbell.
To put out of doors; to expel; to discharge; to release; to set at liberty. Eliminate my spirit, give it range Through provinces of thought yet unexplored.
To strip or deprive of dress; to divest.
To take the tenth part of; to tithe. Johnson.
To sign on the opposite side of (an instrument or writing); hence, to sign in addition to the signature of a principal or superior, in order to attest the authenticity of a writing.
To lead or tend, esp. with reference to a favorable or desirable result; to contribute; -- usually followed by to or toward.
To gain advantage over by arts, stratagem, or deception; to decieve; to delude; to get around. I circumvented whom I could not gain.
To regulate by musical measure. These parting numbers, cadenced by my grief.
To make brutal; beasty; unfeeling; or inhuman.
To quarrel noisily and outrageously. Let a man that is a man consider that he is a fool that brawleth openly with his wife.
To revile or abuse in scurrilous language. Southey.
To increase; to augment. And though power failed, her courage did accrue.
An excessive reverence for, or fear of, that which is unknown or mysterious.
The act of superseding, or the state of being superseded; supersedure. The general law of diminishing return from land would have undergone, to that extent, a temporary supersession.

The act or process of dividing into segments; specifically (Biol.), a self-division into segments as a result of growth; cell cleavage; cell multiplication; endogenous cell formation. Segmentation cavity (Biol.), the cavity formed by the arrangement of the cel
A piece of cloth, usually square and often fine and elegant, carried for wiping the face or hands.
A species of Cardamine (C. pratensis), or lady's smock.
To exclude from fellowship; to refuse intercourse with, as an associate. An attempt to disfellowship an evil, but to fellowship the evildoer.
Belonging to, or inherent in, the constitution, or in the structure of body or mind; as, a constitutional infirmity; constitutional ardor or dullness.
To wit; that is; namely.
Two times; once and again. He twice essayed to cast his son in gold.
Something very inflammable, used for kindling fire from a spark, as scorched linen. German tinder.
Coarse hair or nap; rough, woolly hair. True Witney broadcloth, with its shag unshorn.
A dead body embalmed and dried after the manner of the ancient Egyptians; also, a body preserved, by any means, in a dry state, from the process of putrefaction. Bacon.
The act of binding.
The lower part of the body behind; the buttocks.
Defensive arms for the body; any clothing or covering worn to protect one's person in battle.
The hypodermic injection of tuberculin, which has little or no effect with healthy cattle, but causes a marked rise in temperature in tuberculous animals.
Having a powerful, far-reaching voice or speech.
A pipe wrench having an adjustable L-shaped jaw piece sliding in a sleeve that is pivoted to, and loosely embraces, the handle. Pressure on the handle increases the grip.
Having broad scutella on the front, and small scales on the posterior side, of the tarsus; -- said of certain birds.

A cement having the color of the Portland stone of England, made by calcining an artificial mixture of carbonate of lime and clay, or sometimes certain natural limestones or chalky clays. It contains a large proportion of clay, and hardens under water.
The combination consisting of a generator and a driving motor mechanically connected, usually on a common bedplate and with the two shafts directly coupled or combined into a single shaft.
Having a single floral envelope, that is, a calyx without a corolla, or, possibly, in rare cases, a corolla without a calyx.
Having the margin dentate and also ciliate or fringed with hairs.
Any one of numerous species of stinging hymenopterous insects, esp. any of the numerous species of the genus Vespa, which includes the true, or social, wasps, some of which are called yellow jackets.
The turtledove.
Certainly knowing and believing; confident beyond doubt; implicity trusting; unquestioning; positive. We are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth against them which commit such things.
The Dog Star. See Dog Star.

Any one of several small species of herring which are commonly preserved in olive oil for food, especially the pilchard, or European sardine (Clupea pichardus). The California sardine (Clupea sagax) is similar.

Any plant or species of the genus Papaver, herbs with showy polypetalous flowers and a milky juice. From one species (Papaver somniferum) opium is obtained, though all the species contain it to some extent; also, a flower of the plant.

A tropical plant (Ananassa sativa); also, its fruit; -- so called from the resemblance of the latter, in shape and external appearance, to the cone of the pine tree. Its origin is unknown, though conjectured to be American.

Arsenic sesquisulphide, produced artificially as an amorphous lemonyellow powder, and occurring naturally as a yellow crystalline mineral; -- formerly called auripigment. It is used in king's yellow, in white Indian fire, and in certain technical processes, as
A bitter white crystalline alkaloid found in opium, possessing strong narcotic properties, and much used as an anodyne; -- called also morphia, and morphina.
Any one of many small, delicate, long-legged flies of the Chironomus, and allied genera, which do not bite. Their larvæ are usually aquatic.

A milky or colored juice in certain plants in cavities (called latex cells or latex tubes). It contains the peculiar principles of the plants, whether aromatic, bitter, or acid, and in many instances yields caoutchouc upon coagulation.

The expanded upper end of the windpipe or trachea, connected with the hyoid bone or cartilage. It contains the vocal cords, which produce the voice by their vibrations, when they are stretched and a current of air passes between them.

One who inspects, views, or oversees; one to whom the supervision of any work is committed; one who makes an official view or examination, as a military or civil officer; a superintendent; a supervisor; an overseer. Inspector general (Mil.), a staff officer of
One of several species of flowering plants, much admired for their beauty, and some for their fragrance.
One of several North American burrowing rodents of the genera Geomys and Thomomys, of the family Geomyidæ; -- called also pocket gopher and pouched rat. See Pocket gopher, and Tucan.
The male game fowl.
A thorny evergreen shrub (Ulex Europæus), with beautiful yellow flowers, very common upon the plains and hills of Great Britain; -- called also gorse, and whin. The dwarf furze is Ulex nanus.
Any luminous winged insect, esp. luminous beetles of the family Lampyridæ.

Representing by a figure, or by resemblance; typical; representative. This, they will say, was figurative, and served, by God's appointment, but for a time, to shadow out the true glory of a more divine sanctity.
Inducing to vomit; exciting the stomach to discharge its contents by the mouth. -- n.

A sirupy, or white crystalline, variety of sugar, C6H12O6 (so called from turning the plane of polarization to the right), occurring in many ripe fruits. Dextrose and levulose are obtained by the inversion of cane sugar or sucrose, and hence called invert suga

Of or pertaining to Devon or Devonshire in England; as, the Devonian rocks, period, or system. Devonian age (Geol.), the age next older than the Carboniferous and later than the Silurian; -- called also the Age of fishes.
Any horizontal, molded or otherwise decorated projection which crowns or finishes the part to which it is affixed; as, the cornice of an order, pedestal, door, window, or house. Gwilt.
A bony prominence; particularly, an eminence at the end of a bone bearing a rounded articular surface; -- sometimes applied also to a concave articular surface.
Universal or general; as, the catholic faith. Men of other countries [came] to bear their part in so great and catholic a war.
A short, light musket or rifle, esp. one used by mounted soldiers or cavalry.

(a) A turning or sliding piece which, by the shape of its periphery or face, or a groove in its surface, imparts variable or intermittent motion to, or receives such motion from, a rod, lever, or block brought into sliding or rolling contact with it. (b) A cur
A comparatively rare element related to zinc, and occurring in some zinc ores. It is a white metal, both ductile and malleable.
Full of liveliness and activity; characterized by quickness of motion or action; lively; spirited; quick. Cheerily, boys; be brick awhile.
Forward to meet danger; venturesome; daring; not timorous or shrinking from risk; brave; courageous. Throngs of knights and barons bold.

A volatile, very inflammable liquid, C6H6, contained in the naphtha produced by the destructive distillation of coal, from which it is separated by fractional distillation. The name is sometimes applied also to the impure commercial product or benzole, and als
Behind; toward the stern from; as, abaft the wheelhouse. Abaft the beam.

A bag or sack for carrying about the person, as a bag for carrying the necessaries for a journey; a knapsack; a beggar's receptacle for charity; a peddler's pack. [His hood] was trussed up in his walet.
A living being sacrificed to some deity, or in the performance of a religious rite; a creature immolated, or made an offering of. Led like a victim, to my death I'll go.

Upon any less condition than (the fact or thing stated in the sentence or clause which follows); if not; supposing that not; if it be not; were it not that; except; as, we shall fail unless we are industrious.
The part of a foot lathe, or other machine, which is pressed or moved by the foot.
Granting, admitting, or supposing that; notwithstanding that; if. Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
One who steals; one who commits theft or larceny. See Theft.
The quality or state of being tender (in any sense of the adjective).
A piece split off; a splinter.
The quality or state of being soft; -- opposed to Ant: hardness, and used in the various specific senses of the adjective.
A man or boy habitually negligent of neathess and order; -- the correlative term to slattern, or slut. Pope.

That at which one aims; the thing or end to which the mind directs its view; that which is purposed to be reached or accomplished; hence, ultimate design, aim, or purpose; intention; drift; object. "Shooting wide, do miss the marked scope." Spenser.
One who takes or receives in any manner.
One who, or that which, defends or shields from injury, evil, oppression, etc.; a defender; a guardian; a patron. For the world's protector shall be known.
One who prophesies, or foretells events; a predicter; a foreteller.
Previous warning, notice, or information; forewarning; as, a premonition of danger.

The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting; entire development; consummate culture, skill, or moral excellence; the highest attainable state or degree of excellence; maturity; as, perfection in an art, in a science,

Penal retribution; punishment for crime or offense; the suffering in person or property which is annexed by law or judicial decision to the commission of a crime, offense, or trespass. Death is the penalty imposed.

The state or quality of being patient; the power of suffering with fortitude; uncomplaining endurance of evils or wrongs, as toil, pain, poverty, insult, oppression, calamity, etc. Strenthened with all might, .
A reasoning which is false in point of form, that is, which is contrary to logical rules or formulæ; a formal fallacy, or pseudo- syllogism, in which the conclusion does not follow from the premises.
The quality or state of being parallel.
The planet Venus, when appearing as the morning star; -- applied in Isaiah by a metaphor to a king of Babylon. How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning !

The act of improving; advancement or growth; promotion in desirable qualities; progress toward what is better; melioration; as, the improvement of the mind, of land, roads, etc. I look upon your city as the best place of improvement.
The act of humiliating or humbling; abasement of pride; mortification. Bp.
Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family. And calls, without affecting airs, His household twice a day to prayers.
Glad tidings; especially, the good news concerning Christ, the Kingdom of God, and salvation. And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom.
A lump; a clod.
The state or quality of being flexible; flexibleness; pliancy; pliability; as, the flexibility of strips of hemlock, hickory, whalebone or metal, or of rays of light. Sir I.

A person or thing regarded with peculiar favor; one treated with partiality; one preferred above others; especially, one unduly loved, trusted, and enriched with favors by a person of high rank or authority. Committing to a wicked favorite All public cares.

A cylindrical bundle of small sticks of wood, bound together, used in raising batteries, filling ditches, strengthening ramparts, and making parapets; also in revetments for river banks, and in mats for dams, jetties, etc.

A special business intrusted to a messenger; something to be told or done by one sent somewhere for the purpose; often, a verbal message; a commission; as, the servant was sent on an errand; to do an errand. Also, one's purpose in going anywhere.
An undue or unnatural temper, or disproportionate mixture of parts. Bacon.
The act of disposing, or disposing of, anything; arrangement; orderly distribution; a putting in order; as, the disposal of the troops in two lines.
The quality of being diligent; carefulness; careful attention; -- the opposite of negligence.
The act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind. Pope.
The tail; the end of a thing; especially, a tail-like twist of hair worn at the back of the head; a queue.

The act of consoling; the state of being consoled; allevation of misery or distress of mind; refreshment of spirit; comfort; that which consoles or comforts the spirit. Against such cruelties With inward consolations recompensed.
That which follows something on which it depends; that which is produced by a cause; a result. Shun to taste, And shun the bitter consequence.
The act of concealing; the state of being concealed. But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud, Feed on her damask cheek.
One who seeks what another seeks, or claims what another claims; one who competes; a rival. And can not brook competitors in love.

The act of comparing; an examination of two or more objects with the view of discovering the resemblances or differences; relative estimate. As sharp legal practitioners, no class of human beings can bear comparison with them.
The act of applying color to; also, that which produces color.
The act, process, or time of celebrating. His memory deserving a particular celebration.
A male child, from birth to the age of puberty; a lad; hence, a son. My only boy fell by the side of great Dundee.
A bowman, one skilled in the use of the bow and arrow.
A musical response; alternate singing or chanting. See Antiphony, and Antiphone.
The act of altering or making different. Alteration, though it be from worse to better, hath in it incoveniences.
The right of presenting to a vacant benefice or living in the church. [Originally, the relation of a patron (advocatus) or protector of a benefice, and thus privileged to nominate or present to it.]
Gentle or friendly reproof; counseling against a fault or error; expression of authoritative advice; friendly caution or warning.
The quality of being absurd or inconsistent with obvious truth, reason, or sound judgment. "The absurdity of the actual idea of an infinite number." Locke.

Giving or producing satisfaction; yielding content; especially, relieving the mind from doubt or uncertainty, and enabling it to rest with confidence; sufficient; as, a satisfactory account or explanation.
A tool for turning screws so as to drive them into their place. It has a thin end which enters the nick in the head of the screw.

To apostemate; to form an imposthume or abscess. Arbuthnot.
A group of small wormlike animals, having cilia on the ventral side. The group is regarded as an ancestral or synthetic one, related to rotifers and annelids.
Tending to conciliate; pacific; mollifying; propitiating. The only alternative, therefore, was to have recourse to the conciliatory policy.

An order of Entomostraca; -- so named from the feet of branchiopods having been supposed to perform the function of gills. It includes the fresh-water genera Branchipus, Apus, and Limnadia, and the genus Artemia found in salt lakes.
To render insensible by an anæsthetic. Encyc.
Good against spasms. -- n.
The act of testing or proving; trial; proof.

3d pers. sing.
To regard in a sentimental manner; as, to sentimentalize a subject.
Having prongs or projections like the tines of a fork; as, a three-pronged fork.
To do away with wholly; to annul; to make void; -- said of laws, customs, institutions, governments, etc.; as, to abolish slavery, to abolish folly.
To form into a hydrate; to combine with water.
The yellow part of an egg; the vitellus.
A shop where any manufacture or handiwork is carried on.
One who, or that which, warbles; a singer; a songster; -- applied chiefly to birds. In lulling strains the feathered warblers woo.
One who vends; one who transfers the exclusive right of possessing a thing, either his own, or that of another as his agent, for a price or pecuniary equivalent; a seller; a vendor.

The space inclosed between ranges of hills or mountains; the strip of land at the bottom of the depressions intersecting a country, including usually the bed of a stream, with frequently broad alluvial plains on one or both sides of the stream. Also used figur
The quality or state of being uneasy; restlessness; disquietude; anxiety.
A wall separating two cavities; a partition; as, the nasal septum.
One who retails anything; as, a retailer of merchandise; a retailer of gossip.
One who, or that which, forwards, advances, or promotes; an encourager; as, a promoter of charity or philosophy. Boyle.
Full or adequate supply; enough and to spare; sufficiency; specifically, abundant productiveness of the earth; ample supply for human wants; abundance; copiousness. "Plenty of corn and wine." Gen.
The sliding weight on a steelyard. [Written also pee.]
One who begets, or brings forth, offspring; a father or a mother. Children, obey your parents in the Lord.
In a different manner; in another way, or in other ways; differently; contrarily. Chaucer.
A knot, a knob; a protuberance; a swelling.
The act, process, or art, of measuring.
The act of marrying, or the state of being married; legal union of a man and a woman for life, as husband and wife; wedlock; matrimony. Marriage is honorable in all.
That which settles at the bottom, as, of a cask of liquor (esp. wine); sediment; dregs; -- used now only in the plural.
In man, the joint in the middle part of the leg.
One who gathers or collects.
Habitation; place or house in which a person lives; abode; domicile. Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons.
One who cries; one who makes proclamation. Specifically, an officer who proclams the orders or directions of a court, or who gives public notice by loud proclamation; as, a town-crier.

Hollow and curved or rounded; vaulted; -- said of the interior of a curved surface or line, as of the curve of the of the inner surface of an eggshell, in opposition to convex; as, a concave mirror; the concave arch of the sky.
Usually; generally; ordinarily; frequently; for the most part; as, confirmed habits commonly continue trough life.
The state of burning.
One who, or that which, burns or sets fire to anything.

The act of doing that which begins anything; commencement of an action, state, or space of time; entrance into being or upon a course; the first act, effort, or state of a succession of acts or states. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
One who admires; one who esteems or loves greatly. Cowper.

A expression of gratitude; an acknowledgment expressive of a sense of favor or kindness received; obligation, claim, or desert, or gratitude; -- now generally used in the plural. "This ceremonial thanks." Massinger.
The joint of a finger, particularly when made prominent by the closing of the fingers. Davenant.
A deception for mockery or mischief; a deceptive trick or story; a practical joke. Macaulay.

A handle; that part of an instrument or vessel taken into the hand, and by which it is held and used; -- said chiefly of a knife, sword, or dagger; the hilt. This brandish'dagger I'll bury to the haft in her fair breast.
That which is used for filling anything; as, the stuffing of a saddle or cushion.
Originally, any rough and somewhat heavy piece of timber. Now, commonly, one of the timbers of a roof which are put on sloping, according to the inclination of the roof.
A small compartment in a desk or case for the keeping of letters, documents, etc.; -- so called from the resemblance of a row of them to the compartments in a dovecote. Burke.
A deserted or exposed infant; a child found without a parent or owner. Foundling hospital, a hospital for foundlings.
A steep, rugged rock; a cough, broken cliff, or point of a rock, on a ledge. From crag to crag the signal fiew.
Wrinkled; crumpled; furrowed; contracted into ridges and furrows.

Having a body; consisting of, or pertaining to, a material body or substance; material; -- opposed to spiritual or immaterial. His omnipotence That to corporeal substance could add Speed almost spiritual.

(a) Property of a deceased person, subject by law to the payment of his debts and legacies; -- called assets because sufficient to render the executor or administrator liable to the creditors and legatees, so far as such goods or estate may extend. Story.
Having the characteristic of Zoilus, a bitter, envious, unjust critic, who lived about 270 years before Christ.
Yellow; specifically (Ethnol.), of or pertaining to those races of man which have yellowish, red, auburn, or brown hair.
The largest instrument of the bass-viol kind, having strings tuned an octave below those of the violoncello; the contrabasso; -- called also double bass. [Written also violono.]
Composed of small plates, as of horn or metal, overlapping like tiles; -- said of a kind of ancient armor. Fairholt.
Having a space equal to two diameters or four modules between two columns; -- said of a portico or building. See Intercolumniation.
Having the back hollow or sagged, whether naturally or as the result of injury or weakness; -- said of horses and other animals.
Having the qualities of a speculum, or mirror; having a smooth, reflecting surface; as, a specular metal; a specular surface.
A wind instrument of brass, containing a reed, and partaking of the qualities both of a brass instrument and of a clarinet.
A rare mineral having a velvet-black color and submetallic luster. It is a niobate of uranium, iron, and the yttrium and cerium metals.
Of or pertaining to Roumania.
Having the pallium, or mantle, acting as a gill, as in brachiopods.
Having only one cotyledon, seed lobe, or seminal leaf. Lindley.
Having a heart; having (such) a heart (regarded as the seat of the affections, disposition, or character).
Having wings that are like hands in the structure and arrangement of their bones; -- said of bats. See Cheiroptera.
A genus of birds, with a short, conical, pointed bill. It formerly included all the sparrows and finches, but is now restricted to certain European finches, like the chaffinch and brambling.
Having the color or appearance of unbleached stuff, as silk, linen, or the like.
Containing or involving a declination or refusal, as of submission to a charge or sentence. Blackstone.
Granular; pertaining to, or having the granular structure characteristic of, the class of meteorites called chondrites.
A garment for women, consisting of chemise and drawers united in one. [U.
Having the nature, qualities, taste, form, consistency, or appearance of cheese.
Of or pertaining to brass; having the nature, appearance, or hardness, of brass.

The science which treats of the structure of plants, the functions of their parts, their places of growth, their classification, and the terms which are employed in their description and denomination. See Plant.
Having a black, dark, or gloomy face or aspect.
A wind instrument of the double reed kind, furnished with holes, which are stopped by the fingers, and by keys, as in flutes. It forms the natural bass to the oboe, clarinet, etc.
Broken in place; -- said of rocks having a broken or brecciated structure due to crushing, in contrast to those of brecciated materials brought from a distance.
Having a structure entirely cellular, and no distinct sexual organs; -- a term applied by De Candolle to the lowest order of plants.
Having the form of alveoli, or little sockets, cells, or cavities.

Having power to advise; containing advice; as, an advisory council; their opinion is merely advisory. The General Association has a general advisory superintendence over all the ministers and churches.
Moving from place to place without a settled habitation; wandering. "Vagabond exile." Shak.
To fill up or supply by addition; to add something to. Causes of one kind must be supplemented by bringing to bear upon them a causation of another kind.
To write underneath, as one's name; to sign (one's name) to a document. [They] subscribed their names under them.
To utter a shrill, abrupt scream; to squeak harshly. Squawking thrush (Zoöl.), the missel turush; -- so called from its note when alarmed.
To drive back or away, as with the foot; to kick. [The bird] with his foot will spurn adown his cup.
To die, decay, or become gangrenous, as flesh or bone; to mortify.

To break at once into many pieces; to dash, burst, or part violently into fragments; to rend into splinters; as, an explosion shatters a rock or a bomb; too much steam shatters a boiler; an oak is shattered by lightning. A monarchy was shattered to pieces, and
To wither; to dry up. Shak.

The extraneous matter or impurities which rise to the surface of liquids in boiling or fermentation, or which form on the surface by other means; also, the scoria of metals in a molten state; dross. Some to remove the scum it did rise.

The sin or crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to laymen, or to common purposes, what has been appropriated or consecrated to religious persons or uses. And the hid treasures in her sacred tomb With sacrilege to dig.

A fondness for romantic characteristics or peculiarities; specifically, in modern literature, an aiming at romantic effects; -- applied to the productions of a school of writers who sought to revive certain medi He [Lessing] may be said to have begun the revol
To model or fashion anew; to change the form of. The corporation had been remodeled.
To remove, usually to an inferior position; to consign; to transfer; specifically, to send into exile; to banish. It [the Latin language] was relegated into the study of the scholar.
Reproduced. The earthly author of my blood, Whose youthful spirit, in me regenerate, Doth with a twofold vigor lift me up.
To give echoes; to return back, or be reverberated, as an echo; to resound; to be resonant. And a loud groan reëchoes from the main.
A riddle or obscure question; an enigma; a ridiculous hoax.
To test as to weight and fineness, as the coins deposited in the pyx. [Eng.] Mushet.

To carry or bring (something) forward, or before one; hence, to bring for consideration, acceptance, judgment, etc.; to offer; to present; to proffer; to address; -- said especially of a request, prayer, petition, claim, charge, etc. He spake, and to her hand
To emit or evacuate through the pores of the skin; to sweat; to excrete through pores. Firs .
To become bone; to change from a soft tissue to a hard bony tissue.
To make necessary or indispensable; to render unaviolable. Sickness [might] necessitate his removal from the court.
To perplex greatly; to bewilder; to astonish and confuse; to amaze. South.

An unmarried woman; a girl or woman who has not experienced sexual intercourse; a virgin; a maid. She employed the residue of her life to repairing of highways, building of bridges, and endowing of maidens.
The ear, or its lobe. [Scot.

One versed in the laws, or a practitioner of law; one whose profession is to conduct lawsuits for clients, or to advise as to prosecution or defence of lawsuits, or as to legal rights and obligations in other matters. It is a general term, comprehending attorn
To take (any one) by force or fear, and against one's will, with intent to carry to another place. Abbott.
To unite by twining one with another; to entangle; to interlace. Milton.
To check; to hold back; to restrain; to hinder. Their motions also are excited or inhibited .
To swallow eagerly, or in large draughts; to swallow up; to take down at one swallow. He does not swallow, but he gulps it down.
To fashion into groins; to build with groins. The hand that rounded Peter's dome, And groined the aisles of Christian Rome, Wrought in a sad sincerity.
To make a gash, or long, deep incision in; -- applied chiefly to incisions in flesh. Grievously gashed or gored to death.
To set a value on; to appreciate the worth of; to estimate; to value; to reckon. Then he forsook God, which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.

One moved or actuated by enthusiasm; as: (a) One who imagines himself divinely inspired, or possessed of some special revelation; a religious madman; a fanatic. (b) One whose mind is wholly possessed and heated by what engages it; one who is influenced by a pe
To transport with pleasure; to delight beyond measure; to enravish. Shenstone.

A syllable attached to the first tone of the major diatonic scale for the purpose of solmization, or solfeggio. It is the first of the seven syllables used by the Italians as manes of musical tones, and replaced, for the sake of euphony, the syllable Ut, appli
To cease to use; to discontinue the practice of.
To fail to accord; not to agree; to lack harmony; to differ; to be unlike; to be at variance. They reject the plainest sense of Scripture, because it seems disagree with what they call reason.

A mast, spar, or tall frame, supported at the top by stays or guys, with suitable tackle for hoisting heavy weights, as stones in building. Derrick crane, a combination of the derrick and the crane, having facility for hoisting and also for swinging the load h
A washing away; an overflowing of the land by water; an inundation; a flood; specifically, The Deluge, the great flood in the days of Noah (Gen. vii.).
To reach its highest point of altitude; to come to the meridian; to be vertical or directly overhead. As when his beams at noon Culminate from the equator.
To crush with the teeth; to chew with violence and noise; to crunch. Swift.
To oppose, as another plot, by plotting; to attempt to frustrate, as a stratagem, by stratagem. Every wile had proved abortive, every plot had been counterplotted.
To confine in, or as in, a cloister; to seclude from the world; to immure. None among them are throught worthy to be styled religious persons but those that cloister themselves up in a monastery.
An instrument for measuring or recording intervals of time, upon a revolving drum or strip of paper moved by clockwork. The action of the stylus or pen is controlled by electricity.
To sing in chorus; to exclaim simultaneously. W.
To quicken or animate by chirping; to cherup.
To praise or celebrate in song. The Shepherds at their festivals Carol her goodness.
To show to be false; to convict of, or charge with, falsehood. Their trembling hearts belie their boastful tongues.
To ply diligently; to work carefully upon. "If the earth is belabored with culture, it yieldeth corn." Barrow.
To delude by guile, artifice, or craft; to deceive or impose on, as by a false statement; to lure. The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.
To grudge; to envy the possession of.
A small brook. The brooks, the becks, the rills.
To contend with; to oppose actively; to counteract.
To give a faint shadow or slight representation of; to outline; to shadow forth. Both in the vastness and the richness of the visible universe the invisible God is adumbrated.

To annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor; to repeal; -- applied to the repeal of laws, decrees, ordinances, the abolition of customs, etc. Let us see whether the New Testament abrogates what we so frequently s
To take away surreptitiously by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually by violence; to kidnap.

Previous sentiment, conception, or opinion; previous apprehension; especially, an antecedent impression or conviction of something unpleasant, distressing, or calamitous, about to happen; anticipation of evil; foreboding.
The act or the state of intermitting; the state of being neglected or disused; disuse; discontinuance. B.
The act or state of knowing; the exercise of the understanding.
The act of condemning or pronouncing to be wrong; censure; blame; disapprobation. In every other sense of condemnation, as blame, censure, reproof, private judgment, and the like.
Of or pertaining to rudiments; consisting in first principles; elementary; initial; as, rudimental essays.
The art of writing in cipher, or in characters which are not intelligible except to persons who have the key; cryptography.

An assertion of the contrary to what has been said or affirmed; denial of the truth of a statement or assertion; contrary declaration; gainsaying. His fair demands Shall be accomplished without contradiction.
A reflecting telescope, part of which is made to rotate eccentrically, so as to produce a ringlike image of a star, instead of a point; -- used in studying the scintillation of the stars.
Of or pertaining to sugar; having the qualities of sugar; producing sugar; sweet; as, a saccharine taste; saccharine matter.
Somewhat green; having a tinge of green; as, a greenish yellow. -- Green"ish*ness, n.

Having coincidence; occupying the same place; contemporaneous; concurrent; -- followed by with. Christianity teaches nothing but what is perfectly suitable to, and coincident with, the ruling principles of a virtuous and well- inclined man.
A thin, narrow strip or bar of wood or metal; as, the slats of a window blind.
A spot; a streak; a speckle. "A sunny fleck." Longfellow.

To render other than Protestant; to cause to change from Protestantism to some other form of religion; to deprive of some Protestant feature or characteristic. The attempt to unprotestantize the Church of England.
Preparing the way for anything by previous measures of adaptation; antecedent and adapted to what follows; introductory; preparative; as, a preparatory school; a preparatory condition.
Any one of numerous species of scansorial birds belonging to Picus and many allied genera of the family Picidæ.
Any one of numerous species of snout beetles, or Rhynchophora, in which the head is elongated and usually curved downward. Many of the species are very injurious to cultivated plants.
An earthy substance originally brought from Tripoli, used in polishing stones and metals. It consists almost wholly of the siliceous shells of diatoms.

Support; aid; coöperation; esp., extraordinary aid in money rendered to the sovereign or to a friendly power. They advised the king to send speedy aids, and with much alacrity granted a great rate of subsidy.
A case, box, or receptacle, especially one in which are deposited sacred relics, as the bones of a saint.

A kind of intoxicating liquor distilled from cane juice, or from the scumming of the boiled juice, or from treacle or molasses, or from the lees of former distillations. Also, sometimes used colloquially as a generic or a collective name for intoxicating liquo
A kind of coarse, heavy frieze, formerly used for garments. They spin the choicest rug in Ireland.
The act of revealing, disclosing, or discovering to others what was before unknown to them.
A sacred song; a poetical composition for use in the praise or worship of God. Humus devout and holy psalms Singing everlastingly.

The act of Preferring, or the state of being preferred; the setting of one thing before another; precedence; higher estimation; predilection; choice; also, the power or opportunity of choosing; as, to give him his preference. Leave the critics on either side t
An edifice or place full of intricate passageways which render it difficult to find the way from the interior to the entrance; as, the Egyptian and Cretan labyrinths.
A hump; a protuberance.

Native carbon in hexagonal crystals, also foliated or granular massive, of black color and metallic luster, and so soft as to leave a trace on paper. It is used for pencils (improperly called lead pencils), for crucibles, and as a lubricator, etc.
Decomposed rock, usually reddish or ferruginous (owing to oxidized pyrites), forming the upper part of a metallic vein.
One of several species of insectivorous birds, belonging to Caprimulgus and allied genera, esp. the European species (Caprimulgus Europæus); -- so called from the mistaken notion that it sucks goats.

A porch or waiting room, usually at the west end of an abbey church, where the monks collected on returning from processions, where bodies were laid previous to interment, and where women were allowed to see the monks to whom they were related, or to hear divi
One whose ambition it is to gain admiration by showy dress; a coxcomb; an inferior dandy.
Any foul of filthy substance, as excrement, mud, dust, etc.; whatever, adhering to anything, renders it foul or unclean; earth; as, a wagonload of dirt. Whose waters cast up mire and dirt.

Wood-tar oil; an oily antiseptic liquid, of a burning smoky taste, colorless when pure, but usually colored yellow or brown by impurity or exposure. It is a complex mixture of various phenols and their ethers, and is obtained by the distillation of wood tar, e
Literally, suffering with another; a sensation of sorrow excited by the distress or misfortunes of another; pity; commiseration. Womanly igenuity set to work by womanly compassion.
One who is engaged in the actual use or exercise of any art or profession, particularly that of law or medicine. Crabbe.
One who manufactures.
Having a top, or head, shaped like the top of a covered wagon, or resembling in section or outline an inverted U, thus as, a wagonheaded ceiling.

Having the properties exhibited by gases under very low pressures (one millionth of an atmosphere or less). Matter under this condition, which has been termed the fourth state of matter, is sometimes called radiant matter.
An instrument of torture, consisting of a board with holes into which the fingers were pressed, and fastened with pegs. [Written also pilliewinkles.] [Scot.] Sir W.
A branch of a plumularian hydroid specially modified in structure for the protection of the gonothecæ.
A tumor having the structure of a sacroma in which there is a deposit of bone; sarcoma connected with bone.
Consisting of a series of parallel cones, each made up of many concentric cones closely packed together; -- said of a kind of structure sometimes observed in sedimentary rocks.
To calculate erroneously; to judge wrongly. -- Mis*cal`cu*la"tion, n.

A disappearing gun carriage in which the recoil is checked by cylinders containing liquid and air, the air when compressed furnishing the power for restoring the gun to the firing position. It is used with some English and European heavy guns.
To pronounce an anathema against; to curse. Hence: To condemn publicly as something accursed.

A right-lined quadrilateral figure, whose opposite sides are parallel, and consequently equal; -- sometimes restricted in popular usage to a rectangle, or quadrilateral figure which is longer than it is broad, and with right angles. Parallelogram of velocities

The act of transgressing, or of passing over or beyond any law, civil or moral; the violation of a law or known principle of rectitude; breach of command; fault; offense; crime; sin. Forgive thy people .
The act of recriminating; an accusation brought by the accused against the accuser; a counter accusation. Accusations and recriminations passed back ward and forward between the contending parties.

The act of justifying or the state of being justified; a showing or proving to be just or conformable to law, justice, right, or duty; defense; vindication; support; as, arguments in justification of the prisoner's conduct; his disobedience admits justificatio
A small assemblage of houses in the country, less than a town or city. Village cart, a kind of two-wheeled pleasure carriage without a top.
Shaking; tottering; quivering. -- Trem"bling*ly, adv.
Capable of suiting; fitting; accordant; proper; becoming; agreeable; adapted; as, ornaments suitable to one's station; language suitable for the subject. -- Suit"a*ble*ness, n.
The power or authority of a lord; dominion. O'Neal never had any seigniory over that country but what by encroachment he got upon the English.
Recurring in vicissitude; alternate.
The act or process of one who packs.

A place arched over with brick or stonework, and used for baking, heating, or drying; hence, any structure, whether fixed or portable, which may be heated for baking, drying, etc.; esp., now, a chamber in a stove, used for baking or roasting.
Situated in front; opposite; hence, opposing; adverse; antagonistic. Pope.
A house of religious retirement, or of secusion from ordinary temporal concerns, especially for monks; -- more rarely applied to such a house for females.
The acquisition of knowledge or skill; as, the learning of languages; the learning of telegraphy.
The string that fastens a shoe; a shoestring.
The act or process of inferring by deduction or induction. Though it may chance to be right in the conclusions, it is yet unjust and mistaken in the method of inference.
A small house, hivel, or cabin; a mean lodge or dwelling; a slightly built or temporary structure. Death comes on with equal footsteps To the hall and hut.
A covering or ornament for the head; a headtire. Among birds the males very often appear in a most beautiful headdress, whether it be a crest, a comb, a tuft of feathers, or a natural little plume.
The possessor of a freehold.

Belonging to,or concerning, a focus; as, a focal point. Focal distance, or length,of a lens or mirror (Opt.), the distance of the focus from the surface of the lens or mirror, or more exactly, in the case of a lens, from its optical center.
The act or operation of eroding or eating away.
Of or pertaining to the Dravida. Dravidian languages, a group of languages of Southern India, which seem to have been the idioms of the natives, before the invasion of tribes speaking Sanskrit.

A service of pastry, fruits, or sweetmeats, at the close of a feast or entertainment; pastry, fruits, etc., forming the last course at dinner. "An 't please your honor," quoth the peasant, "This same dessert is not so pleasant." Pope.
A bar of iron sharpened at one end, and used as a lever.
The uppermost cover of a bed or of any piece of furniture. Lay her in lilies and in violets .
A member of a council. [Written also councillor.]
The act or process of converting metal into money. The care of the coinage was committed to the inferior magistrates.
The last of the three names of a person among the ancient Romans, denoting his house or family.
The act or process of inclosing in, or covering with, a case or thin substance, as plaster, boards, etc.
An inhabitant of a borough or walled town, or one who possesses a tenement therein; a citizen or freeman of a borough. Blackstone.
Endowed with life; full of life or spirit; indicating animation; lively; vigorous. "Animated sounds." Pope.
Recording; -- applied to instruments; having an apparatus which registers; as, a registering thermometer. See Recording.
A part of a helmet, arranged so as to lift or open, and so show the face. The openings for seeing and breathing are generally in it.
Giving previous notice; cautioning; admonishing; as, a warning voice. That warning timepiece never ceased.
Neverceasing; continuing forever or for an unlimited time; unfailing; everlasting; continuous. Unto the kingdom of perpetual night.

A person to whose sole decision a controversy or question between parties is referred; especially, one chosen to see that the rules of a game, as cricket, baseball, or the like, are strictly observed. A man, in questions of this kind, is able to be a skillful
A round body; a little wheel.

Of or pertaining to tides; caused by tides; having tides; periodically rising and falling, or following and ebbing; as, tidal waters. The tidal wave of deeper souls Into our inmost being rolls, And lifts us unawares Out of all meaner cares.
A rascal; a swindler; a rogue. De Quincey.

Something demanded or asserted; especially, a position or supposition assumed without proof, or one which is considered as self-evident; a truth to which assent may be demanded or challenged, without argument or evidence.
Of or pertaining to phosphorus; resembling, or containing, from us; specifically, designating those compounds in which phosphorus has a higher valence as contrasted with the phosphorous compounds.
Lifted high up; having great height; towering; high. See lofty Lebanon his head advance.
A tool used by coopers for smoothing and chamfering rheir work, especially the inside of casks.
Once more; again; -- used by the auditors and spectators of plays, concerts, and other entertainments, to call for a repetition of a particular part.
A thick, ill-shapen piece; a clumsy leaden counter used by boys in playing chuck farthing. [Eng.] Smart.
A person easily deceived, tricked, or imposed on; a mean dupe; a gull. I have learned that .
A small fragment or piece; especially, a small piece of bread or other food, broken or cut off. Desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table.
Capable of taking fire and burning; apt to catch fire; inflammable. Sin is to the soul like fire to combustible matter.
Arraignment; as, the clerk of the arraigns. Blackstone.
Having a yellow stipe, or stem.
Of or pertaining to a virgin; becoming a virgin; maidenly. "Chastity and honor virginal." Spenser.
Having the surface covered with a fine and dense silky pubescence; velvety; as, a velutinous leaf.
Having three petals, or flower leaves; three-petaled.
Having vague outlines, and colors and shades so mingled as to give a misty appearance; -- said of a painting.
Hermaphrodite, or having both stamens and pistils in every flower.
Having only one slope or pitch; -- said of a roof. -- n.
Pertaining to, or having the character of, perching birds.
Pertaining to, or having the nature of, fluxion or fluxions; variable; inconstant. The merely human,the temporary and fluxional.
Shaped like a boat; (Bot.) elongated and having the upper surface decidedly concave, as the glumes of many grasses.
Having elevations or depressions in form like one half of a bivalve shell; -- applied principally to a surface produced by fracture.
Of both sexes; hermaphrodite; as a flower with stamens and pistil, or an animal having ovaries and testes.
Having two lips, as the corols of certain flowers.
Furnished with an awn, or long bristle-shaped tip; bearded. Gray.
Having worth or excellence; possessing merit; valuable; deserving; estimable; excellent; virtuous. Full worthy was he in his lordes war.

Long exercised in anything, especially in military life and the duties of a soldier; long practiced or experienced; as, a veteran officer or soldier; veteran skill. The insinuating eloquence and delicate flattery of veteran diplomatists and courtiers.
Growing, or having the power of growing, as plants; capable of vegetating.

Having lost its life and spirit; dead; spiritless; insipid; flat; dull; unanimated; as, vapid beer; a vapid speech; a vapid state of the blood. A cheap, bloodless reformation, a guiltless liberty, appear flat and vapid to their taste.
Not conscious; having no consciousness or power of mental perception; without cerebral appreciation; hence, not knowing or regarding; ignorant; as, an unconscious man. Cowper.
Having lost motion, or the power of exertion and feeling; numb; benumbed; as, a torpid limb. Without heat all things would be torpid.

A game in which a small piece of wood pointed at both ends, called a cat, is tipped, or struck with a stick or bat, so as to fly into the air. In the middle of a game at tipcat, he paused, and stood staring wildly upward with his stick in his hand.
One of a class of theologians who maintain that God has fixed a certain term for the probation of individual persons, during which period, and no longer, they have the offer to grace. Murdock.

The art of healing by manual operation; that branch of medical science which treats of manual operations for the healing of diseases or injuries of the body; that branch of medical science which has for its object the cure of local injuries or diseases, as wou

Of pertaining to, or engaging in, sport or sporrts; exhibiting the character or conduct of one who, or that which, sports. Sporting book, a book containing a record of bets, gambling operations, and the like.
Containing only an outline or rough form; being in the manner of a sketch; incomplete. The execution is sketchy throughout; the head, in particular, is left in the rough.

A portion of Great Britain originally under the supervision of an earl; a territorial division, usually identical with a county, but sometimes limited to a smaller district; as, Wiltshire, Yorkshire, Richmondshire, Hallamshire. An indefinite number of these hu
A dance having five figures, in common time, four couples of dancers being in each set.
Boyish; childish; trifling; silly. The French have been notorious through generations for their puerile affectation of Roman forms, models, and historic precedents.
Consisting of individuals united in a body or mass without order; mingled; confused; undistinguished; as, a promiscuous crowd or mass. A wild, where weeds and flowers promiscuous shoot.
Consisting of land or farms; landed; as, predial estate; that is, real estate. Ayliffe.
A portion of land nearly surrounded by water, and connected with a larger body by a neck, or isthmus.
An outer garment for men or women, originally of fur, or lined with fur; a lady's outer garment, made of silk or other fabric.

A game formerly common in England, in which a wooden ball was driven with a mallet through an elevated hoop or ring of iron. The name was also given to the mallet used, to the place where the game was played, and to the street, in London, still called Pall Mal
An imaginary animal borne as a charge, having wings, an eagle's head, and a short tail; -- sometimes represented without wings.
A small bagpipe formerly in use, having a soft and sweet tone.
The telegraphic code, consisting of dots, dashes, and spaces, invented by Samuel B. Morse.
A fermented beverage made of honey and water; mead. Gay.
Having no desire or inclination; indifferent; heedless; spiritless. " A listless unconcern." Thomson.
Having the quality of softening or mitigating, as pain or acrimony; assuasive; emollient.
A kind of loose robe or gown tied with a sash, worn as an outer garment by Japanese men and women.
A door-keeper; a porter; one who has the care of a public building, or a building occupied for offices, suites of rooms, etc.
Exerting or possessing influence or power; potent; efficacious; effective; strong; having authority or ascendency; as, an influential man, station, argument, etc. A very influential Gascon prefix.
Not mortal; exempt from liability to die; undying; imperishable; lasting forever; having unlimited, or eternal, existance. Unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible.
A liquor consisting of honey diluted in water, and after fermentation called mead.
Having the skin adhering so closely to the ribs and back as not to be easily loosened or raised; -- said of an animal.
A musical instrument, consisting of a series of hemispherical glasses which, by touching the edges with the dampened finger, give forth the tones.
Bold; brave; stout; daring; resolue; intrepid. Hap helpeth hardy man alway.
An apparatus for measuring the amount of hemoglobin in a fluid, by comparing it with a solution of known strength and of normal color.
One who, or that which, grates; especially, an instrument or utensil with a rough, indented surface, for rubbing off small particles of any substance; as a grater for nutmegs.
A method of painting with opaque colors, which have been ground in water and mingled with a preparation of gum; also, a picture thus painted.
A weapon formerly used, consisting of a large blade fixed on the end of a pole, whose edge was on the outside curve; also, a light lance with a long sharp-pointed head. Wilhelm.
A boat with a flat bottom and square ends; -- used for the transportation of bulky freight, especially in shallow waters.
A centerpiece for table decoration, usually consisting of several dishes or receptacles of different sizes grouped together in an ornamental design.
To be suffocated in water or other fluid; to perish in water. Methought, what pain it was to drown.
Play; sport; pastime; diversion; playfulness. Milton.
A white crystalline substance, C3H7NSO2, containing sulphur, occuring as a constituent of certain rare urinary calculi, and occasionally found as a sediment in urine.
Containing the substance oe general principles of a subject or work in a narrow compass; abridged; summarized. More compendious and exeditious ways.
The steersman of a boat; a petty officer who has charge of a boat and its crew.
A flat-floored fishing boat with a lug sail, and a drop rudder extending from two to four feet below the keel. It was originally used on the stormy coast of Yorkshire, England.
A fine, thin, and white fabric made of flax or linen. He hath ribbons of all the colors i' the rainbow; .
Having the appearance or color of a dead human body; pale; ghastly; as, a cadaverous look.
A one-horse carriage with two seats and a calash top.
A kind of close carriage with two or four wheels, usually a public vehicle. "A cab came clattering up." Thackeray.

A system of carrying on the business of government by means of departments or bureaus, each under the control of a chief, in contradiction to a system in which the officers of government have an associated authority and responsibility; also, government conduct
A sword with a broad blade and a cutting edge; a claymore. I heard the broadsword's deadly clang.
To place within brackets; to connect by brackets; to furnish with brackets.
Having the sensibilities deadened by excess or frequency of enjoyment; sated or surfeited with pleasure; used up.

Holding some office or valuable possession, in subordination to another; holding under a feudal or other superior; having a dependent and secondary possession. A feudatory or beneficiary king of England.

A weight used in the East, varying according to the locality; in Turkey, the greater batman is about 157 pounds, the lesser only a fourth of this; at Aleppo and Smyrna, the batman is 17 pounds. Simmonds.
A game at cards, resembling the modern faro, said to have been invented at Venice. Some dress, some dance, some play, not to forget Your piquet parties, and your dear basset.
Made with an arch or curve; covered with an arch; as, an arched door.

A hard, compact variety of mineral coal, of high luster, differing from bituminous coal in containing little or no bitumen, in consequence of which it burns with a nearly non luminous flame. The purer specimens consist almost wholly of carbon.
An elephant goad with a sharp spike and hook, resembling a short-handled boat hook. [India] Kipling.
An instrument for measuring sensations of pain due to pressure. It has a piston rod with a blunted tip which is pressed against the skin.
A grayish green antiseptic powder, consisting of a basic iodide and gallate of bismuth, sometimes used in place of iodoform. [A Trademark]

Any of numerous species of aquatic mites belonging to Hydrachna and allied genera of the family Hydrachnidæ, usually having the legs fringed and adapted for swimming. They are often red or red and black in color, and while young are parasites of fresh-water in
To roll one's self about, as in mire; to tumble and roll about; to move lazily or heavily in any medium; to flounder; as, swine wallow in the mire. I may wallow in the lily beds.
To bear up; to raise aloft; to support in an elevated situation; to sustain. Spenser.
To prate; to talk much and idly; to gabble; to chatter; to twaddle; as, a twattling gossip. L'Estrange.
To walk or march with labor; to jog along; to move wearily. And trudged to Rome upon my naked feet.
To break in pieces by violence; to dash to pieces; to crush. Here everything is broken and smashed to pieces.
To convert into, or to impregnate with, silica, or with the compounds of silicon. The specimens found .
To hear or receive the confession of; to administer confession and absolution to; -- said of a priest as the agent. That they should shrive their parishioners.
To withdraw from fellowship, communion, or association; to separate one's self by a solemn act; to draw off; to retire; especially, to withdraw from a political or religious body.
To return or send back; to repel or drive back; to echo, as sound; to reflect, as light, as light or heat. Who, like an arch, reverberates The voice again.

To commend to the favorable notice of another; to commit to another's care, confidence, or acceptance, with favoring representations; to put in a favorable light before any one; to bestow commendation on; as, he recommended resting the mind and exercising the
To assure anew; to restore confidence to; to free from fear or terror. They rose with fear, .
To make rare, thin, porous, or less dense; to expand or enlarge without adding any new portion of matter to; -- opposed to condense.
To favor; to render successful. "Prosper thou our handiwork." Bk.
To dress or adjust one's self for show; to prank.

To suppose beforehand; to imply as antecedent; to take for granted; to assume; as, creation presupposes a creator. Each [kind of knowledge] presupposes many necessary things learned in other sciences, and known beforehand.
The use of more words than are necessary to express the idea; a roundabout, or indirect, way of speaking; circumlocution. "To describe by enigmatic periphrases." De Quincey.

To beat rapidly and more strongly than usual; to throb; to bound with emotion or exertion; to pulsate violently; to flutter; -- said specifically of the heart when its action is abnormal, as from excitement.
To rise above the top of; to exceed in height; to tower above. "To old Pelion." Shak.
To destroy the organic texture and vital functions of; to produce gangrene in.

Any species of Melilotus, a genus of leguminous herbs having a vanillalike odor; sweet clover; hart's clover. The blue melilot (Melilotus cærulea) is used in Switzerland to give color and flavor to sapsago cheese.
To bring to ripeness or maturity; to ripen. A tree may be maturated artificially.
A government vessel employed for the purposes of war, esp. one of large size; a ship of war.
A sudden thrust or pass, as with a sword.
To wind old rope around, as a cable, to preserve its surface from being fretted, or to wind iron chains around, to defend from the friction of a rocky bottom, or from the ice. Totten.
To run or strike against each other; to encounter; to clash; to jostle. Shak.
To play tricks by sleight of hand; to cause amusement and sport by tricks of skill; to conjure.
To sound harshly or discordantly, as bells out of tune.
To cut into or between; to cut or cross mutually; to divide into parts; as, any two diameters of a circle intersect each other at the center. Lands intersected by a narrow frith Abhor each other.

To obey the law of gravitation; to exert a force Or pressure, or tend to move, under the influence of gravitation; to tend in any direction or toward any object. Why does this apple fall to the ground Because all bodies gravitate toward each other.
To eat greedily; to swallow voraciously; to feed ravenously or like a glutton. Shak.
To intoxicate; to stupefy with drink. I drank .
To judge beforehand, or before hearing the facts and proof; to prejudge.
A festival. Fête champêtre ( Etym: [F.], a festival or entertainment in the open air; a rural festival.
To generate pus; to become imflamed and suppurate; as, a sore or a wound festers. Wounds immedicable Rankle, and fester, and gangrene.
To shed an old covering or condition preliminary to taking on a new one; to molt. There is reason to suppose that very old crayfish do not exuviate every year.
To put out of one's possession; to surrender the ownership of; also, to deprive of possession or proprietary rights. Boyle.
To produce, as figures or designs, on mental, glass, or the like, by means of lines or strokes eaten in or corroded by means of some strong acid.

To withdraw; to withhold; hence, reflexively, to keep at a distance; to cease to be familiar and friendly with. We must estrange our belief from everything which is not clearly and distinctly evidenced.
To betroth; to promise in marriage; to give as spouse. A virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph.
To gorge; to glut. Mir.
To feel absence of trust in; not to confide in or rely upon; to deem of questionable sufficiency or reality; to doubt; to be suspicious of; to mistrust. Not distrusting my health.

A kind of mica containing lithium, often associated with tin ore.
A small, edible, freshwater European perch (Aspro zingel), having a round, elongated body and prominent snout.
A West African buffalo (Bubalus brachyceros) having short horns depressed at the base, and large ears fringed internally with three rows of long hairs. It is destitute of a dewlap.
A low, shrubby, rubiaceous plant (Morinda Royoc) growing along the seacoast of the West Indies. It has small, white, odorous flowers.
A light vehicle for conveying small loads. It has two handles and one wheel, and is rolled by a single person.
An indolent, encysted tumor of the skin; especially, a sebaceous cyst.
Any one of several species of edible marine fishes belonging to the genus Trachinus, of the family Trachinidæ. They have a broad spinose head, with the eyes looking upward.
Any plant of the American genus Hydrophyllum, herbs having white or pale blue bell-shaped flowers. Gray.
One of a system of tubular excretory organs having external openings, found in many invertebrates. They are believed to be analogous in function to the kidneys of vertebrates.
A large gallinule (Gallicrex cristatus) native of Australia, India, and the East Indies. In the breeding season the male is black and has a fleshy red caruncle, or horn, on the top of its head.
A large monkey (Macacus silenus) native of Malabar. It is black, or nearly so, but has a long white or gray beard encircling the face.
A wad, or the materials for wads; any pliable substance of which wads may be made.

An instrument consisting essentially of a glass tube provided with a graduated scale, for exhibiting to the eye the changes of volume of a gas or gaseous mixture resulting from chemical action, and the like.
An arrow or bolt for a crossbow having feathers or brass placed at an angle with the shaft to make it spin in flying.
Any one of several species of actinians belonging to the genus Cerianthus. These animals have a long, smooth body tapering to the base, and two separate circles of tentacles around the mouth.

A poisonous alkaloid obtained from the root hellebore (Veratrum) and from sabadilla seeds as a white crystalline powder, having an acrid, burning taste. It is sometimes used externally, as in ointments, in the local treatment of neuralgia and rheumatism.
A genus including several species of large marine gastropods having massive pyriform shells, with conspicuous folds on the columella.
A narrow superstructure running from stem to stern on the upper deck of a steam cargo vessel having a rounded gunwale and sides curved inward convexly.
A plant (Polianthes tuberosa) with a tuberous root and a liliaceous flower. It is much cultivated for its beautiful and fragrant white blossoms.

The curve described by any point in a wheel rolling on a line; a cycloid; a roulette; in general, the curve described by any point fixedly connected with a moving curve while the moving curve rolls without slipping on a second fixed curve, the curves all being
A Linnæan order of plants having three pistils or styles.
A Linnæan class of plants having three distinct and equal stamens.
A cuban trogon (Priotelus temnurus) having a serrated bill and a tail concave at the end.
A mineral occurring as an aggregation of minute scales having an olive-green color and pearly luster. It is a hydrous silicate of aluminia and iron.
A censer of metal, for burning incense, having various forms, held in the hand or suspended by chains; -- used especially at mass, vespers, and other solemn services. Fairholt.
An artificial red or violet dyestuff consisting of a complex sulphur derivative of certain aromatic diamines, and obtained as a dark crystalline powder; -- called also phenylene violet.
Any one of a group of lizards of the Gecko tribe, having the toes broad, and furnished with a groove in which the claws can be concealed.
Any one of a certain series of basic compounds containing a chain of four nitrogen atoms; for example, ethyl tetrazone, (C2H5)2N.N2.N(C2H5)2, a colorless liquid having an odor of leeks.
A large African antelope (Alcejaphus tora). It has widely divergent, strongly ringed horns.
Any oil substance having a hyacinthine odor, obtained by the action of acids on terpin, and regarded as a related hydrate.
That branch of biological science which treats of monstrosities, malformations, or deviations from the normal type of structure, either in plants or animals.
A short piece of pipe having a lateral outlet, used to connect a line of pipe with a pipe at a right angle with the line; -- so called because it resembles the letter T in shape.

Any one of several species of small fresh-water ducks of the genus Anas and the subgenera Querquedula and Nettion. The male is handsomely colored, and has a bright green or blue speculum on the wings.

(a) The Bull; the second in order of the twelve signs of the zodiac, which the sun enters about the 20th of April; -- marked thus [taurus] in almanacs. (b) A zodiacal constellation, containing the well-known clusters called the Pleiades and the Hyades, in the
A small carnivorous marsupial (Phascogale penicillata) having long, soft fur, and a very long tail with a tuft of long hairs at the end; -- called also brush-tailed phascogale.
Any shrub or tree of the genus Tamarix, the species of which are European and Asiatic. They have minute scalelike leaves, and small flowers in spikes.
A humming bird (Docimastes ensiferus) having a very long, slender bill, exceeding the length of the body of the bird.
A quantity which can not be expressed by rational numbers; thus, *2 is a surd.
The quality, state, or condition of being superior; as, superiority of rank; superiority in merit.
An oxide containing a relatively small amount of oxygen, and less than the normal proportion; as, potassium suboxide, K4O.
Ranked or ranged below; subordinate; inferior; specifically (Mil.), ranking as a junior officer; being below the rank of captain; as, a subaltern officer.
A white crystalline substance having a sweet taste and a hyacinthlike odor, obtained by the decomposition of styracin; -- properly called cinnamic, or styryl, alcohol.
The opinions and maxims of the Stoics.

Elevated as if on stilts; hence, pompous; bombastic; as, a stilted style; stilted declamation. Stilted arch (Arch.), an arch in which the springing line is some distance above the impost, the space between being occupied by a vertical member, molded or ornamen

A pole, or piece of wood, constructed with a step or loop to raise the foot above the ground in walking. It is sometimes lashed to the leg, and sometimes prolonged upward so as to be steadied by the hand or arm.
Antimony hydride, or hydrogen antimonide, a colorless gas produced by the action of nascent hydrogen on antimony. It has a characteristic odor and burns with a characteristic greenish flame.
Any species of bat belonging to the genus Stenoderma, native of the West Indies and South America. These bats have a short or rudimentary tail and a peculiarly shaped nose membrane.
A rate of motion through the water sufficient to render a vessel governable by the helm.
Any one of a group of fishes having the dorsal and anal fins partially covered with scales.
Having the color spots, or structural parts, arranged spirally.
A bit of wood split off; a splinter. [Obs.
An umbelliferous herb (Meum Athamanticum) having finely divided leaves, common in Europe; -- called also baldmoney, mew, and bearwort. [Written also spignel.]
An American shrub (Lindera Benzoin), the bark of which has a spicy taste and odor; -- called also Benjamin, wild allspice, and fever bush.
A kind of dolphin (Platanista Gangeticus) native of the river Ganges; the Gangetic dolphin. It has a long, slender, somewhat spatulate beak.

A poisonous alkaloid glucoside extracted from the berries of common nightshade (Solanum nigrum), and of bittersweet, and from potato sprouts, as a white crystalline substance having an acrid, burning taste; -- called also solonia, and solanina.

A slight frame of wood three or four feet long and about one third as wide, with thongs or cords stretched across it, and having a support and holder for the foot; -- used by persons for walking on soft snow.
A European herbaceous plant (Achillea Ptarmica) allied to the yarrow, having a strong, pungent smell.
A burrowing rodent (Spalax typhlus), native of Russia and Asia Minor. It has the general appearance of a mole, and is destitute of eyes.
An alkaloid occuring in the seeds of mustard. It is extracted, in combination with sulphocyanic acid, as a white crystalline substance, having a hot, bitter taste.
A gibbon (Hylobates syndactylus), native of Sumatra. It has the second and third toes partially united by a web.
The refuse of cattle taken from a drove. [Prov.
Any one of several species of small wrenlike Asiatic birds having short wings and a short tail. They belong to Brachypterix, Callene, and allied genera.
A scarecrow, generally made of feathers tied to a string, hung up to prevent deer from breaking into a place. Halliwell.
An oxide containing three atoms of oxygen with two atoms (or radicals) of some other substance; thus, alumina, Al2O3 is a sesquioxide.
An African wild cat (Felis serval) of moderate size. It has rather long legs and a tail of moderate length.
Any species of Sertularia, or of Sertularidæ, a family of hydroids having branched chitinous stems and simple sessile hydrothecæ. Also used adjectively.

Any one of many species of venomous aquatic snakes of the family Hydrophidæ, having a flattened tail and living entirely in the sea, especially in the warmer parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. They feed upon fishes, and are mostly of moderate size, but so
A kind of seaweed (Chorda Filum) having blackish cordlike fronds, often many feet long.
Any one of numerous species of small owls of the genus Scops having ear tufts like those of the horned owls, especially the European scops owl (Scops giu), and the American screech owl. (S.
Any one of numerous species of marine annelids of the family Polynoidæ, and allies, which have two rows of scales, or elytra, along the back. See Illust.
In the quaternion analysis, a quantity that has magnitude, but not direction; -- distinguished from a vector, which has both magnitude and direction.
Any one of several species of elasmobranch fishes of the genus Pristis. They have a sharklike form, but are more nearly allied to the rays.
A slender marine fish (Scombresox saurus) of Europe and America. It has long, thin, beaklike jaws.
The Indian antelope (Antilope bezoartica, or cervicapra), noted for its beauty and swiftness. It has long, spiral, divergent horns.
Any one of several species of brilliant South American humming birds of the genus Sappho, having very bright-colored and deeply forked tails; -- called also firetail.
An East Indian deer (Rusa Aristotelis) having a mane on its neck. Its antlers have but three prongs.
The act of saving a vessel, goods, or life, goods, or life, from perils of the sea. Salvage of life from a british ship, or a foreign ship in British waters, ranks before salvage of goods.
Waste or rejected matter; anything worthless; valueless stuff; trash; especially, fragments of building materials or fallen buildings; ruins; débris. What rubbish and what offal!
A round of business, amusement, or pleasure, daily or frequently pursued; especially, a course of business or offical duties regularly or frequently returning.
A very large North Atlantic whalebone whale (Physalus antiquorum, or Balænoptera physalus). It has a dorsal fin, and strong longitudinal folds on the throat and belly.
A handsaw with coarse teeth which have but a slight set, used for cutting wood in the direction of the fiber; -- called also ripping saw.
A favorite Italian public entertainment, consisting of music and dancing, -- held generally on fast eves. Brande & C.
An instrument, acting on the principle of Pitot's tube, for measuring the velocity of a fluid current, the speed of a ship, etc.
A muscle which serves to retain an organ or part in place, esp. when retracted.
The act or process of relaxing, or the state of being relaxed; as, relaxation of the muscles; relaxation of a law.
The building and apparatus for refining or purifying, esp. metals and sugar.
(a) A common Old World limicoline bird (Totanus calidris), having the legs and feet pale red. The spotted redshank (T.

The quality or state of being rational; agreement with reason; possession of reason; due exercise of reason; reasonableness. When God has made rationality the common portion of mankind, how came it to be thy inclosure Gov.
Any one of several species of humming birds of the genus Steganura, having two of the tail feathers very long and racket- shaped.
A scraping tool for smoothing metal.

A release or relinquishment of a claim; a deed of release; an instrument by which some right, title, interest, or claim, which one person has, or is supposed to have, in or to an estate held by himself or another, is released or relinquished, the grantor gener
A white crystalline substance, C6H7(OH)5, found in acorns, the fruit of the oak (Quercus). It has a sweet taste, and is regarded as a pentacid alcohol.
A very small deer (Pudua humilis), native of the Chilian Andes. It has simple spikelike antlers, only two or three inches long.
The primary growth from the spore of a moss, usually consisting of branching confervoid filaments, on any part of which stem and leaf buds may be developed.
A summary, plan, or scheme of something proposed, affording a prospect of its nature; especially, an exposition of the scheme of an unpublished literary work.

Any one of several species of very brilliant birds belonging to Promerops, Epimarchus, and allied genera, closely related to the paradise birds, and mostly native of New Guinea. They have a long curved beak and a long graduated tail.
The act or art of foretelling the course and termination of a disease; also, the outlook afforded by this act of judgment; as, the prognosis of hydrophobia is bad.
Any one of numerous species of large shrimplike Crustacea having slender legs and long antennæ. They mostly belong to the genera Pandalus, Palæmon, Palæmonetes, and Peneus, and are much used as food.
Any bird of the Old World genus Glareola, or family Glareolidæ, allied to the plovers. They have long, pointed wings and a forked tail.
Paving or flooring made of small squares or lozenges set diagonally. [Formerly written pointal.]

A unit of force based upon the pound, foot, and second, being the force which, acting on a pound avoirdupois for one second, causes it to acquire by the of that time a velocity of one foot per second. It is about equal to the weight of half an ounce, and is 13
A river tortoise; one of a group of tortoises (Potamites, or Trionychoidea) having a soft shell, webbed feet, and a sharp beak. See Trionyx.
Any one of numerous species of tropical food fishes of the family Polynemidæ. They have several slender filaments, often very long, below the pectoral fin.
One of the two principal groups of Chætopoda. It includes those that have prominent parapodia and fascicles of setæ.
