A Linnæan class of monoclinous or hermaphrodite plants, having many stamens, or any number above twenty, inserted in the receptacle.
A small-leaved North American tree (Planera aquatica) related to the elm, but having a wingless, nutlike fruit.
The act or practice of plagiarizing.
An instrument having two handles and two grasping jaws working on a pivot; -- used for griping things to be held fast, drawing nails, etc.
A wheel, usually with radial handles projecting from the rim, for traversing the saddle of a machine tool, esp. an automatic machine tool, by hand.
A horseman armed with a lance, who in a bullfight receives the first attack of the bull, and excites him by picking him without attempting to kill him.
Any siphonophore which has an air sac for a float, as the Physalia.
Any bat of the genus Phyllostoma, or allied genera, having large membranes around the mouth and nose; a nose-leaf bat.
A yellow crystalline substance, having a geraniumlike odor, regarded as a complex derivative of acetone, and obtained from certain camphor compounds.
A compact, feldspathic, igneous rock containing nephelite, haüynite, etc. Thin slabs give a ringing sound when struck; -- called also clinkstone.
A loose under-garment worn by women, and covering the body below the waist. Petticoat government, government by women, whether in politics or domestic affairs.

An American tree (Diospyros Virginiana) and its fruit, found from New York southward. The fruit is like a plum in appearance, but is very harsh and astringent until it has been exposed to frost, when it becomes palatable and nutritious.
A Linnæan order of plants, having five styles or pistils.
A European titmouse (Parus, or Ægithalus, pendulinus). It is noted for its elegant pendulous purselike nest, made of the down of willow trees and lined with feathers.

A white amorphous or granular substance which consists principally of potassium carbonate, and has a strong alkaline reaction. It is obtained by lixiviating wood ashes, and evaporating the lye, and has been an important source of potassium compounds.
One of a peculiar kind of spines covering the surface of certain starfishes. They are pillarlike, with a flattened summit which is covered with minute spinules or granules.
A kind of pseudomorph, in which there has been a change of physical characters without alteration of chemical composition, as the change of aragonite to calcite.
A treatise which comprehends the whole of any science. [Thou] a pandect mak'st, and universal book.

Any one of numerous species of freshwater pectinibranchiate mollusks, belonging to Paludina, Melantho, and allied genera. They have an operculated shell which is usually green, often with brown bands.
One of a group of aquatic beetles (Palpicornia) having short club-shaped antennæ, and long maxillary palpi.
A large South African antelope (Æpyceros melampus). The male has long lyrate and annulated horns.
An instrument for obtaining directly, without calculation, the true bearing of the sun, and thence the variation of the compass

A small South American rodent (Cologenys paca), having blackish brown fur, with four parallel rows of white spots along its sides; the spotted cavy. It is nearly allied to the agouti and the Guinea pig.
An acid containing oxygen, as chloric acid or sulphuric acid; - - contrasted with the hydracids, which contain no oxygen, as hydrochloric acid. See Acid, and Hydroxy-.
A prefix, also used adjectively, designating: (a) A compound containing oxygen. (b) A compound containing the hydroxyl group, more properly designated by hydroxy-.
One of a series of bases containing the amido and the isonitroso groups united to the same carbon atom.

The male of bovine quadrupeds, especially the domestic animal when castrated and grown to its full size, or nearly so. The word is also applied, as a general name, to any species of bovine animals, male and female.
To do too much; to exceed what is proper or true in doing; to exaggerate; to carry too far. Anything so overdone is from the purpose of playing.
A bursting forth; eruption; insurrection. "Mobs and outbreaks." J.
Singing birds; a group of the Passeres, having numerous syringeal muscles, conferring musical ability.
A back chamber; especially, that part of the naos, or cella, farthest from the main entrance, sometimes having an entrance of its own, and often used as a treasury.

An instrument, consisting of a tube having one end open and the other end covered with a thin flexible membrance to the center of which is attached a small mirror. It is used for exhibiting upon a screen, by means of rays reflected from the mirror, the vibrato
A white crystalline substance, obtained from an exudation from the olive, and having a bitter-sweet taste and acid proporties. [Written also olivile.] Gregory.
An instrument for indicating directly resistance in ohms.
A Linnæan class of plants, in which the flowers have eight stamens not united to one another or to the pistil.

The condition of being oblique; deviation from a right line; deviation from parallelism or perpendicularity; the amount of such deviation; divergence; as, the obliquity of the ecliptic to the equator.
Any one of several species of bombycid moths belonging to Notodonta, Nerice, and allied genera. The caterpillar of these moths has a hump, or spine, on its back.
Any one of a series of nitro derivatives of phenol. They are yellow oily or crystalline substances and have well-defined acid properties, as picric acid.
A genus of parrots with gray heads. of New Zeland and papua, allied to the cockatoos.
The tongue or pole of a cart or other vehicle drawn by two animals. [U.S.]
A European perennial succulent herb (Cotyledon umbilicus), having round, peltate leaves with a central depression; -- also called pennywort, and kidneywort.
A wild sheep (Ovis musimon), inhabiting the mountains of Sardinia, Corsica, etc. Its horns are very large, with a triangular base and rounded angles.

That branch of biology which deals with the structure of animals and plants, treating of the forms of organs and describing their varieties, homologies, and metamorphoses. See Tectology, and Promorphology.
The light of the moon.
A frequent recurrence of the same tone or sound, producing a dull uniformity; absence of variety, as in speaking or singing.
A Linnæan order of plants, including those which have only one style or stigma.
A West African gazelle (Gazella mohr), having horns on which are eleven or twelve very prominent rings. It is one of the species which produce bezoar.
An Asiatic bird (Gracula musica), allied to the starlings. It is black, with a white spot on the wings, and a pair of flat yellow wattles on the head.
A plant (Reseda odorata) having greenish flowers with orange- colored stamens, and exhaling a delicious fragrance. In Africa it is a low shrub, but further north it is usually an annual herb.
An instrument for measuring conductivity.

The mesial plane dividing the body of an animal into similar right and left halves. The line in which it meets the dorsal surface has been called the dorsimeson, and the corresponding ventral edge the ventrimeson.
An ovum, as that of a mammal, only partially composed of germinal matter, that is, consisting of both a germinal portion and an albuminous or nutritive one; -- opposed to holoblast.
A colorless liquid hydrocarbon resembling oil of turpentine, obtained by dehydrating menthol. It has an agreeable odor and a cooling taste.
A yellow powder, C6H3N9, obtained from certain sulphocyanates. It has acid properties and forms compounds called mellonides.
One of a group of univalve shells, having a large aperture or mouth.
A larva, in a stage following the zoëa, in the development of most crabs. In this stage the legs and abdominal appendages have appeared, the abdomen is relatively long, and the eyes are large.

The act of mediating; action or relation of anything interposed; action as a necessary condition, means, or instrument; interposition; intervention. The soul [acts] by the mediation of these passions.
One of the mouth appendages of Crustacea, situated next behind the maxillæ. Crabs have three pairs, but many of the lower Crustacea have but one pair of them.
The condition of a martyr; the death of a martyr; the suffering of death on account of adherence to the Christian faith, or to any cause. Bacon.
A wild cat (Felis manul), having long, soft, light-colored fur. It is found in the mountains of Central Asia, and dwells among rocks.
Of or pertaining to the hand; done or made by the hand; as, manual labor; the king's sign manual. "Manual and ocular examination." Tatham.
An indefinite feeling of uneasiness, or of being sick or ill at ease.
One of a tribe of beetles (Malacodermata), with a soft and flexible body, as the fireflies.
A man who has authority to act, within certain limits, as master of the house; a steward; also, a chief minister or officer.
The act or process of macerating.

A European fish (Peristethus cataphractum), having the body covered with bony plates, and having three spines projecting in front of the nose; -- called also noble, pluck, pogge, sea poacher, and armed bullhead.
Any one of two or three species of Australian birds of the genus Menura. The male is remarkable for having the sixteen tail feathers very long and, when spread, arranged in the form of a lyre.
Any fish belonging to the Dipnoi; -- so called because they have both lungs and gills.
A large tree (Celtis australis), found in the south of Europe. It has a hard wood, and bears a cherrylike fruit.
A quaternary deposit, usually consisting of a fine yellowish earth, on the banks of the Rhine and other large rivers.
A poisonous narcotic alkaloid extracted from the leaves of Indian tobacco (Lobelia inflata) as a yellow oil, having a tobaccolike taste and odor.
A tract of ground laid out for the game of golf; a golfing green.
An Australian myrtaceous tree (Eugenia Smithii), having smooth ovate leaves, and panicles of small white flowers. The wood is hard and fine-grained.
A bitter principle found in the bark of the privet (Ligustrum vulgare), and extracted as a white crystalline substance with a warm, bitter taste; -- called also ligustron.
The lungs of an animal or bird; -- sometimes coarsely applied to the lungs of a human being.

The action of a lever; mechanical advantage gained by the lever. Leverage of a couple (Mech.), the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of two forces which act in parallel and opposite directions.
A device for letting off, releasing, or giving forth, as the warp from the cylinder of a loom.
A West African antelope (Damalis Senegalensis), allied to the sassaby. It is reddish gray, with a black face, and a black stripe on the outside of the legs above the knees.
A large South African antelope (Strepsiceros kudu). The males have graceful spiral horns, sometimes four feet long.
Any pheasant of the genus Pucrasia. The birds of this genus inhabit India and China, and are distinguished by having a long central and two lateral crests on the head.
A nocturnal carnivorous mammal (Cercoleptes caudivolvulus) of South America, about as large as a full-grown cat. It has a prehensile tail and lives in trees.
A black, two-horned, African rhinoceros (Atelodus keitloa). It has the posterior horn about as long as the anterior one, or even longer.
a New Zealand tree, the Cypress cedar (Libocedrus Doniana), having a valuable, fine-grained, reddish wood.
The last and worst of the four ages of the world; -- considered to have begun B. C.
A South American striped frog (Pseudis paradoxa), remarkable for having a tadpole larger than the adult, and hence called also paradoxical frog.
A great Brazilian palm (Maximiliana regia), having immense spathes which are used for baskets and tubs.

A large, handsome, North American woodpecker (Campephilus principalis), having a large, sharp, ivory-colored beak. Its general color is glossy black, with white secondaries, and a white dorsal stripe.

The state, quality, or relation, of two or more isomeric substances. Physical isomerism (Chem.), the condition or relation of certain (metameric) substances, which, while chemically identical (in that they have the same composition, the same molecular weights,
One of a series of compounds containing iodine, and analogous to the chlorhydrins.
The introduction of a tube into an organ to keep it open, as into the larynx in croup.
The time during which a throne is vacant between the death or abdication of a sovereign and the accession of his successor.
The quality or condition of being unstable; want of stability, firmness, or steadiness; liability to give way or to fail; insecurity; precariousness; as, the instability of a building.
The act or process of insinuating; a creeping, winding, or flowing in. By a soft insinuation mix'd With earth's large mass.
The act or process of inflating, or the state of being inflated, as with air or gas; distention; expansion; enlargement. Boyle.

The act or process of increasing; growth in bulk, guantity, number, value, or amount; augmentation; enlargement. The seminary that furnisheth matter for the formation and increment of animal and vegetable bodies.
Any person who maliciously sets fire to a building or other valuable or other valuable property.
The condition of not having reached puberty, or the age of ability to reproduce one's species; want of age at which the marriage contract can be legally entered into.
Having no wings, as some insects.
A Linnæan class of plants, having twenty or more stamens inserted in the calyx.
A superabundance or congestion of blood in an organ or part of the body. Active hyperæmia, cognestion d%ue to increased flow of blood to a part.

A figure consisting of a transference of attributes from their proper subjects to other. Thus Virgil says, "dare classibus austros," to give the winds to the fleets, instead of dare classibus austris, to give the fleets to the winds.
A compound radical, or unsaturated group, HO, consisting of one atom of hydrogen and one of oxygen. It is a characteristic part of the hydrates, the alcohols, the oxygen acids, etc.
One of a series of artificial, organic bases, usually produced as thick viscous liquids by the action of ammonia on ethylene oxide. They have the properties both of alcohol and amines.
The offspring of the union of two distinct species; an animal or plant produced from the mixture of two species. See Mongrel.
A loud noise of many confused voices; a tumult; uproar. Milton.
A pipe with a long, flexible stem, so arranged that the smoke is cooled by being made to pass through water.

A curve described by the moving extremity of a line the other end of which is fixed, this line being constantly parallel to the direction of motion of, and having its length constantly proportional to the velocity of, a point moving in any path; -used in inves
A low bush (Viburnum lantanoides) having long, straggling branches and handsome flowers. It is found in the Northern United States.
One who has high and controlling authority in sacred things; the chief of a sacred order; as, princely hierarchs. Milton.
A white, crystalline substance having a sweetish taste, obtained by the decomposition of hesperidin, and regarded as a complex derivative of caffeic acid.
Any species of Old World geckoes of the genus Hemidactylus. The hemidactyls have dilated toes, with two rows of plates beneath.

An instrument consisting of a mirror moved by clockwork, by which a sunbeam is made apparently stationary, by being steadily directed to one spot during the whole of its diurnal period; also, a geodetic heliotrope.
That part of an elliptical or many-centered arch which has the shorter radius and immediately adjoins the impost.

An electro-negative element or radical, which, by combination with a metal, forms a haloid salt; especially, chlorine, bromine, and iodine; sometimes, also, fluorine and cyanogen. See Chlorine family, under Chlorine.
A dark brown powder containing iron, prepared by the action of zinc dust as a reducing agent upon the coloring matter of the blood, used medicinally as a hematinic.
A rope or hawser by which a vessel is towed or warped along; -- so called because it is necessary to guess at the length to be carried in the boat making the attachment to a distant object.

A cluster, usually nine in number, of small iron balls, put together by means of cast-iron circular plates at top and bottom, with two rings, and a central connecting rod, in order to be used as a charge for a cannon. Formerly grapeshot were inclosed in canvas
A whitish, granular rock, consisting of feldspar and quartz intimately mixed; -- sometimes called whitestone, and leptynite.

The science which treats of the principles of language; the study of forms of speech, and their relations to one another; the art concerned with the right use aud application of the rules of a language, in speaking or writing.
A mineral, consisting of the sulphates of soda and lime.
A trivial mechanism; a device; a toy; a pretty thing. Arbuthnot.
A South African antelope (Oryx Capensis), having long, sharp, nearly straight horns.
A large galley, having some features of the galleon, as broadside guns; esp., such a vessel used by the southern nations of Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries. See Galleon, and Galley.

A yellowish red, crystalline substance, C20H12O5, produced by heating together phthalic anhydride and resorcin; -- so called, from the very brilliant yellowish green fluorescence of its alkaline solutions. It has acid properties, and its salts of the alkalies
A light kind of food, formerly made of flour or meal; a sort of pap. Milk and flummery are very fit for children.
Any bird of the genus Phoenicopterus. The flamingoes have webbed feet, very long legs, and a beak bent down as if broken.
One of several species of pheasants of the genus Euplocamus, having the lower back a bright, fiery red. They inhabit Southern Asia and the East Indies.

Polished to the highest degree of excellence; complete; perfect; as, a finished poem; a finished education. Finished work (Mach.), work that is made smooth or polished, though not necessarily completed.
A perennial plant (Pyrethrum, or Chrysanthemum, Parthenium) allied to camomile, having finely divided leaves and white blossoms; -- so named from its supposed febrifugal qualities.
A measure of length, containing six feet; the space to which a man can extend his arms; -- used chiefly in measuring cables, cordage, and the depth of navigable water by soundings.

Any palm tree having fan-shaped or radiate leaves; as the Chamærops humilis of Southern Europe; the species of Sabal and Thrinax in the West Indies, Florida, etc.; and especially the great talipot tree (Corypha umbraculifera) of Ceylon and Malaya. The leaves o

The impure spirit which comes over first and last in the distillation of whisky; -- the former being called the strong faints, and the latter, which is much more abundant, the weak faints. This crude spirit is much impregnated with fusel oil.
A wild cat (Felis eyra) ranging from southern Brazil to Texas. It is reddish yellow and about the size of the domestic cat, but with a more slender body and shorter legs.
A yellow pigment imported from India and China. It has a strong odor, and is said to be obtained from the urine of herbivorous animals when fed on the mango.
A rock occurring in the Alps, consisting of saussurite and smaragdite; -- sometimes called gabbro.

A fixed point of time, established in history by the occurrence of some grand or remarkable event; a point of time marked by an event of great subsequent influence; as, the epoch of the creation; the birth of Christ was the epoch which gave rise to the Christi
A work in which the contents of a former work are reduced within a smaller space by curtailment and condensation; a brief summary; an abridgement. [An] epitome of the contents of a very large book.
The connective tissue framework and sheath of a nerve which bind together the nerve bundles, each of which has its own special sheath, or perineurium.
To invest or adorn with a robe; to attire.
One of several species of armadillos of the genera Dasypus and Euphractus, having five toes both on the fore and hind feet.
A solid, all plane sections of which are ellipses or circles. See Conoid, n., 2 (a).
Note: Milton, in the following lines, has applied the name to some twinning plant, perhaps the honeysuckle. Through the sweetbrier, or the vine, Or the twisted eglantine.
A cutaneous eruption, consisting of large, round pustules, upon an indurated and inflamed base. Dunglison.
An instrument for intensifying sounds produced by percussion of the thorax. Knight.
A cavity in a rock, having its interior surface studded with crystals and sometimes filled with water; a geode.
A Linnæan class of plants including all that have any number of stamens between twelve and nineteen.
A white, crystalline, aromatic hydrocarbon, C14H14, consisting of two radicals or residues of toluene.
In a dioecious manner. Dioeciously hermaphrodite (Bot.), having flowers structurally perfect, but practically dioecious, -- those on one plant producing no pollen, and those on another no ovules.
A projecting face like the triglyph, but having only two channels or grooves sunk in it.
A volatile, pungent, liquid hydrocarbon, C6H10, consisting of two allyl radicals, and belonging to the acetylene series.
That part of medicine which has to do with ascertaining the nature of diseases by means of their symptoms or signs. His rare skill in diagnostics.
A discharge or flowing of humors or fluid matter, as from the nose in catarrh; -- sometimes used synonymously with inflammation. Dunglison.
In a decursive manner. Decursively pinnate (Bot.), having the leaflets decurrent, or running along the petiole; -- said of a leaf.

A dark blue, edible berry with a white bloom, and its shrub (Gaylussacia frondosa) closely allied to the common huckleberry. The bush is also called blue tangle, and is found from New England to Kentucky, and southward.
The doctrine of the Cynics; the quality of being cynical; the mental state, opnions, or conduct, of a cynic; morose and contemptuous views and opinions.
One of the canine teeth; -- so called from having but one point or cusp on the crown. See Tooth.
An instrument for drawing curved lines.
A peculiar perforated organ of certain spiders (Ciniflonidæ), used for spinning a special kind of silk.
A wooden knife with a long thin blade, used in handling cream or ice cream.
A white, crystalline substance, C12H13NO3, obtained as a product of the decomposition of narcotine. It has weak basic properties, and is usually regarded as an alkaloid.
A garden plant (Chrysanthemum Balsamita) having a strong balsamic smell, and nearly allied to tansy. It is used as a pot herb and salad plant and in flavoring ale and beer.
A train of attendants; a procession.
A noncommissioned officer, next below a sergeant. In the United States army he is the lowest noncomissioned officer in a company of infantry.
An umbelliferous plant, the Coriandrum sativum, the fruit or seeds of which have a strong smell and a spicy taste, and in medicine are considered as stomachic and carminative.
A pulley for driving machines, etc., having two or more parts or steps of different diameters; a pulley having a conical shape.
An instrument for measuring shells, or the angle of their spire.
A plotting together; a confederacy in some evil design; a conspiracy. I know their complot is to have my life.
The act or process of making complete; the getting through to the end; as, the completion of an undertaking, an education, a service. The completion of some repairs.
A series or range of columns placed at regular intervals with all the adjuncts, as entablature, stylobate, roof, etc.
A powerful vegetable alkaloid, C17H19NO5, extracted from the Colchicum autumnale, or meadow saffron, as a white or yellowish amorphous powder, with a harsh, bitter taste; -- called also colchicia.
A utensil with a bottom perforated with little holes for straining liquids, mashed vegetable pulp, etc.; a strainer of wickerwork, perfprated metal, or the like.
The act or process of coercing.
A coarse, composite weed, having a rough or prickly fruit; one of several species of the genus Xanthium; -- called also clotbur.
The end of the vertebral column beyond the sacrum in man and tailless monkeys. It is composed of several vertebræ more or less consolidated.
A utensil to hold a chamber vessel, for the use of the sick and infirm. It is usually in the form of a box, with a seat and tight cover.
An instrument for measuring liquids. It consists of a piston moving in a tube in which is contained the liquid, the quantity expelled being indicated by the graduation upon the piston rod.
The name of a group of minerals, usually of a green color and micaceous to granular in structure. They are hydrous silicates of alumina, iron, and magnesia.
A machine for raising guns or mortar into their carriages.
A table stove or small furnace, usually a cylindrical box of sheet iron, with a grate at the bottem, and an open top.
An ecclesiastic who has a chapel, or who performs religious service in a chapel.

A lizardlike reptile of the genus Chamæleo, of several species, found in Africa, Asia, and Europe. The skin is covered with fine granmulations; the tail is prehensile, and the body is much compressed laterally, giving it a high back.
The act or operation of cutting, to relieve the structure in strangulated hernia. [Frequently written kelotomy.]
To operate on with a catheter. Dunglison.

A one-celled, dry, indehiscent fruit, with a thin membranous pericarp, adhering closely to the seed, so that fruit and seed are incorporated in one body, forming a single grain, as of wheat, barley, etc.

A beetle (Lytta, or Cantharis, vesicatoria), having an elongated cylindrical body of a brilliant green color, and a nauseous odor; the blister fly or blister beetle, of the apothecary; -- also called Spanish fly. Many other species of Lytta, used for the same
A highly stimulating volatile infammable oil, distilled from the leaves of an East Indian tree (Melaleuca cajuputi, etc.) It is greenish in color and has a camphoraceous odor and pungent taste.
A bag or sack with its contents; hence, a stock or store; an accumulation; as, a budget of inventions.

A colorless liquid, CHBr3, having an agreeable odor and sweetish taste. It is produced by the simultaneous action of bromine and caustic potash upon wood spirit, alcohol, or acetone, as also by certain other reactions.
A frame or fender of rope or junk, laid out at the sides or bows of a vessel to secure it from injury by floating ice.

A kind of mineral coal, or brown lignite, burning with a weak flame, and generally a disagreeable odor; -- found at Bovey Tracey, Devonshire, England. It is of geological age of the oölite, and not of the true coal era.
One who keeps accounts; one who has the charge of keeping the books and accounts in an office.
The name of a kind of in used in copperplate printing, prepared from the charred husks of the grape, and residue of the wine press.
A liquor, generally spirituous in which a bitter herb, leaf, or root is steeped.
A papilionaceous plant, the Ornithopus, having a curved, cylindrical pod tipped with a short, clawlike point. Bird's-foot trefoil.
An instrument for measuring depths, esp. one for taking soundings without a sounding line.
A smokeless powder containing equal parts of soluble nitrocellulose and nitroglycerin.
A turning from with dislike; aversion. [Obs.or Archaic] Some men have a natural aversation to some vices or virtues, and a natural affection to others.
An instrument for cleansing the ear, consisting of a small piece of sponge on an ivory or bone handle.
A circle of feathers surrounding the opening of the ear of birds.

Of or pertaining to Attica, in Greece, or to Athens, its principal city; marked by such qualities as were characteristic of the Athenians; classical; refined. Attic base (Arch.), a peculiar form of molded base for a column or pilaster, described by Vitruvius,
An apparatus for effecting atmolysis.
An African sheeplike quadruped (the Ammotragus tragelaphus) having a long mane on the breast and fore legs. It is, perhaps, the chamois of the Old Testament.
A moss or mosslike plant which cellular stems, having usually an upward growth and distinct leaves.
One of a group of perching birds, having the middle toe more or less united to the outer and inner ones.
Vascular tissue of plants, consisting of spiral vessels, dotted, barred, and pitted ducts, and laticiferous vessels.
A soft, pulsating, hollow tumor, containing blood, arising from the preternatural dilation or rupture of the coats of an artery. [Written also aneurysm.]

A resolution of anything, whether an object of the senses or of the intellect, into its constituent or original elements; an examination of the component parts of a subject, each separately, as the words which compose a sentence, the tones of a tune, or the si
A kind of annelid larva having both a dorsal and a ventral circle of special cilia.
The achromatic figure, formed in mitotic cell-division, consisting of two asters connected by a spindle-shaped bundle of rodlike fibers diverging from each aster, and called the spindle.

A unit equal to the product of one complete convolution (of a coiled conductor) into one ampère of current; thus, a conductor having five convolutions and carrying a current of half an ampère is said to have 2½ ampère turns. The magnetizing effect of a coil is

The reciprocal succession of things in time or place; the act of following and being followed by turns; alternate succession, performance, or occurrence; as, the alternation of day and night, cold and heat, summer and winter, hope and fear.
One of a series of compounds that may be regarded as ammonia in which a part of the hydrogen has been replaced by basic, and another part by acid, atoms or radicals.
The clearing off of debt or obligation; a release or discharge from debt or other liability.
A complex, hypothetical radical, composed of two parts of carbon to three of hydrogen and one of oxygen. Its hydroxide is acetic acid.
To pronounce with an accent or with accents.
The feeling of extreme disgust and hatred; abhorrence; detestation; loathing; as, he holds tobacco in abomination.
The act or process of rendering fertile.

(a) An obligation of record entered into before some court of record or magistrate duly authorized, with condition to do some particular act, as to appear at the same or some other court, to keep the peace, or pay a debt. A recognizance differs from a bond, be
Having no precedent or example; not preceded by a like case; not having the authority of prior example; novel; new; unexampled. -- Un*prec"e*dent*ed*ly, adv.
A member of a university or a college who has not taken his first degree; a student in any school who has not completed his course.
A mirror made of glass on which has been placed a backing of some reflecting substance, as quicksilver. There is none so homely but loves a looking-glass.
Having a large or generous heart or disposition; noble; liberal. -- Large"-heart`ed*ness, n.
A fossil bird, of the Jurassic period, remarkable for having a long tapering tail of many vertebræ with feathers along each side, and jaws armed with teeth, with other reptilian characteristics.
One who practices philanthropy; one who loves mankind, and seeks to promote the good of others.
To place; to set in a particular spot or position. The captives and emigrants whom he brought with him were located in the trans-Tiberine quarter.
Bad, evil, or pernicious, in the highest degree, whether in a physical or moral sense. See Worse.
One who wins, or gains by success in competition, contest, or gaming.
pl. of Viscus.

An outlying part of a city or town; a smaller place immediately adjacent to a city; in the plural, the region which is on the confines of any city or large town; as, a house stands in the suburbs; a garden situated in the suburbs of Paris. "In the suburbs of a
Thin dry scales or scabs upon the body; especially, thin scales exfoliated from the cuticle, particularly of the scalp; dandruff.
Superfluous matter separated from that which is useful; dross; scoria; as, the recrement of ore.
The act of navigating; the act of passing on water in ships or other vessels; the state of being navigable.
In a mutual manner.
Machines, in general, or collectively.
Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another; a bandage; a bond. Hawthorne.
One who, or that which, generates, begets, causes, or produces.
One who dances or who practices dancing. The merry dancers, beams of the northern lights when they rise and fall alternately without any considerable change of length.
One who creates, produces, or constitutes. Specifically, the Supreme Being.
Contention; dispute; debate; discussion; agitation of contrary opinions. This left no room for controversy about the title.
A hard or thickened spot or protuberance; a hardening and thickening of the skin or bark of a part, eps. as a result of continued pressure or friction.

One who builds; one whose occupation is to build, as a carpenter, a shipwright, or a mason. In the practice of civil architecture, the builder comes between the architect who designs the work and the artisans who execute it.

That which indicates or fixes a limit or extent, or marks a bound, as of a territory; a bounding or separating line; a real or imaginary limit. But still his native country lies Beyond the boundaries of the skies.
The act of attaining; the act of arriving at or reaching; hence, the act of obtaining by efforts. The attainment of every desired object.
One from whom a person is descended, whether on the father's or mother's side, at any distance of time; a progenitor; a fore father.
Having a flush deck, or with only a moderate depression amidships; -- said of a vessel.
The act of obliterating, or the state of being obliterated; extinction. Sir.
from Sleep. Sleeping car, a railway car or carrriage, arranged with apartments and berths for sleeping.
Consisting of amber; made of amber. "Amber bracelets." Shak.
A very short time; an instant; a moment; -- now used only in the phrase in a trice. "With a trice." Turbervile.

The act of one who trains; the act or process of exercising, disciplining, etc.; education. Fan training (Hort.), the operation of training fruit trees, grapevines, etc., so that the branches shall radiate from the stem like a fan.
To withdraw, or take away, as a part from the whole; to deduct; as, subtract 5 from 9, and the remainder is 4.
To escape. [Obs.
An imaginary being, male or female, like an elf or fairy, represented as a descendant of fallen angels, excluded from paradise till penance is accomplished. Moore.
To surround, inclose, or fortify, with palisades.

That which nourishes; anything which promotes growth and repairs the natural waste of animal or vegetable life; food; aliment. The stomach returns what it has received, in strength and nutriment diffused into all parts of the body.
A dunce; a dolt; a stupid fellow. [Colloq.] They have talked like numskulls.
A market. Where has commerce such a mart .
An eager desire; a craving; a morbid appetite; an earnest wish; an aspiration. Put on my crown; I have immortal longings in me.
A neck or narrow slip of land by which two continents are connected, or by which a peninsula is united to the mainland; as, the Isthmus of Panama; the Isthmus of Suez, etc. Isthmus of the fauces.

One who interviews; especially, one who obtains an interview with another for the purpose of eliciting his opinions or obtaining information for publication. It would have made him the prince of interviewers in these days.

Moisture; dampness; a moderate degree of wetness, which is perceptible to the eye or touch; -- used especially of the atmosphere, or of anything which has absorbed moisture from the atmosphere, as clothing.
A small ax with a short handle, to be used with one hand.
The quality or state of being harsh. O, she is Ten times more gentle than her father 's crabbed, And he's composed of harshness.
A mistress; a sweetheart. I must ever have some Dulcinea in my head.
To keep back or from; to withhold. Detain not the wages of the hireling.
To sail back and forth on the ocean; to sail, as for the potection of commerce, in search of an enemy, for plunder, or for pleasure.
A dunce; a stupid fellow.
A large vesicle or bulla, usually containing a serous fluid; a blister; a bubble, as in water, glass, etc. Arsenic abounds with air blebs.
To determine (something) beforehand. Sir M.
A complex hydrocarbon, C14H10, found in coal tar, and obtained as a white crystalline substance with a bluish fluorescence.
Thin-billed; -- applied to birds with a slender bill, as the humming birds.
Bound with stays. Let nature have scope to fashion the body as she thinks best; we have few well-shaped that are strait-laced.
To outweigh; to overpower by weight; to exceed in weight; to overbalance. An inconsiderable weight, by distance from the center of the balance, will preponderate greater magnitudes.
Applied to sexual zooids of hydroids, that have a saclike form and do not become free; -- opposed to phanerocodonic.
An aquatic American plant (Brasenia peltata) having floating oval leaves, and the covered with a clear jelly.
The state of containing vesicles, or the process by which vesicles are formed.
One of the special defensive zooids of certain hydroids. They have the form of long, slender tentacles, and bear lasso cells.
The process of branching, or the development or offshoots from a stem; also, the mode of their arrangement.

A perennial grass (Agropyrum repens) having long running rootstalks, by which it spreads rapidly and pertinaciously, and so becomes a troublesome weed. Also called couch grass, quick grass, quick grass, twitch grass.
One of a tribe of wading birds (Pressirostres) including those which have a compressed beak, as the plovers.
A Linnæan class of plants having stamens united in three or more bodies or bundles by the filaments.
The state of being pneumatic, or of having a cavity or cavities filled with air; as, the pneumaticity of the bones of birds.

A form of impulse turbine or water wheel, consisting of a row of double cup-shaped buckets arranged round the rim of a wheel and actuated by one or more jets of water playing into the cups at high velocity.
An instrument for showing visually the changes in a varying current; an oscillograph.
A dyestuff, resembling alizarin, obtained from naphthoquinone as a red crystalline substance with a bright green, metallic luster; -- called also naphthalizarin.
A herbaceous climbing vine (Boussingaultia baselloides) very popular in cultivation, having shining entire leaves and racemes of small fragrant white flowers.
The act or state of interfering; as, the stoppage of a machine by the interference of some of its parts; a meddlesome interference in the business of others.
The quality or condition of being imperfect; want of perfection; incompleteness; deficiency; fault or blemish. Sent to my account With all my imperfections on my head.

A peculiarity of physical or mental constitution or temperament; a characteristic belonging to, and distinguishing, an individual; characteristic susceptibility; idiocrasy; eccentricity. The individual mind .
One of the great division of fungi, containing those species which have naked spores borne on free or only fasciculate threads. M.
The warm-blooded vertebrates, comprising the mammals and birds; -- the antithesis to hematocrya.
A tool with a hardened steel point, formerly used instead of a diamond for cutting glass.
An instrument or apparatus for detecting the presence of electrical currents, especially such as are of feeble intensity.

One of a complex series of double cyanides of ferric iron and some other base. Potassium ferricyanide (Chem.), red prussiate of potash; a dark, red, crystalline salt, K6(CN)12Fe2, consisting of the double cyanide of potassium and ferric iron.
One of a breed of large-bodied domestic fowls, having five toes, or the hind toe double. There are several strains, as the white, gray, and silver-gray.
A colorless, volatile, alkaline liquid, NH(C2H5)2, having a strong fishy odor resembling that of herring or sardines. Cf.
The act or process of letting blood or bleeding, as by opening a vein or artery, or by cupping or leeches; -- esp. applied to venesection.
A metallic post attached to electrical apparatus for convenience in making connections.
A small kind of hound with a long body and short legs, used as an earth dog.
Brought forth, as an animal; brought into life; introduced by birth. No one could be born into slavery in Mexico.
A printing process depending on the effect of light on bichromatized gelatin. Paper coated with a mixture of the gelatin and a pigment is called carbon paper or carbon tissue.
Something put into a liquid or mass to make it thicker.
One who, or that which, singes. Specifically: (a) One employed to singe cloth.
The state or quality of being sacred or holy; holiness; saintliness; moral purity; godliness. To sanctity she made no pretense, and, indeed, narrowly escaped the imputation of irreligion.

One who, or that which, revolves; specifically, a firearm ( commonly a pistol) with several chambers or barrels so arranged as to revolve on an axis, and be discharged in succession by the same lock; a repeater.

The quality or state of being incongruous; want of congruity; unsuitableness; inconsistency; impropriety. The fathers make use of this acknowledgment of the incongruity of images to the Deity, from thence to prove the incongruity of the worship of them.
A close, dark prison, commondonjon or keep of a castle, these being used as prisons. Down with him even into the deep dungeon.
One who drives cattle or sheep to market; one who makes it his business to purchase cattle, and drive them to market. Why, that's spoken like an honest drover; so they sell bullocks.
An ordained minister; a man regularly authorized to peach the gospel, and administer its ordinances; in England usually restricted to a minister of the Established Church.

An officer in a king's or a nobleman's household, whose principal business it is to take charge of the liquors, plate, etc.; the head servant in a large house. The butler and the baker of the king of Egypt.
An attempt to assume or exhibit what is not natural or real; false display; artificial show. "An affectation of contempt." Macaulay.
a. & n.
p. p.

To be like something else in the dimensions and arrangement of its parts; -- followed by with or to; as, concurring figures correspond with each other throughout. None of them [the forms of Sidney's sonnets] correspond to the Shakespearean type.
To convert into, or cause to resemble, glass or a glassy substance, by heat and fusion.
To loose from tangles or intricacy; to disentangle; to resolve; as, to untangle thread. Untangle but this cruel chain.
To free from a leash, or as from a leash; to let go; to release; as, to unleash dogs.
To drive from a kennel or hole; as, to unkennel a fox.
To loose from fetters or from restraint; to unchain; to unshackle; to liberate; as, to unfetter the mind.
To cause to be no longer deceived; to free from deception, fraud, fallacy, or mistake. South.
To draw the cork from; as, to uncork a bottle.
To free from tension; to relax; to loose; as, to unbrace a drum; to unbrace the nerves. Spenser.
To remove a bar or bars from; to unbolt; to open; as, to unbar a gate. Heber.
To remove, and plant in another place; as, to transplant trees. Dryden.
To carry or bear; as, to tote a child over a stream; -- a colloquial word of the Southern States, and used esp. by negroes.
To pass through in the manner of a thread or a needle; to make or find a course through; to thread. Some thrid the mazy ringlets of her hair.
To overload; to overburden; to overmatch; to overcharge; as, to surcharge a beast or a ship; to surcharge a cannon. Four charged two, and two surcharged one.
To give suck to; to nurse at the breast. Addison.
To make foolish; to make a fool of; as, to stultify one by imposition; to stultify one's self by silly reasoning or conduct. Burke.
To eject from the stomach; to vomit.
To splash or wet carelessly; as, to sozzle the feet in water. [Local, U.S.] Bartlett.
To cut or divide into long, thin pieces, or into very small pieces; to cut or rend lengthwise; to slit; as, to sliver wood. Shak.
To put into a sheath, case, or scabbard; to inclose or cover with, or as with, a sheath or case. The leopard .
To convert from regular or monastic into secular; as, to secularize a priest or a monk.
To frighten; to strike with sudden fear; to alarm. The noise of thy crossbow Will scare the herd, and so my shoot is lost.
To hew coarsely, without smoothing; as, to roughhew timber.
To make rough.
To cede or grant back; as, to retrocede a territory to a former proprietor.
To touch again, or rework, in order to improve; to revise; as, to retouch a picture or an essay.
To restore to use as money; as, to remonetize silver.
To consider again; as, to reconsider a subject.
To deprive feloniously of the tools used in one's employment (as by breaking or stealing them), for the purpose of annoying; as, to ratten a mechanic who works during a strike. [Trades-union Cant] J.
To take or carry away for one's self; hence, to steal; to take by theft; to filch. Had from his wakeful custody purloined The guarded gold.
To preoccupy, as ground or land; to take previous possession of. Dryden.
To date after the real time; as, to postdate a contract, that is, to date it later than the time when it was in fact made.
To post placards upon or within; as, to placard a wall, to placard the city.
To reduce to pauperism; as, to pauperize the peasantry.
To sleep beyond; as, to oversleep one's self or one's usual hour of rising.
To bite by little at a time; to seize gently with the mouth; to eat slowly or in small bits. Thy turfy mountains, where live nibbling sheep.
To spend amiss or for wrong purposes; to aquander; to waste; as, to misspend time or money. J.
To employ amiss; as, to misemploy time, advantages, talents, etc. Their frugal father's gains they misemploy.
To make lean; to cause to waste away. [Obs.
To utter or do a second time or many times; to repeat; as, to iterate advice. Nor Eve to iterate Her former trespass feared.
To cover by wrapping; to involve; to infold; as, to inwrap in a cloak, in smoke, etc.
To impede by a hopple; to tie the feet of (a horse or a cow) loosely together; to hamper; to hobble; as, to hopple an unruly or straying horse.
To render obtuse; to dull; to blunt; to stupefy; as, to hebetate the intellectual faculties. Southey
To divide into two equal parts; as, to halve an apple; to be or form half of. So far apart their lives are thrown From the twin soul that halves their own.
To contradict; to deny; to controvert; to dispute; to forbid. I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.
To carry or transport over a river, strait, or other narrow water, in a boat.
To fit; to suit; to agree. They shall be made, spite of antipathy, to fadge together.
To make eternal or endless. This other [gift] served but to eternize woe.
To cause to burst forth; to eject; as, to erupt lava. Huxley.
To write or print on the face of (a draft, bill, etc.); as, to enface drafts with memoranda.
To take into, or place in, the bosom; to cherish; to foster. Glad to embosom his affection.
To issue forth from a source; to flow out from more or less constantly; as, fragrance emanates from flowers.
To lengthen; to extend; to stretch; as, to elongate a line.
To bring to pass; to effect; to achieve; to accomplish; to fulfill. A fit instrument to effectuate his desire.

To refuse strongly and solemnly to own or acknowledge; to deny responsibility for, approbation of, an the like; to disclaim; to disown; as, he was charged with embezzlement, but he disavows the crime. A solemn promise made and disavowed.
To impair the strength of; to weaken; to enfeeble; as, to debilitate the body by intemperance. Various ails debilitate the mind.
To cheat, trick, defraud; -- followed by of, or out of; as, to chouse one out of his money. [Colloq.] The undertaker of the afore-cited poesy hath choused your highness.
To make the noise of, or one like that of, a sheep; to cry like a sheep or calf. Then suddenly was heard along the main, To low the ox, to bleat the woolly train.

To put in a black list as deserving of suspicion, censure, or punishment; esp. to put in a list of persons stigmatized as insolvent or untrustworthy, -- as tradesmen and employers do for mutual protection; as, to blacklist a workman who has been discharged.
To alien or alienate; to transfer, as title or property; as, to aliene an estate.

To instigate or encourage by aid or countenance; -- used in a bad sense of persons and acts; as, to abet an ill-doer; to abet one in his wicked courses; to abet vice; to abet an insurrection. "The whole tribe abets the villany." South.
To go before in order of time; to occur first with relation to anything. "Harm precedes not sin." Milton.
To state wrongly; as, to misstate a question in debate. Bp.
To form into a whole by uniting its parts; to frame; to construct; to build; as, to fabricate a bridge or ship.
Varying in from, character, or the like; variable; different; diverse.
OF or pertaining to rotary motion; having power to draw out or turn round. "By art trochilic." Camden.
Having power to awaken or excite; exciting. I begin to feel Some rousing motions in me.
Made of earth; made of burnt or baked clay, or other like substances; as, an earthen vessel or pipe.

Attentive to examine probable effects and consequences of acts with a view to avoid danger or misfortune; prudent; circumspect; wary; watchful; as, a cautious general. Cautious feeling for another's pain.
A small three-masted vessel, with projecting bow stern and convex decks, used in the Mediterranean for transporting merchandise, etc. It carries large square sails, or both.

An ancient expression of good wishes on a festive occasion, especially in drinking to some one. Geoffrey of Monmouth relates, on the authority of Walter Calenius, that this lady [Rowena], the daughter of Hengist, knelt down on the approach of the king, and, pr
A mountain or hill, usually more or less conical in form, from which lava, cinders, steam, sulphur gases, and the like, are ejected; -- often popularly called a burning mountain.
A word; a term; a name; specifically, a word considered as composed of certain sounds or letters, without regard to its meaning. Swamped near to drowning in a tide of ingenious vocables.
To color with vermilion, or as if with vermilion; to dye red; to cover with a delicate red.
A small sack or case, usually of leather, but sometimes of other material, for containing the clothes, toilet articles, etc., of a traveler; a traveling bag; a portmanteau.
A person who has charge of the keys of a prison, for opening and fastening the doors; a warder.
A plant (Sarracenia flava) with long, hollow leaves.
A line of fortifications, usually rough, constructed to prevent the passage of an enemy across a region. [Sp.
A mill worked by persons treading upon steps on the periphery of a wide wheel having a horizontal axis. It is used principally as a means of prison discipline.
Ornamental work with rambled lines. Especially: -- (a) The decorative head of a Gothic window.

Any one of numerous species of batrachians belonging to the genus Bufo and allied genera, especially those of the family Bufonidæ. Toads are generally terrestrial in their habits except during the breeding season, when they seek the water.
To render theological; to apply to divinity; to reduce to a system of theology. School divinity was but Aristotle's philosophy theologized.
From that time; thereafter. If the salt have lost his savor, wherewith shall it be salted it is thenceforth good for nothing.
An optical instrument or toy for showing the presistence of an impression upon the eyes after the luminous object is withdrawn.
Etym: [F. terrier, chien terrier, from terre the earth, L.
An ornamental stand, usually with three legs, having caddies for holding tea.
Combined action; especially (Med.),

To have a resemblance of qualities or properties; to correspond; to harmonize. The pleasing of color symbolizeth with the pleasing of any single tone to the ear; but the pleasing of order doth symbolize with harmony.
An instrument to show the time of day by means of the shadow of a gnomon, or style, on a plate. Sundial shell (Zoöl.), any shell of the genus Solarium.
One who is employed to tend a furnace and supply it with fuel, especially the furnace of a locomotive or of a marine steam boiler; also, a machine for feeding fuel to a fire.
To contend for superiority in an unseemly maner; to scuffle; to struggle; to wrangle; to quarrel.
The sudden issuing of a body of troops, usually small, from a besieged place to attack or harass the besiegers; a sally.
To strive or struggle with a close grapple; to wrestle in a rough fashion.
The case in which the blade of a sword, dagger, etc., is kept; a sheath. Nor in thy scabbard sheathe that famous blade.
Cabbage cut fine and allowed to ferment in a brine made of its own juice with salt, -- a German dish.
A species of red earth colored by iron sesquioxide; red ocher.

The talk of a ribald; low, vulgar language; indecency; obscenity; lewdness; -- now chiefly applied to indecent language, but formerly, as by Chaucer, also to indecent acts or conduct. The ribaldry of his conversation moved Macaulay.
To swallow up. Now lifted by the tide, and now resorbed.
A substance capable of producing with another a reaction, especially when employed to detect the presence of other bodies; a test.
A quadrangle; hence, a prison. [Cant or Slang]
The act of going before, or forward. Lunisolar precession.
An instrument consisting essentially of a polarizer and an analyzer, used for polarizing light, and analyzing its properties.
To make plural by using the plural termination; to attribute plurality to; to express in the plural form.
A piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water. I'll sink him deeper than e'er plummet sounded.
An instrument for measuring angles for determining elevations, distances, etc.
To bear down with a brazen face; to surpass in impudence. T.

A variety of brass made to resemble gold by the use of less zinc and more copper in its composition than ordinary brass contains. Its golden color is often heightened by means of lacquer of some sort, or by use of acids.

A sheet of paper printed and distributed, at stated intervals, for conveying intelligence of passing events, advocating opinions, etc.; a public print that circulates news, advertisements, proceedings of legislative bodies, public announcements, etc.

A new convert or proselyte; -- a name given by the early Christians, and still given by the Roman Catholics, to such as have recently embraced the Christian faith, and been admitted to baptism, esp. to converts from heathenism or Judaism.
Like a medusa; having the fundamental structure of a medusa, but without a locomotive disk; -- said of the sessile gonophores of hydroids. -- n.
The top or head of a mast; the part of a mast above the hounds.
One of a class of sages, or "adepts," reputed to have knowledge and powers of a higher order than those of ordinary men. -- Ma*hat"ma*ism (#), n.
Any species of the genus Scomber, and of several related genera. They are finely formed and very active oceanic fishes.
A money of account in China equal to one tenth of a tael; also, a weight of 57.98 grains. S.
A kitten. Kit fox (Zoöl.), a small burrowing fox (Vulpes velox), inhabiting the region of the Rocky Mountains.
To pierce with a pale; to put to death by fixing on a sharp stake. See Empale.

A court formerly held in several cities of England; specif., a court held in London, before the lord mayor, recorder, and sheriffs, to determine certain classes of suits for the recovery of lands within the city. In the progress of law reform this court has be
To search for plants, or new species of plants, with a view to classifying them. He herborized as he traveled.
A telescope or instrument for viewing the sun without injury to the eyes, as through colored glasses, or with mirrors which reflect but a small portion of light. -- He`li*o*scop`ic, a.
A piece of armor to protect the heels. Chesterfield.
To convert into the Hebrew idiom; to make Hebrew or Hebraistic. J.
To divide (a State) into districts for the choice of representatives, in an unnatural and unfair way, with a view to give a political party an advantage over its opponent. [Political Cant, U.
An instrument for viewing or examining the interior of the stomach.
A highly volatile mixture of fluid hydrocarbons, obtained from petroleum, as also by the distillation of bituminous coal. It is used in making air gas, and in giving illuminating power to water gas.
One who seizes a person by the throat from behind, with a view to strangle and rob him.

One of an ancient and secret association or fraternity, said to have been at first composed of masons or builders in stone, but now consisting of persons who are united for social enjoyment and mutual assistance.
To have previous knowledge of; to know beforehand. Who would the miseries of man foreknow Dryden.
Note: Sometimes called, in New England, old tore. In Scotland, fog is a general name for moss.

A fish which is able to leap from the water, and fly a considerable distance by means of its large and long pectoral fins. These fishes belong to several species of the genus Exocoetus, and are found in the warmer parts of all the oceans.
A little of pigs. Shak.

An efflorescence or discoloration of the skin; an eruption or breaking out, as in measles, smallpox, scarlatina, and the like diseases; -- sometimes limited to eruptions attended with fever. Dunglison.
A medicine designed to be snuffed up the nose, to promote discharges of mucus; a sternutatory. Coxe.
An instrument for measuring the diameters of minute particles or fibers, from the size of the colored rings produced by the diffraction of the light in which the objects are viewed.
An endemic disease. Fear, which is an endemic latent in every human heart, sometimes rises into an epidemic.
To bind with a chain; to hold in chains.
To arrange in order of battle; to array for battle; also, to prepare or arm for battle; to equip as for battle. One in bright arms embattled full strong.
The reflux of tide water; the retiring tide; -- opposed to flood tide.

An instrument for measuring the quantity of dew on the surface of a body in the open air. It consists of a balance, having a plate at one end to receive the dew, and at the other a weight protected from the deposit of dew.
A silver coin among the ancient Greeks, having a different value in different States and at different periods. The average value of the Attic drachma is computed to have been about 19 cents.

A sum of money to be divided and distributed; the share of a sum divided that falls to each individual; a distribute sum, share, or percentage; -- applied to the profits as appropriated among shareholders, and to assets as apportioned among creditors; as, the
Aversion of the taste; dislike, as of food or drink; disrelish. Bacon.

Not to obey; to neglect or refuse to obey (a superior or his commands, the laws, etc.); to transgress the commands of (one in authority); to violate, as an order; as, refractory children disobey their parents; men disobey their Maker and the laws. Not to disob
A piece of music of a mournful character, to accompany funeral rites; a funeral hymn. The raven croaked, and hollow shrieks of owls Sung dirges at her funeral.
Bodily condition or constitution, esp. a morbid habit which predisposes to a particular disease, or class of diseases.
To explode, or cause to explode; to burn with an explosion; to detonate.
To flow; to have origin; to descend; to proceed; to be deduced. Shak.
A leader of the rabble; one who attempts to control the multitude by specious or deceitful arts; an unprincipled and factious mob orator or political leader.
To cut off; to take away or deduct a part of; -- used chiefly of money, accounts, rents, income, etc. To show what may be practicably and safely defalcated from the [the estimates].

Falling off, or subject to fall or be shed, at a certain season, or a certain stage or interval of growth, as leaves (except of evergreens) in autumn, or as parts of animals, such as hair, teeth, antlers, etc.; also, shedding leaves or parts at certain seasons
An ass; esp., one driven by a huckster or greengrocer. [Scot.]
An orthopterous insect of the genus Gryllus, and allied genera. The males make chirping, musical notes by rubbing together the basal parts of the veins of the front wings.
A messenger sent with haste to convey letters or dispatches, usually on public busuness. The wary Bassa .
The young of the equine genus or horse kind of animals; -- sometimes distinctively applied to the male, filly being the female. Cf.
To make the noise, or utter the call, of a brooding hen. Ray.
An instrument for determining the dip of beds or strata, pr the slope of an embankment or cutting; a kind of plumb level. Dana.
A small roll of tobacco, used for smoking. Cigar fish (Zoöl.), a fish (Decapterus punctatus), allied to the mackerel, found on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico.
An instrument for measuring minute intervals of time; used in determining the velocity of projectiles, the duration of short-lived luminous phenomena, etc.
A species of leopard (Cynælurus jubatus) tamed and used for hunting in India. The woolly cheetah of South Africa is C.
A mild kind caustic used to reduce warts and other excrescences. Dunglison.
To cut bend to an upward curve; to construct, as a deck, with an upward curve.
A coarse fabric, made of jute or hemp, used for bagging; also, a finer variety of similar material, used for curtains, etc. [Written also burlaps.]

(a) An elastic apparatus or fender, for deadening the jar caused by the collision of bodies; as, a buffer at the end of a railroad car. (b) A pad or cushion forming the end of a fender, which recieves the blow; -- sometimes called buffing apparatus.
The string of a bow.
An instrument for regulating the electro-motive force in an alternating-current circuit; -- so called because used to "boost", or raise, the pressure in the circuit.
A four-wheeled truck, having a certain amount of play around a vertical axis, used to support in part a locomotive on a railway track.
To make turgid, as with water or air; to cause a swelling of the surface of, from effusion of serum in the cellular tissue, producing a morbid enlargement, often accompanied with softness.

An armor-plated man-of-war built of steel and heavily armed, generally having from ten thousand to fifteen thousand tons displacement, and intended to be fit to meet the heaviest ships in line of battle.
A covered building used chiefly for storing grain, hay, and other productions of a farm. In the United States a part of the barn is often used for stables.

A tree of the same genus as the common fig, and called the Indian fig (Ficus Indica), whose branches send shoots to the ground, which take root and become additional trunks, until it may be the tree covers some acres of ground and is able to shelter thousands
A story or relation of fictitious events, intended to convey some moral truth; a moral fable.
That which produces insensibility to pain, as chloroform, ether, etc.
Deposits of earth, sand, gravel, and other transported matter, made by rivers, floods, or other causes, upon land not permanently submerged beneath the waters of lakes or seas. Lyell.
The cause of continued pain of body or mind, as sickness, losses, etc.; an instance of grievous distress; a pain or grief. To repay that money will be a biting affliction.
An apparatus designed for collecting spores, germs, bacteria, etc., suspended in the air.
One of the Marsipobranchia.

The act of manifesting or disclosing, or the state of being manifested; discovery to the eye or to the understanding; also, that which manifests; exhibition; display; revelation; as, the manifestation of God's power in creation. The secret manner in which acts
One of the Lamellibranchia. Also used adjectively.
One of the grand divisions of the animal kingdom. By many writers it was formerly included in the Radiata.
An instrument for triturating the stone in the bladder; a lithotrite.
To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day; to defer; to postpone; to delay; as, to procrastinate repentance. Dr.
Pertaining to typhoid fever and malaria; as, typhomalarial fever, a form of fever having symptoms both of malarial and typhoid fever.
Vegetable tissue composed of thin-walled rounded cells, -- a modification of parenchyma.
The act of excreting. To promote secretion and excretion.
A transverse bar or piece, as a bar across a door, or as the iron bar or stock which passes through the shank of an anchor to insure its turning fluke down. Russell.
The ground story of a building, either on a level with the street or raised slightly above it; -- said esp. of buildings on the continent of Europe.
To write or engrave (a name, address, inscription, or the like) on the top or surface; to write a name, address, or the like, on the outside or cover of (anything); as, to superscribe a letter.
To some indeterminate place; to some place or other. Driven by the winds of temptation somewhither.

Used as an auxiliary verb, to express a conditional or contingent act or state, or as a supposition of an actual fact; also, to express moral obligation (see Shall); e. g.: they should have come last week; if I should go; I should think you could go.
The power possessed by a substance to refract a ray; as, different substances have different refringencies. Nichol.
A rampart. [Archaic] The Trojans round the place a rampire cast.
To set, place, or establish, as in a rank, office, or condition; to install; to invest; as, to instate a person in greatness or in favor. Shak.

To make public; to several or communicate to the public; to tell (a secret) so that it may become generally known; to disclose; -- said of that which had been confided as a secret, or had been before unknown; as, to divulge a secret. Divulge not such a love as

To make not pleased; to excite a feeling of disapprobation or dislike in; to be disagreeable to; to offend; to vex; -- often followed by with or at. It usually expresses less than to anger, vex, irritate, or provoke.
A cloth; a piece of cloth or leather; a patch; a rag. His garments, nought but many ragged clouts, With thorns together pinned and patched was.
"A wooden pin stuck anciently on the sides of the bedstead, to hold the clothes from slipping on either side." Johnson. Hostess, accommodate us with a bedstaff.
A kind of wine, formerly much esteemed; -- said to have been made near Alicant, in Spain. J.
To free from embarrassment, or perplexity; to clear; to extricate. To disembarrass himself of his companion.
The act of gratifying, or pleasing, either the mind, the taste, or the appetite; as, the gratification of the palate, of the appetites, of the senses, of the desires, of the heart.

An apparatus for making spectroheliograms, consisting of a spectroscopic camera used in combination with a telescope, and provided with clockwork for moving the sun's image across the slit. -- Spec`tro*he`li*o*graph"ic (#), a.
The part which first meets the eye; as: (a) (Arch.) The principal front of a building. [Obs.
A phrase used adjectively sometimes of meretricious attempts to catch or win popular favor.

The act of interpreting; explanation of what is obscure; translation; version; construction; as, the interpretation of a foreign language, of a dream, or of an enigma. Look how we can, or sad or merrily, Interpretation will misquote our looks.
Internal; inward; -- opposed to external. Epilepsies, fierce catarrhs, Intestine stone and ulcers.

A colorless volatile alkaline liquid, N.(CH3)3, obtained from herring brine, beet roots, etc., with a characteristic herringlike odor. It is regarded as a substituted ammonia containing three methyl groups.
Any revolving contrivance for affording amusement; esp., a ring of flying hobbyhorses.

The act of disappointing, or the state of being disappointed; defeat or failure of expectation or hope; miscarriage of design or plan; frustration. If we hope for things of which we have not thoroughly considered the value, our disappointment will be greater o
To sail completely round. Having circumnavigated the whole earth.
Having the quality or power of removing hair. -- n.
Imparting strength or tone; strengthening; invigorating; as, a bracing north wind.
A broad, flat, wooden bar; a slat or sloat.
The act of seeking, or looking after anything; attempt to find or obtain; search; pursuit; as, to rove in quest of game, of a lost child, of property, etc. Upon an hard adventure yet in quest.
A perfumed unguent or composition, chiefly used in dressing the hair; pomade. Wiseman.

One who or that which defends or protects by warding off harm; as: (a) A screen to prevent coals or sparks of an open fire from escaping to the floor. (b) Anything serving as a cushion to lessen the shock when a vessel comes in contact with another vessel or a
Moving with a quick, lively pace, or capable of so doing; dashing. Four spanking grays ready harnessed.
To pledge; to hazard on the event of a contest; to stake; to bet, to lay; to wager; as, to wage a dollar. Hakluyt.

Of or pertaining to Venice in Italy. Venetian blind, a blind for windows, doors, etc., made of thin slats, either fixed at a certain angle in the shutter, or movable, and in the latter case so disposed as to overlap each other when close, and to show a series

To furnish (rooms, carriages, bedsteads, chairs, etc.) with hangings, coverings, cushions, etc.; to adorn with furnishings in cloth, velvet, silk, etc.; as, to upholster a couch; to upholster a room with curtains.
To turn in a reserve way, especially so as to open something; as, to unturn a key. Keats.
To deprive of a string or strings; also, to take from a string; as, to unstring beads.
To open by picking out stitches; to take out, or undo, the stitches of; as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.
To loose from pins; to remove the pins from; to unfasten; as, to unpin a frock; to unpin a frame.
To loose from a hook; to undo or open by loosening or unfastening the hooks of; as, to unhook a fish; to unhook a dress.
To loosen from a fastening; to detach from anything that holds; to unsettle; as, to unfix a bayonet; to unfix the mind or affections.
To cover as under a furrow; to plow in; as, to underfurrow seed or manure.
To dig an underground ditches in, so as to drain the surface; to underdrain; as, to underditch a field or a farm.
To disclose freely; to reveal in confidence, as secrets; to confess; -- often used reflexively; as, to unbosom one's self. Milton.
To generate pus; as, a boil or abscess suppurates.
To heat too much, to overheat; as, to superheat an oven.

To take up into or under, as individual under species, species under genus, or particular under universal; to place (any one cognition) under another as belonging to it; to include under something else. To subsume one proposition under another.
To run very rapidly; to run at full speed. A runner [in a quarter-mile race] should be able to sprint the whole way.
To go or move with one side foremost; to move sidewise; as, to sidle through a crowd or narrow opening. Swift.
To shut up apart from others; to withdraw into, or place in, solitude; to separate from society or intercourse with others. Let Eastern tyrants from the light of heaven Seclude their bosom slaves.
To blunt; to turn, as an edge; figuratively, to cause to be obtuse or dull; as, to retund confidence. Ray.
To set again; as, to reset type; to reset copy; to reset a diamond.
To pass again; to pass or travel over in the opposite direction; to pass a second time; as, to repass a bridge or a river; to repass the sea.
To renew with regard to any state or quality; to restore; to bring again together into a whole, as the parts off anything; to reas, to reintegrate a nation. Bacon.
To hash over again; to prepare or use again; as, to rehash old arguments.
To recover health; to regain strength; to convalesce.
To conquer again; to recover by conquest; as, to reconquer a revolted province.
To twirl; to turn or wind round; to coil; as, to querl a cord, thread, or rope. [Local, U.S.]
The mark, or stamp, of a post office on a letter, giving the place and date of mailing or of arrival.
To slip or slide over; to pass easily or carelessly beyond; to omit; to neglect; as, to overslip time or opportunity.
To shoot over or beyond. "Not to overshoot his game." South.
To plan; to contrive; esp., to form a scheme with the purpose of doing harm; to contrive artfully; to plot. "How long will you machinate!" Sandys.
To make literal; to interpret or put in practice according to the strict meaning of the words; -- opposed to spiritualize; as, to literalize Scripture.

To trouble greatly by numbers or by frequency of presence; to disturb; to annoy; to frequent and molest or harass; as, fleas infest dogs and cats; a sea infested with pirates. To poison vermin that infest his plants.
To bathe; to wash freely; to immerce. And gave her to his daughters to imbathe In nectared lavers strewed with asphodel.
To apply to, in conjunction with mechanical pressure, for the purpose of giving a smooth and glosay surface, or to express oil, etc.; as, to hotpress paper, linen, etc.
To fasten (an animal) by a rope binding the head to one of the fore legs; as, to hamshackle a horse or cow; hence, to bind or restrain; to curb.
To make German, or like what is distinctively German; as, to Germanize a province, a language, a society.
To deprive of calcareous matter; thus, to decalcify bones is to remove the stony part, and leave only the gelatin.

To chamfer or form a depression around the top of (a hole in wood, metal, etc.) for the reception of the head of a screw or bolt below the surface, either wholly or in part; as, to countersink a hole for a screw.
To come to an issue; to turn out; to succed; as, to cheve well in a enterprise. [Prov.
To make a short, shrill, cheerful sound; to chirp. See Chirrup.
To overlay or cover the inner side of the roof of; to furnish with a ceiling; as, to ceil a room. The greater house he ceiled with fir tree.
To slide back; to fall away; esp. to abandon gradually the faith and practice of a religion that has been professed.
To grub up, as trees; to commit an assart upon; as, to assart land or trees. Ashmole.
A genus of extinct crocodilian reptiles of the Jurassic period, having a long and slender snout.

A figure by which an adjective or verb, which agrees with a nearer word, is, by way of supplement, referred also to another more remote; as, "hic illius arma, hic currus fuit;" where fuit, which agrees directly with currus, is referred also to arma.
A piece of orange or lemon peel, or the aromatic oil which may be squeezed from such peel, used to give flavor to liquor, etc.
A small ship's boat, usually rowed by four or six oars. [Written also yaul.]
Sale of goods by the piece or large quantity, as distinguished from retail. By wholesale, in the mass; in large quantities; without distinction or discrimination.
Untrained; undisciplined; unrestrained; hence, loose; free; luxuriant; roving; sportive. "In woods and wanton wilderness." Spenser.
The quality or state of being vain; want of substance to satisfy desire; emptiness; unsubstantialness; unrealness; falsity. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
Not titled; having no title, or appellation of dignity or distinction. Spenser.

The quality or state of being uniform; freedom from variation or difference; resemblance to itself at all times; sameness of action, effect, etc., under like conditions; even tenor; as, the uniformity of design in a poem; the uniformity of nature.
Having no artful, ulterior, or fraudulent purpose; sincere; artless; simple.
A species of time; -- so called from its resemblance in form to a trefoil.
A moundlike Buddhist sepulcher, or memorial monument. often erected over a Buddhish relic.
A piece of canvas used to cover the hammocks which are lashed to the top in action to protect the topmen.
A chain for slinging the lower yards, in time of action, to prevent their falling, if the ropes by which they are hung are shot away.
Extreme pain; violent pang; anguish; agony; especially, one of the pangs of travail in childbirth, or purturition. Prodogious motion felt, and rueful throes.
Feeling thirst; having a painful or distressing sensation from want of drink; hence, having an eager desire. Give me, I pray thee, a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.
A group of fossil saurians having biconcave vertebræ and the teeth implanted in sockets.
Holding fast, or inclined to hold fast; inclined to retain what is in possession; as, men tenacious of their just rights.
An oval figure, whose moldings are oblique to the axis of the work. Moxon.

Any affection produced by the action of the sun on some part of the body; especially, a sudden prostration of the physical powers, with symptoms resembling those of apoplexy, occasioned by exposure to excessive heat, and often terminating fatally; coup de sole
The state of suffering; the bearing of pain; endurance. He must not only die the death, But thy unkindness shall his death draw out To lingering sufferance.
The act of coming under. "The subvention of a cloud." Stackhouse.
A shovel with a turned-up edge, for frit, sand, etc. [Written also strocal, strocle, strokal.]
Piercing, or capable of piercing, with a sting; inflicting acute pain as if with a sting, goad, or pointed weapon; pungent; biting; as, stinging cold; a stinging rebuke. -- Sting"ing*ly, adv.

An instrument consisting of small bars of wood, flat at the bottom and rounded at the top, and resting on the edges of a kind of open box. They are unequal in size, gradually increasing from the smallest to the largest, and are tuned to the diatonic scale.
The position of the king when he can not move without being placed on check and there is no other piece which can be moved.
Anything steeped, or dipped and softened, in any liquid; especially, something dipped in broth or liquid food, and intended to be eaten. He it is to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it.

The doctrine that refers all diseases to morbid changes of the solid parts of the body. It rests on the view that the solids alone are endowed with vital properties, and can receive the impression of agents tending to produce disease.
Manner in which an object is placed; location, esp. as related to something else; position; locality site; as, a house in a pleasant situation.
Having no sinews; hence, having no strength or vigor.
Causing to shake or tremble, as by a blow; especially, causing to recoil with horror or disgust; extremely offensive or disgusting. The grossest and most shocking villainies.

Having a semblance, whether with or without reality; apparent; specious; befitting; as, seeming friendship; seeming truth. My lord, you have lost a friend indeed; And I dare swear you borrow not that face Of seeming sorrow, it is sure your own.
Rough to the touch, like a file; having small raised dots, scales, or points; scabby; scurfy; scaly. Arbuthnot.
Any one of numerous species of large handsome moths belonging to Saturnia and allied genera. The Luna moth, polyphemus, and promethea, are examples.
