Two pieces of bread and butter with a thin slice of meat, cheese, or the like, between them.

A sacred place; a consecrated spot; a holy and inviolable site. Hence, specifically: (a) The most retired part of the temple at Jerusalem, called the Holy of Holies, in which was kept the ark of the covenant, and into which no person was permitted to enter exc
A feast with loose and noisy jollity; riotous festivity or merrymaking; a carousal. This day in mirth and revel to dispend.
The beat of drum, or bugle blast, about break of day, to give notice that it is time for the soldiers to rise, and for the sentinels to forbear challenging. "Sound a reveille." Dryden.
Having power to resolve; causing solution; solvent.
One faithless to principle or party. Specifically: (a) An apostate from Christianity or from any form of religious faith.
The act of refining, or the state of being refined; as, the refinement or metals; refinement of ideas. The more bodies are of kin to spirit in subtilty and refinement, the more diffusive are they.
The Hebrew name of a horned wild animal, probably the Urus.
Vapor; steam; smoke; fume. As hateful to me as the reek of a limekiln.
A piece of canvas sewed across a sail to strengthen it in the part where the eyelet holes for reefing are made. Totten.
To make account of; to care for; to heed; to regard. [Archaic] This son of mine not recking danger.

The act of recanting; a declaration that contradicts a former one; that which is thus asserted in contradiction; retraction. The poor man was imprisoned for this discovery, and forced to make a public recantation.

Prepared for what one is about to do or experience; equipped or supplied with what is needed for some act or event; prepared for immediate movement or action; as, the troops are ready to march; ready for the journey. "When she redy was." Chaucer.

Containing a promise or binding declaration of something to be done or forborne. Promissory note (Law), a written promise to pay to some person named, and at a time specified therein, or on demand, or at sight, a certain sum of money, absolutely and at all eve
An outline, or contour; as, the profile of an apple.

Full of pores; having interstices in the skin or in the substance of the body; having spiracles or passages for fluids; permeable by liquids; as, a porous skin; porous wood. "The veins of porous earth." Milton.
The act of uniting, or an agreement to unite, an aggregation of properties belonging to different persons, with a view to common liabilities or profits.

The act of perverting, or the state of being perverted; a turning from truth or right; a diverting from the true intent or object; a change to something worse; a turning or applying to a wrong end or use. "Violations and perversions of the laws." Bacon.
The quality or state of being partial; inclination to favor one party, or one side of a question, more than the other; undue bias of mind.

The old theory that the egg contains the whole embryo of the future organism and the germs of all subsequent offsprings and is merely awakened to activity by the spermatozoön; -- opposed to spermism or animalculism.
Any spar or projecting timber run out for temporary use, as from a ship's mast, to hold a rope or a sail extended, or from a building, to support hoisting teckle.
An extinct genus of Paleozoic Cephalopoda, having a long, straight, conical shell. The interior is divided into numerous chambers by transverse septa.
Undue attachment to relations; favoritism shown to members of one's family; bestowal of patronage in consideration of relationship, rather than of merit or of legal claim. From nepotism Alexander V.

A decree of the Congregation of the Council declaring invalid [so far as the laws of the Roman Catholic Church are concerned] any marriage of a Roman Catholic, or of a person who has ever been a Roman Catholic, if not contracted before a duty qualified priest
Abounding in mud; besmeared or dashed with mud; as, a muddy road or path; muddy boots.
The theory or doctrine that the human races have a common origin, or constitute a single species.
A mobcap. Goldsmith.
The quality or state of being malevolent; evil disposition toward another; inclination to injure others; ill will. See Synonym of Malice.
A song to quiet babes or lull them to sleep; that which quiets. Shak.
The state or quality of being latent. To simplify the discussion, I shall distinguish three degrees of this latency.
Small steel plates combined together so as to slide one upon the form a piece of armor.
The act or process of irrigating, or the state of being irrigated; especially, the operation of causing water to flow over lands, for nourishing plants.
Having the attention engaged; having emotion or passion excited; as, an interested listener.
Want of activity or exertion; habitual indisposition to action or motion; sluggishness; apathy; insensibility. Glanvill.

A genus of gigantic herbivorous dinosaurs having a birdlike pelvis and large hind legs with three-toed feet capable of supporting the entire body. Its teeth resemble those of the iguana, whence its name.
An instrument for ascertaining the susceptibility of a person to hypnotic influences.
An extinct genus of sharks having conical, compressed teeth.
Containing sensible moisture; damp; moist; as, a humidair or atmosphere; somewhat wet or watery; as, humid earth; consisting of water or vapor. Evening cloud, or humid bow.
An imposition under fair pretenses; something contrived in order to deceive and mislead; a trick by cajolery; a hoax.
A composition consisting of seven lines or verses.
Free from harm; unhurt; as, to give bond to save another harmless.

A sale, gift, or delivery into the hand of another; especially, a sale, gift, delivery, or using which is the first of a series, and regarded as on omen for the rest; a first installment; an earnest; as the first money received for the sale of goods in the mor
A comb for dressing flax, raw silk, etc.; a hatchel.

A subordinary of triangular form having one of its angles at the fess point and the opposite aide at the edge of the escutcheon. When there is only one gyron on the shield it is bounded by two linea drawn from the fess point, one horizontally to the dexter sid

Customary way of speaking or acting; custom; fashion; manner; behavior; mien; mode; practice; -- often used formerly in such phrases as: at his own guise; that is, in his own fashion, to suit himself. Chaucer.
A group of fossil amphibians allied to the labyrinthodonts, having the head defended by bony, sculptured plates, as in some ganoid fishes.
A tumult; a bustle; unnecessary or annoying ado about trifles. Byron.
Having turns, windings, or flexures.
An officer who has authority to direct in the extinguishing of fires, or to order what precautions shall be taken against fires; -- called also fireward.
Honeycomb; having cavities or cells, somewhat resembling those of a honeycomb; alveolate; favose.
The state of being familiar; intimate and frequent converse, or association; unconstrained intercourse; freedom from ceremony and constraint; intimacy; as, to live in remarkable familiarity.
That has lost freshness, color, or brightness; grown dim. "His faded cheek." Milton.
Without previous study or meditation; without preparation; on the spur of the moment; suddenly; extemporaneously; as, to write or speak extempore. Shak.
An officer whose duty it is to observe what escheats have taken place, and to take charge of them. Burrill.
An edict or order of the government prohibiting the departure of ships of commerce from some or all of the ports within its dominions; a prohibition to sail.
Having only one principle or constituent part; consisting of a single element; simple; uncompounded; as, an elementary substance.
An apparatus for determining the amount of oil contained in any substance, or for ascertaining the degree of purity of oil.
Fulfilling duty; dutiful; having the sentiments due to a superior, or to one to whom respect or service is owed; obedient; as, a duteous son or daughter.
grief; sorrow; lamentation. [Archaic] And she died.

One who would apply to political or other practical concerns the abstract doctrines or the theories of his own philosophical system; a propounder of a new set of opinions; a dogmatic theorist. Used also adjectively; as, doctrinaire notions.
A morbid an uncontrollable craving (often periodic) for drink, esp. for alcoholic liquors; also improperly used to denote acute and chronic alcoholism.

One who is wholly devoted; esp., one given wholly to religion; one who is superstitiously given to religious duties and ceremonies; a bigot. While Father Le Blanc was very devout he was not a devotee.
That to which any person or thing is destined; predetermined state; condition foreordained by the Divine or by human will; fate; lot; doom. Thither he Will come to know his destiny.
A suit of light armor covering less than the whole body, as having no protection for the legs below the things, no vizor to the helmet, and the like.

An attempt or disposition to deceive or lead into error; any declaration, artifice, or practice, which misleads another, or causes him to believe what is false; a contrivance to entrap; deception; a wily device; fraud. Making the ephah small and the shekel gre
A kind of knitting done by means of a hooked needle, with worsted, silk, or cotton; crochet work. Commonly used adjectively.
Having short bends, turns, or wrinkles; wrinkled; wavy; zigzag. "The crinkled lightning." Lowell.
Having the appearance of a tuft of hair; having a hairlike tail or train. "Comate, crinite, caudate stars."

Anything created; anything not self-existent; especially, any being created with life; an animal; a man. He asked water, a creature so common and needful that it was against the law of nature to deny him.
An instrument for crushing the head of a fetus, to facilitate delivery in difficult eases.
A diminutive of the bendlet, containing one half its area or one quarter the area of the bend. When a single cottise is used alone it is often called a cost.
Having the power to correct; tending to rectify; as, corrective penalties. Mulberries are pectoral, corrective of billious alkali.
Attempts to attract admoration, notice, or love, for the mere gratification of vanity; trifling in love. "Little affectations of coquetry." Addison.

A contrivance for carrying objects from place to place; esp., one for conveying grain, coal, etc., -- as a spiral or screw turning in a pipe or trough, an endless belt with buckets, or a truck running along a rope.
Having frequent or customary intercourse; familiary associated; intimately acquainted. I have been conversant with the first persons of the age.
That which is conceived, imagined, or formed in the mind; idea; thought; image; conception. In laughing, there ever procedeth a conceit of somewhat ridiculous.
Common; ordinary; trite; as, a commonplace person, or observation.
The network spread by a spider to catch its prey.
A narrow circle of persons associated by common interests or for the accomplishment of a common purpose; -- generally used in a bad sense.
An instrument shaped like a lute, but strung with wire and played with a quill or plectrum. [Written also cithern.] Shak.
An instrument for cutting into the fetal head, to facilitate delivery.
A steward or butler of a monastery or chapter; one who has charge of procuring and keeping the provisions.
Resembling a hair; fine; minute; very slender; having minute tubes or interspaces; having very small bore; as, the capillary vessels of animals and plants.
A machine for spreading out cotton cloths to prepare them for printing.

A fossil plant of the coal formation, having the general form of plants of the modern Equiseta (the Horsetail or Scouring Rush family) but sometimes attaining the height of trees, and having the stem more or less woody within. See Acrogen, and Asterophyllite.
Having the qualities, consistence, or appearance, of butter.
Having or containing bulbs, or a bulb; growing from bulbs; bulblike in shape or structure.
Showing blushes; rosy red; having a warm and delicate color like some roses and other flowers; blooming; ruddy; roseate. The dappled pink and blushing rose.
A tube for directing a jet of air into a fire or into the flame of a lamp or candle, so as to concentrate the heat on some object.
A small piece of cloth worn by children over the breast, to protect the clothes.

To call to mind; to recall or bring to recollection, reflection, or consideration; to think; to consider; -- generally followed by a reflexive pronoun, often with of or that before the subject of thought. I have bethought me of another fault.
Pertaining to, or having the form, nature, or habits of, a beast. Beastly divinities and droves of gods.
The use of a word of common or general signification for the name of a particular thing; as, "He has gone to town," for, "He has gone to London."
A carpenter's tool for boring holes larger than those bored by a gimlet. It has a handle placed crosswise by which it is turned with both hands.
Of or belonging to, or having the qualities of, the ass, as stupidity and obstinacy. "Asinine nature." B.
Having the form, constitution, or habits, of a proper tree, in distinction from a shrub. Loudon.
A person attached to a particular pursuit, study, or science as to music or painting; esp. one who cultivates any study or art, from taste or attachment, without pursuing it professionally.
To cover or saturate with albumen; to coat or treat with an albuminous solution; as, to albuminize paper.
A combination of a stop, or explosive, with an immediately following fricative or spirant of corresponding organic position, as pf in german Pfeffer, pepper, z (= ts) in German Zeit, time.
Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; not present. "Expecting absent friends." Shak.
To change completely, as by a revolution; as, to revolutionize a government. Ames.
The act of forming or producing fruit; the act of fructifying, or rendering productive of fruit; fecundation. The prevalent fructification of plants.
Having two coalescent cotyledons, as the live oak and the horse-chestnut.
An instrument for measuring the amount of force exerted by the lungs in respiration.
An instrument for recording the movements of the thorax or chest wall during respiration; -- also called stethograph.
A delirious picking of bedclothes by a sick person, as if to pick off flocks of wool; carphology; -- an alarming symptom in acute diseases. Dunglison.

An instrument which by means of a prism of a peculiar form, or an arrangement of mirrors, causes an apparent image of an external object or objects to appear as if projected upon a plane surface, as of paper or canvas, so that the outlines may conveniently tra

Formed; shaped; constructed; made; -- often used in composition and preceded by the word denoting the form; as, frigate-built, clipper-built, etc. Like the generality of Genoese countrywomen, strongly built.

Moving or acting with physical strength; urged or impelled with force; excited by strong feeling or passion; forcible; vehement; impetuous; fierce; furious; severe; as, a violent blow; the violent attack of a disease. Float upon a wild and violent sea.
The claw of a predaceous bird or animal, especially the claw of a bird of prey. Bacon.
Of or pertaining to silk; made of, or resembling, silk; silken; silklike; as, a silky luster.
The chief officer of a shire or county, to whom is intrusted the execution of the laws, the serving of judicial writs and processes, and the preservation of the peace.
The skin of a sheep; or, leather prepared from it.
capable of being drawn into a thread, as a glutinous substance; stringy; viscous; tenacious; glutinous; as ropy sirup; ropy lees.
Of or pertaining to a republic. The Roman emperors were republican magistrates named by the senate.
The act or process of bringing or coming into existence; first production. "The origination of the universe." Keill.
Light and quick in motion; moving with ease and celerity; lively; swift. Through the mid seas the nimble pinnace sails.
The fiber by which the petioles of the date palm are bound together, from which various kinds of cordage are made.

In the rear; -- opposed to front; of or pertaining to the part or end which follows or is behind, in opposition to the part which leads or is before; as, the hind legs or hind feet of a quadruped; the hind man in a procession.
The skin of a deer, or the leather which is made from it. Hakluyt.
The lower extremity of the face below the mouth; the point of the under jaw.
A cord of great toughness made from the intestines of animals, esp. of sheep, used for strings of musical instruments, etc.
Pertaining to, or situated under, the northern constellation called the Bear; northern; frigid; as, the arctic pole, circle, region, ocean; an arctic expedition, night, temperature.
Being three times ten; consisting of one more than twenty-nine; twenty and ten; as, the month of June consists of thirty days.
A galvanometer in which current is measured by torsion.
To impregnate or combine with an excess of sulphur.
An instrument with two lenses, by which an image of a single picture projected upon a screen of ground glass is made to present an appearance of relief, and may be viewed by several persons at once.
A double-lens instrument for measuring slight variations of the sun's diameter by photography, utilizing the common chord of two overlapping images.

An artificial nutrient fluid invented by Pasteur for the study of alcoholic fermentation, but used also for the cultivation of bacteria and other organisms. It contains all the elements of protoplasm, and was originally made of the ash of yeast, some ammonia c
A mental disorder in which melancholy and gloomy views torment the affected person, particularly concerning his own health.
Spur gearing having teeth slanting across the face of the wheel, sometimes slanting in opposite directions from the middle.

A yellowish beetle (Doryphora decemlineata), with ten longitudinal, black, dorsal stripes. It has migrated eastwards from its original habitat in Colorado, and is very destructive to the potato plant; -- called also potato beetle and potato bug.
Situated at the farthest point or extremity; farthest out; most distant; extreme; as, the utmost limits of the land; the utmost extent of human knowledge. Spenser.
Recalling to mind, or capable of recalling to mind; having remembrance; reminding one of something. Some other of existence of which we have been previously conscious, and are now reminiscent.

To be set, or to sit, in the place of authority; to occupy the place of president, chairman, moderator, director, etc.; to direct, control, and regulate, as chief officer; as, to preside at a public meeting; to preside over the senate.
To form into grains or small masses; as, to granulate powder, sugar, or metal.
Of or pertaining to Europe, or to its inhabitants. On the European plain, having rooms to let, and leaving it optional with guests whether they will take meals in the house; -- said of hotels.
Consisting of two syllabas, a dissyllabic foot in poetry. B.
A piece of any structure which is fitted or framed crosswise.
Hanging; annexed; adjunct; concomitant; as, a seal appendant to a paper. As they have transmitted the benefit to us, it is but reasonable we should suffer the appendant calamity.
Having the form of a spheroid. -- Sphe*roid"al*ly, adv.
A bounding with juice; succulent. Bacon.
A previous liking; a prepossession of mind in favor of something; predisposition to choose or like; partiality. Burke.
A division of alcyonoid corals, including the seapens and related kinds. They are able to move about by means of the hollow muscular peduncle, which also serves to support them upright in the mud.
An extinct Eocene bird having the jaws strongly serrated, or dentated, but destitute of true teeth. It was found near London.
Having a mutual or reciprocal relation or parallelism; correlative.
The quality or state of being indifferent, or not making a difference; want of sufficient importance to constitute a difference; absence of weight; insignificance.
Having a strong, deep, or glaring color; flushed. Shak.

The act of dispensing or dealing out; distribution; often used of the distribution of good and evil by God to man, or more generically, of the acts and modes of his administration. To respect the dispensations of Providence.
To deprive of synonymous character; to discriminate in use; -- applied to words which have been employed as synonyms. Coleridge.

A coil of small resistance and large inductance, used in an alternating-current circuit to impede or throttle the current, or to change its phase; --called also reactance coil or reactor, these terms being now preferred in engineering usage.

The lantern shown at night by a vessel at anchor. International rules of the road require vessels at anchor to carry from sunset to sunrise a single white light forward if under 150 feet in length, and if longer, two such lights, one near the stern and one for
The act of one who, or that which, turns; also, a winding; a bending course; a fiexure; a meander. Through paths and turnings often trod by day.
The act of one who makes; workmanship; fabrication; construction; as, this is cloth of your own making; the making of peace or war was in his power.
The of causing to burn, or of exciting or inflaming the passions.
That which is found, come upon, or provided; esp. (pl.), that which a journeyman artisan finds or provides for himself; as tools, trimmings, etc.
To go beyond in performance; to excel; to surpass. An imposture outdoes the original.
To inhabit or reside in company, or in the same place or country. The Philistines were worsted by the captived ark .

Of or pertaining to Alessandro Volta, who first devised apparatus for developing electric currents by chemical action, and established this branch of electric science; discovered by Volta; as, voltaic electricity.
Low; base; worthless; mean; despicable. A poor man in vile raiment.

tiono run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want, or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering; to relieve; as, to succor a besieged city. [Written also succour.] He is able to succor them that are tempted.
Characterized by roughness; umpolished; raw; lacking delicacy or refinement; coarse. Such gardening tools as art, yet rude, .
Freed from impurities or alloy; purifed; polished; cultured; delicate; as; refined gold; refined language; refined sentiments. Refined wits who honored poesy with their pens.
Pouring forth with fullness or exuberance; bountiful; exceedingly liberal; giving without stint; as, a profuse government; profuse hospitality. A green, shady bank, profuse of flowers.
possessing nerve; sinewy; strong; vigorous. "Nervous arms." Pope.
Contrary to, or unauthorized by, law; illegal; as, a lawless claim. He needs no indirect nor lawless course.
Not consisting of matter; incorporeal; spiritual; disembodied. Angels are spirits immaterial and intellectual.
Made hard, or compact; made unfeeling or callous; made obstinate or obdurate; confirmed in error or vice.
Of large size or extent; great; extensive; hence, relatively great; greatest; chief; principal; as, a grand mountain; a grand army; a grand mistake. "Our grand foe, Satan." Milton.
Contributing to, or concerned in, propagation or production; generative; procreative; productive. "The genial bed." Milton.

Causing effects; producing results; that makes the effect to be what it is; actively operative; not inactive, slack, or incapable; characterized by energetic and useful activity; as, an efficient officer, power. The efficient cause is the working cause.
Passing from one thing to another; ranging over a wide field; roving; digressive; desultory. "Discursive notices." De Quincey.
Being in the state of a barbarian; uncivilized; rude; peopled with barbarians; as, a barbarous people; a barbarous country.

Wanting dexterity in the use of the hands, or of instruments; not dexterous; without skill; clumsy; wanting ease, grace, or effectiveness in movement; ungraceful; as, he was awkward at a trick; an awkward boy. And dropped an awkward courtesy.
A genus of bats including some of the common small insectivorous species of North America and Europe.
To unfold; to undo; to ravel, as what has been woven.
A genus of Pseudoneuroptera including the white ants, or termites. See Termite.
The act or operation of subtracting or taking away a part.
The process of taking in a reef. Reefing bowsprit, a bowsprit so rigged that it can easily be run in or shortened by sliding inboard, as in cutters.
The vessels or ware made by potters; earthenware, glazed and baked.
A genus of woodpeckers, including some of the common American and European species.

Pertaining to, connected with, produced by, or consisting of, molecules; as, molecular forces; molecular groups of atoms, etc. Molecular attraction (Phys.), attraction acting between the molecules of bodies, and at insensible distances.
The worship of idols, images, or anything which is not God; the worship of false gods. His eye surveyed the dark idolatries Of alienated Judah.

The income of a ruler or of a state; revennue; public money; sometimes, the income of an individual; often used in the plural for funds; available money; resources. All the finances or revenues of the imperial crown.
The act, art, or practice of engraving by means of acid which eats away lines or surfaces left unprotected in metal, glass, or the like. See Etch, v.
To manage; to conduct; to treat. [Our] clergy have with violence demeaned the matter.

A scheme of equalizing the social conditions of life; specifically, a scheme which contemplates the abolition of inequalities in the possession of property, as by distributing all wealth equally to all, or by holding all wealth in common for the equal use and
The name of several evergreen trees. The wood is remarkable for its durability and fragrant odor.
A star of the first magnitude in the southern constellation Argo.
A genus of large univalve mollusks abundant in the arctic seas. It includes the common whelk (B.
The act or process of preparing liquors which are brewed, as beer and ale.
The giving of alms.

In Russia, an elective local district and provincial administrative assembly. Originally it was composed of representatives elected by the peasantry, the householders of the towns, and the landed proprietors.
In a witty manner; wisely; ingeniously; artfully; with it; with a delicate turn or phrase, or with an ingenious association of ideas. Who his own harm so wittily contrives.
A small box, usually jeweled or of precious metal and worn on a chain, containing a mirror, powder puff, and other small toilet articles for a woman.
A kind of woven fabric for waistcoats, having the weft of wool and the warp of silk or cotton. [Written also valentia.]
An instrument for arresting hemorrhage. It consists essentially of a pad or compress upon which pressure is made by a band which is tightened by a screw or other means.
An apparatus for conveying heat, as a case containing material which retains its heat for a considerable period.
A large purse or pouch made of skin with the hair or fur on, worn in front of the kilt by Highlanders when in full dress.

One of a body of students in the universities of Cambridge (Eng.) and Dublin, who, having passed a certain examination, are exempted from paying college fees and charges. A sizar corresponded to a servitor at Oxford.
A taking sides, as with a party, sect, or faction. Bp.
A cake, thinner than a bannock, made of wheat or barley or oat meal. [Written variously, scon, skone, skon, etc.] [Scot.] Burns.
One of a breed of fancy frilled pigeons allied to the owls and turbits, having the body white, the shoulders tricolored, and the tail bluish black with a large white spot on each feather.
A kind of dress goods made of cotton or woolen, with a glossy surface resembling satin.
A kind of apple having the skin streaked with red and yellow, -- a favorite English cider apple. Mortimer.
Concave in front; as, procoelian vertebræ, which have the anterior end of the centra concave and the posterior convex.
A fine cotton fabric, having a linen finish, and often printed on one side, -- used for women's and children's wear.
Moved or worked by the action of the foot or feet on a pedal or treadle.
That branch of the post office having to do with the collection, transmission, and delivery of parcels. The British Inland Parcel Post was established in 1883.
A machine for use in making topographical maps. It is operated by being pushed across country, and not only records distances, like the perambulator, but also elevations.
A rounded seed, rather smaller than a nutmeg, having a hard smooth shell, and a yellowish or bluish color. The seeds grow in the prickly pods of tropical, woody climbers of the genus Cæsalpinia.
A Moorish dance, usually performed by a single dancer, who accompanies the dance with castanets.

A conical rifle bullet, with a cavity in its base plugged with a piece of iron, which, by the explosion of the charge, is driven farther in, expanding the sides to fit closely the grooves of the barrel.
A kind of small roundish olive with a small freestone pit, a fine skin, and a peculiar bitterish flavor. Manzanillas are commonly pitted and stuffed with Spanish pimientos.
Having slipped downward, backward, or away; having lost position, privilege, etc., by neglect; -- restricted to figurative uses. Once more I will renew His lapsed powers, though forfeit.
Foil or wire made of gold, silver, or brass. De Colange.
A cubic measure containing 1000 cubic meters, and equivalent to 35,315 cubic feet.
A kind of soup containing thin slices or shreds of carrots, onions, etc.
A kind of bread made of the meal of maize (Indian corn), mixed with water or milk, etc., and baked. [U.S.] J.
Articles made of iron, as household utensils, tools, and the like.
With a degree of guilt or folly beyond excuse or justification. Inexcusably obstinate and perverse.
A plant (Hyssopus officinalis). The leaves have an aromatic smell, and a warm, pungent taste.
A form of hygrometer having wet and dry bulb thermometers, with an adjustable index showing directly the percentage of moisture in the air, etc.
With a harsh, grating sound or voice.
A book containing the list and pedigrees of one or more herds of choice breeds of cattle; -- also called herd record, or herd register.
A hand containing three of a kind and a pair, as three kings and two tens. It ranks above a flush and below four of a kind.
Ornamental work with a needle or hook, as embroidery, crocheting, netting, etc.
One of a breed of horned sheep of Devonshire, England, having white legs and face and black nostrils. They are esp.
With an even, level, or smooth surface; without roughness, elevations, or depression; uniformly; equally; comfortably; impartially; serenely.
One who has an unusual fancy for, or interest in, dogs; also, one who deals in dogs.
An evergreen shrub or small tree (Ilex cassine) of the southern United States, bearing red drupes and having soft, white, close- grained wood; -- called also dahoon holly.
Having a part cut off or away; having the corners rounded or cut away. Cutaway coat, a coat whose skirts are cut away in front so as not to meet at the bottom.
Having or wearing a crown; surmounted, invested, or adorned, with a crown, wreath, garland, etc.; honored; rewarded; completed; consummated; perfected. "Crowned with one crest." Shak.
That which is held together with another thing; that which is connected with a tenetment, or thing holden, as a certin quantity of land a Burrill.
An instrument or machine for comparing anything to be measured with a standard measure; -- applied especially to a machine for comparing standards of length.
A large hook or crook, as for a pot over a fire; specif., an iron- headed golf club with a straight, narrow face and a long shaft.
A kind of pear that has a rough, astringent taste, and is swallowed with difficulty, or which contracts the mucous membrane of the mouth.
A plant (Agathotes Chirayta) found in Northern India, having medicinal properties to the gentian, and esteemed as a tonic and febrifuge.
An ornamental hook, or brooch worn by a lady at her waist, and having a short chain or chains attached for a watch, keys, trinkets, etc. Also used adjectively; as, a chatelaine chain.

The outer vestment worn by the priest in saying Mass, consisting, in the Roman Catholic Church, of a broad, flat, back piece, and a narrower front piece, the two connected over the shoulders only. The back has usually a large cross, the front an upright bar or

A kind of pie or pudding made by lining a dish with slices of bread, and filling it with bread soaked in milk, and baked. Charlotte Russe (, or Charlotte à la russe Etym: [F., lit., Russian charlotte] (Cookery), a dish composed of custard or whipped cream, inc
A maidservant who has the care of chambers, making the beds, sweeping, cleaning the rooms, etc.
A light covered carriage, having four wheels and seats for four or more persons, usually drawn by one horse.
A small copper coin, with a mixture of silver, formerly current in some parts of Germany and Switzerland. It was worth about four cents.
A stringed instrument of the viol family, used for playing bass. See 3d Bass, n., and Violoncello.

A kind of cake or bread, in shape flat and roundish, commonly made of oatmeal or barley meal and baked on an iron plate, or griddle; -- used in Scotland and the northern counties of England. Jamieson.

Barren regions, especially in the western United States, where horizontal strata (Tertiary deposits) have been often eroded into fantastic forms, and much intersected by canons, and where lack of wood, water, and forage increases the difficulty of traversing t
An officer who has the care or inspection of weights and measures, etc.
A rude apparatus for pulverizing ores, esp. those containing free gold.

Pertaining to, or resembling, a bracelet or ring; consisting of rings or circles. Armillary sphere, an ancient astronomical machine composed of an assemblage of rings, all circles of the same sphere, designed to represent the positions of the important circles

A person, whether negro, Indian, or white, in whom by some defect of organization the substance which gives color to the skin, hair, and eyes is deficient or in a morbid state. An albino has a skin of a milky hue, with hair of the same color, and eyes with dee
A species of macaque (Macacus pileatus) native of India and Ceylon. It has a crown of long erect hair, and tuft of radiating hairs on the back of the head.
A genus of birds comprising the wrynecks.
A genus of plants of the order Hæmodraceæ, having two-ranked, sword-shaped leaves.

A genus of shrubby ranunculaceous plants of North America, including only the species Xanthorhiza apiifolia, which has roots of a deep yellow color; yellowroot. The bark is intensely bitter, and is sometimes used as a tonic.
A sea robin having large, winglike pectoral fins. See Sea robin, under Robin.
A silicate of zinc, usually occurring massive and of a greenish yellow color, also in reddish crystals (troostite) containing manganese.
A somewhat heart-shaped cherry with a whitish skin.
A sudden expulsion of air from the mouth; a quick puff or slight gust, as of air or smoke. But with the whiff and wind of his fell sword The unnerved father falls.

The theories and teachings in regard to heredity propounded by the German biologist August Weismann, esp. in regard to germ plasm as the basis of heredity and the impossibility of transmitting acquired characteristics; -- often called neo-Darwinism.
A European species of Iris (Iris Pseudacorus) having bright yellow flowers.
A large West African chevrotain (Hyæmoschus aquaticus). It has a larger body and shorter legs than the other allied species.
A dog kept to watch and guard premises or property, and to give notice of the approach of intruders.
An extensive tribe of bivalve mollusks of which the genus Venus is the type. The shells are usually oval, or somewhat heartshaped, with a conspicuous lunule.
A genus of small spiral fresh-water gastropods having an operculum.
A salt of valeric acid with glycerin, occurring in butter, dolphin oil., and forming an forming an oily liquid with a slightly unpleasant odor.
Moving without certain direction; wandering; erratic; unsettled. That beauteous Emma vagrant courses took.
A tribe of birds comprising the sheathbills.
A mineral consisting chiefly of uranium oxide with some lead, thorium, etc., occurring in black octahedrons, also in masses with a pitchlike luster; pitchblende.
An extensive group of mammals including all those that have hoofs. It comprises the Artiodactyla and Perissodactyla.
Rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved.
A tribe of ungulates comprising the camels.
An elephant having large tusks.
A knot of turbanlike form worked on a rope with a piece of small line.
A genus of large marine gastropods having a thick heavy shell with conspicuous folds on the columella.
An extensive group of worms which have the body covered externally with vibrating cilia. It includes the Rhabdocoela and Dendrocoela.
One who stays away from business or any duty; especially, one who stays out of school without leave; an idler; a loiterer; a shirk. Dryden.
A division of birds comprising the humming birds.
A lamellibranch which has three muscular scars on each valve.
A division of Coleoptera including those which have but three joints in the tarsi.
A figure having three angles; a triangle.
A suborder of Neuroptera usually having the wings covered with minute hairs. It comprises the caddice flies, and is considered by some to be a distinct order.
A genus of fishes comprising the hairtails. See Hairtail.
A muscle having three heads; specif., the great extensor of the forearm, arising by three heads and inserted into the olecranon at the elbow.
An extensive division of arthropods comprising all those which breathe by tracheæ, as distinguished from Crustacea, which breathe by means of branchiæ.
A genus of fishes comprising the archer fishes. See Archer fish.
A division of swimming birds including those that have totipalmate feet.
The seed of a leguminous tree (Dipteryx odorata), native of Guiana. It has a peculiarly agreeable smell, and is employed in the scenting of snuff.
A genus of transparent marine annelids which swim actively at the surface of the sea. They have deeply divided or forked finlike organs (parapodia).

An alloy of copper and zinc, resembling brass, and containing about 84 per cent of copper; -- called also German, or Dutch, brass. It is very malleable and ductile, and when beaten into thin leaves is sometimes called Dutch metal.
Formerly, a member of an independent body of marksmen in the French army. They were used sometimes in front of the army to annoy the enemy, sometimes in the rear to check his pursuit.

A genus of trees, the lindens, the type of the family Tiliaceæ, distinguished by the winglike bract coalescent with the peduncle, and by the indehiscent fruit having one or two seeds. There are about twenty species, natives of temperate regions.
Any plant of the labiate genus Thymus. The garden thyme (Thymus vulgaris) is a warm, pungent aromatic, much used to give a relish to seasoning and soups.
An order of Pteropoda comprising those species which have a shell. See Pteropoda.
A division of hydroids comprising those which have the hydranths in thecæ and the gonophores in capsules. The campanularians and sertularians are examples.
An oxide having four atoms of oxygen in the molecule; a quadroxide; as, osmium tetroxide, OsO.
An insect having four wings.
A genus of brachiopods which includes many living and some fossil species. The larger valve has a perforated beak, through which projects a short peduncle for attachment.
A division of Ctenophora including those which have two long tentacles.

Of or pertaining to the temple or temples; as, the temporal bone; a temporal artery. Temporal bone, a very complex bone situated in the side of the skull of most mammals and containing the organ of hearing.
An annelid larva having telotrochal bands of cilia.
The bark of the oak, and some other trees, bruised and broken by a mill, for tanning hides; -- so called both before and after it has been used. Called also tan bark.
A block with a tail. See Tail, 9.
A division of Ctenophora including those which have a long, ribbonlike body. The Venus's girdle is the most familiar example.
An artificial group of stony corals including those which have transverse septa in the calicles. The genera Pocillopora and Favosites are examples.
A genus of slender, transparent holothurians which have delicate calcareous anchors attached to the dermal plates. See Illustration in Appendix.

An order of slender eel-like fishes having the gill openings confluent beneath the neck. The pectoral arch is generally attached to the skull, and the entire margin of the upper jaw is formed by the premaxillary.
A variety of the chicken pox, with acuminated vesicles containing a watery fluid; the water pox. Pepys.
A variety of white grape, having a sweet watery juice; -- also called white sweetwater, and white muscadine.
A genus of marine gastropods in which the shell has the outer lip dilated into a broad wing. It includes many large and handsome species commonly called conch shells, or conchs.
A division of birds, including the clamatorial and picarian birds, which do not have well developed singing organs.
To provide with a stipend, or salary; to support; to pay. Evelyn.
Firmly established; not easily moved, shaken, or overthrown; fixed; as, a stable government. In this region of chance, .
A division of edentates having the body covered with large, imbricated horny scales. It includes the pangolins.
A scale cast off from the skin; a thin dry shred consisting of epithelium.
A gephyrean worm of the genus Thalassema, having a spoonlike probiscis.
A genus of common motile microörganisms (Spirobacteria) having the form of spiral-shaped filaments. One species is said to be the cause of relapsing fever.
A tribe of lophobranch fishes having a tubular snout. The female carries the eggs in a ventral pouch.
A suffocating smoke. Grose.
Having the habits of a sloven; negligent of neatness and order, especially in dress. A slovenly, lazy fellow, bolling at his ease.
Water or other liquid carelessly spilled or thrown aboyt, as upon a table or a floor; a puddle; a soiled spot.

The larval form of any salamander while it still has external gills; especially, one of those which, like the axolotl (Amblystoma Mexicanum), sometimes lay eggs while in this larval state, but which under more favorable conditions lose their gills and become n

The art or process of covering metals, wood, paper, glass, etc., with a thin film of metallic silver, or a substance resembling silver; also, the firm do laid on; as, the silvering of a glass speculum.
A genus of caryophyllaceous plants, usually covered with a viscid secretion by which insects are caught; catchfly. Bon Silène.

An instrument used in weaving for passing or shooting the thread of the woof from one side of the cloth to the other between the threads of the warp. Like shuttles through the loom, so swiftly glide My feathered hours.
The edible fruit of a small North American tree of the genus Viburnum (V. Lentago), having white flowers in flat cymes; also, the tree itself.

A mass of iron on which the operation of smelting has failed of its intended effect; -- so called from Shadrach, one of the three Hebrews who came forth unharmed from the fiery furnace of Nebuchadnezzar. (See Dan.
An annelid having setæ; a chætopod.
A genus of delicate branching hydroids having small sessile hydrothecæ along the sides of the branches.
A division of Hymenoptera comprising the sawflies.
A feather which has a plumelike web, with the shaft of an ordinary feather.
A carbohydrate of the glucose group found in the thickened endosperm of certain seeds, and extracted as yellow sirup having a sweetish-bitter taste.
Abounding with seeds; bearing seeds; having run to seeds.
Tending to lead astray; apt to mislead by flattering appearances; tempting; alluring; as, a seductive offer. This may enable us to understand how seductive is the influence of example.
A gorgonian having a simple stem.
An order of fresh-water fishes inhabiting tropical Africa. They have rudimentary electrical organs on each side of the tail.
A genus of oceanic nudibranchiate mollusks having the small branched gills situated on the upper side of four fleshy lateral lobes, and on the median caudal crest.
One who writes; a draughtsman; a writer for another; especially, an offical or public writer; an amanuensis or secretary; a notary; a copyist.
A division of arachnids comprising the scorpions.
A genus of reodents comprising the common squirrels.
A variety of the common cabbage (Brassica oleracea major), having curled leaves, -- much cultivated for winter use.
A variety of agate containing sard.

Leaping or dancing; having the power of, or used in, leaping or dancing. Saltatory evolution (Biol.), a theory of evolution which holds that the transmutation of species is not always gradual, but that there may come sudden and marked variations.
To search a place narrowly. I have often rummaged for old books in Little Britain and Duck Lane.
A division of Artiodactyla having four stomachs. This division includes the camels, deer, antelopes, goats, sheep, neat cattle, and allies.
A variety of tourmaline varying in color from a pale rose to a deep ruby, and containing lithium.
A division of pectinibranchiate gastropods, having the head prolonged into a snout which is not retractile.
A tropical genus of rubiaceous shrubs which often have brilliant flowers.
A genus of plants of the Spurge family, containing but one species (R. communis), the castor-oil plant.
A division of Lepidoptera including all the butterflies. They differ from other Lepidoptera in having club-shaped antennæ.
A bird having small polygonal scales covering the tarsi.
A translucent variety of serpentine, of a honey yellow or greenish yellow color, having a waxy resinlike luster.
Of or pertaining to restoration; having power to restore. Destroys life's enemy, Hunger, with sweet restorative delight.
To sell again; to sell what has been bought or sold; to retail.
Having the faculty of reason; endued with reason; rational; as, a reasonable being.
A Shakespearean word (used once) supposed to mean the same as race, a root.
Slackening; -- a direction to perform a passage with a gradual decrease in time and force; ritardando.

A genus of stemless, leafless plants, living parasitically upon the roots and stems of grapevines in Malaysia. The flowers have a carrionlike odor, and are very large, in one species (Rafflesia Arnoldi) having a diameter of two or three feet.
Having a strong flavor indicating origin; of distinct characteristic taste; tasting of the soil; hence, fresh; rich. The racy wine, Late from the mellowing cask restored to light.
A genus of rosaceous trees and shrubs having pomes for fruit. It includes the apple, crab apple, pear, chokeberry, sorb, and mountain ash.
A genus of large marine gastropods. having a pear-shaped shell.
A variety of garnet, of a poppy or blood-red color, frequently with a tinge of orange. It is used as a gem.
A genus of large marine gastropods having the outer border of the lip divided into lobes; -- called also scorpion shell.
The young tissue of a fibrovascular bundle before its component cells have begun to be differentiated. Sachs.
A pale green mineral occurring in crystalline aggregates having a botryoidal or mammillary structure, and rarely in distinct crystals. It is a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime.

Previous caution or care; caution previously employed to prevent mischief or secure good; as, his life was saved by precaution. They [ancient philosophers] treasured up their supposed discoveries with miserable precaution.
A genus of umbelliferous plants, one species of which (P. pabularia), found in Thibet, Cashmere, Afghanistan, etc., has been used as fodder for cattle.

A genus of bright-colored Siphonophora found floating in the warmer parts of the ocean. The individuals are round and disk-shaped, with a large zooid in the center of the under side, surrounded by smaller nutritive and reproductive zooids, and by slender dacty
A division of trematode worms having more two suckers. Called also Polystomea and Polystoma.
A iodide having more than one atom of iodine in the molecule.
The doctrine that animals of the same species have sprung from more than one original pair.
An old name for those Anthozoa which, like the actinias, have numerous simple tentacles.
The free-swimming larva of sea urchins and ophiurans, having several long stiff processes inclosing calcareous rods.
To fall, drop, or move in any way, with a sudden splash or slap, as on the surface of water.
An animal having broad feet, or a broad foot.
The embryo which has begun its development in the act of germination.
A subdivision of Carnivora having plantigrade feet. It includes the bears, raccoons, and allied species.
An igneous rock of semiglassy nature, having a luster like pitch.
A variety of calcite, or calcium carbonate, consisting of aggregated globular concretions about the size of a pea; -- called also peastone, peagrit.
An apple-green mineral having a greasy feel. It is a hydrous silicate of nickel, magnesia, aluminia, and iron.
A genus of herbaceous plants, some of them having berries which abound in intensely red juice; poke, or pokeweed.
A genus of fresh-water Pulmonifera, having reversed spiral shells. See Pond snail, under Pond.
A foliar part of a plant; any organ homologous with a leaf, or produced by metamorphosis of a leaf.
A gelatin in which the algæ spores have been supposed to vegetate.
A remarkable genus of marine worms having tentacles around the mouth. It is usually classed with the gephyreans.
A genus of liliaceous plants, consisting of one species (Phormium tenax). See Flax-plant.
A basic amido derivative of phloroglucin, having an astringent taste.
The class of flowering plants including all which have true flowers with distinct floral organs; phanerogamia.
A chloride having a higher proportion of chlorine than any other chloride of the same substance or series.
A bromide having a higher proportion of bromine than any other bromide of the same substance or series.
A genus of crinoids belonging to the Blastoidea. They have five petal-like ambulacra.
An extensive division of Coleoptera, including those that normally have five-jointed tarsi. It embraces about half of all the known species of the Coleoptera.
A genus of Bryozoa, of the order Entoprocta, having a bell- shaped body supported on a slender pedicel. See Illust.

A species of hickory (Carya olivæformis), growing in North America, chiefly in the Mississippi valley and in Texas, where it is one of the largest of forest trees; also, its fruit, a smooth, oblong nut, an inch or an inch and a half long, with a thin shell and
Containing pearls; abounding with, or yielding, pearls; as, pearly shells. Milton.
A crayon made of a paste composed of a color ground with gum water. [Sometimes incorrectly written pastil.] "Charming heads in pastel." W.
A genus of herbs growing in wet places, and having white flowers; grass of Parnassus.
The light elastic wood of the Aspidosperma excelsum, a tree of Guiana having a fluted trunk readily split into planks.
A yellow mineral consisting of oxalate of iron.
To rake over, or sweep across, from end to end, as waves that break over a vessel anchored with head to the sea.
To furnish (a vessel) with too long or too heavy a mast or masts.
A fish having a bony skeleton; a teleost.
A genus of minute living Foraminifera having a globular shell.
A genus of living Foraminifera, forming broad, thin, circular disks, containing numerous small chambers.
To bind with a thread or cord; to join; to unite. [Scot.] Jamieson.
A genus of tropical corals, usually branched, and having a very volid texture.
A Linnaean order of plants having eight pistils.
A suborder of Cephalopoda including Octopus, Argonauta, and allied genera, having eight arms around the head; -- called also Octopoda.
A genus of small marine bivalve shells, having a pearly interior.
A genus of algæ. The plants are composed of moniliform cells imbedded in a gelatinous substance.
Of or pertaining to a name or names; having to do with the literal meaning of a word; verbal; as, a nominal definition. Bp.
A nitro derivative of methane, analogous to chloroform, obtained as a colorless oily or crystalline substance, CH.(NO2)3, quite explosive, and having well-defined acid properties.
A report of recent occurences; information of something that has lately taken place, or of something before unknown; fresh tindings; recent intelligence. Evil news rides post, while good news baits.
A compound of naphthalene or its radical with a metallic element; as, mercuric naphthide.
A phylum of the vegetable kingdom consisting of the class Myxomycetes. By some botanists it is not separated from the Thallophyta.

Of or pertaining to mystery; containing a mystery; difficult or impossible to understand; obscure not revealed or explained; enigmatical; incomprehensible. God at last To Satan, first in sin, his doom applied, Thought in mysterious terms.
A large genus of tropical American trees and shrubs, nearly related to the true myrtles (Myrtus), from which they differ in having very few seeds in each berry.
A tumor consisting of muscular tissue.
An insect having many feet, as a myriapod.
A plant of the genus Adoxa (A. moschatellina), the flowers of which are pale green, and have a faint musky smell.
A species of cassowary (Casuarius Bennetti) found in New Britain, and noted for its agility in running and leaping. It is smaller and has stouter legs than the common cassowary.
A division of Foraminifera including those that have only one chamber.
A circular temple consisting of a roof supported on columns, without a cella.
A group of vertebrates, including the birds and reptiles, or those that have only one occipital condyle; the Sauropsida.
The condition of an ovule having but a single embryo. -- Mon*em`bry*on"ic, a.
A genus of Foraminifera, having a porcelanous shell with several longitudinal chambers.
A woman who assists other women in childbirth; a female practitioner of the obstetric art.
A polymeric modification of acrolein obtained by heating it with caustic potash. It is a crystalline substance having an aromatic odor.
A bird having a mesomyodous larynx.
A marriage with a person of inferior social position; a misalliance.
A widely distributed genus of fragrant herbs, including the peppermint, spearmint, etc. The plants have small flowers, usually arranged in dense axillary clusters.
A species of tinamou (Calopezus elegans), having a long slender crest.

A subclass of Mammalia, including nearly all the mammals of Australia and the adjacent islands, together with the opossums of America. They differ from ordinary mammals in having the corpus callosum very small, in being implacental, and in having their young b

A genus of endogenous plants found in tropical America, and some species also in India. They have tuberous roots containing a large amount of starch, and from one species (Maranta arundinacea) arrowroot is obtained.

An optical device for making an indicator diagram for high- speed engines. It consists of a light-tight box or camera having at one end a small convex mirror which reflects a beam of light on to the ground glass or photographic plate at the other end.
An insect having mandibles.
A South American carnivore of the genus Conepatus, allied to the skunk, but larger, and having a longer snout. The tail is not bushy.
A fern of the genus Adiantum (A. pedatum), having very slender graceful stalks.
A subdivision of decapod Crustacea, having the abdomen largely developed. It includes the lobster, prawn, shrimp, and many similar forms.
A genus of acalephs, having a bell-shaped body with eight groups of short tentacles around the margin. It attaches itself by a sucker at the base of the pedicel.
To cover with some protecting substance, as with lute, a crust, coating, or plates.
A bird having lobate toes; esp., a phalarope.
A genus of airbreathing mollusks, including the common garden slugs. They have a small rudimentary shell.
An igneous rock consisting largely of chrysolite, with pyroxene and picotite (a variety of spinel containing chromium).

A genus of wingless thysanurous insects having an elongated flattened body, covered with shining scales and terminated by seven unequal bristles. A common species (Lepisma saccharina) is found in houses, and often injures books and furniture.
A genus of gigantic trees, chiefly Brazilian, of the order Myrtaceæ, having woody capsules opening by an apical lid. Lecythis Zabucajo yields the delicious sapucaia nuts.
Made of lead; of the nature of lead; as, a leaden ball.
A genus of coniferous trees, having deciduous leaves, in fascicles (see Illust. of Fascicle).
A group of rodents, including the hares. They have four incisors in the upper jaw.
An attending male servant; a footman; a servile follower. Like a Christian footboy or a gentleman's lackey.
To break off with an abrupt, sharp noise; to bite; to nibble. [Obs.
A bird of Madagascar (Leptosomus discolor), the only living type of a family allied to the rollers. It has a pair of loral plumes.
A truss, framed with a king-post; -- used in roofs, bridges, etc.
An order of sponges having a skeleton composed of hornlike fibers. It includes the commercial sponges.
A gorgonian coral having a horny axis.
A long-tailed monkey of Borneo (Semnopithecus rubicundus). It has a tuft of long hair on the head.
The sixth month of the year, containing thirty days. And what is so rare as a day in June Then, if ever, come perfect days.
A species of Camellia (Camellia Japonica), a native of Japan, bearing beautiful red or white flowers. Many other genera have species of the same name.
To impress or mark with a seam or cicatrix. Pope.
Having the power of driving or impelling; giving an impulse; moving; impellent. Poor men!
Expressive of command; containing positive command; authoritatively or absolutely directive; commanding; authoritative; as, imperative orders. The suit of kings are imperative.

A genus of plants, several species of which have very beautiful flowers; -- so called because the elastic capsules burst when touched, and scatter the seeds with considerable force. Called also touch-me-not, jewelweed, and snapweed.
An order of small hoofed mammals, comprising the single living genus Hyrax.
An orthorhombic mineral of the pyroxene group, of a grayish or greenish black color, often with a peculiar bronzelike luster (schiller) on the cleavage surface.
The fluid portion of the cell protoplasm, in opposition to stereoplasm, the solid or insoluble portion. The latter is supposed to be partly nutritive and partly composed of idioplasm.
A variety of potash mica containing water. It is less elastic than ordinary muscovite.
A compound of hydriodic acid with a base; -- distinguished from an iodide, in which only the iodine combines with the base.
A derivative of urea, C3H4N2O2, obtained from allantion, as a white, crystalline substance, with a sweetish taste; -- called also glycolyl urea.
A species of the feldspar group containing barium. See Feldspar.

A movable frame of wattled twigs, osiers, or withes and stakes, or sometimes of iron, used for inclosing land, for folding sheep and cattle, for gates, etc.; also, in fortification, used as revetments, and for other purposes.
To separate from the awns; -- said of barley. [Scot.]
A mineral of a transparent vitreous brown color, found in the ejected masses of Vesuvius. It is a silicate of iron and magnesia, containing fluorine.
To render (a building) unfit for habitation, by long continued use as a hospital.
That which has the same fundamental type of structure with something else; thus, the right arm is the homotype of the right leg; one arm is the homotype of the other, etc. Owen.
The condition of having homogonous flowers.
A group of ciliated Infusoria, having cilia all over the body.
An artificial division of gastropods, including those that have an entire aperture.
A genus of plants (herbs, shrubs, or trees), some species of which have large, showy flowers. Some species are cultivated in India for their fiber, which is used as a substitute for hemp.
An order of pelagic Gastropoda, having the foot developed into a median fin. Some of the species are naked; others, as Carinaria and Atlanta, have thin glassy shells.
A division of Coleoptera, having heteromerous tarsi.
A division of Lepidoptera, including the moths, and hawk moths, which have the antennæ variable in form.
A climbing plant of the genus Cardiospermum, having round seeds which are marked with a spot like a heart. Loudon.
An artificial division of insects, including all those with a sucking proboscis.
An instrument with long iron teeth set in a board, for cleansing flax or hemp from the tow, hards, or coarse part; a kind of large comb; -- called also hackle and heckle.

One of a vagabond race, whose tribes, coming originally from India, entered Europe in 14th or 15th centry, and are now scattered over Turkey, Russia, Hungary, Spain, England, etc., living by theft, fortune telling, horsejockeying, tinkering, etc. Cf.
A plant having the stamens inserted in the pistil.
An order of Amphibia, having a long, annulated, snakelike body. See Ophiomorpha.
A group of transparent, free-swimming Annelida, having setae only in the cephalic appendages.

A genus of Gorgoniacea, formerly very extensive, but now restricted to such species as the West Indian sea fan (Gorgonia flabellum), sea plume (G. setosa), and other allied species having a flexible, horny axis.
A plant of the genus Aralia, the root of which is highly valued as a medicine among the Chinese. The Chinese plant (Aralia Schinseng) has become so rare that the American (A.
A chilognath myriapod of the genus Iulus, and allied genera, having numerous short legs along the sides; a milliped or "thousand legs." See Chilognatha.
A plant of the Sedge family (Cyperus longus) having aromatic roots; also, any plant of the same genus. Chaucer.
A state of terror excited by the sudden appearance of danger; sudden and violent fear, usually of short duration; a sudden alarm.
A variety of rhodonite, from Franklin Furnace, New Jersey, containing some zinc.
A viverrine animal of Madagascar (Cryptoprocta ferox). It resembles a cat in size and form, and has retractile claws.
A fish of the genus Aulostoma, having a much elongated tubular snout.
A sudden and brief blast or gust; a light, temporary breeze; as, a flurry of wind.
An order of Infusoria, having one or two long, whiplike cilia, at the anterior end. It includes monads.
A variety of opal occuring in the cavities of volcanic tufa, in smooth and shining globular and botryoidal masses, having a pearly luster; -- so called from Fiora, in Ischia.
A variety of pigeon, with a crest somewhat resembling the mane of a horse. [Written also finikin.]
A group of spores arranged without order and covered with a thin gelatinous envelope, as in certain delicate red algæ.
A bar with an eye at one or both ends.
The surrender or delivery of an alleged criminal by one State or sovereignty to another having jurisdiction to try charge.
A tribe of Ophiuroidea, including the genera Euryale, Astrophyton, etc. They generally have the arms branched.
The quality or condition of having strong reproductive powers; generation with full fertility between different species or races, specif. between hybrids of the first generation.
Having no certain course; roving about without a fixed destination; wandering; moving; -- hence, applied to the planets as distinguished from the fixed stars. The earth and each erratic world.
An American genus of plants, containing but a single species (E. repens), the trailing arbutus.
A genus of nudibranch mollusks having clusters of branchial papillæ along the back. See Ceratobranchia.
A variety of chalcedony containing water.
Without end; having no end or conclusion; perpetual; interminable; -- applied to length, and to duration; as, an endless line; endless time; endless bliss; endless praise; endless clamor.
A species of deer (Elaphurus Davidianus) found in china. It about four feet high at the shoulder and has peculiar antlers.
A genus of shrubs or small trees, having the foliage covered with small silvery scales; oleaster.

Surpassing; extraordinary; distinguished (in a bad sense); -- formerly used with words importing a good quality, but now joined with words having a bad sense; as, an egregious rascal; an egregious ass; an egregious mistake. The egregious impudence of this fell
To remove the epidermis of (a skin) with a concave knife, blunt in its middle part, -- as in making chamois leather.
A curious fungus of the genus Geaster, in which the outer coating splits into the shape of a star, and the inner one forms a ball containing the dustlike spores.
The wife or widow of a duke; also, a lady who has the sovereignty of a duchy in her own right.
A passerine bird of the family Dicruridæ. They are usually black with a deeply forked tail.
A drip, when made of stone. See Drip, 2.
A genus of nudibranchiate mollusks having a wreath of branchiæ on the back.
A binary compound of sulphur containing two atoms of sulphur in each molecule; -- formerly called disulphuret. Cf.
A genus of Branchiopoda, having a disklike shell, attached by one valve, which is perforated by the peduncle.
A group of spiders having only two lunglike organs. [Written also Dipneumones.]
An order of myriapods having two pairs of legs on each segment; the Chilognatha.
A compound of a binary type containing two atoms of iodine; -- called also biniodide.
The curve which on a given surface and with a given perimeter contains the greatest area. Tait.
An animal having only two digits.
A salt of chromic acid containing two equivalents of the acid radical to one of the base; -- called also bichromate.
The Evil One; Satan, represented as the tempter and spiritual of mankind. [Jesus] being forty days tempted of the devil.
A wearing off or away. Phonograms which by process long-continued detrition have reached a step of extreme simplicity.
A genus of marine mollusks belonging to the Scaphopoda, having a tubular conical shell.

The act of delivering or freeing from restraint, captivity, peril, and the like; rescue; as, the deliverance of a captive. He hath sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to preach deliverance to the captives.
Having certain or distinct; determinate in extent or greatness; limited; fixed; as, definite dimensions; a definite measure; a definite period or interval. Elements combine in definite proportions.
A vessel used to decant liquors, or for receiving decanted liquors; a kind of glass bottle used for holding wine or other liquors, from which drinking glasses are filled.
A genus consisting mostly of tropical perennial herbs (Commelina), having ephemeral flowers.
A coniferous tree of the genus Cupressus. The species are mostly evergreen, and have wood remarkable for its durability.
A division of Bryozoa, in which the cells have circular apertures.
The coloring principle of turmeric, or curcuma root, extracted as an orange yellow crystalline substance, C14H14O4, with a green fluorescence.
A group of fishes, established by Agassiz, characterized by having scales with a pectinated margin, as in the perch. The group is now generally regarded as artificial.
A salt formed by the union of croconic acid with a base.
Having the qualities of chalk;abounding with chalk; chalky; as, cretaceous rocks and formations. See Chalk.
The peculiar fruit of fennel, carrott, parsnip, and the like, consisting of a pair of carpels pendent from a supporting axis.
A comprehensive division of the Vertebrata, including all those that have a skull.

A leguminous climbing plant of the genus Mucuna, having crooked pods covered with sharp hairs, which stick to the fingers, causing intolerable itching. The spiculæ are sometimes used in medicine as a mechanical vermifuge.
To copy, as a design or painting, by tracing with a pencil on oiled paper, or other transparent substance.
An American tree of the genus Populus or polar, having the seeds covered with abundant cottonlike hairs; esp., the P. monilifera and P.
A vain, trifling woman, who endeavors to attract admiration from a desire to grafity vanity; a flirt; -- formerly sometimes applied also to men.
A mineral of a black color, submetallic luster, and high specific specific gravity. It is a niobate (or columbate) of iron and manganese, containing tantalate of iron; -- first found in New England.

A solution of pyroxylin (soluble gun cotton) in ether containing a varying proportion of alcohol. It is strongly adhesive, and is used by surgeons as a containing for wounds; but its chief application is as a vehicle for the sensitive film in photography.
A casket, chest, or trunk; especially, one used for keeping money or other valuables. Chaucer.
A variety of Cratægus, or hawthorn (C. Crus-galli), having long, straight thorns; -- called also Cockspur thorn.
A small species of titmouse, with a black head; the coletit.

To put on the other tack by dropping the lee anchor as soon as the wind is out of the sails (which brings the vessel's head to the wind), and by cutting the cable as soon as she pays off on the other tack. Clubhauling is attempted only in an exigency.
A thickened glandular portion of the body of the adult earthworm, consisting of several united segments modified for reproductive purposes.
A mass composed of several bricks run together by the action of the fire in the kiln.
A genus of freshwater leeches, furnished with a proboscis. They feed upon mollusks and worms.
A genus of flowering plants, of many species, mostly climbers, having feathery styles, which greatly enlarge in the fruit; -- called also virgin's bower.
A group of beetles having club-shaped antennæ.
An order of Crustacea including the barnacles. When adult, they have a calcareous shell composed of several pieces.

Denudation around or in the neighborhood of an object. Hills of circumdenudation, hills which have been produced by surface erosion; the elevations which have been left, after denudation of a mass of high ground.
A comprehensive division of animals including all Vertebrata together with the Tunicata, or all those having a dorsal nervous cord.
To treat or prepare with a chloride, as a plate with chloride of silver, for the purposes of photography. R.
An order of mammalia, including the bats, having four toes of each of the anterior limbs elongated and connected by a web, so that they can be used like wings in flying. See Bat.
An edible species of mushroom (Agaricus campestris). Fairy ring champignon, the Marasmius oreades, which has a strong flavor but is edible.
A bird of Europe (Fringilla coelebs), having a variety of very sweet songs, and highly valued as a cage bird; -- called also copper finch.
The larval form of a trematode worm having the shape of a tadpole, with its body terminated by a tail-like appendage.
A genus of poisonous African serpents, with a horny scale over each eye; the horned viper.
A weed with a sterm of many joints (Illecebrum verticillatum); also, the Polygonum aviculare or knotgrass.
A plant with the joints of the stem, and sometimes other parts, covered with a viscid secretion to which small insects adhere. The species of Silene are examples of the catchfly.
A black variety of diamond, found in Brazil, and used for diamond drills. It occurs in irregular or rounded fragments, rarely distinctly crystallized, with a texture varying from compact to porous.
A soldier armed with a carbine.
To upset or overturn, as a vessel or other body. But what if carrying sail capsize the boat Byron.
A limpid, colorless oil with a peculiar odor, obtained from beech tar. Watts.
Having capacity; able to contain much; large; roomy; spacious; extended; broad; as, a capacious vessel, room, bay, or harbor. In the capacious recesses of his mind.

A plant of the Pink family (Cucubalus bacciferus), bearing berries regarded as poisonous. Bladder campion, a plant of the Pink family (Cucubalus Behen or Silene inflata), having a much inflated calyx.
A person who stands at the door of an omnibus to open and shut it, and to receive fares; an idle hanger-on about innyards. [Eng.] Dickens.
A fresh-water fish of the genus Lota, having on the nose two very small barbels, and a larger one on the chin. [Written also burbolt.]

A species of Smilax (S. Pseudo-China) growing from New Jersey to the Gulf of Mexico, which has very large tuberous and farinaceous rootstocks, formerly used by the Indians for a sort of bread, and by the negroes as an ingredient in making beer; -- called also
A variety of enstatite, often having a bronzelike luster. It is a silicate of magnesia and iron, of the pyroxene family.
The snaffle and rein of a military bridle, which acts independently of the bit, at the pleasure of the rider. It is used in connection with a curb bit, which has its own rein.

The curved channel in which a breast wheel turns. It is closely adapted to the curve of the wheel through about a quarter of its circumference, and prevents the escape of the water until it has spent its force upon the wheel.
A group of Coleoptera having short wings; the rove beetles.
A division of the Crinoidea, including those furnished with long jointed arms. See Crinoidea.
A Flemish sloop with a castle at each end. Sir W.
A genus of fungi having the under side of the pileus or cap composed of a multitude of fine separate tubes. A few are edible, and others very poisonous.
The berry of several species of Vaccinium, and ericaceous genus, differing from the American huckleberries in containing numerous minute seeds instead of ten nutlets. The commonest species are V.
A genus of herbs (Blitum) with a fleshy calyx. Blitum capitatum is the strawberry blite.
A disease of the eyelids, consisting in chronic inflammation of the margins, with a gummy secretion of sebaceous matter. Dunglison.
A composition for blacking shoes, boots, etc.; also, one for taking impressions of engraved work.
A wading bird of the genus Botaurus, allied to the herons, of various species.
A sulphide having two atoms of sulphur in the molecule; a disulphide, as in iron pyrites, FeS2; -- less frequently called bisulphuret.
A salt having two equivalents of oxalic acid to one of the base; an acid oxalate.
Having a beard. "Bearded fellow." Shak.
An oxide of barium (or barytum); a heavy earth with a specific gravity above 4.
A combination of auric acid with a base; as, aurate or potassium.
Having the power or quality of attracting or drawing; as, the attractive force of bodies. Sir I.
A small marine fish of the family Atherinidæ, having a silvery stripe along the sides. The European species (Atherina presbyter) is used as food.
A genus of ophiurans having the arms much branched.

A genus of plants including the milkweed, swallowwort, and some other species having medicinal properties. Asclepias butterfly (Zoöl.), a large, handsome, red and black butterfly (Danais Archippus), found in both hemispheres.
A large division of Articulata, embracing all those that have jointed legs. It includes Insects, Arachnida, Pychnogonida, and Crustacea.
A compound of arsenic and hydrogen, AsH3, a colorless and exceedingly poisonous gas, having and odor like garlic; arseniureted hydrogen.

A genus of New Zealand birds about the size of a hen, with only short rudiments of wings, armed with a claw and without a tail; the kiwi. It is allied to the gigantic extinct moas of the same country.
Capable of being applied; fit or suitable to be applied; having relevance; as, this observation is applicable to the case under consideration. -- Ap"pli*ca*ble*ness, n.
A primary division of gastropods, including those having spiral shells. The two sides of the body are unequally developed.
A mineral of a white a slightly bluish color, usually massive. It is anhydrous sulphate of lime, and differs from gypsum in not containing water (whence the name).
A plant which has its seeds inclosed in a pericarp.
A terminal combining form: Having a stamen or stamens; staminate; as, monandrous, with one stamen; polyandrous, with many stamens.
A spore of some algæ, which has male functions.
A genus of leguminous shrubs, having long clusters of purple flowers; false or bastard indigo. Longfellow.
A small circle of the sphere parallel to the horizon; a circle or parallel of altitude. Two stars which have the same almucantar have the same altitude.
An imaginary art which aimed to transmute the baser metals into gold, to find the panacea, or universal remedy for diseases, etc. It led the way to modern chemistry.
A genus of plants, one species of which (A. Mexicanum) has lavender-blue flowers in dense clusters.
Plighted faith; marriage contract or promise.
A group of Coelenterata, comprising the Anthozoa Ctenophora. The sea anemone, or actinia, is a familiar example.
A combination of aceric acid with a salifiable base.
A shout of approbation, favor, or assent; eager expression of approval; loud applause. On such a day, a holiday having been voted by acclamation, an ordinary walk would not satisfy the children.
A group of annelids, so called because the species composing it have no special organs of respiration.
A group of cirripeds having abdominal appendages.

The goddess of retribution or vengeance; hence, retributive justice personified; divine vengeance. This is that ancient doctrine of nemesis who keeps watch in the universe, and lets no offense go unchastised.
An affectation of excessive elegance and refinement of language; high-flown diction.
A sentence in which the ideas fall, or become less important and striking, at the close; -- the opposite of climax. It produces a ridiculous effect.
To change, as a state, into a republic; to republican principles; as, France was republicanized; to republicanize the rising generation. D.
A preparation containing quinine and many other ingredients, often used in the treatment of malarial affections. It was invented by Dr.
A current which, though too feeble to blow the usual fuse or to injure at once telegraph or telephone instruments, will in time burn them out.
Neglect or failure to observe or fulfill.

The act of falsifying, or making false; a counterfeiting; the giving to a thing an appearance of something which it is not. To counterfeit the living image of king in his person exceedeth all falsifications.
The act of one who wears; the manner in which a thing wears; use; conduct; consumption. Belike he meant to ward, and there to see his wearing.
Beneath; below; in a lower place; under; as, a channel underneath the soil. Or sullen mole, that runneth underneath.
Three times. "Thrice in vain." Spenser.
The protuberance through which milk is drawn from the udder or breast of a mammal; a nipple; a pap; a mammilla; a dug; a tit.
The fat and fatty tissues of an animal, especially the harder fat about the kidneys and loins in beef and mutton, which, when melted and freed from the membranes, forms tallow.

In Greek choruses and dances, the movement of the chorus while turning from the right to the left of the orchestra; hence, the strain, or part of the choral ode, sung during this movement. Also sometimes used of a stanza of modern verse.
Settled pay or compensation for services, whether paid daily, monthly, or annually.
