A poetic foot of two long syllables, as in the Latin word leges.
A little sphere or spherical body; as, quicksilver, when poured upon a plane, divides itself into a great number of minute spherules.
A body or figure approaching to a sphere, but not perfectly spherical; esp., a solid generated by the revolution of an ellipse about one of its axes. Oblate spheroid, Prolate spheroid.
One who shuts or closes.
This or that female; the woman understood or referred to; the animal of the female sex, or object personified as feminine, which was spoken of. She loved her children best in every wise.
Rarely; not often; not frequently. Wisdom and youth are seldom joined in one.

One of the larger bodies of salt water, less than an ocean, found on the earth's surface; a body of salt water of second rank, generally forming part of, or connecting with, an ocean or a larger sea; as, the Mediterranean Sea; the Sea of Marmora; the North Sea
A deep bright red tinged with orange or yellow, -- of many tints and shades; a vivid or bright red color.
A riddle or sieve. [Prov.
imp. & p.
The act of one who renders, or that which is rendered. Specifically: (a) A version; translation; as, the rendering of the Hebrew text.
The act of remembering; a holding in mind, or bringing to mind; recollection. Lest fierce remembrance wake my sudden rage.

A bow or arch exhibiting, in concentric bands, the several colors of the spectrum, and formed in the part of the hemisphere opposite to the sun by the refraction and reflection of the sun's rays in drops of falling rain.
An ultimate atom, or simple, unextended point; something ultimate and indivisible.
One of the very small invisible particles of which all matter is supposed to consist.
Infectious particles or germs floating in the air; air made noxious by the presence of such particles or germs; noxious effluvia; malaria.
The human race; man, taken collectively. The proper study of mankind is man.
Length; measure or distance along the longest line; -- distinguished from breadth or thickness; as, the longitude of a room; rare now, except in a humorous sense. Sir H.
That part of a bridle or halter which encompasses the head. Shak.
Making hard or harder.
Figure; dress; array. [Colloq.] Were they all in full fig, the females with feathers on their heads, the males with chapeaux bras Prof.
Soon; in good season; seasonably; betimes; as, come early. Those that me early shall find me.
In the form of a cross; across; transversely. Longfellow.
A minute particle; an atom; a molecule.
A close union or junction of bodies; a touching or meeting.
False accusation of a crime or offense, maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another; malicious misrepresentation; slander; detraction. "Infamouse calumnies." Motley.
The part at the back of the hip, which, in man, forms one of the rounded protuberances on which he sits; the rump.
Consumed with, or as with, fire; scorched or dried, as with fire or heat; baked or hardened in the fire or the sun. Burnt ear, a black, powdery fungus which destroys grain.
The quality or state of being bright; splendor; luster; brilliancy; clearness. A sudden brightness in his face appear.
One who boils.
A plant, drug, or medicine, characterized by a fragrant smell, and usually by a warm, pungent taste, as ginger, cinnamon spices.
A substance which prevents or retards putrefaction, or destroys, or protects from, putrefactive organisms; as, salt, carbolic acid, alcohol, cinchona.

A misplacing or error in the order of time; an error in chronology by which events are misplaced in regard to each other, esp. one by which an event is placed too early; falsification of chronological relation.
A narrow passage; especially a walk or passage in a garden or park, bordered by rows of trees or bushes; a bordered way. I know each lane and every alley green.
Whole; not divided; entire; full; complete; absolute; as, a total departure from the evidence; a total loss. " Total darkness." "To undergo myself the total crime." Milton.
A star, usually five pointed and pierced; -- when used as a difference it indicates the third son.
A soluble, nitrogenous ferment, capable of converting starch and dextrin into sugar.
Having a bottom made of copper, as a tin boiler or other vessel, or sheathed with copper, as a ship.

A method of pronouncing Latin and Greek in which the vowels have their more familiar Continental values, as in German and Italian, the consonants being pronounced mostly as in English. The stricter form of this method of pronouncing Latin approaches the Roman,
Having the structure of the palate like that of the ostrich and emu.
To make conventional; to bring under the influence of, or cause to conform to, conventional rules; to establish by usage.
A period of seven days, usually that reckoned from one Sabbath or Sunday to the next. I fast twice in the week.

A portrait or representation of the face of our Savior on the alleged handkerchief of Saint Veronica, preserved at Rome; hence, a representation of this portrait, or any similar representation of the face of the Savior. Formerly called also Vernacle, and Verni

Resembling a worm in form or motions; vermicular; as, the vermiform process of the cerebellum. Vermiform appendix (Anat.), a slender blind process of the cæcum in man and some other animals; -- called also vermiform appendage, and vermiform process.
The flesh of a calf when killed and used for food.
The right of using and enjoying the profits of an estate or other thing belonging to another, without impairing the substance. Burrill.
In an erect position or posture; perpendicular; vertical, or nearly vertical; pointing upward; as, an upright tree. With chattering teeth, and bristling hair upright.
Situated beyond, or on the farther side; thither; -- correlative with hither.
Of the age of, or pertaining to, the Trias. -- n.
A union of three; three objects treated as one; a ternary; a trinity; as, a triad of deities.
Lying or being across, or in a crosswise direction; athwart; -- often opposed to Ant: longitudinal. Transverse axis (of an ellipse or hyperbola) (Geom.), that axis which passes through the foci.
A pit in which the dead body of a human being is deposited; a grave; a sepulcher. As one dead in the bottom of a tomb.
Situated or placed across something else; transverse; oblique. Moved contrary with thwart obliquities.
Of or pertaining to the end or extremity; forming the extremity; as, a terminal edge.
Strong; lusty; vigorous; robust; sinewy; muscular; hence, firm; resolute; dauntless. With hearts stern and stout.
Soft, and full of cavities; of an open, loose, pliable texture; as, a spongy excrescence; spongy earth; spongy cake; spongy bones.
Supreme or highest in power; superior to all others; chief; as, our sovereign prince.
The crime of buying or selling ecclesiastical preferment; the corrupt presentation of any one to an ecclesiastical benefice for money or reward. Piers Plowman.
Of or pertaining to the country of the ancient Silures; -- a term applied to the earliest of the Paleozoic eras, and also to the strata of the era, because most plainly developed in that country.
Pertaining to, consisting in, or affecting, the sense, or bodily organs of perception; relating to, or concerning, the body, in distinction from the spirit. Pleasing and sensual rites and ceremonies.
The half of a circle; the part of a circle bounded by its diameter and half of its circumference. (b) A semicircumference.
A roll of paper or parchment; a writing formed into a roll; a schedule; a list. The heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll.
Removed to a distance; not near; far away; distant; -- said in respect to time or to place; as, remote ages; remote lands. Places remote enough are in Bohemia.

Belonging to, or concerning, an individual person, company, or interest; peculiar to one's self; unconnected with others; personal; one's own; not public; not general; separate; as, a man's private opinion; private property; a private purse; private expenses o
The act or right of purchasing before others. Specifically: (a) The privilege or prerogative formerly enjoyed by the king of buying provisions for his household in preference to others.

The art of apprehending and interpreting ideas by the faculty of imagination; the art of idealizing in thought and in expression. For poetry is the blossom and the fragrance of all human knowledge, human thoughts, human passions, emotions, language.
Inclined to persist; having staying qualities; tenacious of position or purpose.

Capable or susceptible of passion, or of different passions; easily moved, excited or agitated; specifically, easily moved to anger; irascible; quick-tempered; as, a passionate nature. Homer's Achilles is haughty and passionate.
The last letter of the Greek alphabet. See Alpha.
The act or practice of recording anything by marks, figures, or characters.
A state or government in which the supreme power is lodged in the hands of a monarch.
The number of ten hundred thousand, or a thousand thousand, -- written 1,000, 000. See the Note under Hundred
Being at, or pertaining to, midday; belonging to, or passing through, the highest point attained by the sun in his diurnal course. "Meridian hour." Milton.
The office or dignity of a magistrate. Blackstone.
A solution of alkaline salts extracted from wood ashes; hence, any solution obtained by lixiviation.

An established formula for public worship, or the entire ritual for public worship in a church which uses prescribed forms; a formulary for public prayer or devotion. In the Roman Catholic Church it includes all forms and services in any language, in any part
That part of a garment which is turned back; specifically, the lap, or fold, of the front of a coat in continuation of collar. [Written also lappel and lapelle.]
The coarse, strong fiber of the East Indian Corchorus olitorius, and C. capsularis; also, the plant itself.
Of the age of the middle Mesozoic, including, as divided in England and Europe, the Lias, Oölite, and Wealden; -- named from certain rocks of the Jura mountains. -- n.
A line connecting points on the earth's surface having the same mean summer temperature.
A line connecting points on the earth's surface having the same mean temperature in the coldest month of the year.
Strained; tightly drawn; kept on the stretch; strict; very close or earnest; as, intense study or application; intense thought.
A collection of pus or purulent matter in any part of an animal body; an abscess.

Contrary to good, in a physical sense; contrary or opposed to advantage, happiness, etc.; bad; evil; unfortunate; disagreeable; unfavorable. Neither is it ill air only that maketh an ill seat, but ill ways, ill markets, and ill neighbors.
The business of a hosier.
A retailer of vegetables or fruits in their fresh or green state.

Pertaining to generation, or to the generative organs. Genital cord (Anat.), a cord developed in the fetus by the union of portions of the Wolffian and Müllerian ducts and giving rise to parts of the urogenital passages in both sexes.

The solemn rites used in the disposition of a dead human body, whether such disposition be by interment, burning, or otherwise; esp., the ceremony or solemnization of interment; obsequies; burial; -- formerly used in the plural. King James his funerals were pe
Deficient in physical strenght; weak; infirm; debilitated. Carried all the feeble of them upon asses.
Waiting in expectation; looking for; (Med.)
The scaling off of a bone, a rock, or a mineral, etc.; the state of being exfoliated.
Pregnant; with child.
The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
Ill-boding; portentous; as, dire omens.
One who, or that which, dips; especially, a vessel used to dip water or other liquid; a ladle.
The principal meal of the day, eaten by most people about midday, but by many (especially in cities) at a later hour.
Extending downward; -- said of a leaf whose base extends downward and forms a wing along the stem. -- De*cur"rent*ly, adv.
The business of a cutler.
The angle formed by the parting of two legs or branches; a fork; the point where a trunk divides; as, the crotch of a tree.
A high officer in the monarhical establishments of the Middle Ages.
The process of concreting; the process of uniting or of becoming united, as particles of matter into a mass; solidification.
A small slice of meat; a piece of flesh. God knows thou art a collop of my flesh.
An oblong case in which the silkworn lies in its chrysalis state. It is formed of threads of silk spun by the worm just before leaving the larval state.
A long outer garment formerly worn by men and women, as well as by soldiers as part of their uniform.

A rich stuff for shawls, acaris, etc., originally made in Cashmere from the soft wool found beneath the hair of the goats of Cashmere, Thibet, and the Himalayas. Some cashmere, of fine quality, is richly embroidered for sale to Europeans.
The natural color of flesh; rosy pink. Her complexion of the delicate carnation.

An indignity offered to God in words, writing, or signs; impiously irreverent words or signs addressed to, or used in reference to, God; speaking evil of God; also, the act of claiming the attributes or prerogatives of deity.
An animal of the genus Bos, especially the common species, B. taurus, including the bull, cow, and ox, in their full grown state; esp., an ox or cow fattened for food.
A bar or beam of wood or iron, connecting the opposite wheels of a carriage, on the ends of which the wheels revolve.
Performed with, or characterized by, art or skill. [Archaic] "Artful strains." "Artful terms." Milton.
The quality or principle of plants or other substances which constitutes their fragrance; agreeable odor; as, the aroma of coffee.
A taste which remains in the mouth after eating or drinking.
Swallowing, engrossing; as, an absorbing pursuit. -- Ab*sorb"ing, adv.
A person who has the use of property and reaps the profits of it. Wharton.
Having a siphon, or siphons, to convey water to the gills; belonging or pertaining to the Siphonobranchiata. -- n.

A high and narrow tank, with a central cylinder for the introduction of compressed air, used in the agitation and settling of pulp (pulverized ore and water) during treatment by the cyanide process; -- so named because, though originally devised in New Zealand
A pilot who has a branch or commission, as from Trinity House, England, for special navigation.

A projectile constructed so as to take the grooves of a rifle by means of a soft copper band firmly attached near its base or, formerly, by means of an envelope of soft metal. In small arms the modern projectile, having a soft core and harder jacket, is subjec
A vegetable tissue consisting of tracheæ.
Bred from the best blood through a long line; pure-blooded; -- said of stock, as horses. Hence, having the characteristics of such breeding; mettlesome; courageous; of elegant form, or the like.
Having a thin skin; hence, sensitive; irritable.
A genus of tropical apocynaceous shrubs having singularly twisted flowers. One species (Strophanthus hispidus) is used medicinally as a cardiac sedative and stimulant.
A shrubby species of wormwood (Artemisia Abrotanum) having aromatic foliage. It is sometimes used in making beer.
A suborder of Gephyrea, including those which have the body unarmed and the intestine opening anteriorly.
A genus of coarse herbs having small flowers in panicled cymes; figwort.
A suborder of Urodela, comprising salamanders.
A group of Coleoptera having a snoutlike head; the snout beetles, curculios, or weevils.
A ganoid fish having rhombic enameled scales; one of the Rhomboganoidei.
A suborder of Medusæ which includes very large species without marginal tentacles, but having large mouth lobes closely united at the edges. See Illust.
A division of Foraminifera including those having a manychambered shell.
A sulphide having more than one atom of sulphur in the molecule; -- contrasted with monosulphide.
A division of Radiolaria. It includes those having one more central capsules.
A division of Nudibranchiata including those which have numerous branchiæ on the back.
A tissue consisting of long and slender tubular cells, of which wood is mainly composed.
An order of fishes having barbels on the jaws. It includes the catfishes, or siluroids.
A foraminifer having but one chamber.
A myrtaceous genus of trees or shrubs, found in Australia and the South Sea Islands, and having very hard wood. Metrosideros vera is the true ironwood.
A genus of nemertean worms, parasitic in the gill cavity of clams and other bivalves. They have a large posterior sucker, like that of a leech.
A genus of evergreen shrubs from the Cape of Good Hope, having handsome foliage. Leucadendron argenteum is the silverboom of the colonists.
A genus of hepatic mosses, now much circumscribed, but formerly comprising most plants of the order, which is sometimes therefore called Jungermanniaceæ.
A compound of hydrocyanic acid with a base; -- distinguished from a cyanide, in which only the cyanogen so combines.

A brief poetical sentiment; hence, any brief sentiment, motto, or legend; especially, one inscribed on a ring. "The posy of a ring." Shak.
That which portends, or foretoken; esp., that which portends evil; a sign of coming calamity; an omen; a sign. Shak.
Any tree of the genus Populus; also, the timber, which is soft, and capable of many uses.
A knife with one or more blades, which fold into the handle so as to admit of being carried in the pocket.

A piece of leather stuffed or padded, worn by fencers to protect the breast. Dryden.
A plantigrade animal, or one that walks or steps on the sole of the foot, as man, and the bears.
(a) A leaflet of a pinnate leaf. See Illust.
A disease (morbus pediculous) consisting in the excessive multiplication of lice on the human body.
Purulent inflammation of the cellular or areolar tissue.
Having the quality of enduring; physically able to suffer or bear. Patient of severest toil and hardship.
A pie. See Patty.

The hairy or feathery appendage of the achenes of thistles, dandelions, and most other plants of the order Compositæ; also, the scales, awns, or bristles which represent the calyx in other plants of the same order.
Any American marsupial of the genera Didelphys and Chironectes. The common species of the United States is Didelphys Virginiana.

A little nucleus.
The quality or state of being novel; newness; freshness; recentness of origin or introduction. Novelty is the great parent of pleasure.

An elementary substance which forms one of the constituents of didymium. Symbol Nd.

That part of a blossom which secretes nectar, usually the base of the corolla or petals; also, the spur of such flowers as the larkspur and columbine, whether nectariferous or not. See the Illustration of Nasturtium.
A kind of shell limestone, whose strata form the middle one of the three divisions of the Triassic formation in Germany. See Chart, under Geology.
The act of sorrowing or expressing grief; lamentation; sorrow.
A single and continuous vegetable axis; -- opposed to sympodium.
The least quantity assignable, admissible, or possible, in a given case; hence, a thing of small consequence; -- opposed to Ant: maximum.
A mania for writing verses.
A light, colorless, gaseous, inflammable hydrocarbon, CH4; marsh gas. See Marsh gas, under Gas.
Gayety, with laughter; mirth; frolic. "Follies and light merriment." Spenser.
A pool or lake. Drayton.
A fibrous and muscular band lying within the longitudinal axis of the tongue in many mammals, as the dog.
A square sail bent upon a yard that hangs obliquely to the mast and is raised or lowered with the sail. Totten.

(a) A name of several kinds of water lilies; as Nelumbium speciosum, used in religious ceremonies, anciently in Egypt, and to this day in Asia; Nelumbium luteum, the American lotus; and Nymphæa Lotus and N. cærulea, the respectively white-flowered and blue-flo
In a general sense, any hatshaped, or conical, gastropod shell.

An officer who supplies the place of a superior in his absence; a representative of, or substitute for, another in the performance of any duty. The lawful magistrate, who is the vicegerent or lieutenant of God.
The six-legged young, or larva, of certain mites; -- sometimes used as a generic name. See Harvest mite, under Harvest.
Freedom from occupation or business; vacant time; time free from employment. The desire of leisure is much more natural than of business and care.
The Viburnum Tinus, an evergreen shrub or tree of the south of Europe, which flowers during the winter mouths. [Written also laurustine and laurestina.]
Formerly, a part or division of a county among the Anglo- Saxons. At present it consists of four or five hundreds, and is confined to the county of Kent.
A kind of feldspar commonly showing a beautiful play of colors, and hence much used for ornamental purposes. The finest specimens come from Labrador.
A cookroom; the room of a house appropriated to cookery. Cool was his kitchen, though his brains were hot.

Any one of numerous species of birds constituting the family Alcedinidæ. Most of them feed upon fishes which they capture by diving and seizing then with the beak; others feed only upon reptiles, insects, etc.
A catkin or ament. See Ament.
A partial, secondary, or small involucre. See Illust.
The act of intimating; also, the thing intimated.
Intervening space. Bp.
Total loss of reputation; public disgrace; dishonor; ignominy; indignity. The afflicted queen would not yield, and said she would not .

Not dependent; free; not subject to control by others; not relying on others; not subordinate; as, few men are wholly independent. A dry, but independent crust.
The act of indenting or state of being indented.
A Japanese measure of length equal to about two and one twelfth yards. [Written also ink.]
Exemption or freedom from punishment, harm, or loss. Heaven, though slow to wrath, Is neimpunity defied.
Any animal of the genus Hyrax, of which about four species are known. They constitute the order Hyracoidea.
One of the nutritive zooids of a hydroid colony. Also applied to the proboscis or manubrium of a hydroid medusa.
One who holds to a heresy; one who believes some doctrine contrary to the established faith or prevailing religion. A man that is an heretic, after the first and second admonition, reject.
The first, or preaxial, digit of the hind limb, corresponding to the pollux in the fore limb; the great toe; the hind toe of birds.
One of several species of sea birds of the genus Puffinus; esp., P. major, the greater shearwarter, and P.
A kind of plum of medium size, roundish shape, greenish flesh, and delicious flavor. It is called in France Reine Claude, after the queen of Francis I.
A white or gray tasteless powder, the oxide of the element glucinum; -- formerly called glucine.
The opening from the pharynx into the larynx or into the trachea. See Larynx.
Any one of a genus (Gentiana) of herbaceous plants with opposite leaves and a tubular four- or five-lobed corolla, usually blue, but sometimes white, yellow, or red. See Illust.
One of the Gastropoda. [Written also gasteropod.]
(a) A mass or knot of nervous matter, including nerve cells, usually forming an enlargement in the course of a nerve. (b) A node, or gland in the lymphatic system; as, a lymphatic ganglion.
A round gall produced on the leaves and shoots of various species of the oak tree. See Gall, and Nutgall.

A market place or public place in Rome, where causes were judicially tried, and orations delivered to the people.
Presage of coming ill; expectation of misfortune.
The European polecat; also, its fur.
A hook for catching fish.

A genus (Abies) of coniferous trees, often of large size and elegant shape, some of them valued for their timber and others for their resin. The species are distinguished as the balsam fir, the silver fir, the red fir, etc.
A deed or act; especially, a heroic act; a deed of renown; an adventurous or noble achievement; as, the exploits of Alexander the Great. Ripe for exploits and mighty enterprises.

A flag; a banner; a standard; esp., the national flag, or a banner indicating nationality, carried by a ship or a body of soldiers; -- as distinguished from flags indicating divisions of the army, rank of naval officers, or private signals, and the like. Hang
A large Australian bird, of two species (Dromaius Novæ- Hollandiæ and D. irroratus), related to the cassowary and the ostrich.
Dryness; want of rain or of water; especially, such dryness of the weather as affects the earth, and prevents the growth of plants; aridity. The drought of March hath pierced to the root.
(Anat.) See Meson.
The act of giving or bestowing; a grant. After donation there an absolute change and alienation of the property of the thing given.
A dividing membrane or thin partition, commonly with an opening through it.
A casting down; depression. [Obs.
The act of defining; determination of the limits; as, the telescope accurate in definition.
One who affects special finery or gives undue attention to dress; a fop; a coxcomb.
That with which one dabs; hence, a pad or other device used by printers, engravers, etc., as for dabbing type or engraved plates with ink.
A mongrel or inferior dog. They .
One of the classes of the arthropods, including lobsters and crabs; -- so called from the crustlike shell with which they are covered.

The act of nailing or fastening a person to a cross, for the purpose of putting him to death; the use of the cross as a method of capital punishment.
A forked support; a crotch. The crotchets of their cot in columns rise.
A conspicuous wild flower (Centaurea Cyanus), growing in grainfields.

Cerium oxide, CeO2, a white infusible substance constituting about one per cent of the material of the common incandescent mantle.
A large bird, of the genus Casuarius, found in the east Indies. It is smaller and stouter than the ostrich.
A window sash opening on hinges affixed to the upright side of the frame into which it is fitted. (Poetically) A window.
The complex radical, CO.OH, regarded as the essential and characteristic constituent which all oxygen acids of carbon (as formic, acetic, benzoic acids, etc.) have in common; -- called also oxatyl.

The great band commissural fibers which unites the two cerebral hemispheres. See corpus callosum, under Carpus.

Alkarsin; a colorless, poisonous, arsenical liquid, As2(CH3)4, spontaneously inflammable and possessing an intensely disagreeable odor. It is the type of a series of compounds analogous to the nitrogen compounds called hydrazines.

The act of battering or beating.
A positive or nonacid constituent of compound, either elementary, or, if compound, performing the functions of an element.
A valuable grain, of the family of grasses, genus Hordeum, used for food, and for making malt, from which are prepared beer, ale, and whisky. Barley bird (Zoöl.), the siskin.
A gigantic African tree (Adansonia digitata), also naturalized in India. See Adansonia.

The back and sides of a pig salted and smoked; formerly, the flesh of a pig salted or fresh. Bacon beetle (Zoöl.), a beetle (Dermestes lardarius) which, especially in the larval state, feeds upon bacon, woolens, furs, etc.
One attached to another person or thing, as a part of a suite or staff. Specifically: One attached to an embassy.

One of the classes of vertebrates.

A tree, usually growing in moist land, and belonging to the genus Alnus. The wood is used by turners, etc.; the bark by dyers and tanners.

A web-footed bird, of the genus Diomedea, of which there are several species. They are the largest of sea birds, capable of long- continued flight, and are often seen at great distances from the land.
A spore borne at the extremity of the cells of fructification in fungi.

The act of becoming, or state of being, intemperate; excess in any kind of action or indulgence; any immoderate indulgence of the appetites or passions. God is in every creature; be cruel toward none, neither abuse any by intemperance.

An instrument for measuring or comparing the intensites of the colors of the spectrum.

The act of retracting what has been said; recantation.
To estimate too highly; to overvalue.

An extensive suborder of fresh-water physostomous fishes having the anterior vertebræ united and much modified; the Eventognathi.

A division of opisthobranchiate mollusks, having no shell except while very young. The gills are naked and situated upon the back or sides.
A group of nudibranchiate Mollusca having on the back papilliform or branched organs serving as gills.
A genus of plants of the order Nyctoginaceæ, from tropical South America, having the flowers surrounded by large bracts.

One who mends or repairs.

The quality or state of being hard, literally or figuratively. The habit of authority also had given his manners some peremptory hardness.
A light, liquid food, made by boiling meal of maize, oatmeal, or fiour in water or milk; thin porridge.
The act of moving in any manner; traveling; as, the going is bad.

The act of distending; the act of stretching in breadth or in all directions; the state of being Distended; as, the distention of the lungs.

The act of ascribing, imputing, or affirming to belong; also, that which is ascribed.

Any one of numerous species of American singing birds belonging to Vireo and allied genera of the family Vireonidæ. In many of the species the back is greenish, or olive-colored.

Any one of several species of large sting rays belonging to Trygon and allied genera.
Any one of numerous species of marine univalve shells belonging to Trochus and many allied genera of the family Trochidæ. Some of the species are called also topshells.

Spun yarn used in racking ropes.

A dance performed by two persons in circular figures with a whirling motion; also, a piece of music composed in triple measure for this kind of dance.

To make, or give forth, small, quick, sharp sounds, as a piece of metal does when struck; to clink. As sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
Any one of several species of fishes belonging to Polynemus and allied genera. They have numerous long pectoral filaments.

To quell; to crush; to silence or put down. [Colloq.] Oh 't was your luck and mine to be squelched.
To sprout; to bud; to germinate, as barley steeped for malt.
To utter a soliloquy; to talk to one's self.
A contrivance for turning a spit by means of a fly or wheel moved by the current of ascending air in a chimney.

To tremble or shake with fear, horrer, or aversion; to shiver with cold; to quake. "With shuddering horror pale." Milton.

To walk awkwardly and unsteadily, as if the knees were weak; to shuffle along.

To utter a harsh, shrill cry; to make a sharp outcry, as in terror or acute pain; to scream; to shriek. "The screech owl, screeching loud." Shak.
Any plant of the umbelliferous genus Sanicula, reputed to have healing powers.
The willow; willow twigs. [Poetic] Tennyson.
To make a low, heavy, continued sound; as, the thunder rumbles at a distance. In the mean while the skies 'gan rumble sore.

One who, in the 17th century and the early part of the 18th, claimed to belong to a secret society of philosophers deeply versed in the secrets of nature, -- the alleged society having existed, it was stated, several hundred years.
To render turbid or muddy; to stir up; to roil.
To make over again; to restore to freshness or vigor; to renew. All nature feels the reniovating force Of winter.

To rekindle; to light again. Relumed her ancient light, not kindled new.

To move backward and forward; to vibrate like a pendulum; to swing; to sway.

A large drinking cup, with a wide mouth, supported on a foot or standard.
Any thing or being regarded as having the power of spontaneous motion or action. Huxley.

A sect of dissenters from the ecclesiastical system of the Roman Catholic Church, who in the 13th century were driven by persecution to the valleys of Piedmont, where the sect survives. They profess substantially Protestant principles.
A genus of polypetalous herbaceous plants, including all kinds of violets.

The formation of varices; varicosity.

The female of the tiger. Holland.

A machine consisting of many pulleys; specifically, an apparatus formerly used for reducing luxations.
A medicine for affections of the lungs.

Capable of producing bone; having the power to change cartilage or other tissue into bone.

The sense by which the impressions made on the olfactory organs by the odorous particles in the atmosphere are perceived.

A tract of soft, wet ground; a marsh; a fen. Morass ore.

The animals of any given area or epoch; as, the fauna of America; fossil fauna; recent fauna.

The science of Mollusca, and of the shells which they form; malacology.
The chief officer of a regiment; an officer ranking next above a lieutenant colonel and next below a brigadier general.
A squirrel-like animal of the genus Tamias, sometimes called the striped squirrel, chipping squirrel, ground squirrel, hackee. The common species of the United States is the Tamias striatus.
The pincherlike claw of Crustacea and Arachnida.

An unctuous preparation for external application, of a consistence intermediate between that of an ointment and a plaster, so that it can be spread upon cloth without the use of heat, but does not melt when applied to the skin.
A remedy for all diseases; a panacea.
The curve formed by a rope or chain of uniform density and perfect flexibility, hanging freely between two points of suspension, not in the same vertical line.

To move in a caracole, or in caracoles; to wheel. Prince John caracoled within the lists.
A plant of the genus Ranunculus, or crowfoot, particularly R. bulbosus, with bright yellow flowers; -- called also butterflower, golden cup, and kingcup.

A mineral of great hardness, and, when transparent, of much beauty. It occurs in hexagonal prisms, commonly of a green or bluish green color, but also yellow, pink, and white.
A small building, or a part of a building, more or less open, constructed in a place commanding a fine prospect.
A species of Capsicum, or Guinea pepper (C. annuum).
A genus of plants, mostly of tropical America, many species of which are grown as ornamental plants. The leaves are curiously one- sided, and often exhibit brilliant colors.
A window forming a bay or recess in a room, and projecting outward from the wall, either in a rectangular, polygonal, or semicircular form; -- often corruptly called a bow window.
A perennial herbaceous plant of almost treelike size (Musa sapientum); also, its edible fruit. See Musa.
A two-masted Arab or Indian trading vessel, used in Indian Ocean.

A genus of plants; also, the most important species (Arnica montana), native of the mountains of Europe, used in medicine as a narcotic and stimulant.
The light of an arc lamp.
A transparent, pale green variety of beryl, used as a gem. See Beryl.
A genus of insects belonging to the order Hemiptera and family Aphidæ, including numerous species known as plant lice and green flies.
The great artery which carries the blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs; the main trunk of the arterial system.
A description of blood vessels and lymphatics.
A genus of water fowls, of the order Anseres, including certain species of fresh-water ducks.
The constructive metabolism of the body, as distinguished from katabolism.
Inclined to love; having a propensity to love, or to sexual enjoyment; loving; fond; affectionate; as, an amorous disposition.
The study or science of algæ or seaweeds.
A red star of the first magnitude, situated in the eye of Taurus; the Bull's Eye. It is the bright star in the group called the Hyades.
A diseased condition of the system, brought about by the continued use of alcoholic liquors.
The placenta and membranes with which the fetus is connected, and which come away after delivery.

A sack or bag of wool; specifically, the seat of the lord chancellor of England in the House of Lords, being a large, square sack of wool resembling a divan in form.

The quality or condition of being urgent; insistence; pressure; as, the urgency of a demand or an occasion.
The commotion or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar, and confusion of voices; hurly-burly; noisy confusion. What meaneth the noise of this tumult 1 Sam.
The art of dressing up; artifice; stratagem; fraud; imposture.
The doing or performing of any business; management of any affair; performance.

Affected by tabes; tabetic.
A consonance or harmony of sounds, agreeable to the ear, whether the sounds are vocal or instrumental, or both. The trumpets sound, And warlike symphony in heard around.

The light of the sun, or the place where it shines; the direct rays of the sun, the place where they fall, or the warmth and light which they give. But all sunshine, as when his beams at noon Culminate from the equator.
The working room of an artist.

An impropriety or incongruity of language in the combination of words or parts of a sentence; esp., deviation from the idiom of a language or from the rules of syntax. A barbarism may be in one word; a solecism must be of more.
The condition of a slave; the state of entire subjection of one person to the will of another. Disguise thyself as thou wilt, still, slavery, said I, still thou art a bitter draught!
A member of a senate. The duke and senators of Venice greet you.
Tending to calm, moderate, or tranquilize; specifically (Med.), allaying irritability and irritation; assuaging pain.
The art or science of projecting or delineating shadows as they fall in nature. Gwilt.
A peasant or cultivator of the soil. [India] The Indian ryot and the Egyptian fellah work for less pay than any other laborers in the world.

The act or process of renovating; the state of being renovated or renewed. Thomson.
The act or process of reclaiming.
The acts, arts, or boastful pretensions of a quack; false pretensions to any art; empiricism. Carlyle.

A nice point of exactness in conduct, ceremony, or proceeding; particularity or exactness in forms; as, the punctilios of a public ceremony. They will not part with the least punctilio in their opinions and practices.
The act, practice, or art of singing psalms or sacred songs; also, psalms collectively, or a collection of psalms.
A game of chance, in which four sea shells, each called a prop, are used instead of dice.
A follower of Plato; a Platonist.
An allowance of food bestowed in charity; a mess of victuals; hence, a small charity gift; a dole. "A good pitaunce." Chaucer.
The art and science of discovering the predominant temper, and other characteristic qualities of the mind, by the outward appearance, especially by the features of the face.
A description of the laws of the human voice, or sounds uttered by the organs of speech.

The act or process of penetrating, piercing, or entering; also, the act of mentally penetrating into, or comprehending, anything difficult. And to each in ward part, With gentle penetration, though unseen, Shoots invisible virtue even to the deep.
The act or process of making a pad or of inserting stuffing.
The amount of coal or ore put out from one or more mines, or the quantity of material produced by, or turned out from, one or more furnaces or mills, in a given time.
The answer of a god, or some person reputed to be a god, to an inquiry respecting some affair or future event, as the success of an enterprise or battle. Whatso'er she saith, for oracles must stand.

The power of choosing; the right of choice or election; an alternative. There is an option left to the United States of America, whether they will be respectable and prosperous, or contemptible and miserable, as a nation.
The condition of being numb; that state of a living body in which it loses, wholly or in part, the power of feeling or motion.
The act or process of negotiating; a treating with another respecting sale or purchase. etc.
An official expounder of Mohammedan law.
A minute portion of time; a point of time; an instant; as, at thet very moment. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.
The articles made or sold by milliners, as headdresses, hats or bonnets, laces, ribbons, and the like.
The study of physiognomy; the art of discovering the character of persons by their features, or the lines of the face.

The union of man and woman as husband and wife; the nuptial state; marriage; wedlock. If either of you know any impediment, why ye may not be lawfully joined together in matrimony, ye do now confessit.
The quality or condition of being major or greater; superiority. Specifically: (a) The military rank of a major.

Doing grand things; admirable in action; displaying great power or opulence, especially in building, way of living, and munificence. A prince is never so magnificent As when he's sparing to enrich a few With the injuries of many.
A spring of water; hence, water, or a pure, transparent liquid like water. A fountain bubbled up, whose lymph serene Nothing of earthly mixture might distain.
The act or process of litigating; a suit at law; a judicial contest.

A discharge of atmospheric electricity, accompanied by a vivid flash of light, commonly from one cloud to another, sometimes from a cloud to the earth. The sound produced by the electricity in passing rapidly through the atmosphere constitutes thunder.

A book in which a summary of accounts is laid up or preserved; the final book of record in business transactions, in which all debits and credits from the journal, etc., are placed under appropriate heads. [Written also leger.]
The rank, quality, state, or attributes of a king; royal authority; sovereign power; rule; dominion; monarchy. Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom.
Incapable of being seen; not perceptible by vision; not visible. To us invisible, or dimly seen In these thy lowest works.

The entrance of an enemy into a country with purposes of hostility; a sudden or desultory incursion or invasion; raid; encroachment. The loss of Shrewsbury exposed all North Wales to the daily inroads of the enemy.
The act of writing on the back of a note, bill, or other written instrument.

The act or process of using formulas sung or spoken, with occult ceremonies, for the purpose of raising spirits, producing enchantment, or affecting other magical results; enchantment. "Mysterious ceremony and incantation." Burke.

Not possible; incapable of being done, of existing, etc.; unattainable in the nature of things, or by means at command; insuperably difficult under the circumstances; absurd or impracticable; not feasible. With men this is impossible; but with God all things a
The work of one who makes images or visible representation of objects; imitation work; images in general, or in mass. "Painted imagery." Shak.
An expression of frolic and exultation, and sometimes of wonder. B.
The doctrine of the Hedonic sect.
A book of reference, to be carried in the hand; a manual; a guidebook.
A book of directions and information for travelers, tourists, etc.
The act or result of guiding; the superintendence or assistance of a guide; direction; government; a leading. His studies were without guidance and without plan.
The act or operation of melting or rendering fluid by heat; the act of melting together; as, the fusion of metals.
A contemptuous name for a liveried servant or a footman.
A pavement or sidewalk of flagstones; flagstones, collectively.

A hobby ; freak; whim. -- Fad"dist, n.
The act or process of extricating or disentangling; a freeing from perplexities; disentanglement.
The fling of a horse, or ordinary kicking back of his heels; a gambol.

The public function of an ambassador; the charge or business intrusted to an ambassador or to envoys; a public message to; foreign court concerning state affairs; hence, any solemn message. He sends the angels on embassies with his decrees.
The act or process of producing or refining with labor; improvement by successive operations; refinement.

The act of edifying, or the state of being edified; a building up, especially in a moral or spiritual sense; moral, intellectual, or spiritual improvement; instruction. The assured edification of his church.

A heap of dung.

The termination of union; separation; disjunction; as, the disunion of the body and the soul.
The art and practice of conducting negotiations between nations (particularly in securing treaties), including the methods and forms usually employed.
The cessation of use; disuse; discontinuance of practice, custom, or fashion. The desuetude abrogated the law, which, before, custom had established.
The power, spirit, or principles of a despot; absolute control over others; tyrannical sway; tyranny. "The despotism of vice." Byron.

A mistress of a family, who is a lady; a womam in authority; especially, a lady. Then shall these lords do vex me half so much, As that proud dame, the lord protector's wife.

The outline of a figure or body, or the line or lines representing such an outline; the line that bounds; periphery. Titian's coloring and contours.

A judicial court of chancery, which in England and in the United States is distinctively a court with equity jurisdiction.
The young of the cow, or of the Bovine family of quadrupeds. Also, the young of some other mammals, as of the elephant, rhinoceros, hippopotamus, and whale.
The younger of two brothers; a younger brother or son; the youngest son. The cadet of an ancient and noble family.
The property of floating on the surface of a liquid, or in a fluid, as in the atmosphere; specific lightness, which is inversely as the weight compared with that of an equal volume of water.
An arm or branch of a tree, esp. a large arm or main branch.

The rising light of the morning; the dawn of day; the redness of the sky just before the sun rises.

The art of measuring altitudes, or heights.
Proper to be added; positive; -- opposed to subtractive.

A garment worn below another.
The daughter of one's son or daughter.
Inclosed, or nearly inclosed, with land; as, the Mediterranean Sea, between Europe and Africa.

Having but one gill, as certain molluscs.

Like or pertaining to the genus Trichiurus or family Trichiuridæ, comprising the scabbard fishes and hairtails.
Having three acute or setigerous points; tricuspidate.
Having four leaves; consisting of four distinct leaves or leaflets.
Containing four distinct petals, or flower leaves; as, a tetrapetalous corolla.
An adjustable traveling bag consisting of two cases, the larger slipping over the other.
Occupying the same time; pertaining to, or having the properties of, a tautochrone.

Having a forked tongue, as that of snakes and some lizards.
Having but one hand, or one workman; also, alone; unassisted.

Having four horns, or hornlike organs; as, a quadricornous beetle.

Having seeds inclosed in a pod or other pericarp.

Any item of movable or immovable property except the freehold, or the things which are parcel of it. It is a more extensive term than goods or effects.
One who balances, or uses a balance.
One of a group of squirrels, of the genera Pteromus and Sciuropterus, having parachute-like folds of skin extending from the fore to the hind legs, which enable them to make very long leaps.
To produce counter irritation in; to treat with one morbid process for the purpose of curing another.

The quality or state of being universal; unlimited extension or application; generality; -- distinguished from particularity; as, the unversality of a proposition; the unversality of sin; the unversality of the Deluge.

One of the triad of Hindoo gods. He is the avenger or destroyer, and in modern worship symbolizes the reproductive power of nature.
One who signs or subscribes his name; as, a memorial with a hundred signers.

One who kills or who murders a king; specifically (Eng.Hist.), one of the judges who condemned Charles I. to death.
Like pulp; consisting of pulp; soft; fleshy; succulent; as, the pulpy covering of a nut; the pulpy substance of a peach or a cherry.

The ninth part of movable goods, formerly payable to the clergy on the death of persons in their parishes. Mozley & W.
To labialize. Brewer.
A board, as upon a guidepost having upon it directions or information as to the road. Lowell.
To some, or any, other place; as, you will have to go elsewhither for it. R.

An atmosphere of rare matter, composed principally of incandescent hydrogen gas, surrounding the sun and enveloping the photosphere. Portions of the chromosphere are here and there thrown up into enormous tongues of flame.
The act or practice of prostituting or offering the body to an indiscriminate intercourse with men; common lewdness of a woman.

Of or pertaining to the shell of a tortoise; resembling a tortoise shell; having the color or markings of a tortoise shell.

A division of pulmonate mollusks having the breathing organ situated on the neck, as in the common snail.
A group of extinct Reptilia, intermediate in structure (especially with regard to the pelvis) between reptiles and birds. -- Or`ni*tho*scel"i*dan, a.
Having many pods or seed vessels.
A rock showing under the microscope the structure of a graphic granite (pegmatite). -- Mi`cro*peg`ma*tit"ic, a.
Having the pallial line entire, or without a sinus, as certain bivalve shells.
A show or exhibition having a great number of scenes or views.
