To treat (cotton fiber or fabrics) with a solution of caustic alkali. Such treatment causes the fiber to shrink in length and become stronger and more receptive of dyes.
To discharge the menses; to have the catamenial flow.

In the southwestern part of the united States, a bullock or heifer that has not been branded, and is unclaimed or wild; -- said to be from Maverick, the name of a cattle owner in Texas who naglected to brand his cattle.
A kind of coarse punch with a rasplike face, used for making a rough surface on etching ground, or on the naked copper, the effect after biting being very similar to stippled lines.
To move quickly, esp. with a sudden turn; hence, to dodge; to escape by a quick turn; --obs.
To link together; to unite closely or firmly, as by a chain. Two bosoms interchained with an oath.
To fasten or bind, as with a knot; to knot together. Fuller.
A figurative construction, changing or inverting the natural order of words or clauses; as, "echoed the hills" for "the hills echoed." With a violent hyperbaton to transpose the text. Milton.

(a) The representation made of the aspect of the heavens at the moment of a person's birth, by which the astrologer professed to foretell the events of the person's life; especially, the sign of the zodiac rising above the horizon at such a moment. (b) The dia
A post at the fork of a road, with a guideboard on it, to direct travelers.
To shiver; to have chills. [Obs.
A stone laid over, or erected near, a grave, usually with an inscription, to preserve the memory of the dead; a tombstone.
To play or game for money or other stake.
To commit fornication; to have unlawful sexual intercourse.
Having a tendency to flop or flap; as, a floppy hat brim. G.
To lock with two bolts; to fasten with double security. Tatler.
One who, or that which, has power to dissolve or dissipate. Thou kind dissolver of encroaching care.
To drop the bait gently on the surface of the water. To catch a club by dapping with a grasshoper.
One who comes, or who has come; one who has arrived, and is present. All comers, all who come, or offer, to take part in a matter, especially in a contest or controversy.

To adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast, especially by twining round or embracing; as, the tendril of a vine clings to its support; -- usually followed by to or together. And what hath life for thee That thou shouldst cling to it thus Mrs.
Work consisting of or showing checkers varied alternately as to colors or materials.

A shrub (the Myrica cerifera, or wax-bearing myrtle), common in North America, the little nuts of which are covered with a greenish white wax, which was formerly, used for hardening candles; -- also called bayberry tree, bayberry, or candleberry.
A kind of tobacco for smoking, made of the dried leaves, coarsely broken; -- so called from the rush baskets in which it is packed in South America. McElrath.
A kind of pipe, used by the North American Indians for smoking tobacco. The bowl is usually made of soft red stone, and the tube is a long reed often ornamented with feathers.
To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor; -- usually with the reciprocal pronoun. You have so bestirred your valor.
To pommel; to beat, as with a stick; figuratively, to assail or criticise in conversation, or in writing. Thackeray.
To cover as with a muffler; to wrap up. Bemuffled with the externals of religion.
To furnish with a fringe; to form a fringe upon; to adorn as with fringe. Fuller.
A bickern; a bench anvil with a long beak, adapted to reach the interior surface of sheet metal ware; the horn of an anvil.
To become barbarous. The Roman empire was barbarizing rapidly from the time of Trajan.
One of a primitive people supposed to have lived in prehistoric times, in Central Asia, east of the Caspian Sea, and north of the Hindoo
A letting or renting, esp. a license to inclose land in a forest with a low hedge and a ditch, under a yearly rent.

(a) An imaginary belt in the heavens, 16º or 18º broad, in the middle of which is the ecliptic, or sun's path. It comprises the twelve constellations, which one constituted, and from which were named, the twelve signs of the zodiac.
Passionate ardor in the pursuit of anything; eagerness in favor of a person or cause; ardent and active interest; engagedness; enthusiasm; fervor. "Ambition varnished o'er with zeal." Milton.
Ay; yea; -- a word which expresses affirmation or consent; -- opposed to Ant: no.
The earth and the surrounding heavens; the creation; the system of created things; existent creation; the universe. The invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen.
Tending to wither; causing to shrink or fade. -- With"er*ing*ly, adv.
The act of withdrawing; withdrawment; retreat; retraction. Fielding.
Proof against penetration or permeation by water; impervious to water; as, a waterproof garment; a waterproof roof.

A molding, or other projection, in the wall of a building, to throw off the water, -- generally used in the United States for the first table above the surface of the ground (see Table, n., 9), that is, for the table at the top of the foundation and the beginn
A tower in which a sentinel is placed to watch for enemies, the approach of danger, or the like.
A variety of allanite from Sweden supposed to contain wasium.
An outbuilding for washing, esp. one for washing clothes; a laundry.
A storehouse for wares, or goods. Addison.
One who wards or keeps; a keeper; a guard. "The warders of the gate." Dryden.
The Chinese name of one or two species of bamboo, or jointed cane, of the genus Phyllostachys. The slender stems are much used for walking sticks.
a. & n.
Full of delight or pleasure, especially that of the senses; ministering to sensuous or sensual gratification; exciting sensual desires; luxurious; sensual. Music arose with its voluptuous swell.

A unit of electric measurement equal to the product of a volt and an ampere. For direct current it is a measure of power and is the same as a watt; for alternating current it is a measure of apparent power.
A hydrous phosphate of iron of a blue to green color, growing darker on exposure. It occurs in monoclinic crystals, also fibrous, massive, and earthy.

A structure of considerable magnitude, usually with arches or supported on trestles, for carrying a road, as a railroad, high above the ground or water; a bridge; especially, one for crossing a valley or a gorge. Cf.
A rare metallic element of which little is known. It is said by Scacchi to have been extracted from a yellowish incrustation from the cracks of a Vesuvian lava erupted in 1631.
Full of venom; noxious to animal life; poisonous; as, the bite of a serpent may be venomous.
The act of vacillating; a moving one way and the other; a wavering. His vacillations, or an alternation of knowledge and doubt.

The act of usurping, or of seizing and enjoying; an authorized, arbitrary assumption and exercise of power, especially an infringing on the rights of others; specifically, the illegal seizure of sovereign power; -- commonly used with of, also used with on or u
A morbid swelling of the scrotum due to extravasation of urine into it.
Aloft; on high; in a direction contrary to that of gravity; toward or in a higher place or position; above; -- the opposite of Ant: down. But up or down, By center or eccentric, hard to tell.
p. p.
The quality or state of being uncertain.
A machine for setting type or for casting lines of type and setting them.
(a) The ear drum, or middle ear. Sometimes applied incorrectly to the tympanic membrane.
pl. of Turf.
Any plant of the liliaceous genus Tulipa. Many varieties are cultivated for their beautiful, often variegated flowers.
Belief; faith; fidelity. Bid her alight And hertroth plight.
A tree-legged stool, table, or other support; especially, a stand to hold a kettle or similar vessel near the fire; a tripod. [Written also trevet.]
The seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice.
Fitted to trench or cut; gutting; sharp. " Trenchant was the blade." Chaucer.
An overhead rail forming a track on which a trolley runs to convey a load, as in a shop.
One who trains; an instructor; especially, one who trains or prepares men, horses, etc., for exercises requiring physical agility and strength.
A plate of timber for the end of a beam or joist to rest on. Gwilt
A tackle used in hoisting and lowering the topmast.
A rope used for hoisting and lowering a topmast, and for other purposes.
Folly; trifling.
The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
The quality or state of being timid; timorousness; timidness.
Wanting courage to meet danger; easily frightened; timorous; not bold; fearful; shy. Poor is the triumph o'er the timid hare.

A very large and powerful carnivore (Felis tigris) native of Southern Asia and the East Indies. Its back and sides are tawny or rufous yellow, transversely striped with black, the tail is ringed with black, the throat and belly are nearly white.
Lacking thought; careless; inconsiderate; rash; as, a thoughtless person, or act.
A mineral of a brown to black color, or, as in the variety orangite, orange-yellow. It is essentially a silicate of thorium.
Any one of several prickly composite plants, especially those of the genera Cnicus, Craduus, and Onopordon. The name is often also applied to other prickly plants.
A solid figure inclosed or bounded by four triangles.
One who governs by terrorism or intimidation; specifically, an agent or partisan of the revolutionary tribunal during the Reign of Terror in France. Burke.
Literally, a boundary; a border; a limit.

A state of holding on in a continuous course; manner of continuity; constant mode; general tendency; course; career. Along the cool sequestered vale of life They kept the noiseless tenor of their away.
The quality or state of being tenacious; as, tenacity, or retentiveness, of memory; tenacity, or persistency, of purpose.

The process of giving the requisite degree of hardness or softness to a substance, as iron and steel; especially, the process of giving to steel the degree of hardness required for various purposes, consisting usually in first plunging the article, when heated

A tree of East Indies (Tectona grandis) which furnishes an extremely strong and durable timber highly valued for shipbuilding and other purposes; also, the timber of the tree. [Written also teek.] African teak, a tree (Oldfieldia Africana) of Sierra Leone; als

An ancient and celebrated Christian hymn, of uncertain authorship, but often ascribed to St. Ambrose; -- so called from the first words "Te Deum laudamus." It forms part of the daily matins of the Roman Catholic breviary, and is sung on all occasions of thanks
Consisting of, or covered with, tar; like tar.
A plant of the genus Artemisa (A. dracunculus), much used in France for flavoring vinegar.
One of the Tardigrada.
A rod carrying a tappet or tappets, as one for closing the valves in a Cornish pumping engine.
That which takes up or tightens; specifically, a device in a sewing machine for drawing up the slack thread as the needle rises, in completing a stitch.
A small table or flat surface.
The lapping of chamfered edges of planks to make a smooth surface, as for a bulkhead.
A theory of generation in which each germ is supposed to contain the germs of all subsequent generations; -- the opposite of epigenesis.

The state of being suspended; specifically, a state of uncertainty and expectation, with anxiety or apprehension; indetermination; indecision; as, the suspense of a person waiting for the verdict of a jury. Ten days the prophet in suspense remained.

The act of overturning, or the state of being overturned; entire overthrow; an overthrow from the foundation; utter ruin; destruction; as, the subversion of a government; the subversion of despotic power; the subversion of the constitution. The subversion [by

Fitted or disposed to subserve; useful in an inferior capacity; serving to promote some end; subordinate; hence, servile, truckling. Scarce ever reading anything which he did not make subservient in one kind or other.
The quality or state of being sublime (in any sense of the adjective).
The act of subjugating, or the state of being subjugated.

Firm as a stub or stump; stiff; unbending; unyielding; persistent; hence, unreasonably obstinate in will or opinion; not yielding to reason or persuasion; refractory; harsh; -- said of persons and things; as, stubborn wills; stubborn ore; a stubborn oak; as st
A Russian river craft used for transporting freight.
An artifice or trick in war for deceiving the enemy; hence, in general, artifice; deceptive device; secret plot; evil machination. Fit for treasons, stratagems, and spoils.

An affection of one or both eyes, in which the optic axes can not be directed to the same object, -- a defect due either to undue contraction or to undue relaxation of one or more of the muscles which move the eyeball; squinting; cross-eye.
The act of stipulating; a contracting or bargaining; an agreement.
An apparatus for measuring the external movements of a given point of the chest wall, during respiration; -- also called thoracometer.

A narrowing of the opening or hollow of any passage, tube, or orifice; as, stenosis of the pylorus. It differs from stricture in being applied especially to diffused rather than localized contractions, and in always indicating an origin organic and not spasmod

The state or quality of being stable, or firm; steadiness; firmness; strength to stand without being moved or overthrown; as, the stability of a structure; the stability of a throne or a constitution.
A supposed spongelike expansion of the tip of a rootlet for absorbing water; -- called also spongelet.
Great brightness; brilliant luster; brilliancy; as, the splendor ot the sun. B.
A wet meter used to determine the breathing capacity of the lungs.
An instrument for recording the respiratory movements, as the sphygmograph does those of the pulse.
The quality or state of being spiny or thorny; spininess.
A small sac connected with the female reproductive organs of insects and many other invertebrates, serving to receive and retain the spermatozoa.
A regulus consisting essentially of nickel, obtained as a residue in fusing cobalt and nickel ores with silica and sodium carbonate to make smalt.
Habitual soberness or temperance as to the use of spirituous liquors; as, a man of sobriety. Public sobriety is a relative duty.
A curved plank, placed edgewise, to work in the bows of a vessel. R.
Close and warm; as, an infant lies snug.
Half-roasted ore.
A woman who is negligent of her dress or house; one who is not neat and nice.
The act of falling, or coming short; as: (a) The failure of a crop, or the like. (b) Neglect of, or failure in, performance of duty.
The breaking in pieces, or shattering, of a ship or other vessel by being cast ashore or driven against rocks, shoals, etc., by the violence of the winds and waves.
The game of hockey; -- so called because of the liability of the players to receive blows on the shin. Halliwell.
A kind of herpes (Herpes zoster) which spreads half way around the body like a girdle, and is usually attended with violent neuralgic pain.
The head of an Arab family, or of a clan or a tribe; also, the chief magistrate of an Arab village. The name is also applied to Mohammedan ecclesiastics of a high grade.

One who serves, or does services, voluntarily or on compulsion; a person who is employed by another for menial offices, or for other labor, and is subject to his command; a person who labors or exerts himself for the benefit of another, his master or employer;
In regular order; one after the other; severally.
Of or pertaining to burial, to the grave, or to monuments erected to the memory of the dead; as, a sepulchral stone; a sepulchral inscription.

Of or pertaining to the sensorium or sensation; as, sensory impulses; -- especially applied to those nerves and nerve fibers which convey to a nerve center impulses resulting in sensation; also sometimes loosely employed in the sense of afferent, to indicate n

Full ofscrupules; inclined to scruple; nicely doubtful; hesitating to determine or to act, from a fear of offending or of doing wrong. Abusing their liberty, to the offense of their weak brethren which were scrupulous.

(a) A strip of plaster of the thickness proposed for the coat, applied to the wall at intervals of four or five feet, as a guide. (b) A wooden straightedge used to lay across the plaster screed, as a limit for the thickness of the coat.

Offense caused or experienced; reproach or reprobation called forth by what is regarded as wrong, criminal, heinous, or flagrant: opprobrium or disgrace. O, what a scandal is it to our crown, That two such noble peers as ye should jar!
A division of Reptilia formerly established to include the Lacertilia, Crocodilia, Dinosauria, and other groups. By some writers the name is restricted to the Lacertilia.

The state of being satiated or glutted; fullness of gratification, either of the appetite or of any sensual desire; fullness beyond desire; an excess of gratification which excites wearisomeness or loathing; repletion; satiation. In all pleasures there is sati
An attendant attached to a prince or other powerful person; hence, an obsequious dependent. "The satellites of power." I.

A muscle of the thigh, called the tailor's muscle, which arises from the hip bone and is inserted just below the knee. So named because its contraction was supposed to produce the position of the legs assumed by the tailor in sitting.
A genus of trees with entire opposite leaves and small apetalous flowers. There are less than a dozen species, occuring from India to Australia and the Pacific Islands.
An exception; a reservation; an excuse. They admit many salvos, cautions, and reservations.
The act of saving; preservation or deliverance from destruction, danger, or great calamity.
An East Indian timber tree (Shorea robusta), much used for building purposes. It is of a light brown color, close-grained, and durable.
Free from harm, injury, or risk; untouched or unthreatened by danger or injury; unharmed; unhurt; secure; whole; as, safe from disease; safe from storms; safe from foes. "And ye dwelled safe." 1 Sam.
To go into or reside in the country; to ruralize. Pope.
A fugitive; a vagabond; an apostate; a renegade. See Renegade.
The quality or state of being rough.
A small piece of spun yarn or marline, used to fasten the head of the sail to the spar. [Written also roband, and robbin.]
A species of lyric poetry so composed as to contain a refrain or repetition which recurs according to a fixed law, and a limited number of rhymes recurring also by rule.
An instrument for reversing the direction of an electric current. [Written also reotrope.]
A metallic wire used for regulating the resistance of a circuit, or varying the strength of an electric current, by inserting a greater or less length of it in the circuit.
A strong pulling or drawing back; withdrawal. "Revulsions and pullbacks." SSir T.
The act of revolving, or turning round on an axis or a center; the motion of a body round a fixed point or line; rotation; as, the revolution of a wheel, of a top, of the earth on its axis, etc.
The act of retributing; repayment. In good offices and due retributions, we may not be pinching and niggardly.
Unwilling to go on; obstinate in refusing to move forward; stubborn; drawing back. Restive or resty, drawing back, instead of going forward, as some horses do.
Submissive; yielding; not disposed to resist or murmur. A firm, yet cautious mind; Sincere, thought prudent; constant, yet resigned.
The act of resigning or giving up, as a claim, possession, office, or the like; surrender; as, the resignation of a crown or comission.

A system of lines forming small squares of standard size, which is photographed, by a separate exposure, on the same plate with star images to facilitate measurements, detect changes of the film, etc. (b) In lace, a ground or foundation of regular meshes, like

Disposed to fight against; hostile; at war with; being at variance; contrary; inconsistent; refractory; disobedient; also, distasteful in a high degree; offensive; -- usually followed by to, rarely and less properly by with; as, all rudeness was repugnant to h
The act of repudiating, or the state of being repuddiated; as, the repudiation of a doctrine, a wife, a debt, etc.
A machine or implement for applying fresh primers to spent cartridge shells, so that the shells be used again.
One who reports. Specifically: (a) An officer or person who makees authorized statements of law proceedings and decisions, or of legislative debates.
That part of a circulating decimal which recurs continually, ad infinitum: -- sometimes indicated by a dot over the first and last repetend is 283.
The act of renewing, restoring, etc., or the state of being renewed or repaired; as, the reparation of a bridge or of a highway; -- in this sense, repair is oftener used. Arbuthnot.
A name of many different kinds of apples. Cf.
The act of renewing, or the state of being renewed; as, the renewal of a treaty.
Act of rejecting, or state of being rejected.
The act of passing back or returning; retrogression; retrogradation. Sir T.
The act of refreshing, or the state of being refreshed; restoration of strength, spirit, vigor, or liveliness; relief after suffering; new life or animation after depression.
The female of the ruff.
The act of recovering, regaining, or retaking possession.

The act of recognizing, or the state of being recognized; acknowledgment; formal avowal; knowledge confessed or avowed; notice. The lives of such saints had, at the time of their yearly memorials, solemn recognition in the church of God.
A royal jurisdiction or domain; a region which is under the dominion of a king; a kingdom. The absolute master of realms on which the sun perpetually alone.
Being, causing, or favoring reaction; as, reactionary movements.

The influence of a coil of wire upon an alternating current passing through it, tending to choke or diminish the current, or the similar influence of a condenser; inductive resistance. Reactance is measured in ohms.
Not altered from its natural state; not prepared by the action of heat; as, raw sienna; specifically, not cooked; not changed by heat to a state suitable for eating; not done; as, raw meat.
A fixed daily allowance of provisions assigned to a soldier in the army, or a sailor in the navy, for his subsistence.
A fine eruption or efflorescence on the body, with little or no elevation. Canker rash.
The quality or state of being rare; rareness; thinness; as, the rarity (contrasted with the density) of gases.

A French political group, also known as the Constitutional Right from its position in the Chambers, mainly monarchists who rallied to the support of the Republic in obedience to the encyclical put forth by Pope Leo XIII. in Feb., 1892.
Violent excitement; eager passion; extreme vehemence of desire, emotion, or suffering, mastering the will. "In great rage of pain." Bacon.
A fibrous material used for tying plants, said to come from the leaves of a palm tree of the genus Raphia. J.
An arc of a circle which is equal to the radius, or the angle measured by such an arc.
Discharge from a debt or an obligation; acquittance. Omittance is no quittance.
The hypothetical radical of certain quinone derivatives related to rhodizonic acid.
A mineral which is opaque in its natural state, but is said to change its color and become transparent by heat.

A niobate of calcium, cerium, and other bases, occurring usually in octahedrons of a yellowish or brownish color and resinous luster; -- so called from its becoming grass-green on being subjected to heat under the blowpipe.
A small image in the human form; a doll.
The aperture in the iris; the sight, apple, or black of the eye. See the Note under Eye, and Iris.
The quality or state of being punctual; especially, adherence to the exact time of an engagement; exactness.
A walk for pleasure, display, or exercise. Burke.
The falling down of a part through the orifice with which it is naturally connected, especially of the uterus or the rectum. Dunglison.
The act of moving forward; a proceeding in a course; motion onward.
The act of one who is profuse; a lavishing or pouring out without sting. Thy vast profusion to the factious nobles Rowe.
An armed private vessel which bears the commission of the sovereign power to cruise against the enemy. See Letters of marque, under Marque.
One who is confined in a prison. Piers Plowman.
First in order of time; original; primeval; primitive; primary. "Prime forests." Tennyson.
Being with young, as a female; having conceived; great with young; breeding; teeming; gravid; preparing to bring forth.
One who, or that which, precedes an event, and indicates its approach; a forerunner; a harbinger. Evil thoughts are the invisible, airy precursors of all the storms and tempests of the soul.
Destitute of power, force, or energy; weak; impotent; not able to produce any effect. -- Pow"er*less*ly, adv.
The gunwale of a ship. To lower the yards a-portoise, to lower them to the gunwale.

A fine translucent or semitransculent kind of earthenware, made first in China and Japan, but now also in Europe and America; -- called also China, or China ware. Porcelain, by being pure, is apt to break.
A stone marked with dendrites and black lines, and so disposed as to represent rivers, marshes, etc.
The act of polluting, or the state of being polluted (in any sense of the verb); defilement; uncleanness; impurity.
An instrument for determining the amount of polarization of light, or the proportion of polarized light, in a partially polarized ray.
The art of casting and working in lead, and applying it to building purposes; especially, the business of furnishing, fitting, and repairing pipes for conducting water, sewage, etc. Gwilt.
A mixture of hair and tar for covering the bottom of a ship.

(Arch.) In classical architecture, a vertically faced member immediately below the circular base of a column; also, the lowest member of a pedestal; hence, in general, the lowest member of a base; a sub-base; a block upon which the moldings of an architrave or

Capable of plying or bending; readily yielding to force or pressure without breaking; flexible; pliable; lithe; limber; plastic; as, a pliant thread; pliant wax. Also used figuratively: Easily influenced for good or evil; tractable; as, a pliant heart.
Pleasing; grateful to the mind or to the senses; agreeable; as, a pleasant journey; pleasant weather. Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
An apparatus for measuring the capacity of condensers, or the inductive capacity of dielectrics.
A cant word for anything petty or small. It is used by Drayton as the name of a fairy.

An extensive division of birds which includes the woodpeckers, toucans, trogons, hornbills, kingfishers, motmots, rollers, and goatsuckers. By some writers it is made to include also the cuckoos, swifts, and humming birds.
An open square in a European town, especially an Italian town; hence (Arch.), an arcaded and roofed gallery; a portico. In the United States the word is popularly applied to a veranda.
An instrument for registering the movements of the diaphragm, or midriff, in respiration.
A condition of the penis in which the prepuce can not be drawn back so as to uncover the glans penis.
An instrument for studying the mechanism of accommodation.
The mildest form of epilepsy, with momentary faintness or unconsciousness, but without convulsions; -- opposed to grand mal.
A short mortar used formerly for throwing stone shot. Hakluyt.
The act of permuting; exchange of the thing for another; mutual transference; interchange. The violent convulsions and permutations that have been made in property.
A genus of birds including the common European partridge. Formerly the word was used in a much wider sense to include many allied genera.
An order of fishes including the gray mullets (Mugil), the barracudas, the silversides, and other related fishes. So called from their relation both to perches and to pikes.
A division of Arachnida, including the whip scorpions (Thelyphonus) and allied forms. Sometimes used in a wider sense to include also the true scorpions.
The strong ligament of the back of the neck in quadrupeds. It connects the back of the skull with dorsal spines of the cervical vertebræ, and helps to support the head.
One who protects, supports, or countenances; a defender. "Patron of my life and liberty." Shak.
Of or pertaining to shepherds; hence, relating to rural life and scenes; as, a pastoral life.
An upstart; a man newly risen into notice.
A combining form used to indicate connection with, or relation to, the parietal bones or the parietal segment of the skull; as, the parieto-mastoid suture.

A word, phrase, or sentence, by way of comment or explanation, inserted in, or attached to, a sentence which would be grammatically complete without it. It is usually inclosed within curved lines (see def.
A term used to denote all of the elements or factors which constitute vitality or vital energy. H.

An instrument for copying plans, maps, and other drawings, on the same, or on a reduced or an enlarged, scale. [Written also pantagraph, and incorrectly pentagraph.] Skew pantograph, a kind of pantograph for drawing a copy which is inclined with respect to the
Serving to palliate; serving to extenuate or mitigate.
An ancient Greek hymn in honor of Apollo as a healing deity, and, later, a song addressed to other deities.
The fragrant roots of the Saussurea Costus, exported from India to China, and used for burning as incense. It is supposed to be the costus of the ancients.
The means of nutriment to animals or plants; food; nourishment; hence, that which feeds or sustains, as fuel for a fire; that upon which the mind or soul is nourished; as, intellectual pabulum.
An apparatus employed to indicate the presence, or the amount, of ozone.
A rope used for hauling out a sail upon a spar; -- opposite of inhaul.
A vehement or loud cry; a cry of distress, alarm, opposition, or detestation; clamor.
The quality or state of being original. Macaulay.
A genus of bombycid moths whose caterpillars (esp. those of Orgyia leucostigma) are often very injurious to fruit trees and shade trees.
An instrument for measuring the distance of distinct vision, mainly for the selection of eveglasses.
An instrument or machine for measuring work done, especially for ascertaining the number of rotations made by a machine or wheel in manufacturing cloth; a counter. Ure.
A free fold of the peritoneum, or one serving to connect viscera, support blood vessels, etc.; an epiploön.
An instrument for ascertaining the weight and purity of oil; an elaiometer.
A hydrocarbon radical formerly supposed to exist in oenanthic acid, now known to be identical with heptyl.
The quality or state of being odd; singularity; queerness; peculiarity; as, oddity of dress, manners, and the like. That infinitude of oddities in him.
One who is new in any business, profession, or calling; one unacquainted or unskilled; one yet in the rudiments; a beginner; a tyro. I am young; a novice in the trade.

The quality or condition of being notorious; the state of being generally or publicly known; -- commonly used in an unfavorable sense; as, the notoriety of a crime. They were not subjects in their own nature so exposed to public notoriety.
No person; no one; not anybody.
An apparatus for determining the amount of nitrogen or some of its compounds in any substance subjected to analysis; an azotometer.
The quality or state of being nice (in any of the senses of that word.). The miller smiled of her nicety.

The state or quality of being neutral; the condition of being unengaged in contests between others; state of taking no part on either side; indifference. Men who possess a state of neutrality in times of public danger, desert the interest of their fellow subje
Of necessity; necessarily; indispensably; -- often with must, and equivalent to of need. A man must needs love mauger his head.
The belief or doctrine that attributes everything to nature as a sanative agent.
A pearly substance which lines the interior of many shells, and is most perfect in the mother-of-pearl. [Written also nacker and naker.] See Pearl, and Mother-of-pearl.
The summit of an eminence. [Prov.
One given to mysticism; one who holds mystical views, interpretations, etc.; especially, in ecclesiastical history, one who professed mysticism. See Mysticism.
An instrument for determining and recording the different phases, as the intensity, velocity, etc., of a muscular contraction.

A small animal of Java (Paradoxirus fasciatus), allied to the civets. It swallows, but does not digest, large quantities of ripe coffee berries, thus serving to disseminate the coffee plant; hence it is called also coffee rat.
Masking; frolic in disguise; buffoonery. The mummery of foreign strollers.
Exceedingly; very; very much. "A monstrous thick oil on the top." Bacon.
The state of being monstrous, or out of the common order of nature; that which is monstrous; a monster. South.
One who admonishes; one who warns of faults, informs of duty, or gives advice and instruction by way of reproof or caution. You need not be a monitor to the king.
The progeny resulting from a cross between two breeds, as of domestic animals; anything of mixed breed. Drayton.
One who, or that which, moderates, restrains, or pacifies. Sir W.
The act of moderating, or of imposing due restraint.
Imitating, esp. in derision, or so as to cause derision; mimicking; derisive.

The act of mocking, deriding, and exposing to contempt, by mimicry, by insincere imitation, or by a false show of earnestness; a counterfeit appearance. It is, as the air, invulnerable, And our vain blows malicious mockery.

The act of mitigating, or the state of being mitigated; abatement or diminution of anything painful, harsh, severe, afflictive, or calamitous; as, the mitigation of pain, grief, rigor, severity, punishment, or penalty.
A title of courtesy prefixed to the name of a man or youth. It is usually written in the abbreviated form Mr.

A thousand years; especially, thousand years mentioned in the twentieth chapter in the twentieth chapter of Revelation, during which holiness is to be triumphant throughout the world. Some believe that, during this period, Christ will reign on earth in person
An allowance for traveling expenses at a certain rate per mile.
An instrument for measuring the size of the womb. Knight.
An alcoholate of methyl alcohol in which the hydroxyl hydrogen is replaced by a metal, after the analogy of a hydrate; as, sodium methylate, CH3ONa.
One who bears a message; the bearer of a verbal or written communication, notice, or invitation, from one person to another, or to a public body; specifically, an office servant who bears messages.
Serving to preserve remembrance; commemorative; as, a memorial building. There high in air, memorial of my name, Fix the smooth oar, and bid me live to fame.
A kind of mental unsoundness characterized by extreme depression of spirits, ill-grounded fears, delusions, and brooding over one particular subject or train of ideas.
The quality of being mediocre; a middle state or degree; a moderate degree or rate. "A mediocrity of success." Bacon.
A speculum for examining a natural passage, as the urethra.

A name of several maritime grasses, as the sea sand-reed (Ammophila arundinacea) which is used in Holland to bind the sand of the seacoast dikes (see Beach grass, under Beach); also, the Lygeum Spartum, a Mediterranean grass of similar habit.

Adherence to a peculiar style or manner; a characteristic mode of action, bearing, or treatment, carried to excess, especially in literature or art. Mannerism is pardonable,and is sometimes even agreeable, when the manner, though vicious, is natural .
The act of maintaining; sustenance; support; defense; vindication. Whatsoever is granted to the church for God's honor and the maintenance of his service, is granted to God.
Inclined to wild sports; delighting in rash, absurd, or dangerous amusements. "The merry madcap
The quality or state of being lucid.
A heavy, clumsy, or awkward fellow; a sturdy drone; a clown. Lingering lubbers lose many a penny.
A vessel used to receive the washings of ores of metals.

A division of beetles, including a large number of species, in which the antennæ are very long. Most of them, while in the larval state, bore into the wood or beneath the bark of trees, and some species are very destructive to fruit and shade trees.
Of or pertaining to a particular place, or to a definite region or portion of space; restricted to one place or region; as, a local custom. Gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.
A genus of elongated bivalve shells, allied to the mussels, and remarkable for their ability to bore holes for shelter, in solid limestone, shells, etc. Called also Lithophagus.

Descent in a line from a common progenitor; progeny; race; descending line of offspring or ascending line of parentage. Both the lineage and the certain sire From which I sprung, from me are hidden yet.
Eager; craving; urged by desire; eager to taste or enjoy; greedy. "The lickerish palate of the glutton." Bp.

The quality of weighing less than something else of equal bulk; relative lightness, especially as shown by rising through, or floating upon, a contiguous substance; buoyancy; -- opposed to gravity. He gave the form of levity to that which ascended; to that whi
A tube for producing Lenard rays.
pl. of Leaf.
The state or quality of being lax; want of tenseness, strictness, or exactness.
A genus of trees including, according to modern authors, only the true laurel (Laurus nobilis), and the larger L. Canariensis of Madeira and the Canary Islands.
A workman whose business it is to shape boots or shoes, or place leather smoothly, on lasts; a tool for stretching leather on a last.
A state of the body or mind which is caused by exhaustion of strength and characterized by a languid feeling; feebleness; lassitude; laxity.
A genus of great seaweeds with long and broad fronds; kelp, or devil's apron. The fronds commonly grow in clusters, and are sometimes from thirty to fifty feet in length.
An instrument for measuring, and recording graphically, the pressure of the blood in any of the blood vessels of a living animal; -- called also kymographion.
A condition in which the knees are bent in so as to touch each other in walking; inknee.
A member of a common form of truss, as a roof truss. It is strictly a tie, intended to prevent the sagging of the tiebeam in the middle.
A mineral of a brownish black color, related to titanite in form. It consists chiefly of silica, titanium dioxide, lime, and yttria.
A fragment of any solid substance; a thick piece. See Chunk.
One who works by the job.
A machine for bending or straightening rails.

Originally, one belonging to the tribe or kingdom of Judah; after the return from the Babylonish captivity, any member of the new state; a Hebrew; an Israelite. Jew's frankincense, gum styrax, or benzoin.
A machine of great antiquity, used in Bengal for raising water to irrigate land. Knight.
Dissimulation; ignorance feigned for the purpose of confounding or provoking an antagonist.
An herb of the Mint family (Sideritis), supposed to heal sword cuts; also, a species of Galeopsis.
The act of investing, or the state of being invested.
Carelessness; heedlessness; thoughtlessness; unconcern.
A plane for shaving or dressing the concave or inside faces of barrel staves.
An order of birds, formerly established to include the perching birds, but now generally regarded as an artificial group.
Disturbed state; uneasiness either of body or mind; restlessness; disquietude. Sir H.
A hint; an intimation. The least inkling or glimpse of this island.
The act of enjoining; the act of directing, commanding, or prohibiting.
Unlimited extent of time, space, or quantity; eternity; boundlessness; immensity. Sir T.
The act or process of infecting. There was a strict order against coming to those pits, and that was only to prevent infection.
In reality; in truth; in fact; verily; truly; -- used in a variety of sense. Esp.: (a) Denoting emphasis; as, indeed it is so.

Not credible; surpassing belief; too extraordinary and improbable to admit of belief; unlikely; marvelous; fabulous. Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead Acts xxvi.
Not correct; not according to a copy or model, or to established rules; inaccurate; faulty. The piece, you think, is incorrect.
Not competent; wanting in adequate strength, power, capacity, means, qualifications, or the like; incapable; unable; inadequate; unfit. Incompetent to perform the duties of the place.
The state or quality of being inactive; inertness; as, the inactivity of matter.
Want of action or activity; forbearance from labor; idleness; rest; inertness. Berkeley.
In transit; during passage; as, goods in transitu.
The quality of being improper; unfitness or unsuitableness to character, time place, or circumstances; as, improperiety of behavior or manners.
The condition or quality of being impetuous; fury; violence.
Not pervious; not admitting of entrance or passage through; as, a substance impervious to water or air. This gulf impassable, impervious.
Things which impede or hinder progress; incumbrances; baggage; specif. (Mil.),

The act or practice of a hypocrite; a feigning to be what one is not, or to feel what one does not feel; a dissimulation, or a concealment of one's real character, disposition, or motives; especially, the assuming of false appearance of virtue or religion; a s

A cyst in which some unicellular organisms temporarily inclose themselves, from which they emerge unchanged, after a period of drought or deficiency of food. In some instances, a process of spore formation seems to occur within such cysts.
Care of domestic affairs; economy; domestic management; thrift. There's husbandry in heaven; Their candles are all out.

A violent storm, characterized by extreme fury and sudden changes of the wind, and generally accompanied by rain, thunder, and lightning; -- especially prevalent in the East and West Indies. Also used figuratively.

The state or quality of being humble; freedom from pride and arrogance; lowliness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth; a sense of one's own unworthiness through imperfection and sinfulness; self-abasement; humbleness. Serving the Lord with all humili
Entrails of a deer. [Written also umbles.] Johnson.
The quality of being human; the peculiar nature of man, by which he is distinguished from other beings.
A small line of three strands used for seizing; -- called also housing. Totten.

Belonging or appropriate to an enemy; showing the disposition of an enemy; showing ill will and malevolence, or a desire to thwart and injure; occupied by an enemy or enemies; inimical; unfriendly; as, a hostile force; hostile intentions; a hostile country; ho
An umbelliferous plant of the genus Sison (S.Amomum); -- so called because used to cure a swelling called a hone.
A consecrated day; religious anniversary; a day set apart in honor of some person, or in commemoration of some event. See Holyday.
The act of hindering, or the state of being hindered.
The act of hesitating; suspension of opinion or action; doubt; vacillation.
The expectoration of blood, due usually to hemorrhage from the mucous membrane of the lungs.
A medicine designed to improve the condition of the blood.
Heath. [Scot.] Gorse and grass And heather, where his footsteps pass, The brighter seem.

A part (usually separate from the bed or frame) for supporting some of the principal working parts of a machine; as: (a) The part of a lathe that holds the revolving spindle and its attachments; -- also called poppet head, the opposite corresponding part being
A stag; the male of the red deer. See the Note under Buck.
The apartments or portion of the house allotted to females in Mohammedan families.
The refuse or coarse part of fiax; tow.
A stackyard. [Prov.
An instrument devised by Hermann, for regulating and measuring the thickness of a layer of blood for spectroscopic examination.

A modification of the gyroscope, consisting essentially of a fly wheel fixed inside a rigid case to which is attached a thin flange of metal for supporting the instrument. It is used in studying the dynamics of rotating bodies.
Athletic or disciplinary exercises; the art of performing gymnastic exercises; also, disciplinary exercises for the intellect or character.
Nice or keen appreciation or enjoyment; relish; taste; fancy. Dryden.
That which forms the foundation or support of anything; the basis; the essential or fundamental part; first principle. Dryden.
A grated iron utensil for broiling flesh and fish over coals.
A father's or mother's father; an ancestor in the next degree above the father or mother in lineal ascent. Grandfather longlegs.
A sponsor; a godfather or a godmother. Should a great lady that was invited to be a gossip, in her place send her kitchen maid, 't would be ill taken.
A disease of the teeth, which causes them to loosen and fall out of their sockets.

The process of germinating; the beginning of vegetation or growth in a seed or plant; the first development of germs, either animal or vegetable. Germination apparatus, an apparatus for malting grain.
A disposition to turn or incline towards the earth; the influence of gravity in determining the direction of growth of an organ.

That branch of applied mathematics which determines, by means of observations and measurements, the figures and areas of large portions of the earth's surface, or the general figure and dimenshions of the earth; or that branch of surveying in which the curvatu
A writer of news, or an officer appointed to publish news by authority. Johnson.
Splendor of appearance; ostentatious finery. [Archaic] Guess the gallantry of our church by this .
Excitement; commotion; enthusiasm.
Droll; comical; amusing; laughable. Funny bone.
A cord, baud, or bundle of fibers; esp., one of the small bundles of fibers, of which large nerves are made up; applied also to different bands of white matter in the brain and spinal cord.
A name formerly given to cellulose found in certain fungi and mushrooms.
The institutions or the practices of freemasons.
A method of forming a joint at the intersection of window-sash bars, by cutting away only enough wood to show a miter.
An uproar; a noisy quarrel; a disturbance; a brawl.
The condition or quality of being formal, strictly ceremonious, precise, etc.
The act of forfeiting; the loss of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office, or effects, by an offense, crime, breach of condition, or other act. Under pain of foreiture of the said goods.
A piece of timber placed across the stem, to unite the bows and strengthen the fore part of the ship; a breast hook.
The act of forbearing or waiting; the exercise of patience. He soon shall findForbearance no acquittance ere day end.
A leaf of a book or manuscript.
An instrument for observing or exhibiting fluorescence.
A commissioned or noncommissioned officer posted in the rear of a line, or on the flank of a column, of soldiers, to rectify mistakes and insure steadiness and promptness in the ranks.
A genus of small beetles, of which one species (the grapevine Fidia, F. longipes) is very injurious to vines in America.
The bow, strung with horsehair, used in playing the fiddle; a fiddle bow.
A combination of kindred to avenge injuries or affronts, done or offered to any of their blood, on the offender and all his race.
Heat; excessive warmth. The fevor of ensuing day.
The mechanism for closing the breech of a breech-loading firearm, in artillery consisting principally of the breechblock, obturator, and carrier ring.
A member of a secret organization, consisting mainly of Irishment, having for its aim the overthrow of English rule in ireland.

The act of fascinating, bewhiching, or enchanting; enchantment; witchcraft; the exercise of a powerful or irresistible influence on the affections or passions; unseen, inexplicable influence. The Turks hang old rags .

A failing short; a becoming deficient; failure; deficiency; imperfection; weakness; lapse; fault; infirmity; as, a mental failing. And ever in her mind she cas about For that unnoticed failing in herself.
The act of extorting; the act or practice of wresting anything from a person by force, by threats, or by any undue exercise of power; undue exaction; overcharge.
The act of extinguishing or making extinct; a putting an end to; the act of putting out or destroying light, fire, life, activity, influence, etc.
A muscle which serves to extend or straighten any part of the body, as an arm or a finger; -- opposed to flexor.
An apparatus for drying substances or preserving them from moisture; a desiccator; also, less frequently, an agent employed to absorb moisture, as calcium chloride, or concentrated sulphuric acid.

Carefully selected or sought out; hence, of distinguishing and surpassing quality; exceedingly nice; delightfully excellent; giving rare satisfaction; as, exquisite workmanship. Plate of rare device, and jewels Of reach and exquisite form.
The act of disburdening, discharging, or freeing morally from a charge or imputation; also, the state of being disburdened or freed from a charge.

The state of being exigent; urgent or exacting want; pressing necessity or distress; need; a case demanding immediate action, supply, or remedy; as, an unforeseen exigency. "The present exigency of his affairs." Ludlow.

The act of exempting; the state of being exempt; freedom from any charge, burden, evil, etc., to which others are subject; immunity; privilege; as, exemption of certain articles from seizure; exemption from military service; exemption from anxiety, suffering,
From office; by virtue, or as a consequence, of an office; officially.
. See Evil eye under Evil, a.
In an eventual manner; finally; ultimately.
The act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogation; artful means of eluding. Thou .
Liable to vanish or pass away like vapor; vanishing; fleeting; as, evanescent joys. So evanescent are the fashions of the world in these particulars.
The act of emptying, clearing of the contents, or discharging. Specifically: (a) (Mil.) Withdrawal of troops from a town, fortress, etc.
The art or process of determining he constituents of a gaseous mixture by means of the eudiometer, or for ascertaining the purity of the air or the amount of oxygen in it.
A dike of piles in the sea, a river, etc., to check the approach of an enemy.

A genus of dipterous insects whose young (called rat-tailed larvæ) are remarkable for their long tapering tail, which spiracles at the tip, and for their ability to live in very impure and salt waters; -- also called drone fly.
An iron needle for piercing the cartridge of a cannon before priming.
The epidermal cells of rootlets, specially adapted to absorb liquids. Goodale.
Act of environing; state of being environed.
The quality of being an enemy; hostile or unfriendly disposition. No ground of enmity between us known.
The act of bestowing a dower, fund, or permanent provision for support.
An instrument for examining the interior of the rectum, the urethra, and the bladder.
A tract of land or a territory inclosed within another territory of which it is independent. See Exclave.
In passing; in the course of any procedure; -- said specif. (Chess),
A choice or select body; the flower; as, the élite of society.
A variety of hephelite, usually massive, of greasy luster, and gray to reddish color. Elæolite syenite, a kind of syenite characterized by the presence of elæolite.
The sound of a patient's voice so modified as to resemble the bleating of a goat, heard on applying the ear to the chest in certain diseases within its cavity, as in pleurisy with effusion.

The image, likeness, or representation of a person, whether a full figure, or a part; an imitative figure; -- commonly applied to sculptured likenesses, as those on monuments, or to those of the heads of princes on coins and medals, sometimes applied to portra
A current of air or water running back, or in a direction contrary to the main current.
Deviating or departing from the center, or from the line of a circle; as, an eccentric or elliptical orbit; pertaining to deviation from the center or from true circular motion.
A condition of bone cartilage occurring in certain diseases of these tissues, in which they acquire an unnatural density, and come to resemble ivory.
A boiling or bubbling up of a liquid; the motion produced in a liquid by its rapid conversion into vapor.

A shaking, trembling, or concussion of the earth, due to subterranean causes, often accompanied by a rumbling noise. The wave of shock sometimes traverses half a hemisphere, destroying cities and many thousand lives; -- called also earthdin, earthquave, and ea
A bag filled with earth, used commonly to raise or repair a parapet.

A concretionary nodule of clay ironstone, of the size of a walnut or larger, so called by the ancients, who believed that the eagle transported these stones to her nest to facilitate the laying of her eggs; aëtites.
The state or quality of being eager; ardent desire. "The eagerness of love." Addison.
A disease attended with inflammation and ulceration of the colon and rectum, and characterized by griping pains, constant desire to evacuate the bowels, and the discharge of mucus and blood.
A collection of cattle driven, or cattle collected for driving; a number of animals, as oxen, sheep, or swine, driven in a body.
A contrivance for holding and turning a drill. Knight.
A draining; a gradual flowing off of any liquid; also, that which flows out of a drain.
A piece of canvas fastened by lacing to the bonnet of a sail, to give it a greater depth, or more drop.
A sudden fall; a body of things falling. Those cataracts or downfalls aforesaid.
A small vane of bunting, feathers, or any other light material, carried at the masthead to indicate the direction of the wind. Totten.
A book; esp., a collection of poems written by one author; as, the divan of Hafiz. [Persia]
The act of dissipating or dispersing; a state of dispersion or separation; dispersion; waste. Without loss or dissipation of the matter.

Inequality; difference in age, rank, condition, or excellence; dissimilitude; -- followed by between, in, of, as to, etc.; as, disparity in, or of, years; a disparity as to color. The disparity between God and his intelligent creatures.
The act of disjoining; disunion; separation; a parting; as, the disjunction of soul and body.
A flat round plate; (Biol.)
An instrument for measuring the dilatation or expansion of a substance, especially of a fluid.
An instrument designed for transmitting pictures by telegraph. Fallows.
The act of devoting; consecration.
The act of destining or appointing.
The act of despairing or becoming desperate; a giving up of hope. This desperation of success chills all our industry.
A genus of coleopterous insects, the larvæ of which feed animal substances. They are very destructive to dries meats, skins, woolens, and furs.
A place of deposit storing of goods; a warehouse; a storehouse. The islands of Guernsey and Jersey are at present the great depots of this kingdom.
The act of defying, putting in opposition, or provoking to combat; a challenge; a provocation; a summons to combat. A war without a just defiance made.
The act or the state of declining; declination; descent; slope. The declension of the land from that place to the sea.
Full of, or characterized by, deceit; serving to mislead or insnare; trickish; fraudulent; cheating; insincere. Harboring foul deceitful thoughts.
Fallen, as to physical or social condition; affected with decay; rotten; as, decayed vegetation or vegetables; a decayed fortune or gentleman. -- De*cay"ed*ness, n.
A modification of the kaleidoscope; -- used to reflect images so as to form beautiful designs.
The act of debasing or the state of being debased. Milton.
Capable of causing death; mortal; fatal; destructive; certain or likely to cause death; as, a deadly blow or wound.
A pneumatic or hydraulic cushion for a falling weight, as in the valve gear of a steam engine, to prevent shock.

A genus of plants native to Mexico and Central America, of the order Compositæ; also, any plant or flower of the genus. The numerous varieties of cultivated dahlias bear conspicuous flowers which differ in color.

One of a sect or school of philosophers founded by Antisthenes, and of whom Diogenes was a disciple. The first Cynics were noted for austere lives and their scorn for social customs and current philosophical opinions.
An instrument for exhibiting and measuring wave motion; specif. (Elec.),
A surface of the fourth degree, having certain special relations to spherical surfaces. The tore or anchor ring is one of the cyclides.
A variety of cellulose, occuring as a fine transparent membrane covering the aerial organs of plants, and forming an essential ingredient of cork; by oxidation it passes to suberic acid.
A scoop or ring with either a blunt or a cutting edge, for removing substances from the walls of a cavity, as from the eye, ear, or womb.
A genus of euphorbiaceous plants belonging to tropical countries. Croton oil (Med.), a viscid, acrid, brownish yellow oil obtained from the seeds of Croton Tiglium, a small tree of the East Indies.
Qualified to criticise, or pass judgment upon, literary or artistic productions. It is submitted to the judgment of more critical ears to direct and determine what is graceful and what is not.
