The operation of opening the fetal head, in order to effect delivery.
A lamb reared without the aid of the dam. Hence: A pet, in general.
The act corrugating; contraction into wrinkles or alternate ridges and grooves.

Pertaining to, or composed of, corpuscles, or small particles. Corpuscular philosophy, that which attempts to account for the phenomena of nature, by the motion, figure, rest, position, etc., of the minute particles of matter.
A cord or ribbon bestowed or borne as a badge of honor; a broad ribbon, usually worn after the manner of a baldric, constituting a mark of a very high grade in an honorary order. Cf.
The act of coöperating, or of operating together to one end; joint operation; concurrent effort or labor. Not holpen by the coöperation of angels.
The act of convicting; the act of proving, finding, or adjudging, guilty of an offense. The greater certainty of conviction and the greater certainty of punishment.
The act of coming together; the state of being together; union; coalition. The conventions or associations of several particles of matter into bodies of any certain denomination.
Rudeness compounded of haughtiness and contempt; scornful insolence; despiteful treatment; disdain; contemptuousness in act or speech; disgrace. The oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely.
The state or quality of being contrary; opposition; repugnance; disagreement; antagonism. There is a contrariety between those things that conscience inclines to, and those that entertain the senses.

Propositions which directly and destructively contradict each other, but of which the falsehood of one does not establish the truth of the other. If two universals differ in quality, they are contraries; as, every vine is a tree; no vine is a tree.
Union or connection; the state of touching or contact. "Point of contingency." J.
Fond of contention; given to angry debate; provoking dispute or contention; quarrelsome. Despotic and contentious temper.
The act of constraining, or the state of being constrained; that which compels to, or restrains from, action; compulsion; restraint; necessity. Long imprisonment and hard constraint.
That which is not subject to change; that which is invariable.
Correspondence in form, manner, or character; resemblance; agreement; congruity; -- followed by to, with, or between.
Expression of sympathy with another in sorrow or grief. Their congratulations and their condolences.
Agreement; accordance. Contrasts, and yet concordances.
Belonging to a close or termination; decisive; convincing; putting an end to debate or question; leading to, or involving, a conclusion or decision. Secret reasons .
The act of conceiving in the womb; the initiation of an embryonic animal life. I will greaty multiply thy sorrow and thy conception.
A preparation of fruit in sirup in such a manner as to preserve its form, either whole, halved, or quartered; as, a compote of pears. Littr
The act of complying; a yielding; as to a desire, demand, or proposal; concession; submission. What compliances will remove dissension Swift.
A stuffed or quilted coverlet for a bed; a comforter; a comfort. [U.
An instrument, intended to represent the revolution of a comet round the sun. Hutton.
A variety of cabbage (Brassica oleracea), cultivated for its seeds, which yield an oil valued for illuminating and lubricating purposes; summer rape.
The act of striking together; a striking together, as of two hard bodies; a violent meeting, as of railroad trains; a clashing.
Existence at the same time with another; -- contemporary existence. Without the help, or so much as the coexistence, of any condition.
A fabulous serpent whose breath and look were said to be fatal. See Basilisk.

A game in which questions are asked for the purpose of enabling the questioners to discover a word or thing previously selected by two persons who answer the questions; -- so called because the players take sides in two "clumps" or groups, the "clump" which gu
A series of muscular contractions due to sudden stretching of the muscle, -- a sign of certain neuropathies.

A work of acknowledged excellence and authrity, or its author; -- originally used of Greek and Latin works or authors, but now applied to authors and works of a like character in any language. In is once raised him to the rank of a legitimate English classic.
An instrument of iron, with sharp prongs, attached to a boot or shoe to enable the wearer to walk securely upon ice; a creeper. Kane.

A disease of the liver in which it usually becomes smaller in size and more dense and fibrous in consistence; hence sometimes applied to similar changes in other organs, caused by increase in the fibrous framework and decrease in the proper substance of the or
The act of moving in a circle, or in a course which brings the moving body to the place where its motion began. This continual circulation of human things.
The fragrant flowers of the Chloranthus inconspicuus, used in China for perfuming tea.
An instrument for measuring time; a timekeeper.
A general name for coloring matter of plants other than chlorophyll, especially that of petals.
St. Vitus's dance; a disease attended with convulsive twitchings and other involuntary movements of the muscles or limbs.
Pertaining to chivalry or knight-errantry; warlike; heroic; gallant; high-spirited; high-minded; magnanimous. In brave pursuit of chivalrous emprise.
One who prates much in his own favor, and makes unwarrantable pretensions; a quack; an impostor; an empiric; a mountebank.
Love; universal benevolence; good will.

One who engages in any contest; esp. one who in ancient times contended in single combat in behalf of another's honor or rights; or one who acts or speaks in behalf of a person or a cause; a defender; an advocate; a hero.
A shark of the genus Cestracion, and of related genera. The posterior teeth form a pavement of bony plates for crushing shellfish.
Cayenne pepper. Cayenne pepper.
A hollow place in the earth, either natural or artificial; a subterraneous cavity; a cavern; a den.
A military man serving on horseback; a knight.
A rope used in hoisting the anchor to the cathead. Totten.
That which comes without design or without being foreseen; contingency. Losses that befall them by mere casualty.
An order of Mammallia including the lion, tiger, wolf bear, seal, etc. They are adapted by their structure to feed upon flesh, though some of them, as the bears, also eat vegetable food.
An apparatus in which coal gas, hydrogen, or air is passed through or over a volatile hydrocarbon, in order to confer or increase illuminating power. [Written also carburettor.]
Governed or characterized by caprice; apt to change suddenly; freakish; whimsical; changeable. "Capricious poet." Shak.
As much as will fill a cap. A capful of wind (Naut.), a light puff of wind.
A law or rule. Or that the Everlasting had not fixed His canon 'gainst self- slaughter.
A genus of composite herbaceous plants. One species, Calendula officinalis, is the common marigold, and was supposed to blossom on the calends of every month, whence the name.
A comblike structure on the metatarsus of the hind legs of certain spiders (Ciniflonidæ), used to curl certain fibers in the construction of their webs.

The decoration of a fluted shaft of a column or of a pilaster with reeds, or rounded moldings, which seem to be laid in the hollows of the fluting. These are limited in length to about one third of the height of the shaft.
A boy servant, or page, -- in allusion to the buttons on his livry. [Colloq.] Dickens.

A projecting beam or boom; as: (a) One projecting from each bow of a vessel, to haul the fore tack to, called a tack bumpkin. (b) Onr from each quarter, for the main-brace blocks, and called brace bumpkin.
The quality of being brutal; inhumanity; savageness; pitilessness.
The state of being brothers or a brother.
A salt of bromic acid.
A thick piece of timber in the form of a knee, placed across the stem of a ship to strengthen the fore part and unite the bows on each side. Totten.
A large rope to fasten the midship part of a ship to a wharf, or to another vessel.
A band for the breast. Specifically: (Naut.) A band of canvas, or a rope, fastened at both ends to the rigging, to support the man who heaves the lead in sounding.
Bold; courageous; daring; intrepid; -- opposed to cowardly; as, a brave man; a brave act.
A gill; a respiratory organ for breathing the air contained in water, such as many aquatic and semiaquatic animals have.
A man who uses a bow; an archer. The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen.
As much of an action as is performed at one time; a going and returning, as of workmen in reaping, mowing, etc.; a turn; a round. In notes with many a winding bout Of linked sweetness long drawn out.

A mineral of a steel-gray to black color and metallic luster, occurring crystallized, often in twin crystals shaped like cogwheels (wheel ore), also massive. It is a sulphide of antimony, lead, and copper.

A dipterous insect of the family (Estridæ, of many different species, some of which are particularly troublesome to domestic animals, as the horse, ox, and sheep, on which they deposit their eggs. A common species is one of the botflies of the horse (Gastrophi

A rare variety of camphor, C10H17.OH, resembling ordinary camphor, from which it can be produced by reduction. It is said to occur in the camphor tree of Borneo and Sumatra (Dryobalanops camphora), but the natural borneol is rarely found in European or America

A very singular missile weapon used by the natives of Australia and in some parts of India. It is usually a curved stick of hard wood, from twenty to thirty inches in length, from two to three inches wide, and half or three quarters of an inch thick.
The hero of a mediæval French nursery legend, who, leaving home, enjoined his young wife not to open a certain room in his castle. She entered it, and found the murdered bodies of his former wives.
A chain in which the alternate links are broad blocks connected by thin side links pivoted to the ends of the blocks, used with sprocket wheels to transmit power, as in a bicycle.

The quality or state of being bitter, sharp, or acrid, in either a literal or figurative sense; implacableness; resentfulness; severity; keenness of reproach or sarcasm; deep distress, grief, or vexation of mind. The lip that curls with bitterness.
The state of mind of a bigot; obstinate and unreasoning attachment of one's own belief and opinions, with narrow-minded intolerance of beliefs opposed to them.

A liquid consisting mainly of the lighter and more volatile hydrocarbons of petroleum or kerosene oil, used as a solvent and for cleansing soiled fabrics; -- called also petroleum spirit, petroleum benzine. Varieties or similar products are gasoline, naphtha,
A messenger or crier of a court; a servitor; one who cites or bids persons to appear and answer; -- called also an apparitor or summoner.
The quality or condition of being base; degradation; vileness. I once did hold it a baseness to write fair.
A variety of paralysis, peculiar to India and the Malabar coast; -- considered by many to be the same as beriberi in chronic form.
An uncivilized state or condition; rudeness of manners; ignorance of arts, learning, and literature; barbarousness. Prescott.
A plant of the family of grasses, and genus Bambusa, growing in tropical countries.
An ancient military engine, in the form of a crossbow, used for hurling large missiles.
A vessel for holding hot water in which another vessel may be heated without scorching its contents; -- used for warming or preparing food or pharmaceutical preparations.
An apparatus for measuring or determining the proportion of nitrogen; a nitrometer.
An instrument for examining the condition of the ear.
A hearer or listener. Macaulay.
A public sale of property to the highest bidder, esp. by a person licensed and authorized for the purpose; a vendue.
One who sustains a great burden.
Roughness of surface; unevenness; -- opposed to smoothness. "The asperities of dry bodies." Boyle.
On, or to, one side; out of a straight line, course, or direction; at a little distance from the rest; out of the way; apart. Thou shalt set aside that which is full.
The act of rising; motion upward; rise; a mounting upward; as, he made a tedious ascent; the ascent of vapors from the earth. To him with swift ascent he up returned.
Instruments or weapons of offense or defense. He lays down his arms, but not his wiles.
A person skilled in the art of building; one who understands architecture, or makes it his occupation to form plans and designs of buildings, and to superintend the artificers employed.
pl. of Arch, n.
A genus of tall conifers of the pine family. The species are confined mostly to South America and Australia.
A driving or running towards; approach; impulse; also, the act of striking against. In all consonants there is an appulse of the organs.
Exciting appetite; as, appetizing food. The appearance of the wild ducks is very appetizing.
A genus of small beetles, several of which, in the larval state, are very destructive to woolen goods, fur, etc. The common "museum pest" is A.
Opposition of action; counteraction or contrariety of things or principles.
A division of the Articulata, including the annelids and allied groups; sometimes made to include also the helminths and echinoderms. [Written also Annuloidea.]
The act of animating, or giving life or spirit; the state of being animate or alive. The animation of the same soul quickening the whole frame.
A prefix, or combining form, in numerous compounds, usually relating to seed or blood vessels, or to something contained in, or covered by, a vessel.
An instrument for measuring the force or velocity of the wind; a wind gauge.
Entire or partial loss or absence of feeling or sensation; a state of general or local insensibility produced by disease or by the inhalation or application of an anæsthetic.
A fresh-water weed of the frog's-bit family (Hydrocharidaceæ), native to America. Transferred to England it became an obstruction to navigation.
A genus of fishes, remarkable for their power of living long out of water, and of making their way on land for considerable distances, and for climbing trees; the climbing fishes.
State of being ample; extent of surface or space; largeness of dimensions; size. The cathedral of Lincoln .
A genus of fresh-water ganoid fishes, exclusively confined to North America; called bowfin in Lake Champlain, dogfish in Lake Erie, and mudfish in South Carolina, etc. See Bowfin.

The quality or state of being ambiguous; doubtfulness or uncertainty, particularly as to the signification of language, arising from its admitting of more than one meaning; an equivocal word or expression. No shadow of ambiguity can rest upon the course to be
An alloy of mercury with another metal or metals; as, an amalgam of tin, bismuth, etc.
At all times; ever; perpetually; throughout all time; continually; as, God is always the same. Even in Heaven his [Mammon's] looks and thoughts.

The state of being allied; the act of allying or uniting; a union or connection of interests between families, states, parties, etc., especially between families by marriage and states by compact, treaty, or league; as, matrimonial alliances; an alliance betwe
An instrument for viewing pictures by means of a lens, so as to present them in their natural proportions and relations.
A term used in hailing; as, "Ship ahoy."
Gaping, as with wonder, expectation, or eager attention. Dazzles the crowd and sets them all agape.
On foot. We 'll walk afoot a while.
Borne on the water; floating; on board ship. On such a full sea are we now afloat.
Acting against, or in a contrary direction; opposed; contrary; opposite; conflicting; as, adverse winds; an adverse party; a spirit adverse to distinctions of caste.
Floating at random; in a drifting condition; at the mercy of wind and waves. Also fig.
. At one's pleasure; as one wishes.
One who practices rope dancing, high vaulting, or other daring gymnastic feats.
The act of acquitting; discharge from debt or obligation; acquittance.
A pustular affection of the skin, due to changes in the sebaceous glands.

The measurement of the strength of acids, especially by a chemical process based on the law of chemical combinations, or the fact that, to produce a complete reaction, a certain definite weight of reagent is required. -- Ac`id*i*met"ric*al, a.
An instrument for ascertaining the strength of acids. Ure.
The act of achieving or performing; an obtaining by exertion; successful performance; accomplishment; as, the achievement of his object.
A compound of aniline with acetyl, used to allay fever or pain; -- called also antifebrine.
Agreement; harmony; conformity. "In strict accordance with the law." Macaulay.

Accompanying as a subordinate; aiding in a secondary way; additional; connected as an incident or subordinate to a principal; contributing or contributory; said of persons and things, and, when of persons, usually in a bad sense; as, he was accessory to the ri
A coming to; the act of acceding and becoming joined; as, a king's accession to a confederacy.
The act of abstracting, separating, or withdrawing, or the state of being withdrawn; withdrawal. A wrongful abstraction of wealth from certain members of the community.
An absolving, or setting free from guilt, sin, or penalty; forgiveness of an offense. "Government .
The act of abasing, humbling, or bringing low; the state of being abased or humbled; humiliation.
A flowering; the putting forth and unfolding of blossoms.
The act of forcing or letting out of its proper vessels or ducts, as a fluid; effusion; as, an extravasation of blood after a rupture of the vessels.
The act of adorning, or the state of being adorned; adornment. In the selection of their ground, as well as in the embellishment of it.

To distinguish or mark by a specific difference; to effect a difference in, as regards classification; to develop differential characteristics in; to specialize; to desynonymize. The word then was differentiated into the two forms then and than.

The formation of a fetus at the result of an impregnation occurring after another impregnation but before the birth of the offspring produced by it. This is possible only when there is a double uterus, or where menstruation persists up to the time of the secon
The act, process, or result of scorifying, or reducing to a slag; hence, the separation from earthy matter by means of a slag; as, the scorification of ores.
A camera for obtaining a circular panoramic view of the horizon. The photographic plate is placed horizontally with a vertical lens above.
The process of forming a cicatrix, or the state of being cicatrized.
A squad of inapt recruits assembled for special drill.
The act or process of transcribing, or copying; as, corruptions creep into books by repeated transcriptions.
A meeting or assembly for conversation, particularly on literary or scientific subjects. Gray.

The relation of person by blood, is distinction from affinity or relation by marriage; blood relationship; as, lineal consanguinity; collateral consanguinity. Invoking aid by the ties of consanguinity.
The act or product of transliterating, or of expressing words of a language by means of the characters of another alphabet.

A headquarters for torpedo vessels and their supplies, usually having facilities for repairs and for instruction and experiments. The principal torpedo station of the United States is at Newport, R.I.

The photography of distant objects in more enlarged form than is possible by the ordinary means, usually by a camera provided with a telephoto lens or mounted in place of the eyepiece of a telescope, so that the real or a magnified image falls on the sensitive
Having dorsal vertebræ with long and divided transverse processes; -- applied to certain reptiles.

Twice and a half as great (as another thing); having the ratio of two and a half to one. Sesquiduplicate ratio (Math.), the ratio of two and a half to one, or one in which the greater term contains the lesser twice and a half, as that of 50 to 20.
Having a forked tongue, like a serpent.
Having all the toes turned forward, as the colies.
Having bones in the fins, as certain fishes.
Placed at the same node with a leaf, but separated from it by the whole diameter of the stem; as, an oppositifolious peduncle.
Having a cylindrical body with a convex head of larger diameter; having a head like that of a mushroom.
Having the first and second toes turned backward, as in the trogons.
Having a form intermediate between dentate and sinuate.
A beautiful warbler of the United States (Dendroica Blackburniæ). The male is strongly marked with orange, yellow, and black on the head and neck, and has an orange-yellow breast.
To go from place to place without any certain purpose or direction; to rove; to wander. He roameth to the carpenter's house.
The condition or quality of being opposable. In no savage have I ever seen the slightest approach to opposability of the great toe, which is the essential distinguishing feature of apes.
The act of ejecting phlegm or mucus from the throat or lungs, by coughing, hawking, and spitting.

A method adopted in etching, to keep the acid from those parts which are already sufficiently corroded, by applying varnish or other covering matter with a brush, but allowing the acid to act on the other parts.
A close-fitting cap represented in Greek art as worn by Orientals, assumed to have been conical in shape. It has been adopted in modern art as the so-called liberty cap, or cap of liberty.
To have an erroneous remembrance of; to suppose erroneously that one recollects. Hitchcock.
In an homonymous manner; so as to have the same name or relation.
So as to have motion or direction parallel to the equator.
A mineral of a violet-blue color, inclining to gray and white. It is a hydrous fluoride of cerium, yttrium, and calcium.
An instrument to indicate the state of the atmosphere, especially changes of atmospheric pressure, and hence changes of weather, as a barometer or baroscope. Poor man's weatherglass.
(a) That side of a vessel which is toward the wind; the windward side. (b) A piece of plank placed in a porthole, or other opening, to keep out water.
An instrument for viewing the interior of the urethra.
Want of conformity; incongruity; inconsistency. South.
A third somewhat; something mediating, or regarded as being, between two diverse or incompatible substances, natures, or positions.
The quality or state of being technical; technicalness.

The connection of two coils diagrammatically as a letter T, chiefly used as a connection for passing transformers. When the three free ends are connected to a source of three-phase current, two-phase current may be derived from the secondary circuits.
Essential parts. Ayliffe.
An extensive division of gastropod Mollusca in which the loop or visceral nerves is twisted, and the sexes separate. It is nearly to equivalent to Prosobranchiata.
An instrument for ascertaining the velocity of the blood in a vessel.
An apparatus for examining the interior of the mouth.
An electrical instrument for determining by the ear the rhythm of the pulse of a person at a distance.
An instrument for measuring the strength of the pulse beat; a sphygmograph.
A mineral of a bright metallic luster and tin-white to pale lead-gray color. It consist of arsenic and cobalt.
The act of regenerating, or the state of being regenerated.
An instrument for measuring the size of the pupil of the pupil of the eye.
The act of presenting, or the state of being presented; a setting forth; an offering; bestowal. Prayers are sometimes a presentation of mere desires.
An instrument, similar to the phenakistoscope, for presenting to view, or projecting upon a screen, images the natural motions of real objects.
A bent tube used to determine the velocity of running water, by placing the curved end under water, and observing the height to which the fluid rises in the tube; a kind of current meter.
The application of light for therapeutic purposes, esp. for treating diseases of the skin.
The act of perturbing, or the state of being perturbed; esp., agitation of mind.
The change of one mineral species to another, so as to involve a change in physical characters without alteration of chemical composition.
An instrument for measuring the amount which a ship heels at sea.

The indirect division of cells in which, prior to division of the cell protoplasm, complicated changes take place in the nucleus, attended with movement of the nuclear fibrils; -- opposed to karyostenosis. The nucleus becomes enlarged and convoluted, and final
That can not be successfully resisted or opposed; superior to opposition; resistless; overpowering; as, an irresistible attraction. An irresistible law of our nature impels us to seek happiness.
The state or quality of being irregular; that which is irregular.
Serving to introduce something else; leading to the main subject or business; preliminary; prefatory; as, introductory proceedings; an introductory discourse.
The act of intervening; interposition. Sound is shut out by the intervention of that lax membrane.

The act of installing or giving possession of an office, rank, or order, with the usual rites or ceremonies; as, the installation of an ordained minister in a parish. On the election, the bishop gives a mandate for his installation.
An instrument for measuring or ascertaining the degree or rate of electrical induction.

Not defensible; not capable of being defended, maintained, vindicated, or justified; unjustifiable; untenable; as, an indefensible fortress, position, cause, etc. Men find that something can be said in favor of what, on the very proposal, they thought utterly
An apparatus for determining the amount of sugar in diabetic urine.
An instrument for measuring the number of red blood corpuscles in the blood.
The act of bending the knee, particularly in worship. Bp.
A beating or flogging; a whipping; a scourging. Garth.
A wandering beyond proper limits; an excursion or sally from the usual way, course, or limit.
The state of being eccentric; deviation from the customary line of conduct; oddity.
The act of lessening, or seeking to lessen, price, value, or reputation.
With careful consideration, or deliberation; circumspectly; warily; not hastily or rashly; slowly; as, a purpose deliberately formed.
A machine for decorticating wood, hulling grain, etc.; also, an instrument for removing surplus bark or moss from fruit trees.
A horizontal row of corbels, with the panels or filling between them; also, less properly used to include the stringcourse on them.
The act of confirming or strengthening; the act of establishing, ratifying, or sanctioning; as, the confirmation of an appointment. Their blood is shed In confirmation of the noblest claim.
A compound of chloral and formic amide used to produce sleep.
The science, art, or practice of healthful exercise of the body and limbs, to promote strength and gracefulness; light gymnastics.
The theory which seeks to explain certain physiological and pathological by means of animalcules.
Absence of sexual appetite.
A house where beasts are butchered for the market.
One more that nineteen; twice; as, twenty men.
fr. Smooth, v.

A piece of strong steel wire with the ends curved and pointed, used on toe or quarter cracks to bind the edges together and prevent motion. It is clasped into two notches, one on each side of the crack, burned into the wall with a cautery iron.
The doctrine of symptoms; that part of the science of medicine which treats of the symptoms of diseases; semeiology.
The operation for restoring or replacing the soft palate when it has been lost. Dunglison.
A solid, the faces of which are six parallelograms, the opposite pairs being parallel, and equal to each other; a prism whose base is a parallelogram.

An apparatus in which the images of extermal objects, formed by a convex lens or a concave mirror, are thrown on a paper or other white surface placed in the focus of the lens or mirror within a darkened chamber, or box, so that the oulines may be traced.
The tenets of Sabbatarians. Bp.
The act or process of naturalizing, esp. of investing an alien with the rights and privileges of a native or citizen; also, the state of being naturalized.

The act or process of multiplying, or of increasing in number; the state of being multiplied; as, the multiplication of the human species by natural generation. The increase and multiplication of the world.
A photograph of the sun made by monochromatic light, usually of the calcium line (k), and showing the sun's faculæ and prominences.
Having knowledge; knowing; enlightened; of extensive information; erudite; learned. They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.
Moving with a bound or bounds. The bounding pulse, the languid limb.
Under cover; screened; sheltered; not exposed; hidden. Covered way (Fort.), a corridor or banquette along the top of the counterscarp and covered by an embankment whose slope forms the glacis.
Having a certain look or appearance; -- often compounded with adjectives; as, good-looking, grand-looking, etc.
Of or pertaining to science; used in science; as, scientific principles; scientific apparatus; scientific observations.
A cast, or facsimile copy, of an engraved block, matter in type, etc. (see citation); as, a polytype in relief.
To do or perform; to carry through; to execute, commonly in a bad sense; to commit (as a crime, an offense); to be guilty of; as, to perpetrate a foul deed. What the worst perpetrate, or best endure.

The act of disfranchising, or the state disfranchised; deprivation of privileges of citizenship or of chartered immunities. Sentenced first to dismission from the court, and then to disfranchisement and expulsion from the colony.

Not to believe; to refuse belief or credence to; to hold not to be true or actual. Assertions for which there is abundant positive evidence are often disbelieved, on account of what is called their improbability or impossibility.
To form or turn into allegory; as, to allegorize the history of a people.

Having the power of breathing impaired by the rupture, dilatation, or running together of air cells of the lungs, so that while the inspiration is by one effort, the expiration is by two; affected with pulmonary emphysema or with heaves; -- said of a horse. Yo
Having or covering an angle wider than the ordinary; -- applied to certain lenses of relatively short focus. Lenses for ordinary purposes have an angle of 50º or less.
Having whelks, ridges, or protuberances; hence, streaked; striated.
Having upright intentions or honorable purposes. Dutchmen who had sold themselves to France, as the wellintentioned party.
Furnished with wattles, or pendent fleshy processes at the chin or throat. The wattled cocks strut to and fro.
Having no tent or tents, as a soldier or a field.
Having made journeys; having gained knowledge or experience by traveling; hence, knowing; experienced. [Written also travelled.] The traveled thane, Athenian Aberdeen.
Consisting of three distinct webs inwrought together in weaving, as cloth or carpeting; having three strands; threefold.
Having strong or large thews or muscles; muscular; sinewy; strong.
A sight consisting of a small telescope, as on a compass or rifle.
Having the form of, or resembling, a style, pin, or pen; styloid.
Resembling tow; having long, loose scales, or matted filaments, like tow; stupose.
One who conceals himself board of a vessel about to leave port, or on a railway train, in order to obtain a free passage.
Provided with a step or steps; having a series of offsets or parts resembling the steps of stairs; as, a stepped key. Stepped gear, a cogwheel of which the teeth cross the face in a series of steps.

A thin plate of metal, leather, or other material, used in painting, marking, etc. The pattern is cut out of the plate, which is then laid flat on the surface to be marked, and the color brushed over it.

Partaking of, or exemplifying, the characteristics of a statue; having the symmetry, or other excellence, of a statue artistically made; as, statuesquelimbs; a statuesque attitude. Their characters are mostly statuesque even in this respect, that they have no
A round mass of snow pressed or roller together, or anything resembling such a mass.
A slight, superficial knowledge of something; sciolism. I had a great desire, not able to attain to a superficial skill in any, to have some smattering in all.
Having little wit; not wise; having scanty intellect or judgment.
Having the appearance or qualities of a shopkeeper, or shopman.
A costume consisting of a plain belted waist and skirt of the same material.
A split of a sheepskin; one of the thin sections made by splitting a sheepskin with a cutting knife or machine.
Made by one's self. Self-made man, a man who has risen from poverty or obscurity by means of his own talentss or energies.
A bed of oysters or mussels. [Scot.]
Consisting of scabs; rough; itchy; leprous; as, scabious eruptions. Arbuthnot.
The act or process of ruminating, or chewing the cud; the habit of chewing the cud. Rumination is given to animals to enable them at once to lay up a great store of food, and afterward to chew it.
Having the tail, or lower part of the body, bright red.
Having the frames, stem, and sternpost adjusted; -- said of a ship on the stocks.
A flattened ring-shaped piece of iron, to be pitched at a fixed object in play; hence, any heavy flat missile used for the same purpose, as a stone, piece of iron, etc. (b) pl.
A mill for grinding grain, the upper stone of which was turned by hand; -- used before the invention of windmills and watermills. Shak.
Shriveled or shrunken; -- said especially of grain which has lost its juices from the ravages of insects, such as the wheat midge, or Trips (Thrips cerealium).
Having the villi of the placenta collected into definite patches, or cotyledons.
Having phthisis, or some symptom of it, as difficulty in breathing.
Having (such) a nature, temper, or disposition; disposed; -- used in composition; as, good-natured, ill-natured, etc.
An inhabitant of a mountain; one who lives among mountains.
Having or causing mistrust, suspicions, or forebodings. Their light blown out in some mistrustful wood.
Of, pertaining to, or having a character of, a minim or minimum; least; smallest; as, a minimal amount or value.

Composed of, or covered with, lozenge-shaped scales; having lozenge-shaped divisions. Mascled armor, armor composed of small lozenge-shaped scales of metal fastened on a foundation of leather or quilted cloth.
Having a lap joint, or lap joints, as many kinds of woodwork and metal work.
A short club with a knobbed end used as a missile weapon by Kafir and other native tribes of South Africa.
Having the surface decorated with cloudings and streaks, somewhat as if imitating jasper.
Double-faced; deceitful. Janus-faced lock, one having duplicate faces so as to go upon a right or a left hand door, the key entering on either side indifferently.
Having power to inform, animate, or vivify. Dr.

The imagine-making power of the mind; the power to create or reproduce ideally an object of sense previously perceived; the power to call up mental imagines. Our simple apprehension of corporeal objects, if present, is sense; if absent, is imagination.
Pertaining to, or denoting, a compound consisting of a double fluoride of hydrogen and silicon; silicofluoric. See Silicofluoric.
Having the nature of, pertaining to, or covered with, herbs or herbage. "Herby valleys." Chapman.
Without a visible hammer; -- said of a gun having a cock or striker concealed from sight, and out of the way of an accidental touch.
The point of a spear, or an arrowhead.
Having the odor, taste, or appearance of fruit; also, fruitful. Dickens.
The freezing, or effect of a freezing, of some part of the body, as the ears or nose. Kane.
Gathered, or having the map gathered, into little tufts, knots, or protuberances. Cf.
Having small pits or depression, as the receptacle in some composite flowers.
Having a flat foot, with little or no arch of the instep.
Having broad, loose, dependent ears. Shak.
Having one's mental imagery prevailingly of the visual type; having one's thoughts and memories mainly in the form of visual images. -- Eye"-mind`ed*ness, n.
An operation that consists in inserting needless in the part affected, and connecting them with the poles of a galvanic apparatus.
Having eyes wanting brightness, liveliness, or vivacity. Shak.

A small craft used in the West India Islands to take off sugars, rum, etc., to the merchantmen; also, a vessel for transporting lumber, cotton, etc., coastwise; as, a lumber drogher. [Written also droger.] Ham.
Having the form of a cucumber; having the form of a cylinder tapered and rounded at the ends, and either straight or curved.
Having a crevice or crevices; as, a creviced structure for storing ears of corn. Trickling through the creviced rock.
Having crannies, chinks, or fissures; as, a crannied wall. Tennyson.

The right of an author or his assignee, under statute, to print and publish his literary or artistic work, exclusively of all other persons. This right may be had in maps, charts, engravings, plays, and musical compositions, as well as in books.
Encompassed with a coma, or bushy appearance, like hair; hairy.
Having ridges or bunches of flesh, like collops. With that red, gaunt, and colloped neck astrain.
Circular; as, a circulatory letter. Johnson.
Pertaining to, consisting, of resembling, turf; turfy. A cespitous or turfy plant has many stems from the same root, usually forming a close, thick carpet of matting.

A machine, used for the purpose of giving cloth, paper, etc., a smooth, even, and glossy or glazed surface, by cold or hot pressure, or for watering them and giving them a wavy appearance. It consists of two or more cylinders revolving nearly in contact, with
Made of silk; having a silky or flaxlike appearance. Coles.
Having bluffs, or bold, steep banks.

A breed of large and powerful dogs, with long, smooth, and pendulous ears, and remarkable for acuteness of smell. It is employed to recover game or prey which has escaped wounded from a hunter, and for tracking criminals.
Having two valves, as the oyster and some seed pods; bivalve.
An instrument or weapon with two prongs.
Having a white face or a white mark on the face, as a stag.
The disbelief or denial of the existence of a God, or supreme intelligent Being. Atheism is a ferocious system, that leaves nothing above us to excite awe, nor around us to awaken tenderness.
Ornamented with a pattern (which has been cut out of another color or stuff) applied or transferred to a foundation; as, appliqué lace; appliqué work.
Having a round, broad face, like an apple. "Apple-faced children." Dickens.
Having lost, or tending to lose, inflections by phonetic decay; as, anaptotic languages.
Of or pertaining to the genus Allium, or garlic, onions, leeks, etc.; having the smell or taste of garlic or onions.
Belonging to the order of fishes having spinose fins, as the perch. -- n.
Having a spiny head, as one of the Acanthocephala.
The maws, or stomachs, of young calves, used a rennet for curdling milk. [Scot.]
The anemone; -- so called because formerly supposed to open only when the wind was blowing. See Anemone.

(a) Contagious or poisonous matter, as of specific ulcers, the bite of snakes, etc.; -- applied to organic poisons. (b) The special contagion, inappreciable to the senses and acting in exceedingly minute quantities, by which a disease is introduced into the or
A stringed instrument of music; a bass viol of four strings, or a bass violin with long, large strings, giving sounds an octave lower than the viola, or tenor or alto violin.
A road way. Via Lactea Etym: [L.] (Anat.), the Milky Way, or Galaxy.

Want of power to produce the desired or proper effect; inefficiency; ineffectualness; futility; uselessness; fruitlessness; as, the inefficacy of medicines or means. The seeming inefficacy of censures.

A bass instrument of the saxhorn family.

Originally, a shield-bearer or armor-bearer, an attendant on a knight; in modern times, a title of dignity next in degree below knight and above gentleman; also, a title of office and courtesy; -- often shortened to squire.
An injection, or clyster, thrown into the rectum as a medicine, or to impart nourishment. Hoblyn.

The keyboard of an organ, pianoforte, or harmonium.
Having cirri along the margin of a part or organ.
A short, suppressed laugh; the expression of satisfaction, exultation, or derision.
Mean or unfair artifice to perplex a cause and obscure the truth; stratagem; sharp practice; sophistry. Irritated by perpetual chicanery.

Art to catch at faults; disposed to find fault or to cavil; eager to object; difficult to please. A captius and suspicious.

A light skiff or rowboat used on the Bosporus; also, a Levantine vessel of larger size.

A person appointed, or chosen, by parties to determine a controversy between them.
Literally: One sent forth; a messenger. Specifically: One of the twelve disciples of Christ, specially chosen as his companions and witnesses, and sent forth to preach the gospel.

To express or represent in the characters of another alphabet; as, to transliterate Sanskrit words by means of English letters. A.

Rounded stones containing tin ore, lying at the surface of the ground, and indicating a vein. Raymond.
An office or feast celebrated with less solemnity than the double ones. See Double, n., 8.
The customary certificate of national character which neutral merchant vessels are bound to carry in time of war; a passport for a vessel and cargo.
The act of dividing with an instrument having a sharp edge. Wiseman.
A small pan with a handle, in which sauce is prepared over a fire; a stewpan.
The act or practice of robbing; theft. Thieves for their robbery have authority When judges steal themselves.
An instrument employed for replacing a displaced organ or part.
A list of drams, operas, pieces, parts, etc., which a company or a person has rehearsed and is prepared to perform.
The parliament of Austria (exclusive of Hungary, which has its own diet, or parliament). It consists of an Upper and a Lower House, or a House of Lords and a House of Representatives.
A dish made of pieces of meat, stewed, and highly seasoned; as, a ragout of mutton.
A polishing material made of potter's clay that has failed in baking.
A rawhide whip plaited with two thongs of buffalo hide T. Roosevelt.
A form of crystal common with quartz, consisting of two six- sided pyramids, base to base.
A magistrate who, having been pretor at home, was appointed to the government of a province. [Written also proprætor.]
A clergyman of a superior order, as an archbishop or a bishop, having authority over the lower clergy; a dignitary of the church.
A soldier armed with a pike. Knolles.

A form of sentence among the ancient Syracusans by which they banished for five years a citizen suspected of having dangerous influence or ambition. It was similar to the ostracism in Athens; but olive leaves were used instead of shells for ballots.
A verse of five feet.
The act or process of laying a pavement, or covering some place with a pavement.
A proteidlike body found in the fluid from ovarian cysts and elsewhere. It is generally associated with a substance related to, if not identical with, glycogen.
Having the form or figure of an egg; egg-shaped; as, an oviform leaf.
A book composed of sheets each of which is folded into eight leaves; hence, indicating more or less definitely a size of book so made; -- usually written 8vo or 8º.
A young bird which has not abandoned the nest. Piers Plowman.
One of a denomination of Christians formerly living under the government of the Moors in Spain, and having a liturgy and ritual of their own. [Written also Mozarab, Mostarab.] Brande & C.
A soldier armed with a musket.
Having many segments; cleft into several parts by linear sinuses; as, a multifid leaf or corolla.

A follower of Mintanus, a Phrygian enthusiast of the second century, who claimed that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, dwelt in him, and employed him as an instrument for purifying and guiding men in the Christian life. -- Mon`ta*nis"tic, Mon`ta*nis"tic*al, a.
A composition consisting of one verse only.
A single algebraic expression; that is, an expression unconnected with any other by the sign of addition, substraction, equality, or inequality.
A pie made of mince-meat.
An old form of gunlock containing a match for firing the priming; hence, a musket fired by means of a match.
A silk or woolen vestment without sleeves worn by cardinals, bishops, abbots, and the prelates of the Roman court. It has a low collar, is fastened in front, and reaches almost to the knees.
Composed of dactyls and trochees so arranged as to produce a movement like that of ordinary speech.
Of or relating to the cell or compartment of an ovary, etc.; in composition, having cells; as trilocular. Gray.
An instrument for crushing stones in the bladder.
An instrument for performing laryngotomy.
Laminate. Laminated arch (Arch.), a timber arch made of layers of bent planks secured by treenails.
A curved bugle, having six finger keys or stops, by means of which the performer can play upon every key in the musical scale; -- called also keyed bugle, and key bugle. Moore.

A paper having on it these letters, with a sum named, and duly signed; -- in use in England as an acknowledgment of a debt, and taken as evidence thereof, but not amounting to a promissory note; a due bill. Wharton.

A figure of speech in which the expression is an evident exaggeration of the meaning intended to be conveyed, or by which things are represented as much greater or less, better or worse, than they really are; a statement exaggerated fancifully, through excitem
A water jar; esp., one with a large rounded body, a small neck, and three handles. Some of the most beautiful Greek vases are of this form.

The product of ten mulitplied by ten, or the number of ten times ten; a collection or sum, consisting of ten times ten units or objects; five score. Also, a symbol representing one hundred units, as 100 or C.
One of two or more words identical in orthography, but having different derivations and meanings; as, fair, n., a market, and fair, a., beautiful.
Consisting of gum; viscous; adhesive; producing or containing gum; covered with gum or a substance resembling gum. Kindles the gummy bark of fir or pine.

A crystalline, nitrogenous substance, with a sweet taste, formed from hippuric acid by boiling with hydrochloric acid, and present in bile united with cholic acid. It is also formed from gelatin by decomposition with acids.
A kind of verbal noun, having only the four oblique cases of the singular number, and governing cases like a participle.
An American machine gun, consisting of a cluster of barrels which, being revolved by a crank, are automatically loaded and fired.
A member of the Fronde.
Furnished with a fringe. Fringed lear (Bot.), a leaf edged with soft parallel hairs.
The cooling room of the Roman thermæ, furnished with a cold bath.
A beak flute, an older form of the flute, played with a mouthpiece resembling a beak, and held like a flageolet.

Having conspicuous flowers; -- used as an epithet with many names of plants; as, flowering ash; flowering dogwood; flowering almond, etc. Flowering fern, a genus of showy ferns (Osmunda), with conspicuous bivalvular sporangia.
A simple fieldwork, consisting of two faces forming a salient angle pointing outward and open at the gorge.
An old form of gunlock, as the flintlock, which ignites the priming by a spark; perhaps originally, a matchlock. Hence, a gun having such a lock.

A male of the human species castrated; commonly, one of a class of such persons, in Oriental countries, having charge of the women's apartments. Some of them, in former times, gained high official rank.
A euphemistic name for the Furies of Erinyes.
The action of a horse, when, to get rid of his rider, he rears, plunges, and kicks furiously.
A six-pointed star whose rays are wavy, instead of straight like those of a mullet. [Written also étoile.] Estoile of eight points, a star which has four straight and four wavy rays.
Having the form of a sword blade; sword-shaped; as, an ensiform leaf. Ensiform cartilage, and Ensiform process.
Having some object, as the head of a man or beast, impaled upon it; as, a sword which is said to be "enfiled of" the thing which it pierces.
A composition of dust of ivory or of bone with a cement; -- used for imitations of valuable stones and in making moldings, seals, etc. Knight.
A vase or drinking cup having two handles or ears.

One of a group of extinct reptiles having the jaws armed with a horny beak, as in turtles, and in the genus Dicynodon, supporting also a pair of powerful tusks. Their remains are found in triassic strata of South Africa and India.
The daughter of Jupiter and Latona; a virgin goddess who presided over hunting, chastity, and marriage; -- identified with the Greek goddess Artemis. And chaste Diana haunts the forest shade.
A glass vessel or bottle with a large body and small neck, inclosed in wickerwork.
A roof having a double slope, or composed, on each side, of two parts which have unequal inclination; a gambrel roof.
The god of love, son of Venus; usually represented as a naked, winged boy with bow and arrow. Pretty dimpled boys, like smiling cupids.
A soldier armed with a cuirass. Milton.
A tribe or confederacy of North American Indians, including the Muskogees, Seminoles, Uchees, and other subordinate tribes. They formerly inhabited Georgia, Florida, and Alabama.

The creation of the world or universe; a theory or account of such creation; as, the poetical cosmogony of Hesoid; the cosmogonies of Thales, Anaxagoras, and Plato. The cosmogony or creation of the world has puzzled philosophers of all ages.
The conductor, chief, or leader of the dramatic chorus; hence, the chief or leader of a party or interest. That noted corypheus [Dr.
(a) An obsolete rude reed instrument (Ger. Zinken), of the oboe family.

Formed in columns; having the form of a column or columns; like the shaft of a column. Columnar epithelium (Anat.), epithelium in which the cells are priismatic in form, and set upright on the surface they cover.
A foot consisting of four syllables, of which the first and last are long, and the other short (- ~ ~ -); that is, a choreus, or trochee, and an iambus united.
Having the form a piece of turf, i. e., many stems from one rootstock or from many entangled rootstocks or roots.
A garment worn throughout the Levant, consisting of a long gown with sleeves reaching below the hands. It is generally fastened by a belt or sash.
A size of type between long primer and brevier. See Type.
A charge representing a leather vessel for carrying water; -- also called water bouget.
The dysentery, a disease in which the flux or discharge from the bowels has a mixture of blood. Arbuthnot.
A dignity or degree of honor next below a baron and above a knight, having precedency of all orders of knights except those of the Garter. It is the lowest degree of honor that is hereditary.
An instrument for recording automatically the variations of atmospheric pressure.
A kind of banjo, with a short neck, tuned a fourth higher than the common banjo; -- popularly so called.
The precincts within which a bailiff has jurisdiction; the limits of a bailiff's authority.
Provided with antlers, as a stag.
A movement of the atmosphere opposite in character, as regards direction of the wind and distribution of barometric pressure, to that of a cyclone. -- An`ti*cy*clon"ic, a.
A man sphinx; a sphinx having the head of a man and the body of a lion.
A colorless liquid prepared from herring brine and containing amines, used as a local antiseptic.
Of, pertaining to, or resembling, alveoli or little cells, sacs, or sockets. Alveolar processes, the processes of the maxillary bones, containing the sockets of the teeth.

A trick or stratagem practiced for insnaring or deception; a sly, insidious; artifice; a beguilement; an allurement. Put on the whole armor of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Having weight; heavy; ponderous; as, a weighty body.

Any wheel for propelling machinery or for other purposes, that is made to rotate by the direct action of water; -- called an overshot wheel when the water is applied at the top, an undershot wheel when at the bottom, a breast wheel when at an intermediate poin

The granting or dedication of property in trust for a pious purpose, that is, to some object that tends to the good of mankind, as to support a mosque or caravansary, to provide for support of one's family, kin, or neighbors, to benefit some particular person
Not limited; having no bounds; boundless; as, an unlimited expanse of ocean.
Not happy or fortunate; unfortunate; unlucky; as, affairs have taken an unhappy turn.

A white to gray volcanic tufa, formed of decomposed trachytic cinders; -- sometimes used as a cement. Hence, a coarse sort of plaster or mortar, durable in water, and used to line cisterns and other reservoirs of water.
Like trash; containing much trash; waste; rejected; worthless; useless; as, a trashy novel.
Having the top or upper part too heavy for the lower part. Sir H.
Any species of Tinea, or of the family Tineidæ, which includes numerous small moths, many of which are injurious to woolen and fur goods and to cultivated plants. Also used adjectively.
The right which the owner of a mill possesses, by contract or law, to compel the tenants of a certain district, or of his sucken, to bring all their grain to his mill for grinding. Erskine.
One whose occupation is to cut out and make men's garments; also, one who cuts out and makes ladies' outer garments. Well said, good woman's tailor .
A thought, imagination, or conjecture, which is based upon feeble or scanty evidence; suspicion; guess; as, the surmisses of jealousy or of envy. [We] double honor gain From his surmise proved false.
Fat; thick; plump; bulky. Nor the squab daughter nor the wife were nice.
A little or spot in or anything, of a different substance or color from that of the thing itself. An huge great serpent, all with speckles pied.
Having the power of dissolving; dissolving; as, a solvent fluid. "the solvent body." Boyle.

The state or quality of being solid; density; consistency, -- opposed to fluidity; compactness; fullness of matter, -- opposed to openness or hollowness; strength; soundness, -- opposed to weakness or instability; the primary quality or affection of matter by
Boiled; seethed; also, soaked; heavy with moisture; saturated; as, sodden beef; sodden bread; sodden fields.
Resembling soap; having the qualities of, or feeling like, soap; soft and smooth.
One who sleeps; a slumberer; hence, a drone, or lazy person.
Moving with a dragging, scraping step. "A shuffling nag." Shak.

A process used in preparing certain kinds of leather, which consists in frizzing the skin, and working oil into it to supply the place of the astringent (tannin, alum, or the like) ordinarily used in tanning.

One who, or that which, scorifies; specifically, a small flat bowl-shaped cup used in the first heating in assaying, to remove the earth and gangue, and to concentrate the gold and silver in a lead button.
Circuitous; going round; indirect; as, roundabout speech. We have taken a terrible roundabout road.

The hard, amber-colored resin left after distilling off the volatile oil of turpentine; colophony. Rosin oil, an oil obtained from the resin of the pine tree, -- used by painters and for lubricating machinery, etc.
Having taken root; firmly implanted; fixed in the heart. "A rooted sorrow." Shak.
A rent or long aperture; a chink; a fissure; a crack. Sir T.
Tending to produce reformation; reformative.
Fruit, as grapes, plucked from the cluster. Ray.
One who, or that which, rams or drives. Specifically: (a) An instrument for driving anything force; as, a rammer for driving stones or piles, or for beating the earth to more solidity.
To germinate; to bud; to multiply abundantly. Warburton.

A new convert especially a convert to some religion or religious sect, or to some particular opinion, system, or party; thus, a Gentile converted to Judaism, or a pagan converted to Christianity, is a proselyte. Ye [Scribes and Pharisees] compass sea and land
Bustle; confusion; tumult; flutter; bother. [Written also potter, and pudder.] "What a pother and stir!" Oldham.
Capable of being weighed; having appreciable weight. -- Pon"der*a*ble*ness, n.
Having the qualities or effects of poison; venomous; baneful; corrupting; noxious. Shak.
A kind of small pinchers with long jaws, -- used for bending or cutting metal rods or wire, for handling small objects such as the parts of a watch, etc.
A fork, or farming utensil, used in pitching hay, sheaves of grain, or the like.

One of a sect or party among the Jews, noted for a strict and formal observance of rites and ceremonies and of the traditions of the elders, and whose pretensions to superior sanctity led them to separate themselves from the other Jews.
Tending to persuade; having the power of persuading; as, persuasive eloquence. "Persuasive words." Milton.
A body so suspended from a fixed point as to swing freely to and fro by the alternate action of gravity and momentum. It is used to regulate the movements of clockwork and other machinery.
Having no beaten path or way; untrodden; impenetrable; as, pathless woods. Trough the heavens' wide, pathless way.
An honorary title given to officers of high rank in Turkey, as to governers of provinces, military commanders, etc. The earlier form was bashaw.
A burden; an obligation. Onus probandi ( Etym: [L.], obligation to furnish evidence to prove a thing; the burden of proof.
Having one side only, or one side prominent; hence, limited to one side; partial; unjust; unfair; as, a one-sided view or statement. "Unguarded and one-sided language." T.

Pertinaciously adhering to an opinion, purpose, or course; persistent; not yielding to reason, arguments, or other means; stubborn; pertinacious; -- usually implying unreasonableness. I have known great cures done by obstinate resolution of drinking no wine.
Variegated in color; consisting of different colors; dappled; party-colored; as, a motley coat.
Of or pertaining to a mode or mood; consisting in mode or form only; relating to form; having the form without the essence or reality. Glanvill.

The act of sending, or the state of being sent; a being sent or delegated by authority, with certain powers for transacting business; comission. Whose glorious deeds, but in these fields of late, Made emulous missions' mongst the gods themselves.
Wrong conduct; bad behavior; mismanagement. Addison.
Disposed; inclined; having a mind. Joseph...
The act of plundering.
Being alive; having life; as, a living creature.
Of or pertaining to a line; consisting of lines; in a straight direction; lineal.
Having light; lighted; not dark or gloomy; bright. White walls make rooms more lightsome than black.
A medicine to check the secretion of milk, or to dispel a supposed accumulation of milk in any part of the body.
Full of knots; having knots knurled; as, a knotted cord; the knotted oak. Dryden.
A house; esp., one which is a resort for thieves. [Slang, Eng.]
An iota; a point; a tittle; the smallest particle. Cf.
Made of jet, or like jet in color. The people .

Of very bad report; having a reputation of the worst kind; held in abhorrence; guilty of something that exposes to infamy; base; notoriously vile; detestable; as, an infamous traitor; an infamous perjurer. False errant knight, infamous, and forsworn.
Not active; having no power to move; that does not or can not produce results; inert; as, matter is, of itself, inactive.
Abounding with husks; consisting of husks. Dryden.
Resemblance between different plants or animals, in external shape, in general habit, or in organs, which is not due to descent from a common ancestor, but to similar surrounding circumstances.
Wide and general destruction; devastation; waste. As for Saul, he made havoc of the church.
One who provides lodgings; especially, the officer of the English royal household who formerly preceded the court when traveling, to provide and prepare lodgings. Fuller.
In the middle; at half the distance; imperfectly; partially; as, he halfway yielded. Temples proud to meet their gods halfway.
a small fascine or fagot, steeped in wax, pitch, and glue, used in various ways, as for igniting buildings or works, or to light ditches and ramparts. Farrow.
Pleasant; agreeable; desirable. We have many goodly days to see.
Partial or total darkness; thick shade; obscurity; as, the gloom of a forest, or of midnight.
Like a ghost in appearance; deathlike; pale; pallid; dismal. Each turned his face with a ghastly pang.
One who founds, establishes, and erects; one who lays a foundation; an author; one from whom anything originates; one who endows.
Having a fever; suffering from, or affected with, a moderate degree of fever; showing increased heat and thirst; as, the patient is feverish.
A nonsensical exclamation attributed to giants and ogres; hence, any expression calculated to impose upon the timid and ignorant. "Impudent fee-faw-fums." J.
To think out; to find out or discover by thinking; to devise; to contrive. "Excogitate strange arts." Stirling.

The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay or yield; compulsion to give or furnish; a levying by force; a driving to compliance; as, the exaction to tribute or of obedience; hence, extortion. Take away your exactions from my people.
To speak or write in commendation of (another); to extol in speech or writing; to praise.

Having two significations equally applicable; capable of double interpretation; of doubtful meaning; ambiguous; uncertain; as, equivocal words; an equivocal sentence. For the beauties of Shakespeare are not of so dim or equivocal a nature as to be visible only
A warehouse; a magazine for depositing goods, stores, etc.; a mart or place where merchandise is deposited; as, an entrepôt for shipping goods in transit.
Having a power of enchantment; charming; fascinating. -- En*chant"ing*ly, adv.
Double; twofold. Duplex escapement, a peculiar kind of watch escapement, in which the scape-wheel has two sets of teeth.
Fagots, boughs, or loose materials of any kind, laid on the bottom of the hold for the cargo to rest upon to prevent injury by water, or stowed among casks and other cargo to prevent their motion.

A composition, in prose or poetry, accommodated to action, and intended to exhibit a picture of human life, or to depict a series of grave or humorous actions of more than ordinary interest, tending toward some striking result. It is commonly designed to be sp
A rope to haul down, or to assist in hauling down, a sail; as, a staysail downhaul; a trysail downhaul.
Want of esteem; low estimation, inclining to dislike; disfavor; disrepute. Disesteem and contempt of the public affairs.
A slight natural depression or indentation on the surface of some part of the body, esp. on the cheek or chin.
Any textile fabric (esp. linen or cotton toweling) woven in diaper pattern.
A dweller; an inhabitant. "Denizens of air." Pope.
Having the power to create; exerting the act of creation. "Creative talent." W.
Primarily, a place of standing or staying together; hence, any solemn assembly or council. To council summons all his mighty peers, Within thick clouds and dark tenfold involved, A gloomy consistory.

A curve invented by Diocles, for the purpose of solving two celebrated problems of the higher geometry; viz., to trisect a plane angle, and to construct two geometrical means between two given straight lines.
Granted or established by charter; having, or existing under, a charter; having a privilege by charter. The sufficiency of chartered rights.
The soft naked sheath at the base of the beak of birds of prey, parrots, and some other birds. See Beak.
A compound medicinal powder, used by the ancients to sprinkle on ulcers, to absorb perspiration, etc. Dunglison.
One of the short ropes or iron cramps used to brace in the shrouds toward the masts so a to give freer sweep to the yards.

A groove in any cylinder; specif., a groove around the cylinder of an elongated bullet for small arms to contain a lubricant, or around the rotating band of a gun projectile to lessen the resistance offered to the rifling. Also, a groove around the base of a c
A broad-leaved plant (Petasites vulgaris) of the Composite family, said to have been used in England for wrapping up pats of butter.
A clumsy boat, used for conveying provisions, fruit, etc., for sale, to vessels lying in port or off shore.
Report; rumor; fame. The bruit thereof will bring you many friends.

An upright wooden or iron post in a boat or on a dock, used in veering or fastening ropes. Bollard timber (Naut.), a timber, also called a knighthead, rising just within the stem in a ship, on either side of the bowsprit, to secure its end.
an Australian eagle (Aquila audax), which destroys lambs and even the kangaroo. -- To make bold, to take liberties or the liberty; to venture.
Having largeness of size; of much bulk or magnitude; of great size; large. "He's too big to go in there." Shak.
A small inflammatory tumor; a pustule. [Prov.
A public proclamation or edict; a public order or notice, mandatory or prohibitory; a summons by public proclamation.
Having the qualities of balm; odoriferous; aromatic; assuaging; soothing; refreshing; mild. "The balmy breeze." Tickell.
An infant or young child of either sex; a babe.
An excessive or inordinate desire of gain; greediness after wealth; covetousness; cupidity. To desire money for its own sake, and in order to hoard it up, is avarice.
Conferring aid or help; helping; aiding; assisting; subsidiary; as auxiliary troops. Auxiliary scales (Mus.), the scales of relative or attendant keys.
A person who sells by auction; a person whose business it is to dispose of goods or lands by public sale to the highest or best bidder.
Profound debility of children due to lack of food and to unhygienic surroundings. --A*threp"tic (#), a.
Supplemental; not inherent or original; adscititious; additional; assumed. Homer has been reckoned an ascititious name.

Doubtful or uncertain, particularly in respect to signification; capable of being understood in either of two or more possible senses; equivocal; as, an ambiguous course; an ambiguous expression. What have been thy answers What but dark, Ambiguous, and with do
An officer selected by a general to carry orders, also to assist or represent him in correspondence and in directing movements.
Conjoined; attending; consequent. Though that my death were adjunct to my act.

An overflowing fullness; ample sufficiency; great plenty; profusion; copious supply; superfluity; wealth: -- strictly applicable to quantity only, but sometimes used of number. It is lamentable to remember what abundance of noble blood hath been shed with smal
Pertaining to, or formed by, concretion or aggregation; producing or containing concretions.
Having a rough grain or fiber; hence, figuratively, having coarse traits of character; not polished; brisque.
One who believes that past changes in the structure of the earth have proceeded from cataclysms or causes more violent than are now operating; -- called also nonuniformitarian.
Having a feather-edge; also, having one edge thinner than the other, as a board; -- in the United States, said only of stuff one edge of which is made as thin as practicable.
Having the petals free, that is, entirely separate from each other; -- said of both plant and flower.

In the Ptolemaic system, the outermost of the revolving concentric spheres constituting the universe, the motion of which was supposed to carry with it all the inclosed spheres with their planets in a daily revolution from east to west. See Crystalline heavens

The quality or state of being inconsistent; discordance in respect to sentiment or action; such contrariety between two things that both can not exist or be true together; disagreement; incompatibility. There is a perfect inconsistency between that which is of
A trifle; trifling talk; nonsense. [Colloq.] Spectator.

The act of commemorating; an observance or celebration designed to honor the memory of some person or event. This sacrament was designed to be a standing commemoration of the death and passion of our Lord.
Examination of the abdomen to detect abdominal disease.
The act of one who, or that which, weaves; the act or art of forming cloth in a loom by the union or intertexture of threads.
A collar or neck chain, usually twisted, especially as worn by ancient barbaric nations, as the Gauls, Germans, and Britons.

The act of shedding, separating, or casting off or out; as, the shedding of blood.
A small beaklike process or extension of some part; a small rostrum; as, the rostellum of the stigma of violets, or of the operculum of many mosses; the rostellum on the head of a tapeworm.
imp. of Run.
pl. of Penny.

The whole body of salt water which covers more than three fifths of the surface of the globe; -- called also the sea, or great sea. Like the odor of brine from the ocean Comes the thought of other years.
The act of one who lends.
The act of throwing with force.
of Hang. Hung beef, the fleshy part of beef slightly salted and hung up to dry; dried beef.
A touching, controlling, managing, using, etc., with the hand or hands, or as with the hands. See Handle, v.
A false die. See Gord.
The brow or hairy arch above the eye. Shak.
The pendulous skin under the neck of an ox, which laps or licks the dew in grazing.
A dirty or clotted lock of wool on a sheep; a taglock.

The change from a liquid to a thickened, curdlike, insoluble state, not by evaporation, but by some kind of chemical reaction; as, the spontaneous coagulation of freshly drawn blood; the coagulation of milk by rennet, or acid, and the coagulation of egg albumi

Pertaining to chemistry; characterized or produced by the forces and operations of chemistry; employed in the processes of chemistry; as, chemical changes; chemical comnbinations. Chemical attraction or affinity.

That piece of armor which protected the lower part of the face, whether forming a part of the helmet or fixed to the breastplate. It was so constructed (with joints or otherwise) that the wearer could raise or lower it to eat and drink.
A kind of flag attached to a spear or pike by a crosspiece, and used by a chief as his standard in battle. Hang out our banners on the outward walls.
A form of hydrometer, specially graduated, for finding the density of milk, and thus discovering whether it has been mixed with water or some of the cream has been removed.

A variety of bronze possessing great hardness, elasticity, and toughness, obtained by melting copper with tin phosphide. It contains one or two per cent of phosphorus and from five to fifteen per cent of tin.
A machine for converting an alternating current into an alternating current of a different number of phases and the same frequency.
A cross formed of two strips of different metals, to illustrate the Peltier effect.
The hard pearly internal layer of several kinds of shells, esp. of pearl oysters, river mussels, and the abalone shells; nacre.
The state of interdigitating; interdigital space. Owen.
A form of apparatus (somewhat different from the hemadrometer) for measuring the velocity of the blood.
An instrument for registering the velocity of the blood.

A piece of timber or an iron barrel traversed with iron-pointed spikes or spears, five or six feet long, used to defend a passage, stop a breach, or impede the advance of cavalry, etc. Obstructions of chain, boom, and cheval-de-frise.
A photometer for measuring the brightness of stars.
Not willing; loath; disinclined; reluctant; as, an unwilling servant. And drop at last, but in unwilling ears, This saving counsel, "Keep your piece nine years." Pope.
Not usual; uncommon; rare; as, an unusual season; a person of unusual grace or erudition. -- Un*u"su*al*ly, adv.
Giving trouble or anxiety; vexatious; burdensome; wearisome. This troublesome world.
The large stomach of ruminating animals, when prepared for food. How say you to a fat tripe finely broiled Shak.
Occurring every third day; as, a tertian fever.
Of or pertaining to the genus Taurus, or cattle.

Cleaning off surfaces, or cleaning away dust, dirt, or litter, as a broom does; moving with swiftness and force; carrying everything before it; including in its scope many persons or things; as, a sweeping flood; a sweeping majority; a sweeping accusation. --
The quality or condition of being striated.
