Any plant of the genus Lithospermum, herbs having a fruit composed of four stony nutlets.
A North American plant (Collinsonia Canadensis) having a very hard root; horse balm. See Horse balm, under Horse.

The space, or any of the spaces, in front of the boilers of a ship, from which the furnaces are fed; the stokehole of a ship; also, a room containing a ship's boilers; as, forced draft with closed stokehold; -- called also, in American ships, fireroom.
To stop; to choke.
A name given to several kinds of wood with an unpleasant smell, as that of the Foetidia Mauritiana of the Mauritius, and that of the South African Ocotea bullata.
The quality or state of being stiff; as, the stiffness of cloth or of paste; stiffness of manner; stiffness of character. The vices of old age have the stiffness of it too.
Any one of numerous species of small fishes of the genus Gasterosteus and allied genera. The back is armed with two or more sharp spines.
A special podlike or fusiform branch containing tetraspores. It is found in certain red algæ.
A herald, in the Iliad, who had a very loud voice; hence, any person having a powerful voice.
Having a small or narrow mouth; -- said of certain small ground snakes (Opoterodonta), which are unable to dilate their jaws.
A cyst containing matter like suet.
Pertaining to, or of the nature of, steatite; containing or resembling steatite.
Any humming bird of the genus Heliomaster. The feathers of the throat have a brilliant metallic luster.
A curious American mole (Condylura cristata) having the nose expanded at the end into a stellate disk; -- called also star-nosed mole.
Any marine gastropod shell of the genus Apporhais having an elongated siphon. See Illust.
A tracing, called a pulse tracing, consisting of a series of curves corresponding with the beats of the heart, obtained by the application of the sphygmograph.
Any one of numerous species of sand wasps of the genus Sphex and allied genera. These wasps have the abdomen attached to the thorax by a slender pedicel.

An instrument for facilitating the practical use of spherics in navigation and astronomy, being constructed of two cardboards containing various circles, and turning upon each other in such a manner that any possible spherical triangle may be readily found, an
A very large toothed whale (Physeter macrocephalus), having a head of enormous size. The upper jaw is destitute of teeth.
A name given to several species of crowfoot (Ranunculus) which have spear-shaped leaves.
A vessel with a perforated cover, for sprinkling with a liquid; a sprinkler.
A suspicion; a suggestion; hence, a very small portion; a taste; as, coffee with a soupçon of brandy; a soupçon of coquetry.
Causing sleep; tending to cause sleep; soporiferous; as, the soporific virtues of opium.
A showy leguminous plant (Calliandra purpurea) of the West Indies. The flowers have long tassels of purple stamens.
An alkaloid produced by the decomposition of solanine, as a white crystalline substance having a harsh bitter taste.
A hemispherical or rounded head to a rivet or bolt; also, a swaging tool with a cavity in its face for forming such a rounded head.
A young salmon two or three years old, when it has acquired its silvery color.

Any species of Pleurotomaria, a genus of beautiful, pearly, spiral gastropod shells having a deep slit in the outer lip. Many fossil species are known, and a few living ones are found in deep water in tropical seas.
Any cephalopod having a siphonate shell.
Ferruginous quartz, of a blood-red or brownish red color, sometimes with a tinge of yellow.
A long-tailed monkey (Semnopitchecus melalophus) native of Sumatra. It has a crest of black hair.
A perennial rosaceous herb (Potentilla Anserina) having the leaves silvery white beneath.
Any one of numerous species of butterflies of the genus Argynnis and allied genera, having silvery spots on the under side of the wings. See Illust.
Any one of several species of small fishes of the family Atherinidæ, having a silvery stripe along each side of the body. The common species of the American coast (Menidia notata) is very abundant.
A shock; a jog; a violent concussion or impulse. [R.
Any species of small burrowing snakes of the family Uropeltidæ, native of Ceylon and Southern Asia. They have a small mouth which can not be dilated.
To subject to the process of vapor galvanizing (which see, below).
A peculiar gregarious burrowing rodent (Haplodon rufus), native of the coast region of the Northwestern United States. It somewhat resembles a muskrat or marmot, but has only a rudimentary tail.
A swimming leg (of an insect) having a fringe of hairs on the margin.
To energize or excite (the field magnets of a dynamo) by induction from the residual magnetism of its cores, leading all or a part of the current thus produced through the field-magnet coils.
A reaping machine containing mechanism for binding the grain into sheaves.
One of a family of beetles having the maxillary palpi terminating in a hatchet-shaped joint.
A kind of blackish seaweed (Himanthalia lorea) found on the northern coasts of the Atlantic. It has a thonglike forking process rising from a top-shaped base.
A large American holothurian (Lophothuria Fabricii) having a bright orange convex body covered with finely granulated scales. Its expanded tentacles are bright red.
Any bird with a schizognathous palate.
A tool with a semicircular edge, -- used by engravers to clear away the spaces between the lines of an engraving. Fairholt.
An arctic seal (Lobodon carcinophaga), having the molars serrated; -- called also crabeating seal.
A small North American owl (Nyctale Acadica), destitute of ear tufts and having feathered toes; -- called also Acadian owl.
A coarse cloth made of hemp, and used for packing goods, etc. [Written also sarpelere.] Tyrwhitt.
A small South American opossum (Didelphys opossum), having four white spots on the face.
Any species of the genus Sarcoptes and related genera of mites, comprising the itch mites and mange mites. -- a.
Any one of several species of South American monkeys of the genus Cebus, having long and prehensile tails. Some of the species are called also capuchins.
A colorless crystalline substance, isomeric with piperonal, but having weak acid properties. It is extracted from sandalwood.
A metal urn used in Russia for making tea. It is filled with water, which is heated by charcoal placed in a pipe, with chimney attached, which passes through the urn.
A white crystalline substance consisting of phenol salicylate.
A boat propelled by a sail or sails.
A kind of ketch very common in the Levant, which has neither topgallant sail nor mizzen topsail.
A kind of turnip commonly with a large and long or ovoid yellowish root; a Swedish turnip. See Turnip.
To chew the cud; to chew again what has been slightly chewed and swallowed. "Cattle free to ruminate." Wordsworth.

A European gold wasp (Chrysis ignita) which has the under side of the abdomen bright red, and the other parts deep bluish green with a metallic luster. The larva is parasitic in the nests of other wasps and of bees.
A boat designed to be propelled by oars instead of sails.
Any one of several species of large hawks of the genus Archibuteo, having the legs feathered to the toes. Called also rough- legged hawk, and rough-legged buzzard.
Bovine. -- n.
A fleshy-leaved herb (Rhodiola rosea); rosewort; -- so called because the roots have the odor of roses.
A green micaceous mineral occurring in minute scales. It is essentially a silicate of aluminia and potash containing vanadium.
Any species of small marine fishes of the genera Onos and Rhinonemus (formerly Motella), allied to the cod. They have three or four barbels.
The reed bunting. It has a collar of white feathers.
One of the Rhipiptera, a group of insects having wings which fold like a fan; a strepsipter.
Any species of the genus Rhinilophus, or family Rhinolophidæ, having a horseshoe-shaped nasal crest; a horseshoe bat.
Any one of several species of bryozoans of the genus Retepora. They form delicate calcareous corals, usually composed of thin fenestrated fronds.
To make a remark or remarks; to comment.
A kind of dry fruit, consisting of three or more cells, each which at length breaks open at the inner angle.
To fashion anew; to form or mold into shape a second time. MacKnight.
To embody again.
To put, or go, on board a vessel again; to embark again.
Any one of several species of marine food fishes of the genus Diabasis, or Hæmulon, of the Southern United States, having the inside of the mouth bright red. Called also flannelmouth, and grunt.
A small North American dace (Minnilus cornutus, or Notropis megalops). The male, in the breeding season, has bright red fins.
To arrange again; to arrange in a different way.
To adjust or settle again; to put in a different order or relation; to rearrange.
To transport with excitement; to enrapture. [Poetic] Thomson.

Having a general affinity to ranunculaceous plants. Ranal alliance (Bot.), a name proposed by Lindley for a group of natural orders, including Ranunculaceæ, Magnoliaceæ, Papaveraceæ, and others related to them.
A plant (Campanula Rapunculus) of the Bellflower family, with a tuberous esculent root; -- also called ramps.
A long, flexible stick, rod, or branch, which is interwoven with others, between upright posts or stakes, in making a kind of hedge or fence.
A small sloop-rigged racing yacht carrying about six hundred square feet of sail, distinguished from a knockabout by having a short bowsprit.
Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the fatty acid series, containing fifteen atoms of carbon; called also pentadecylic acid.
Butane, each molecule of which has four carbon atoms.
A punting pole with a broad flange near the end to prevent it from sinking into the mud; a setting pole.
Ruby silver; dark red silver ore. It is a sulphide of antimony and silver, occurring in rhombohedral crystals or massive, and is of a dark red or black color with a metallic adamantine luster.
To murmur as a cat. See Pur.
To become a pupa.
A punt made from the goal line by a player of the side which has made a touchdown to one of his own side for a fair catch, from which an attempt to kick a goal may be made.
Any one of numerous species of beautiful humming birds of the genus Eriocnemis having large tufts of downy feathers on the legs.
birds whose young at first have down on the pterylæ only; -- called also Gymnopædes.
To combine with oxygen, as any elementary substance, in such proportion as to form a protoxide.
That one of a series of oxides having the lowest proportion of oxygen. See Proto-, 2 (b).
A kind of granite or gneiss containing a silvery talcose mineral.
A colorless gaseous hydrocarbon (C3H6) of the ethylene series, having a garlic odor. It occurs in coal gas, and is produced artificially in various ways.
One of the fleshy legs found on the abdominal segments of the larvæ of Lepidoptera, sawflies, and some other insects. Those of Lepidoptera have a circle of hooks.
One who has presbyopia; a farsighted person.
The act of previous determination; a purpose formed beforehand; as, the predetermination of God's will. Hammond.
The quality or state of being precise; exact limitation; exactness; accuracy; strict conformity to a rule or a standard; definiteness. I have left out the utmost precisions of fractions.
A metallic handle with a clasp for holding a crayon.
A utensil for popping corn, usually a wire basket with a long handle.
A Linnæan order of plants having many styles.
One who maintains that animals of the same species have sprung from more than one original pair; -- opposed to monogenist.
A bromide containing more than one atom of bromine in the molecule.
To apply pollen to (a stigma). -- Pol`li*na"tion, n.
Of, pertaining to, or containing, lead; -- used specifically to designate those compounds in which it has a lower valence as contrasted with plumbic compounds.
Of, pertaining to, resembling, or containing, lead; -- used specifically to designate those compounds in which it has a higher valence as contrasted with plumbous compounds; as, plumbic oxide.

A vote by universal male suffrage; especially, in France, a popular vote, as first sanctioned by the National Constitution of 1791. [Written also plebiscit.] Plebiscite we have lately taken, in popular use, from the French.
To appease; to pacify; to concilate. "Therefore is he always propitiated and placated." Cudworth.
A large voracious fresh-water fish (Serrasalmo piraya) of South America, having lancet-shaped teeth.
To go before, and prepare or open a way for; to act as pioneer.
A compact granular cryptocrystalline mineral of a dull grayish or greenish white color. It is a hydrous alkaline silicate, and is derived from the alteration of other minerals, as iolite.
Having a firing pin to explode the cartridge; as, a pin-fire rifle.
An alkaloid extracted from jaborandi (Pilocarpus pennatifolius) as a white amorphous or crystalline substance which has a peculiar effect on the vasomotor system.
Of or pertaining to Phyllorhina and other related genera of bats that have a leaflike membrane around the nostrils.

An apparatus consisting of a large wheel with spokes, which when turning very rapidly is illuminated by momentary flashes of light passing through slits in a rotating disk. By properly timing the succession of flashes the wheel is made to appear to be motionle
An instrument for recording minute intervals of time. The record is made by the power of a magnetic field, due to an electric signaling current, to turn the plane of polarization of light.
A colorless gas, PH3, analogous to ammonia, and having a disagreeable odor resembling that of garlic. Called also hydrogen phosphide, and formerly, phosphureted hydrogen.
A South American butterfly (Ithonia phono) having nearly transparent wings.
Any species of Phalaropus and allied genera of small wading birds (Grallæ), having lobate toes. They are often seen far from land, swimming in large flocks.
Any marsupial belonging to Phalangista, Cuscus, Petaurus, and other genera of the family Phalangistidæ. They are arboreal, and the species of Petaurus are furnished with lateral parachutes.

One of the compartments in a church which are separated by low partitions, and have long seats upon which several persons may sit; - - sometimes called slip. Pews were originally made square, but are now usually long and narrow.
A common baptismal name for a man. The name of one of the apostles, Peter boat, a fishing boat, sharp at both ends, originally of the Baltic Sea, but now common in certain English rivers.
To pass or flow through, as an aperture, pore, or interstice; to permeate. That labyrinth is easily pervaded.
To disturb; to agitate; to vex; to trouble; to disquiet. Ye that .
A sulphide containing more sulphur than some other compound of the same elements; as, iron pyrites is a persulphide; -- formerly called persulphuret.

One of a group of shooting stars which appear yearly about the 10th of August, and cross the heavens in paths apparently radiating from the constellation Perseus. They are beleived to be fragments once connected with a comet visible in 1862.
To oxidize to the utmost degree, so as to form a peroxide.
An oxide containing more oxygen than some other oxide of the same element. Formerly peroxides were regarded as the highest oxides.
A silk-producing moth (Attacus Pernyi) which feeds upon the oak. It has been introduced into Europe and America from China.

Any small marine gastropod shell of the genus Littorina. The common European species (Littorina littorea), in Europe extensively used as food, has recently become naturalized abundantly on the American coast.
An oxide containing five atoms of oxygen in each molecule; as, phosphorus pentoxide, P2O5.
A Linnæan class of plants having five separate stamens.
Capable of neutralizing, or combining with, five molecules of a monobasic acid; having five hydrogen atoms capable of substitution by acid residues; -- said of certain complex bases.
Any one of numerous species of Pennatula, Pteroides, and allied genera of Alcyonaria, having a featherlike form; a sea-pen. The zooids are situated along one edge of the side branches.
Abnormal regularity; the state of certain flowers, which, being naturally irregular, have become regular through a symmetrical repetition of the special irregularity.
A method of treatment, devised by Pasteur, for preventing certain diseases, as hydrophobia, by successive inoculations with an attenuated virus of gradually increasing strength.
(a) That circuit of ground committed to the charge of one parson or vicar, or other minister having cure of souls therein. Cowell.
A flourish made with the pen at the end of a signature. In the Middle Ages, this formed a sort of rude safeguard against forgery.
A kind of mica related to muscovite, but containing soda instead of potash. It is characteristic of the paragonite schist of the Alps.
An alkaloid found in opium. It has a weaker therapeutic action than morphine.
A small Asiatic mammal (Ailurus fulgens) having fine soft fur. It is related to the bears, and inhabits the mountains of Northern India.
One of a family of clavicorn beetles, including those which have very long maxillary palpi.
A South African plant (Prionium Palmita) of the Rush family, having long serrated leaves. The stems have been used for making brushes.
Of, pertaining to, or containing, palladium; -- used specifically to designate those compounds in which palladium has a lower valence as compared with palladic compounds.
Of, pertaining to, or derived from, palladium; -- used specifically to designate those compounds in which the element has a higher valence as contrasted with palladious compounds.
One of a family of bats, including those which have thick external ears.
A bird or other animal having thick toes.
To task too heavily.
To hear more of (anything) than was intended to be heard; to hear by accident or artifice. Shak.
To cast or cover over; hence, to cloud; to darken. Those clouds that overcast your morn shall fly.
To exceed in vying. Dryden.
To come out to the surface of the ground; -- said of strata.
An apparatus, consisting of a number of cells whose sides are of parchment paper, for conducting the process of osmosis. It is used esp.

Denoting those compounds of osmium in which the element has a valence relatively lower than in the osmic compounds; as, osmious chloride. [Written also osmous.] Osmious acid (Chem.), an acid derived from osmium, analogous to sulphurous acid, and forming unstab
A cloth made of worsted and cotton, -- used for wearing apparel.
An American ranunculaceous plant (Hidrastis Canadensis), having a yellow tuberous root; -- also called yellowroot, golden seal, etc.

A telescope with a diagonal eyepiece, suspended vertically in gimbals by the object end beneath a fixed diagonal plane mirror. It is used for delineating landscapes, by means of a pencil at the eye end which leaves the delineation on paper.
An instrument with a revolving wheel for measuring a curved line, as on a map.
An oily liquid, obtained by distillation of calcium oleate, and probably consisting of the ketone of oleic acid.
Copper wire with a strong but light insulation, used in wiring houses, etc.
The state of being under oestrual influence, or of having sexual desire.
A volatile liquid obtained by boiling sulphur with linseed oil. It has an unpleasant garlic odor.
One who occupies, or has possession.

To darken; to obscure; to becloud; hence, to confuse; to bewilder. His head, like a smokejack, the funnel unswept, and the ideas whirling round and round about in it, all obfuscated and darkened over with fuliginous matter.
Any Australian bat of the genus Nyctophilus, having a very simple nasal appendage.
of Number. The fourth book of the Pentateuch, containing the census of the Hebrews.

A person or thing of a sort that there is no other such; something extraordinary; a thing that has not its equal. It is given as a name to various objects, as to a choice variety of apple, a species of medic (Medicago lupulina), a variety of pottery clay, etc.
A coarse umbelliferous plant (Ligusticum actæifolium) with a large aromatic root. It is found chiefly in the Alleghany region.
The head; -- used jocosely or contemptuously. Come, master, I have a project in my noddle.
To combine, or impregnate, with nitrogen or its compounds.

To wink; to nictate. Nictitating membrance (Anat.), a thin membrance, found in many animals at the inner angle, or beneath the lower lid, of the eye, and capable of being drawn across the eyeball; the third eyelid; the haw.
One who has lately come.
A tumor developed on, or connected with, a nerve, esp. one consisting of new-formed nerve fibers.
Having the quality of acting upon or affecting the nerves; quieting nervous excitement. -- n.
An essential oil obtained by distillation from the flowers of the orange. It has a strong odor, and is used in perfumery, etc.
A peculiar kind of fructification on certain red algæ, consisting of an external mass of filaments at length separating into tetraspores.
To utter the cry of the horse; to whinny.

The act of denying; assertion of the nonreality or untruthfulness of anything; declaration that something is not, or has not been, or will not be; denial; -- the opposite of Ant: affirmation. Our assertions and negations should be yea and nay.
Seasickness; hence, any similar sickness of the stomach accompanied with a propensity to vomit; qualm; squeamishness of the stomach; loathing.
A European toad (Bufo calamita), having a yellow line along its back.
Any one of a series of hydroxyl derivatives of naphthalene, analogous to phenol. In general they are crystalline substances with a phenol (carbolic) odor.
To mingle, saturate, or impregnate, with naphtha.
Having a head like that of a nail; formed so as to resemble the head of a nail. Nail-headed characters, arrowheaded or cuneiform characters.
A name given to several varieties of Old World grapes, differing in color, size, etc., but all having a somewhat musky flavor. The muscat of Alexandria is a large oval grape of a pale amber color.
Any mollusk which has a shell composed of more than two pieces.
A brown, amorphous, bitter substance having a strong emetic action, extracted from the root of the mudar.

Any one of several species of long-tailed, passerine birds of the genus Momotus, having a strong serrated beak. In most of the species the two long middle tail feathers are racket-shaped at the tip, when mature.
A small abscess or tumor having a resemblance to a mulberry. Dunglison.
An apparatus for raising a liquid by pressure of air or steam in a reservoir containing the liquid.
A Linnæan order of plants, having solitary flowers with united anthers, as in the genus Lobelia.
Having one oblique inclination; -- applied to strata that dip in only one direction from the axis of elevation.
A painting or drawing in a single color; a picture made with a single color.
A trader; a dealer; -- now used chiefly in composition; as, fishmonger, ironmonger, newsmonger.
A Linnæan class of plants embracing those having but a single stamen.
A Linnæan class of plants having the stamens united into a tube, or ring, by the filaments, as in the Mallow family.
A small, handsome, long-tailed West American monkey (Cercopithecus mona). The body is dark olive, with a spot of white on the haunches.
A cutaneous disease characterized by numerous tumors, of various forms, filled with a thick matter; -- so called from the resemblance of the tumors to some molluscous animals. Dunglison.
An agricultural implement used in Flanders, consisting of a kind of large shovel drawn by a horse and guided by a man. [Written also mollebært and mouldebært.] Simmonds.

Any plant of the genus Mitella, -- slender, perennial herbs with a pod slightly resembling a bishop's miter; bishop's cap. False miterwort, a white-flowered perennial herb of the United States (Tiarella cardifolia).
Mistake of the meaning; error; misconception. Bacon.
To rule badly; to misgovern.
To reckon wrongly; to miscalculate. Swift.
To slight or undervalue. O, for those vanished hours, so much misprized!
To put in a wrong place; to set or place on an improper or unworthy object; as, he misplaced his confidence.
To match unsuitably.
To judge erroneously or unjustly; to err in judgment; to misconstrue.
One of a group of mammals having a small size as a typical characteristic. It includes the lower orders, as the Insectivora, Cheiroptera, Rodentia, and Edentata.
An instrument consisting of a short pendulum with a sliding weight. It is set in motion by clockwork, and serves to measure time in music.
A light, volatile liquid, H2C(OCH3)2, regarded as a complex ether, and having a pleasant ethereal odor. It is obtained by the partial oxidation of methyl alcohol.
To find the quantity, dimensions, or capacity of, by any rule or standard; to measure.
To change by a metabolic process. See Metabolism.
A radioactive product intermediate between thorium and radiothorium, with a period of 5.5 years.
Any bird of the genus Merganser, and allied genera. They are allied to the ducks, but have a sharply serrated bill.
Tissue composed of spheroidal cells.

Having the qualities fabled to belong to the god Mercury; swift; active; sprightly; fickle; volatile; changeable; as, a mercurial youth; a mercurial temperament. A mercurial man Who fluttered over all things like a fan.
Full of mercy; having or exercising mercy; disposed to pity and spare offenders; unwilling to punish. The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious.
The objects of commerce; whatever is usually bought or sold in trade, or market, or by merchants; wares; goods; commodities. Spenser.
A piano having a mechanical attachment which enables the player to prolong the notes at will.
A climbing plant (Ullucus officinalis) of the Andes, having tuberous roots which are used as a substitute for potatoes.
One of a family of fresh-water pectinibranchiate mollusks, having a turret-shaped shell.
A discharge from the bowels of black matter, consisting of altered blood.
One of a group which includes the higher orders of mammals, having a large size as a typical characteristic.
To tincture or impregnate with anything medicinal; to drug. "Medicated waters." Arbuthnot.
A large European sciænoid fish (Sciæna umbra or S. aquila), having white bloodless flesh.
A wife or a widow, especially, one who has borne children; a woman of staid or motherly manners. Your wives, your daughters, Your matrons, and your maids.
An excitant containing opium, much used by the Turks. Dunglison.
Any spiral marine shell of the genus Persona, having a curiously twisted aperture.
A perforated stone-faced runner for grinding.
One skillful to hit a mark with a missile; one who shoots well.
A large wild goat (Capra megaceros), having huge flattened spiral horns. It inhabits the mountains of Northern India and Cashmere.

Of, pertaining to, designating, those compounds of manganese in which the element has a lower valence as contrasted with manganic compounds; as, manganous oxide. Manganous acid, a hypothetical compound analogous to sulphurous acid, and forming the so-called ma
To treat ill; to abuse; to treat roughly.
A tool somewhat like a chisel with a groove in it, used by calkers of ships to finish the seams after the oakum has been driven in.
A South African lemur (Galago maholi), having very large ears. [Written also moholi.]
A South American stork (Euxenara maguari), having a forked tail.
To spot; to stain; to blur. Maculate the honor of their people.
One of a group of wading birds (Macrodactyli) having very long toes. [Written also macrodactyle.]
An immensely long blackish seaweed of the Pacific (Macrocystis pyrifera), having numerous almond-shaped air vessels.

Any one of several metameric alkaloids, C5H3N.(CH3)2, of the pyridine series, obtained from bone oil as liquids, and having peculiar pungent odors. These alkaloids are also called respectively dimethyl pyridine, ethyl pyridine, etc.
To lie hid; to lie in wait. Like wild beasts, lurking in loathsome den.

A large marine annelid (Arenicola marina) having a row of tufted gills along each side of the back. It is found burrowing in sandy beaches, both in America and Europe, and is used for bait by European fishermen.
A leguminous plant (Medicago sativa), having bluish purple cloverlike flowers, cultivated for fodder; -- called also alfalfa. [Written also lucerne.]
To bend; to box; to stoop. [Archaic] Chaucer.
A perennial herb (Phryma Leptostachya), having slender seedlike fruits.
A kind of crystallite having a (slender) acicular form.
One of a tribe of beetles, having long maxillary palpi.
To feel extreme disgust at, or aversion for. Loathing the honeyed cakes, I Ionged for bread.
Any one of several small, fresh-water, cyprinoid fishes of the genera Cobitis, Nemachilus, and allied genera, having six or more barbules around the mouth. They are found in Europe and Asia.
A hard, or stony, plantlike organism, as the gorgonians, corals, and corallines, esp. those gorgonians having a calcareous axis.
A sac containing small, calcareous concretions (otoliths). They are found in many Medusæ, and other invertebrates, and are supposed to be auditory organs.
To make antiseptic.
To treat or regard as a lion or object of great interest. J.
Rising or having risen from rest; -- said of cattle. See Couchant and levant, under Couchant.
A bird or other animal having slender toes. [Written also lepodactyle.]
To make legal.

A large sea turtle (Sphargis coriacea), having no bony shell on its back. It is common in the warm and temperate parts of the Atlantic, and sometimes weighs over a thousand pounds; -- called also leather turtle, leathery turtle, leather-backed tortoise, etc.
Having a leaflike membrane on the nose; -- said of certain bats, esp. of the genera Phyllostoma and Rhinonycteris.
A white crystalline substance extracted from the fruit of the bay (Laurus nobilis), and consisting of a complex mixture of glycerin ethers of several organic acids.
One of a series of organic compounds, regarded as anhydrides of certain hydroxy acids. In general, they are colorless liquids, having a weak aromatic odor.
An acid amide derived from lactic acid, and obtained as a white crystalline substance having a neutral reaction. It is metameric with alanine.
Generating or shedding tears; given to shedding tears; suffused with tears; tearful. You should have seen his lachrymose visnomy.
To treat by, or subject to, the Krupp process.
A long-tailed ape (Macacus cynomolgus) of India and Sumatra. It is reddish olive, spotted with black, and has a black tail.
A protuberance; a swelling; a knob; a button; hence, rising ground; a summit. See Knob, and Knop.
A northern gull (Rissa tridactyla), inhabiting the coasts of Europe and America. It is white, with black tips to the wings, and has but three toes.
To bring forth a young goat.

One of a series of series of complex nitrogenous substances, represented by methyl ketol and related to indol. Methyl ketol, a weak organic base, obtained as a white crystalline substance having the odor of fæces.
One of a series of organic bases obtained by the reduction of certain isonitroso compounds of the ketones. In general they are unstable oily substances having a pungent aromatic odor.
A large New Zealand parrot (Nestor notabilis), notorious for having acquired the habit of killing sheep; -- called also mountain parrot.
A large, green, arboreal, orthopterous insect (Cyrtophyllus concavus) of the family Locustidæ, common in the United States. The males have stridulating organs at the bases of the front wings.

An instrument for measuring the rain that falls; a rain gauge.

Goddess of the seasons, or of the hours of the day. Lo!
Queer, and fitted to provoke laughter; ludicrous from oddity; amusing and strange.
A public assembly of the Roman people for electing officers or passing laws.

Eating or feeding on flesh. The term is applied: (a) to animals which naturally seek flesh for food, as the tiger, dog, etc.; (b) to plants which are supposed to absorb animal food; (c) to substances which destroy animal tissue, as caustics.

A florid, brilliant style of music, written for effect, to show the range and flexibility of a singer's voice, or the technical force and skill of a performer; virtuoso music. Aria di bravura ( Etym: [It.], a florid air demanding brilliant execution.
Expressed in articles or in separate items or particulars. [Archaic] Bacon.
One of the chief magistrates in ancient Athens, especially, by preëminence, the first of the nine chief magistrates. -- Ar*chon"tic, a.

A term used to denote a duty or charge laid upon goods, at a certain rate per cent upon their value, as stated in their invoice, - - in opposition to a specific sum upon a given quantity or number; as, an ad valorem duty of twenty per cent.
Situated in front of the maxillary bones; pertaining to the premaxillæ; intermaxillary. -- n.

A certificate issued by a government that there has been deposited with it silver to a specified amount, payable to the bearer on demand. In the United States and its possessions, it is issued against the deposit of silver coin, and is not legal tender, but is
Having yellow fruit.
A steamboat having a stern wheel instead of side wheels. [Colloq.
A thick batter pudding made of Indian meal stirred into boiling water; mush. [U.
The chief commander of an army; especially, the commander in chief of an army consisting of two or more grand divisions under separate commanders; -- a title used in most foreign countries.
A winding so arranged as to divide the armature current and lead a portion of it around the field-magnet coils; -- opposed to series winding. --Shunt"-wound` (#), a.

Differing in kind; having unlike qualities; possessed of different characteristics; dissimilar; -- opposed to homogeneous, and said of two or more connected objects, or of a conglomerate mass, considered in respect to the parts of which it is made up. -- Het`e
Having, or relating to the power of producing heat; -- applied to foods which, being rich in carbon, as the fats, are supposed to give rise to heat in the animal body by oxidation.
A man employed in labor, whether in tillage or manufactures; a worker.
One who, or that which, works; a laborer; a performer; as, a worker in brass. Professors of holiness, but workers of iniquity.
A witty saying; a sentence or phrase which is affectedly witty; an attempt at wit; a conceit. Milton.
, pl. of Villus.

A semifluid or fluid oleoresin, primarily the exudation of the terebinth, or turpentine, tree (Pistacia Terebinthus), a native of the Mediterranean region. It is also obtained from many coniferous trees, especially species of pine, larch, and fir.
A braid, knot, or curl, of hair; a ringlet. Her yellow hair was braided in a tress.
One who transcribes, or writes from a copy; a copier; a copyist.
One who trades; a shopkeeper.
The act of clipping the hair, or of shaving the crown of the head; also, the state of being shorn.
The quality or state of being thin (in any of the senses of the word).
The number four; a collection of four things; a quaternion.
Extreme fear; fear that agitates body and mind; violent dread; fright. Terror seized the rebel host.
A cover or covering; an integument.
The act of sewing; also, the line along which two things or parts are sewed together, or are united so as to form a seam, or that which resembles a seam.
A meal taken at the close of the day; the evening meal.
A furrow; a groove; a fissure.
A fastness; a fort or fortress; fortfield place; a place of security.
One who is strange, foreign, or unknown. Specifically: -- (a) One who comes from a foreign land; a foreigner.
imp. of Steal.
An old French copper coin, equivalent in value to, and now displaced by, the five-centime piece (sou.
An opening; a hollow; a bending.
A shopkeeper; a retailer. Dryden.
A trader who sells goods in a shop, or by retail; -- in distinction from one who sells by wholesale. Addison.
The state or quality of being hidden; as, his movements were detected in spite of their secrecy. The Lady Anne, Whom the king hath in secrecy long married.

The quality of being sagacious; quickness or acuteness of sense perceptions; keenness of discernment or penetration with soundness of judgment; shrewdness. Some [brutes] show that nice sagacity of smell.
Sorrow for the misery of another; pity; tenderness. [Poetic] "They weep for ruth." Chaucer.
a. & n.

The act of turning, as a wheel or a solid body on its axis, as distinguished from the progressive motion of a revolving round another body or a distant point; thus, the daily turning of the earth on its axis is a rotation; its annual motion round the sun is a
One who, or that which, reflects. Boyle.
The act of recreating, or the state of being recreated; refreshment of the strength and spirits after toil; amusement; diversion; sport; pastime.
The quality or state of being pubescent, or of having arrived at puberty. Sir T.
The earliest age at which persons are capable of begetting or bearing children, usually considered, in temperate climates, to be about fourteen years in males and twelve in females.

The state of being prosperous; advance or gain in anything good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; attainment of the object desired; good fortune; success; as, commercial prosperity; national prosperity. Now prosperity begins to m
Descendants of the human kind, or offspring of other animals; children; offspring; race, lineage. " Issued from the progeny of kings." Shak.
Knowledge of events before they take place; foresight. God's certain prescience of the volitions of moral agents.
The morning star; Phosphor.

One who pays; one who compensates, rewards, or requites; specifically, an officer or agent of a government, a corporation, or an employer, whose duty it is to pay salaries, wages, etc., and keep account of the same.
A small dish, pan, or vase.

A lover, of either sex; a wooer or a mistress (formerly in a good sense, now only in a bad one); one who takes the place, without possessing the rights, of a husband or wife; -- used of a man or a woman. The seducer appeared with dauntless front, accompanied b
Any minute nipplelike projection; as, the papillæ of the tongue.
A form of government in which the supreme power is placed in the hands of a few persons; also, those who form the ruling few. All oligarchies, wherein a few men domineer, do what they list.
Often; frequently; not rarely; many times. [Poetic] Chaucer.
One who offends; one who violates any law, divine or human; a wrongdoer. I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders.
The shell or hard external covering in which the kernel of a nut is inclosed.
The act of confining a ship to a particular place, by means of anchors or fastenings.
A little mount; a hillock; a small elevation or prominence. [Written also monticule.]
One of two equal parts; a half; as, a moiety of an estate, of goods, or of profits; the moiety of a jury, or of a nation. Shak.
A model or measure.
Bad fortune or luck; calamity; an evil accident; disaster; mishap; mischance. Consider why the change was wrought, You 'll find his misfortune, not his fault.
A Russian village community. D.
Anything very minute; as, the minims of existence; -- applied to animalcula; and the like.
Aspect; air; manner; demeanor; carriage; bearing. Vice is a monster of so frightful mien, As, to be hated, needs but to be seen.
A sweet or agreeable succession of sounds. Lulled with sound of sweetest melody.
pl. of Medium.
A brick or tile. Knight.

A resinous substance produced mainly on the banyan tree, but to some extent on other trees, by the Coccus lacca, a scale-shaped insect, the female of which fixes herself on the bark, and exudes from the margin of her body this resinous substance.
One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a person who does work that requires strength rather than skill, as distinguished from that of an artisan.
A buffoon; a merry-andrew; a court fool. This .
The act of insulating, or the state of being insulated; detachment from other objects; isolation.
A hospital, or place where the infirm or sick are lodged and nursed gratuitously, or where out-patients are treated.
Drunkenness; inebriation. E.
That which is imposed or levied; a tax, tribute, or duty; especially, a duty or tax laid by goverment on goods imported into a country. Even the ship money .
That which impedes or hinders progress, motion, activity, or effect. Thus far into the bowels of the land Have we marched on without impediment.
A pendent, and usually conical, mass of ice, formed by freezing of dripping water; as, the icicles on the eaves of a house.
The home place; a home and the inclosure or ground immediately connected with it. Dryden.
A handle; especially, the handle of a sword, dagger, or the like.
Herbs collectively; green food beasts; grass; pasture. "Thin herbage in the plaims." Dryden.
One who, or that which, heats.
The state of being hale, sound, or whole, in body, mind, or soul; especially, the state of being free from physical disease or pain. There is no health in us.
One who sells wares by crying them in the street; hence, a peddler or a packman.
The hip; the projecting region of the lateral parts of the pelvis and the hip joint; the hind part.
A thick, viscid fluid; a clot, as of blood. Quincy.
The juice or other liquid matter that drips from flesh in cooking, made into a dressing for the food when served up.

The state or quality of being grand; vastness; greatness; splendor; magnificence; stateliness; sublimity; dignity; elevation of thought or expression; nobility of action. Nor doth this grandeur and majestic show Of luxury .
A concrete juice, or gum resin, produced by several species of trees in Siam, Ceylon, and Malabar. It is brought in masses, or cylindrical rolls, from Cambodia, or Cambogia, -- whence its name.
A prop or support.
The finger next to the thumb; the index.
A soldier who marches and fights on foot; a foot soldier.
The act of flowing. Cotgrave.
The part a chimney appropriated to the fire; a hearth; -- usually an open recess in a wall, in which a fire may be built.

An implacable or malicious foe; one who is diabolically wicked or cruel; an infernal being; -- applied specifically to the devil or a demon. Into this wild abyss the wary fiend Stood on the brink of Hell and looked a while.
A small fiber; the branch of a fiber; a very slender thread; a fibrilla. Cheyne.
An authoritative command or order to do something; an effectual decree. His fiat laid the corner stone.
One who farms; as: (a) One who hires and cultivates a farm; a cultivator of leased ground; a tenant. Smart.
Sight of the eye; the sense of seeing; view; observation. Josephus sets this down from his own eyesight.
The act or state of expecting or looking forward to an event as about to happen. "In expectation of a guest." Tennyson.
At any time; at any period or point of time. No man ever yet hated his own flesh.
One who employs another; as, an employer of workmen.
The scum or refuse matter which is thrown off, or falls from, metals in smelting the ore, or in the process of melting; recrement.
A separating tissue; a partition; a septum.
A conversation between two or more persons; particularly, a formal conservation in theatrical performances or in scholastic exercises.
Right-handedness.
Act of injuring another's reputation by any slanderous communication, written or oral; the wrong of maliciously injuring the good name of another; slander; detraction; calumny; aspersion.
One who owes a debt; one who is indebted; -- correlative to creditor. [I 'll] bring your latter hazard back again, And thankfully rest debtor for the first.
A narrow opening resulting from a split or crack or the separation of a junction; a cleft; a fissure; a rent. The mouse, Behind the moldering wainscot, shrieked, Or from the crevice peered about.

A small, narrow opening, fissure, crevice, or chink, as in a wall, or other substance. In a firm building, the cavities ought not to be filled with rubbish, but with brick or stone fitted to the crannies.
Two taken together; a pair or couple; especially two lines of verse that rhyme with each other. A sudden couplet rushes on your mind.
A twisting; a writhing; wry motion; a twist; as, the contortion of the muscles of the face. Swift.

The "beans" or "berries" (pyrenes) obtained from the drupes of a small evergreen tree of the genus Coffea, growing in Abyssinia, Arabia, Persia, and other warm regions of Asia and Africa, and also in tropical America.
from Cleave, v. t.

The body of men set apart, by due ordination, to the service of God, in the Christian church, in distinction from the laity; in England, usually restricted to the ministers of the Established Church. Hooker.
The Anointed; an appellation given to Jesus, the Savior. It is synonymous with the Hebrew Messiah.
A shift, or undergarment, worn by women.
A large, deep, hollow place in the earth; a large cave.
A tenacious, elastic, gummy substance obtained from the milky sap of several plants of tropical South America (esp. the euphorbiaceous tree Siphonia elastica or Hevea caoutchouc), Asia, and Africa.
Brush; a thicket or coppice of small trees and shrubs.
A woman newly married, or about to be married. Has by his own experience tried How much the wife is dearer than the bride.
Respiration; the act of inhaling and exhaling air. Subject to a difficulty of breathing.
imp. & p.
The act of bequeathing or leaving by will; as, a bequest of property by A. to B.
Note: [Called also benjamin.]
That which is written with one's own hand; an original manuscript; a person's own signature or handwriting.
The act of assisting; help; aid; furtherance; succor; support. Without the assistance of a mortal hand.
A ring; a ringlike part or space.
The act of mixing; mixture.
The act of adjuring; a solemn charging on oath, or under the penalty of a curse; an earnest appeal. What an accusation could not effect, an adjuration shall.

A soft, unctuous, or waxy substance, of a light brown color, into which the fat and muscle tissue of dead bodies sometimes are converted, by long immersion in water or by burial in moist places. It is a result of fatty degeneration.
The quality of being acute or pointed; sharpness; as, the acuteness of an angle.
The quality of being sour; sourness; tartness; sharpness to the taste; as, the acidity of lemon juice.
Extreme hatred or detestation; the feeling of utter dislike.
Laughingly gay; overflowing with good humor and good spirits; jovial; inclined to laughter or play ; sportive. They drank, and were merry with him.
Permitting water or other fluid to leak in or out; as, a leaky roof or cask.
Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid (called also thioarsenic acid) analogous to arsenic acid, and known only in its salts.
The act of consummating, or the state of being consummated; completed; completion; perfection; termination; end (as of the world or of life). "Tis a consummation Devoutly to be wished.
A pit in the form of an inverted cone or pyramid, constructed as an obstacle to the approach of an enemy, and having a pointed stake in the middle. The pits are called also trapholes.
A name given to some species of morning-glory (Ipomoea) having the leaves lobed in pedate fashion.
Any species of Thalaassinidæ, a family of burrowing macrurous Crustacea, having a long and soft abdomen.
A Linnæan class of plants having six stamens, four of which are longer than the others.

An instrument for recording and reproducing sound by local magnetization of a steel wire, disk, or ribbon, moved against the pole of a magnet connected electrically with a telephone receiver, or the like.
A carbonate containing an excess of the basic constituent.
An engine moved by steam.

The male germ cell in animals and plants, the essential element in fertilization; a microscopic animalcule-like particle, usually provided with one or more cilia by which it is capable of active motion. In animals, the familiar type is that of a small, more or
To convert (a magnesian silicate) into serpentine. -- Ser`pen*tin`i*za"tion, n.

A mechanism (usually one operated by electricity, compressed air, a spring, or an explosive gas), attached to an internal- combustion engine, as on an automobile, and used as a means of starting the engine without cranking it by hand.
A leguminous plant (Ornithopus scorpides) of Southern Europe, having curved pods.

A tyrant flycatcher (Milvulus forficatus) of the Southern United States and Mexico, which has a deeply forked tail. It is light gray above, white beneath, salmon on the flanks, and fiery red at the base of the crown feathers.
To invigorate anew.
A chloride containing more than one atom of chlorine in the molecule.
An American sparrow (Zonotrichia albicollis) having a conspicuous white throat. The name is imitative of its note.
An elephant that is furnished with a pad for carrying burdens instead of with a howdah for carrying passengers.
Nitrate of calcium, a substance having a grayish white color, occuring in efforescences on old walls, and in limestone caves, especially where there exists decaying animal matter.
Untrue representation; false or incorrect statement or account; -- usually unfavorable to the thing represented; as, a misrepresentation of a person's motives. Sydney Smith.
To take in a wrong sense; to misunderstand. Locke.
A larval crustacean in a stage following the nauplius, and having about seven pairs of appendages.
A plant (Sedum Telephium) with fleshy leaves, which has extreme powers of resisting drought; garden ox-pine.
Any one of a division (Lepidoganoidei) of ganoid fishes, including those that have scales forming a coat of mail. Also used adjectively.
An annual weed (Polygonum Persicaria), having a lanceolate leaf with a dark spot in the middle.
A box through which the main conductors of a system of electric distribution pass, and where connection is made with branch circuits.
Meteoric iron; a meteorite consisting of metallic iron without stony matter.
Those insects which have a complete metamorphosis; metabola.
Those insects which have an incomplete metamorphosis.
An instrument for measuring the harmonic relations of sounds. It is often a monochord furnished with movable bridges.
The art or process of reducing gold to extremely thin leaves, by beating with a hammer. Ure.
A form of annelid larva having cilia on the ventral side.

A tropical leguminous bush (Poinciana, or Cæsalpinia, pulcherrima) with prickly branches, and showy yellow or red flowers; -- so named from its having been sometimes used for hedges in the West Indies. Baird.
One of a group of stalked rotifers, having ciliated tentacles around the lobed disk.
A large, venomous serpent (Trigonocephalus lanceolatus) of Brazil and the West Indies. It is allied to the rattlesnake, but has no rattle.
An aquatic plant (Hottonia palustris), having finely divided leaves.
The actors in a drama or play.
One of the secondary, and usually sexual, zooids produced by budding or fission from the primary zooids, in animals having alternate generations. In the tapeworms, the joints are deuterozooids.
A naked human skull as the emblem of death; the head of the conventional personification of death. I had rather be married to a death's-head with a bone in his mouth.
To cause to wheel or turn in an opposite direction.

Examination of the brain for the diagnosis of diseas; esp., the act or process of diagnosticating the condition of the brain by examination of the interior of the eye (as with an ophthalmoscope). Buck.
(Zoöl.) A peculiar early larval stage of certain starfishes, having a bilateral structure, and swimming by means of bands of vibrating cilia.

The act of accelerating, or the state of being accelerated; increase of motion or action; as, a falling body moves toward the earth with an acceleration of velocity; -- opposed to retardation. A period of social improvement, or of intellectual advancement, con
Glued together; united, as by some adhesive substance.
The placing of a before another, which, by ordinary rules, ought to follow it.
A liquid oil made from animal fats (esp. beef fat) by separating the greater portion of the solid fat or stearin, by crystallization.
The theory or method of suggesting an effect or impression without elaboration of the details; -- a disignation of a recent fashion in painting and etching.
Suitable; adapted; fit; corresponding; congruous; conformable; in accord or agreement; obedient; willing. Action correspondent or repugnant unto the law.
Counteracting scurvy. -- n.
A medicine tending to cause parturition, or to give relief in childbearing. Dunglison.

The act of vibrating, or the state of being vibrated, or in vibratory motion; quick motion to and fro; oscillation, as of a pendulum or musical string. As a harper lays his open palm Upon his harp, to deaden its vibrations.
A little hillock; a knoll. Ainsworth.
Material for filling a cavity.
A woman who spins, or whose occupation is to spin. She spake to spinster to spin it out.

The state or quality of being ripe; maturity;; completeness; perfection; as, the ripeness of grain; ripeness of manhood; ripeness of judgment. Time, which made them their fame outlive, To Cowley scarce did ripeness give.
A wild, romping young person. [Low] Marrya
One who provides gratification for the lust of others; a procurer; a pander. Swift.
Rude, boisterous play. Too much given to horseplay in his raillery.

Decoration by means of flutes or channels; a flute, or flutes collectively; as, the fluting of a column or pilaster; the fluting of a lady's ruffle. Fluting iron, a laundry iron for fluting ruffles; -- called also Italian iron, or gaufering iron.
A riding, or the act of riding, on horseback; horsemanship. The pretender to equitation mounted.
That which nourishes; food; nutriment; anything which feeds or adds to a substance in natural growth. Hence: The necessaries of life generally: sustenance; means of support.
Of a dark hue; moderately black; swarthy; tawny. "Swart attendants." Trench.
Pertaining to rebels or rebellion; acting in revolt; rebellious; as, rebel troops. Whoso be rebel to my judgment.
Pertaining to, made of, or resembling, brass.
The branch of dendrology treating of the gross and minute structure of wood.

Act of one who wrestles; specif., the sport consisting of the hand-to-hand combat between two unarmed contestants who seek to throw each other. The various styles of wrestling differ in their definition of a fall and in the governing rules.
A mill operated by the power of the wind, usually by the action of the wind upon oblique vanes or sails which radiate from a horizontal shaft. Chaucer.
With which; -- used relatively. The love wherewith thou hast loved me.
To roll, as the body of an animal; to tumble about, especially in anything foul or defiling; to wallow. When we welter in pleasures and idleness, then we eat and drink with drunkards.
To render volatile; to cause to exhale or evaporate; to cause to pass off in vapor. The water .
To rise; to get up; to appear from below the horizon. "Uprose the sun." Cowley.
To raise; to lift up.
To throw from one's seat; to deprive of a seat. Cowper.
To strip of a saddle; to take the saddle from, as a horse.
To destroy the form and qualities of; to deprive of being; to uncreate. God does not make or unmake things to try experiments.
To drive from a house or habitation; to dislodge; hence, to deprive of shelter.
To rate too low; to rate below the value; to undervalue. Burke.
To lie under; to rest beneath; to be situated under; as, a stratum of clay underlies the surface gravel.
To lay beneath; to put under.
To deprive of a crown; to take the crown from; hence, to discrown; to dethrone. He hath done me wrong, And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long.
To mutually agree to meet at a certain place. [Scot.]
To impress with terror; to coerce by intimidation. Humiliated by the tyranny of foreign despotism, and terrorized by ecclesiastical authority.
A system of apparatus for electric signals providing for automatic transmission of a definite number of different signals or calls, as in connection with hotel annunciators.
To prate; to talk idly; to use many words with little meaning; to chat. The tattling quality of age, which is always narrative.
To lay an impost upon; to cause to pay tallage.
To comprise in, or reduce to, a summary; to present briefly. Chambers.
A demon or fiend; especially, a lascivious spirit supposed to have sexual intercourse with the men by night; a succuba. Cf.
To hesitate or stumble in uttering words; to speak with spasmodic repetition or pauses; to stammer. Trembling, stuttering, calling for his confessor.
To cease to flow; to be motionless; as, blood stagnates in the veins of an animal; hence, to become impure or foul by want of motion; as, air stagnates in a close room.

A sharp, narrow spade, usually with a long handle, used by farmers for digging up large-rooted weeds; a similarly shaped implement used for various purposes. My spud these nettles from the stone can part.
Having the mind set on spiritual things, or filled with holy desires and affections. -- Spir"it*u*al-mind`ed*ness, n.

A close garnment with straight sleeves, and skirts reaching to the ankles, and buttoned in front from top to bottom; especially, the black garment of this shape worn by the clergy in France and Italy as their daily dress; a cassock.
To perform with solemn or ritual ceremonies, or according to legal forms. Baptism to be administered in one place, and marriage solemnized in another.
To fight slightly or in small parties; to engage in a skirmish or skirmishes; to act as skirmishers.

To offend the feelings of the conscience of (a person) by some action which is considered immoral or criminal; to bring shame, disgrace, or reproach upon. I demand who they are whom we scandalize by using harmless things.
To run with speed; to run or move in a quick, hurried manner; to hasten away. Macaulay.

To sink, in the middle, by its weight or under applied pressure, below a horizontal line or plane; as, a line or cable supported by its ends sags, though tightly drawn; the floor of a room sags; hence, to lean, give way, or settle from a vertical position; as,
To cry or shout; hence, to sell by auction. [Scot.] Jamieson.
To buy back or again; to regain by purchase. Sir M.
To send, give, or grant back; torelease a claim to; to resign or surrender by deed; to return. Blackstone.

To put (one) in mind of something; to bring to the remembrance of; to bring to the notice or consideration of (a person). When age itself, which will not be defied, shall begin to arrest, seize, and remind us of our mortality.
To freeze together again; to undergo regelation, as ice.
To curve in an opposite or unusual direction; to bend back or down.
To recover or recall the knowledge of; to bring back to the mind or memory; to remember.
To bellow again; to repeat or echo a bellow. The cave rebellowed, and the temple shook.
To take away by violence or by stealth; to snatch away; to rob; to despoil; to bereave. [Archaic].
To assert again or anew; to maintain after an omission to do so. Let us hope .
To drink with relish; to drink copiously of; to swallow in large draughts. "Quaffed off the muscadel." Shak.
The state of being a pupil. As sons of kings, loving in pupilage, Have turned to tyrants when they came to power.
To eject the contests of the stomach; to vomit; to spew. The infant Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms.
To wander about and beg; to seek food or other supplies by low arts; to seek for advantage by mean shift or tricks. [Low] A perfect artist in progging for money.
To prefigure; to exhibit previously in a type. Bp.
To engage by previous contract; to bind or attach previously; to preoccupy. But he was preëngaged by former ties.
To concert or arrange beforehand; to settle by previous agreement.
To make light of; to treat with derision or contempt, as if by saying pooh! pooh!
To write as a poet; to compose verse; to idealize. I versify the truth, not poetize.
To steal or purloin from the writings of another; to appropriate without due acknowledgement (the ideas or expressions of another).
To deal in trifles; to concern one's self with trivial matters rather than with those that are important. Ascham.
To make love to women; to play the male flirt. You can't go philandering after her again.
To interchange; to transfer reciprocally.
To appropriate to one's own use the property of the public; to steal public moneys intrusted to one's care; to embezzle. An oppressive, .
To exceed in weight; to overbalance; to weigh down. Drayton.
To dose to excess; to give an overdose, or too many doses, to.
To make or place an arch over; to hang over like an arch. "Brown with o'erarching shades." Pope.
To exceed in the number of votes given; to defeat by votes. South.
To excel or overcome in staring; to face down. I would outstare the sternest eyes that look.
To exceed in duration; to survive; to endure longer than. Milton.
To surpass in growing; to grow more than. Shak.
To exceed in generalship; to gain advantage over by superior military skill or executive ability; to outmaneuver. Chesterfield.
To outweight; to exceed in weight or effect. Let dull Ajax bear away my right When all his days outbalance this one night.
To lead the life of a nomad; to wander with flocks and herds for the sake of finding pasturage. The Vogules nomadize chiefly about the Rivers Irtish, Obi, Kama, and Volga.
To make natural; as, custom naturalizes labor or study.
Meal (esp. Indian meal) boiled in water; hasty pudding; supawn.
To furnish with mullions; to divide by mullions.

A wind blowing part of the year from one direction, alternating with a wind from the opposite direction; -- a term applied particularly to periodical winds of the Indian Ocean, which blow from the southwest from the latter part of May to the middle of Septembe
To shape ill; to give an ill or unnatural from to; to deform. "Figures monstrous and misshaped." Pope.
To report erroneously; to give an incorrect account of. Locke.
To call by the wrong name; to give a wrong or inappropriate name to.
To construe wrongly; to interpret erroneously. Do not, great sir, misconstrue his intent.
To call by a wrong name; to name improperly.
To transform into a mineral. In these caverns the bones are not mineralized.
