Of or pertaining to the act or power of perceiving; having the faculty or power of perceiving; used in perception. "His perceptive and reflective faculties." Motley.
A noun having five cases.
An instrument similar to a mariner's compass, but without magnetic needles, and having two sight vanes by which bearings are taken, esp. such as cannot be taken by the compass.
Like paste, as in color, softness, stickness. "A pasty complexion." G.
A word having an acute accent on the penultimate syllable.
Having panes; provided with panes; also, having openings; as, a paned window; paned window sash. "Paned hose." Massinger.
An aneroid barometer having a second scale that gives the approximate elevation above sea level of the place where the observation is made.
A genus of American Eocene mammals allied to the horse, but having four toes in front and three behind.
Having a large estate or property; wealthy; rich; affluent; as, an opulent city; an opulent citizen. -- Op"u*lent*ly, adv.
Having the nature or qualities of oil; oily; unctuous.
Having or emitting an odor or scent, esp. a sweet odor; fragrant; sweet-smelling.
An extinct order of ostrichlike aquatic birds having teeth, which are set in a groove in the jaw. It includes Hesperornis, and allied genera.
An extensive genus of fossil ferns, of which species have been found from the Devonian to the Triassic formation.

Of or pertaining to murder; characterized by, or causing, murder or bloodshed; having the purpose or quality of murder; bloody; sanguinary; as, the murderous king; murderous rapine; murderous intent; a murderous assault. "Murderous coward." Shak.

A genus of extinct marine reptiles allied to the lizards, but having the body much elongated, and the limbs in the form of paddles. The first known species, nearly fifty feet in length, was discovered in Cretaceous beds near Maestricht, in the Netherlands.
A noun having only one case. Andrews.
An extinct Miocene mammal of the Horse family, closely related to the genus Anhithecrium, and having three usable hoofs on each foot.
A word having more than one form of the root.
An extinct mammal of the Horse family, but not larger than a sheep, and having three toes on each foot.

Of or pertaining to merchants, or the business of merchants; having to do with trade, or the buying and selling of commodities; commercial. The expedition of the Argonauts was partly mercantile, partly military.
A work of twelve volumes, each containing the offices in the Greek Church for a month; also, each volume of the same. Shipley.
Of, pertaining to, or having to do with, the art of healing disease, or the science of medicine; as, the medical profession; medical services; a medical dictionary; medical jurisprudence.

Compacted into, or consisting of, a mass; having bulk and weight ot substance; ponderous; bulky and heavy; weight; heavy; as, a massy shield; a massy rock. Your swords are now too massy for your strengths, And will not be uplifted.
Bordering on, or situated near, the ocean; connected with the sea by site, interest, or power; having shipping and commerce or a navy; as, maritime states. "A maritime town." Addison.
A compound of the so-called margaric acid with a base.
Having qualities that excite, or are fitted to excite, love; worthy of love. Elaine the fair, Elaine the lovable, Elaine, the lily maid of Astolat.
Having a long life; having constitutional peculiarities which make long life probable; lasting long; as, a long-lived tree; they are a longlived family; long-lived prejudices.
Sovereign; independent; having authority or right to allegiance; as, a liege lord. Chaucer.
Belonging to a legion; consisting of a legion or legions, or of an indefinitely great number; as, legionary soldiers; a legionary force. "The legionary body of error." Sir T.
Bearing or containing milk or a milky fluid; as, the lactiferous vessels, cells, or tissue of various vascular plants.
Designating a club in London, to which Addison and Steele belonged; -- so called from Christopher Cat, a pastry cook, who served the club with mutton pies.
Having no issue or progeny; childless. "The heavens .
Possessed of genius, or the faculty of invention; skillful or promp to invent; having an aptitude to contrive, or to form new combinations; as, an ingenious author, mechanic. A man .
Having the qualities, or showing the characteristics, of an imp.
Pertaining to, having the nature of, fire; containing fire; resembling fire; as, an igneous appearance.
An outwork composed of two demibastions joined by a curtain. It is connected with the works in rear by long wings.
Having the same name or designation; standing in the same relation; -- opposed to heteronymous.
A fossil coral of the genus Heliolites, having twelve-rayed cells. It is found in the Silurian rocks.
A fossil cephalopod of the genus Hamites, related to the ammonites, but having the last whorl bent into a hooklike form.
Having a gorge or throat.
Smooth; having a surface without hairs or any unevenness.
Consisting of a small cord or fiber.
Tawny; dull yellow, with a mixture of gray and brown. Lindley.
Having leaves, or leaflike projections; as, a foliated shell.
Having the shape of a thread or filament; as, the filiform papillæ of the tongue; a filiform style or peduncle. See Illust.
A genus of fossil corals abundant in the Silurian and Devonian rocks, having polygonal cells with perforated walls.
Like a father in affection and care; paternal; tender; protecting; careful. You have showed a tender, fatherly regard.
Consisting or made of meal or flour; as, a farinaceous diet.
A follower of Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus (4th century A. D.), who held that Christ was not God but a created being, having a nature different from that of the Father.
Having equal power or force; equivalent. Bacon.
Attended by, or having the character of, emotion. H.
The operation performed with an écraseur.
A level having a short telescope (hence its name) rigidly fixed to a table capable only of rotatory movement in a horizontal plane. The telescope is usually an inverting one.
Containing dregs or lees; muddy; foul; feculent. Boyle.
A noun which has only two cases. Andrews.
The fifth book of the Pentateuch, containing the second giving of the law by Moses.
Having the form of a tooth or of teeth; tooth-shaped.
Made up like a dandy; having the dress or manners of a dandy; buckish.
Having a wavy, floating light; opalescent; chatoyant.
An extinct genus of Devonian ganoid fishes, having the broad plates about the head studded with berrylike tubercles.
Composed of clots or clods; having the quality or form of a clot; sticky; slimy; foul. "The clotted glebe." J.
Having a sharp, distinct outline, like that of a cameo. She has .
Like ashes; having the color of ashes, -- as the cortical substance of the brain.
Having the lower chop or jaw depressed; hence, crestfallen; dejected; dispirited;downcast. See Chapfallen.

Having the ground engraved or cut out in the parts to be enameled; inlaid in depressions made in the ground; -- said of a kind of enamel work in which depressions made in the surface are filled with enamel pastes, which are afterward fired; also, designating t

Having a large, strong, or gross body; stout; lusty; -- now used chiefly of human beings, but formerly of animals, in the sense of stately or beautiful, and of inanimate things that were huge and bulky. "Burly sacks." Drayton.

An old name for a fossil consisting of the petrified teeth and palatal bones of fishes belonging to the family of Pycnodonts (thick teeth), whose remains occur in the oölite and chalk formations; toadstone; -- so named from a notion that it was originally form
Red and inflamed; suffused with blood, or having the vessels turgid with blood, as when the conjunctiva is inflamed or irritated. His eyes were bloodshot, .
Having two grooves or furrows.
Being in two parts; having two correspondent parts, as a legal contract or writing, one for each party; shared by two; as, a bipartite treaty.
A solid consisting of a double twelve-sided pyramid; -- so called because the planes of this form occur on crystals of beryl.
Having a beak or a beaklike point; beak-shaped. "Each beaked promontory." Milton.
A diminutive of the bar, having one fourth its width.
Prevented from growing, by having the bark too firm or close.
Independent in government; having the right or power of self- government.
A noun which has no distinction of cases; an indeclinable noun.

A repetition of the last word or any prominent word in a sentence or clause, at the beginning of the next, with an adjunct idea; as, "He retained his virtues amidst all his misfortunes -- misfortunes which no prudence could foresee or prevent."
Pertaining to or containing alum, or alumina; as, aluminous minerals, aluminous solution.
With a crook or bend; with the hand on the hip and elbow turned outward. "With one arm akimbo." Irving.
Professing ignorance; involving no dogmatic; pertaining to or involving agnosticism. -- Ag*nos"tic*al*ly, adv.
Old; having lived long; having lived almost to or beyond the usual time allotted to that species of being; as, an aged man; an aged oak.
Containing excessive praise or compliment; servilely praising; flattering; as, an adulatory address. A mere rant of adulatory freedom.
Liable to be accused or censured; chargeable with a crime or fault; blamable; -- with of.
Having a sound, strong body; physically competent; robust. "Able-bodied vagrant." Froude.
The band of the sleeve of a shirt, or other garment, which covers the wrist.
To wake; to cease to sleep; to be awakened. Early, Turnus wakening with the light.
A four-wheeled vehicle for the transportation of goods, produce, etc.; a wagon. The wardens see nothing but a wain of hay.
To confirm; to render valid; to give legal force to. The chamber of deputies .
To deprive of a stock; to remove the stock from; to loose from that which fixes, or holds fast.
To draw the screws from; to loose from screws; to loosen or withdraw (anything, as a screw) by turning it.
To cause to be one; to make into a unit; to unite; to view as one. A comprehensive or unifying act of the judging faculty.
To injure by working secretly; to destroy or overthrow by clandestine measure; to undermine. But thou from loving England art so far, That thou hast underwrought his lawful king.
To swell; to cause to swell, or puff up. To swell, tumefy, stiffen, not the diction only, but the tenor of the thought.

To adjust or devise so as to emit or respond to electric oscillations of a certain wave length; to tune; specif., to put (two or more instruments or systems of wireless telegraphy) in syntony with each other. -- Syn`to*ni*za"tion (#), n.

A coat worn over the other garments; especially, the long and flowing garment of knights, worn over the armor, and frequently emblazoned with the arms of the wearer. A long surcoat of pers upon he had..
To keep within limits; to restain; to cause to stop, or cease; to stint. Then would he weep, he might not be stent.
To give scant measure; to squeeze or pinch in order to effect a saving. [Prev.
To put under a sheal or shelter. [Scot.]
To make sensual; to subject to the love of sensual pleasure; to debase by carnal gratifications; to carnalize; as, sensualized by pleasure. Pope.

One of a board of town officers chosen annually in the New England States to transact the general public business of the town, and have a kind of executive authority. The number is usually from three to seven in each town.
To render rural; to give a rural appearance to.
To forge again or anew; hence, to fashion or fabricate anew; to make over. Udall.

To roll back, as a wave or flood; to be sent or driven back; to flow back, as a consequence or effect; to conduce; to contribute; to result. The evil, soon Driven back, redounded as a flood on those From whom it sprung.
To comfort again; to console anew; to give new strength to. Bacon.
A strain given on the horn to call back the hounds when they have lost track of the game.
To rise, mount, or climb again.
An apparatus for the production of sound by the action of luminous or thermal rays. It is essentially the same as the photophone.
To utter a low, murmuring, continued sound, as a cat does when pleased. [Written also purr.]
To forename; to name beforehand; to tell by name beforehand. Shak.
To bring under the influence of prelacy. Palfrey.

To cause to violate an oath or a vow; to cause to make oath knowingly to what is untrue; to make guilty of perjury; to forswear; to corrupt; -- often used reflexively; as, he perjured himself. Want will perjure The ne'er-touched vestal.
To act or perform to excess; to exaggerate in acting; as, he overacted his part.
To go faster than; to outrun; to advance beyond; to leave behing. Appetites which .
To excel, or to leave behind, in sailing; to sail faster than. Beau.
To gaze beyond; to exceed in sharpness or persistence of seeing or of looking; hence, to stare out of countenance.
to render Oriental; to cause to conform to Oriental manners or conditions.
The organ of sight; an eye. The difference is as great between The optics seeing, as the object seen.
A place or building for making observations on the heavenly bodies. The new observatory in Greenwich Park.

A large water wheel, turned by the action of a stream against its floats, and carrying at its circumference buckets, by which water is raised and discharged into a trough; used in Arabia, China, and elsewhere for irrigating land; a Persian wheel.
To decline or fail to prosecute; to allow to be dropped (said of a suit); to enter judgment against (a plaintiff who fails to prosecute); as, the plaintiff was non-prossed.
To be unwilling; to refuse to act. The actions of the will are "velle" and "nolle," to will and nill.
A rural custom in England, of visiting one's parents on Midlent Sunday, -- supposed to have been originally visiting the mother church to make offerings at the high altar.
To cause to be mongrel; to cross breeds, so as to produce mongrels.

The misnaming of a person in a legal instrument, as in a complaint or indictment; any misnaming of a person or thing; a wrong or inapplicable name or title. Many of the changes, by a great misnomer, called parliamentary "reforms".
To kindle amiss; to inflame to a bad purpose; to excite wrongly.

To enroll; to enter in a register; specifically, to enter or admit to membership in a body or society, particularly in a college or university, by enrolling the name in a register. In discovering and matriculating the arms of commissaries from North America.
One who, or that which, mashes; also (Brewing), a machine for making mash.
The science which relates to the structure and habits of mollusks.

One who has a license to exercise a profession; as, a licentiate in medicine or theology. The college of physicians, in July, 1687, published an edict, requiring all the fellows, candidates, and licentiates, to give gratuitous advice to the neighboring poor.
To give Latin terminations or forms to, as to foreign words, in writing Latin.
To bruise; to grind coarsely; as, kibbled oats. [Prov.Eng.] Halliwell.
To enter or record in a journal or diary. Johnson.
To wriggle or frisk about; to move awkwardly; to shake up and down.

A kind of prison; a building for the confinement of persons held in lawful custody, especially for minor offenses or with reference to some future judicial proceeding. [Written also gaol.] This jail I count the house of liberty.
To run between parties and intercept without right the advantage that one should gain from the other; to traffic without a proper license; to intrude; to forestall others; to intermeddle.
To dry in, or to expose to, the sun's rays; to ripen or prepare by such exposure. Johnson.
To work in, as lace; to embellish with work resembling lace; also, to lace or enlace. P.
To bend; to cause to become curved; to make crooked; to deflect. J.
To dwell in; to abide within; to remain in possession. The Holy Ghost became a dove, not as a symbol, but as a constantly indwelt form.

To distinguish from others from others of the species; to endow with individuality; to divide into individuals; to discriminate. The soul, as the prime individuating principle, and the said reserved portion of matter as an essential and radical part of the ind
To sit, as on eggs for hatching; to brood; to brood upon, or keep warm, as eggs, for the purpose of hatching.
Not personal; not representing a person; not having personality. An almighty but impersonal power, called Fate.
The natural history of fishes; that branch of zoölogy which relates to fishes, including their structure, classification, and habits.
A horizontal section of a building or other object, showing its true dimensions according to a geometric scale; a ground plan; a map; also, the art of making such plans.
A condition of overgrowth or excessive development of an organ or part; -- the opposite of atrophy.
Have or have not; -- a familiar invitation to reciprocal drinking. Shak.
A fountain on Mount Helicon in Boeotia, fabled to have burst forth when the ground was struck by the hoof of Pegasus. Also, its waters, which were supposed to impart poetic inspiration.
The natural history of reptiles; that branch of zoölogy which relates to reptiles, including their structure, classification, and habits.
One who, or that which, hems with a needle. Specifically: (a) An attachment to a sewing machine, for turning under the edge of a piece of fabric, preparatory to stitching it down.
A small, flat, wind instrument of music, in which the notes are produced by the vibration of free metallic reeds.
A large piece of woolen or cotton cloth worn by Arabs as an outer garment. [Written also hyke.] Heyse.
The science which treats of the structure and diseases of women. -- Gyn`e*col"o*gist.
A small piece of cloth inserted in a garment, for the purpose of strengthening some part or giving it a tapering enlargement. Seam and gusset and band.
To squint; to look obliquely; to overlook things. [Scot.] Jamieson.

To investigate or apprehend geometrical quantities or laws; to make geometrical constructions; to proceed in accordance with the principles of geometry. Nature geometrizeth, and observeth order in all things.

The science which treats: (a) Of the structure and mineral constitution of the globe; structural geology. (b) Of its history as regards rocks, minerals, rivers, valleys, mountains, climates, life, etc.; historical geology.

The science which treats of the world and its inhabitants; a description of the earth, or a portion of the earth, including its structure, fetures, products, political divisions, and the people by whom it is inhabited.
To agree; to harmonize. [Colloq.
To shoot; to dart like lightning; to fulminate; to utter with authority or vehemence. She fulmined out her scorn of laws Salique.
To deposit eggs upon, as a flesh fly does on meat; to cause to be maggoty; hence, to taint or contaminate, as if with flyblows. Bp.
A small shrill pipe, resembling the piccolo flute, used chiefly to accompany the drum in military music. Fife major (Mil.), a noncommissioned officer who superintends the fifers of a regiment.

One who, or that which, extracts; as: (a) (Surg.) A forceps or instrument for extracting substances. (b) (Breech-loading Firearms) A device for withdrawing a cartridge or spent cartridge shell from the chamber of the barrel.
To banish; to drive or force (a person) from his own country; to make an exile of. The expatriated landed interest of France.
To cause to become like the Europeans in manners or character; to habituate or accustom to European usages. A state of society .
To register; to enroll or record; to inregister. To read enregistered in every nook His goodness, which His beauty doth declare.
To purge of faults; to make better; to correct; esp., to make corrections in (a literary work); to alter for the better by textual criticism, generally verbal.
To throw up a bank so as to confine or to defend; to protect by a bank of earth or stone.
To lose flesh gradually and become very lean; to waste away in flesh. "He emaciated and pined away." Sir T.
To disrobe; to strip of apparel; to make naked. Drink disapparels the soul.
The science which treats of the skin, its structure, functions, and diseases.

With a constantly increasing volume of voice; with gradually increasing strength and fullness of tone; -- a direction for the performance of music, indicated by the mark, or by writing the word on the score.

The science of the world or universe; or a treatise relating to the structure and parts of the system of creation, the elements of bodies, the modifications of material things, the laws of motion, and the order and course of nature.
To collect or gather into a mass or aggregate; to bring together; to accumulate. To what will thy congested guilt amount Blackmore.
To cause (a liquid) to change into a curdlike or semisolid state, not by evaporation but by some kind of chemical reaction; to curdle; as, rennet coagulates milk; heat coagulates the white of an egg.
A temporary structure sometimes used in the funeral solemnities of eminent persons, for the public exhibition of the remains, or their conveyance to the place of burial.
To dress or finish up (cloth); to pick knots, burs, loose threads, etc., from, as in finishing cloth. Burling iron, a peculiar kind of nippers or tweezers used in burling woolen cloth.
To utter or tell unnecessarily, or in a thoughtless manner; to publish (secrets or trifles) without reserve or discretion. Udall.
To cover with dung, as for manuring; to bedaub or defile, literally or figuratively. Bp.
To bind fast; to constrict; to contract; to cause parts to draw together; to compress. Which contraction .
To transform, as the venous blood, into arterial blood by exposure to oxygen in the lungs; to make arterial.
The malicious burning of a dwelling house or outhouse of another man, which by the common law is felony; the malicious and voluntary firing of a building or ship. Wharton.
To impregnate with aroma; to render aromatic; to give a spicy scent or taste to; to perfume. Bacon.
To admit or accept the tenets of the Arians; to become an Arian.
To raise to the state of an angel; to render angelic. It ought not to be our object to angelize, nor to brutalize, but to humanize man.
A morbid condition in which the blood is deficient in quality or in quantity.
To convert into an alkali; to give alkaline properties to.
To commit the first act of hostility or offense; to begin a quarrel or controversy; to make an attack; -- with on.
To turn the mind or attention; to refer; to take heed or notice; -- with to; as, he adverted to what was said. I may again advert to the distinction.
Able and apt to invent; quick at contrivance; ready at expedients; as, an inventive head or genius. Dryden.
Having the quality of incising, cutting, or penetrating, as with a sharp instrument; cutting; hence, sharp; acute; sarcastic; biting. "An incisive, high voice." G.
One who, or that which, extinguishes; esp., a hollow cone or other device for extinguishing a flame, as of a torch or candle.
To make fourfold; to double twice; to quadruple.
To give wrong proportions to; to join without due proportion.
Two cats fabled, in an Irish story, to have fought till nothing was left but their tails. It is probably a parable of a local contest between Kilkenny and Irishtown, which impoverished both towns.
A blank paper, with a person's signature, etc., at the bottom, given to another person, with permission to superscribe what conditions he pleases. Hence: Unconditional terms; unlimited authority.

A document used in shipping goods by sea. In the case of free goods the shipping notes are the receiving note, addressed by the shipper to the chief officer of the vessel, requesting him to receive on board specified goods, and a receipt for the mate to sign,
To form or divide into syllables.
To be inherent; to stick (in); to be fixed or permanently incorporated with something; to cleave (to); to belong, as attributes or qualities. They do but inhere in the subject that supports them.
Six times ten; fifty-nine and one more; threescore.
Five and ten; one more than fourteen.
Excessively hot; as, a broiling sun. -- n.
A torsion balance used for measuring electric attraction or repulsion.
Pertaining to, or designating, a yellow crystalline substance (called also perthiocyanic acid), analogous to sulphocyanic acid, but containing more sulphur.
A railway passenger car made so as to facilitate seeing the scenery en route; a car open, or with glass sides, or with a kind of open balcony at the rear.
A sporangium or conceptacle containing only very minute spores. Cf.
A sporangium or conceptacle containing only large spores; -- opposed to microsporangium. Both are found in the genera Selaginella, Isoctes, and Marsilia, plants remotely allied to ferns.
Having the skin modified to serve as a gill.
To fertilize, as the stigmas of a flower or plant, with the pollen from another individual of the same species.

A play in which one person is blindfolded, and tries to catch some one of the company and tell who it is. Surely he fancies I play at blindman's buff with him, for he thinks I never have my eyes open.
Consisting of starch; resembling starch; stiff; precise.
Six and ten; consisting of six and ten; fifteen and one more.
Of or pertaining to an ancient Greek martial dance. " ye have the pyrrhic dance as yet." Byron.
Having many angles. Polygonal numbers, certain figurate numbers.
Consisting of hazels, or of the wood of the hazel; pertaining to, or derived from, the hazel; as, a hazel wand. I sit me down beside the hazel grove.
Made of giblets; as, a giblet pie.
Composed of corallines; as, coralline limestone.
Having the character of a commensal.
Consisting of clay; abounding with clay; partaking of clay; like clay.
Containing three letters or characters, or three sets of letters or characters.
Having a disposition or temper habitually sober. -- So"ber-mind`ed*ness, n.
Having a right or honest mind. -- Right"-mind`ed*ness, n.

Full of presumption; presuming; overconfident or venturesome; audacious; rash; taking liberties unduly; arrogant; insolent; as, a presumptuous commander; presumptuous conduct. A class of presumptuous men, whom age has not made cautious, nor adversity wise.
Giving, indicating, or having a preference or precedence; as, a preferential claim; preferential shares.
Having the nature or qualities of a pestilence. "Sends the pestilential vapors." Longfellow.
A word which has the circumflex accent on the last syllable. Goodwin.
An order of extinct toothed birds having the teeth in sockets, as in the genus Ichthyornis. See Ichthyornis.
Having a bad countenance or appearance; ill-favored; blemished; deformed. Bacon.
Granting, or authorized to grant, dispensations. "Dispensatory power." Bp.
Serving to commend; containing praise or commendation; commending; praising. "Commendatory verses." Pope.
The operation of forming a new canthus, when one has been destroyed by injury or disease.
A genus of gigantic American Jurassic dinosaurs, having large cavities in the bodies of the dorsal vertebræ.
Having affection or warm regard; loving; fond; as, an affectionate brother.
To cause to become not secular; to detach from secular things; to alienate from the world.

A judicial writ, founded upon some record, and requiring the party proceeded against to show cause why the party bringing it should not have advantage of such record, or (as in the case of scire facias to repeal letters patent) why the record should not be ann
To reason like a philosopher; to search into the reason and nature of things; to investigate phenomena, and assign rational causes for their existence. Man philosophizes as he lives.
The act or process of building a nest.
The science or theory of church building and decoration.
A process by which copper matte is treated by passing through it a blast of air, to oxidize and remove sulphur. It is analogous in apparatus to the Bessemer process for decarbonizing cast iron.
Having the surface roughly shaped or faced with the stonecutter's hammer; -- said of building stone.
Having the structure of a filoplume.
The quality or state of being yellow; as, the yellowness of an orange.
Any room or apartment used especially for labor.
A storm characterized by high wind with little or no rain.

The act of one who, or that which, v Bp. Hall.
One who utters. Spenser.
An exclamation indicating check, rebuke, or contempt; as, tush, tush! do not speak of it.
Either the thymus gland or the pancreas, the former being called neck, or throat, sweetbread, the latter belly sweetbread. The sweetbreads of ruminants, esp.
imp. & p.
In a strong manner; so as to be strong in action or in resistance; with strength; with great force; forcibly; powerfully; firmly; vehemently; as, a town strongly fortified; he objected strongly.

Any one of a number of similar complex resins obtained from the bark of several trees and shrubs of the Styrax family. The most common of these is liquid storax, a brown or gray semifluid substance of an agreeable aromatic odor and balsamic taste, sometimes us
from Sink. Sinking fund.
obs. 3d pers.
Popularly, any plant or plants growing in the sea.
Adapted for removing scales, as from a fish; as, a scaling knife; adapted for removing scale, as from the interior of a steam boiler; as, a scaling hammer, bar, etc.
One who, or that which, reproduces. Burke.
A petty king; a ruler of little power or consequence.
The act of trimming, or removing what is superfluous.
In a principal manner; primarily; above all; chiefly; mainly.
A woman who officiated in sacred rites among pagans. Abp.
Beforehand; antecedently; as, a plan previously formed.
The act of throwing or casting; a cast; a pitch; as, wild pitching in baseball.
A stiff thick kind of paper board, formed of several single sheets pasted one upon another, or of paper macerated and pressed into molds, etc.
One who partakes; a sharer; a participator. Partakers of their spiritual things.
One who opposes; an opponent; an antagonist; an adversary.
The act of contracting, or of making or becoming less in breadth or extent.
One who narrates; one who relates a series of events or transactions.
The act of one who, or that which, lays.
One who, or that which, kindles, stirs up, or sets on fire."Kindlers of riot." Gay.
One who, or that which, interrupts.
A country in Central Europe, now a part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Hungary water, a distilled "water," made from dilute alcohol aromatized with rosemary flowers, etc.
One who howls.
One who harangues, or is fond of haranguing; a declaimer. With them join'd all th' harangues of the throng, That thought to get preferment by the tongue.
In a graphic manner; vividly.
A son's or daughter's son.
One who frequents; one who often visits, or resorts to customarily.
In time past, either in time immediately preceding or at any indefinite distance; of old; heretofore.
One who fines or purifies.
The latter part and close of the day, and the beginning of darkness or night; properly, the decline of the day, or of the sum. In the ascending scale Of heaven, the stars that usher evening rose.
The state of being dry. See Dry.
One who disputes, or who is given to disputes; a controvertist. Where is the disputer of this world 1 Cor.
One who defends; one who maintains, supports, protects, or vindicates; a champion; an advocate; a vindicator. Provinces .
That which constricts, draws together, or contracts.
The act or state of sticking together; close union.
One confined to the bed by sickness.
A fortress in or near a fortified city, commanding the city and fortifications, and intended as a final point of defense. Syn.

One of an ancient race of people, who formerly inhabited a great part of Central and Western Europe, and whose descendants at the present day occupy Ireland, Wales, the Highlands of Scotland, and the northern shores of France. [Written also Kelt.
One who, or that which, catches.
One who brings. Yet the first bringer of unwelcome news Hath but a losing office.
One who whitens, or whose occupation is to whiten, by bleaching.
In ancient times.
One who adapts.
One who, or that which, absorbs.
To perform inefficiently, as a play; to act feebly.
To announce beforehand. Coleridge.
To bear down or carry down, as by excess of weight, power, force, etc.; to overcome; to suppress. The point of reputation, when the news first came of the battle lost, did overbear the reason of war.
To blossom forth. Carlyle.
To dip. [Prov.
To cover (an animal or vegatable substance) into a residue of carbon by the action of fire or some corrosive agent; to char.

A crystalline nitrogenous body closely related to both uric acid and hypoxanthin, present in muscle tissue, and occasionally found in the urine and in some urinary calculi. It is also present in guano.
The act of providong with a seat or seats; as, the seating of an audience.
The act of piercing or puncturing with a sharp point. "There is that speaketh like the prickings of a sword." Prov.

State of being dual or twofold; a twofold division; any system which is founded on a double principle, or a twofold distinction; as: (a) (Philos.) A view of man as constituted of two original and independent elements, as matter and spirit. (Theol.) (b) A syste
One of a breed of hardy cattle originating in the country of Devon, England. Those of pure blood have a deep red color.
Relating to, or derived from, a city or citizen; relating to man as a member of society, or to civil affairs. Civic crown (Rom.
Cloth or other material for bags.
Of or pertaining to Astrakhan in Russia or its products; made of an Astrakhan skin. -- n.
To go at the easy gait called an amble; -- applied to the horse or to its rider.
A spore formed by the union of the contents of two similar cells, either of the same or of distinct individual plants. Zygosperms are found in certain orders of algæ and fungi.
A fluosilicate of alumina occurring in tetrahedral crystals at the Zuñi mine in Colorado.
A genus of birds that comprises the white-eyes. See White-eye.
A genus of plants of the Naiadaceæ, or Pondweed family. Zostera marina is commonly known as sea wrack, and eelgrass.
A division of Mammalia in which the placenta is zonelike.
A peculiar larval stage of certain decapod Crustacea, especially of crabs and certain Anomura. [Written also zoæa.]

A genus of Actinaria, including numerous species, found mostly in tropical seas. The zooids or polyps resemble small, elongated actinias united together at their bases by fleshy stolons, and thus forming extensive groups.
The zooids of a compound anthozoan, collectively.
A suborder of Actinaria, including Zoanthus and allied genera, which are permanently attached by their bases.
A genus of grasses including Indian rice. See Indian rice, under Rice.

A rare element of the carbon-silicon group, intermediate between the metals and nonmetals, obtained from the mineral zircon as a dark sooty powder, or as a gray metallic crystalline substance. Symbol Zr.

The oxide of zirconium, obtained as a white powder, and possessing both acid and basic properties. On account of its infusibility, and brilliant luminosity when incandescent, it is used as an ingredient of sticks for the Drummomd light.
A salt of zirconic acid.
A combining form (also used adjectively) designating zirconium as an element of certain double compounds; zircono-; as in zircofluoric acid, sodium zircofluoride.
The upper division of the Permian (Dyas) of Europe. The prevailing rock is a magnesian limestone.
A large noxious fly of Abyssinia, which like the tsetse fly, is destructive to cattle.
A genus of large grasses of which the Indian corn (Zea Mays) is the only species known. Its origin is not yet ascertained.
A genus of flowering plants. Zauschneria Californica is a suffrutescent perennial, with showy red flowers much resembling those of the garden fuchsia.
A hydrous carbonate of nickel occurring as an emerald-green incrustation on chromite; -- called also emerald nickel.

An old solfeggio name for B flat; the seventh harmonic, as heard in the or æolian string; -- so called by Tartini. It was long considered a false, but is the true note of the chord of the flat seventh.
A species of Magnolia (M. conspicua) with large white blossoms that open before the leaves.
A silicate of iron and lime occurring in black prismatic crystals; -- also called ilvaite. [Spelt also jenite.]
An animal that yelps, or makes a yelping noise. Specifically: (Zoöl.) (a) The avocet; -- so called from its sharp, shrill cry.

The wood of any one of several different kinds of trees; also, any one of the trees themselves. Among the trees so called are the Cladrastis tinctoria, an American leguminous tree; the several species of prickly ash (Xanthoxylum); the Australian Flindersia Oxl
Either half of a square-rigged vessel's yard, from the center or mast to the end.
The power of moving, or being managed, at sea; -- said with reference to a ship. Sir T.

A nickname for a native of citizen of New England, especially one descended from old New England stock; by extension, an inhabitant of the Northern States as distinguished from a Southerner; also, applied sometimes by foreigners to any inhabitant of the United
A West Indian name for two large timber trees (Podocarpus coriaceus, and P. Purdicanus) of the Yew family.
A genus of endogenous herbs with grassy leaves and small yellow flowers in short, scaly-bracted spikes; yellow-eyed grass. There are about seventeen species in the Atlantic United States.
A genus of marine bivalves closely allied to Teredo, and equally destructive to timber. One species (Xylotrya fimbriata) is very common on the Atlantic coast of the United States.
An unfermentable sugar of the pentose class, C5H10O5, formed by the hydrolysis of xylan; wood sugar.
A derivative of xylene obtained as a white crystalline substance which on exposure in the air becomes red; -- called also betaorcin.
A genus of marine bivalves which bore holes in wood. They are allied to Pholas.
A genus of hymenopterous insects including the carpenter. See Carpenter bee, under Carpenter.
A salt of xylic acid.
An acid amide derivative of xylic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance.
A salt of xeronic acid.
The radical characteristic of xenylic compounds.
A native phosphate of yttrium occurring in yellowish-brown tetragonal crystals.
A suborder of soft-rayed fresh-water fishes of which the blackfish of Alaska (Dallia pectoralis) is the type.
An Arctic fork-tailed gull (Xema Sabinii).
A genus of prickly shrubs or small trees, the bark and rots of which are of a deep yellow color; prickly ash.
The yellow discoloration often observed in cancerous tumors.
A genus of composite plants in which the scales of the involucre are united so as to form a kind of bur; cocklebur; clotbur.
A compound or derivative of xanthogen. [Archaic]
A salt of xanthic; a xanthogenate.
An amido derivative of xanthic acid obtained as a white crystalline substance, C2H5O.CS.NH2; -- called also xanthogen amide.
A species of elm (Ulmus montana) found in Northern and Western Europe; Scotch elm.
The art or skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making anything. Due reward For her praiseworthy workmanship to yield.
A genus of ferns, one species of which (Woodwardia radicans) is a showy plant in California, the Azores, etc.
A striped variety of hornstone, resembling wood in appearance.
A compact woodlike variety of asbestus.
The technical name of the element tungsten. See Tungsten.
A salt of wolframic acid; a tungstate.
A variety of epidote, of a reddish color, found in Scotland.
A genus of climbing leguminous plants bearing long, pendulous clusters of pale bluish flowers.
The land-locked variety of the common salmon. [Canada]
One of the casks stowed in the wings of a vessel's hold, being smaller than such as are stowed more amidships. Totten.

A tract of land, or a region, uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings, whether a forest or a wide, barren plain; a wild; a waste; a desert; a pathless waste of any kind. The wat'ry wilderness yields no supply.
an arsenide of copper from Lake Superior.
The common beam tree of England (Pyrus Aria); -- so called from the white, woolly under surface of the leaves.
A flock of snipe.
A bird that feeds on wheat, especially the chaffinch.
A kind of stand, or piece of furniture, having shelves for books, ornaments, etc.; an étagère.
A man who owns, or has the care of, a wharf.
The state or condition of being well; welfare; happiness; prosperity; as, virtue is essential to the well-being of men or of society.
The visible regions of the air; the vault of heaven; the sky. On the welkne shoon the sterres lyght.
A hydrous sulphate of alumina occurring in white reniform masses.
The action of the elements on a rock in altering its color, texture, or composition, or in rounding off its edges.
A turn of the cable about the end of the windlass, without the bits.
The wax-covered fruit of the wax myrtle, or bayberry. See Bayberry, and Candleberry tree.
A hydrous phosphate of alumina, occurring usually in hemispherical radiated forms varying in color from white to yellow, green, or black.

Heavy plank or timber extending fore and aft the whole length of a vessel's deck at the line of junction with the sides, forming a channel to the scuppers, which are cut through it. In iron vessels the waterway is variously constructed.
A variety of chicken pox, or varicella. Dunglison.
A blossom or plant of any species of the genus Nymphæa, distinguished for its large floating leaves and beautiful flowers. See Nymphæa.
The edible fruit of two species of passion flower (Passiflora laurifolia, and P. maliformis); -- so called in the West Indies.
The rapacious larva of a large water beetle (Hydrophilus piceus), and of other similar species. See Illust.
A goose-neck apparatus for supplying water from an elevated tank, as to the tender of a locomotive.
Any one of several species of Nuphar; the yellow frog lily; -- so called from the shape of the seed vessel. See Nuphar, and cf.
The edible tuber of a species of arrowhead (Sagittaria variabilis); -- so called by the Indians of Oregon. [Written also wappato.]
A black variety of the jaguar; -- called also tapir tiger. [Written also walla.]
A genus of brachiopods of which many species are found in the fossil state. A few still exist in the deep sea.
A piece of plank two yard Bailey.
A fluophosphate of magnesia, occurring in yellowish crystals, and also in massive forms.
The young of the great black-backed gull (Larus marinus), formerly considered a distinct species. [Prov.
A scaly granular variety of anhydrite of a grayish white color, used for ornamental purposes.
A genus of Carnivora including the foxes.
One who votes; one who has a legal right to vote, or give his suffrage; an elector; a suffragist; as, as, an independent voter.
An oxysulphide of lead occurring in implanted spherical globules of a yellowish or brownish color; -- called also voltzine.
In the greater part of Russia, a division for local government consisting of a group of mirs, or village communities; a canton.

The way or fashion of people at any particular time; temporary mode, custom, or practice; popular reception for the time; -- used now generally in the phrase in vogue. One vogue, one vein, One air of thoughts usurps my brain.

A list or collection of words arranged in alphabetical order and explained; a dictionary or lexicon, either of a whole language, a single work or author, a branch of science, or the like; a word-book.

A councilor of state; a high executive officer in Turkey and other Oriental countries. [Written also visier, vizir, and vizer.] Grand vizier, the chief minister of the Turkish empire; -- called also vizier-azem.
The dissection of an animal while alive, for the purpose of making physiological investigations.
The quality or condition of being viviparous. H.
An artificial division of vertebrates including those that produce their young alive; -- opposed to Ovipara.
A genus of carnivores which comprises the civets.
A genus of plants including all true grapevines.
A rare skin disease consisting in the development of smooth, milk-white spots upon various parts of the body.
A form of machine for exhibiting animated pictures.
The doctrine that all the functions of a living organism are due to an unknown vital principle distinct from all chemical and physical forces.
An old French variety of pear, of little value.
An arrow, having a rotary motion, formerly used with the crossbow. Cf.
Any tropical humming bird of the genus Petasophora, having violet or purplish ear tufts.
A dyestuff of the induline group, made from aniline, and used as a substitute for indigo in dyeing wool and silk a violet-blue or a gray-blue color.
The produce of the vine for one season, in grapes or in wine; as, the vintage is abundant; the vintage of 1840.
An inclosure or yard for grapevines; a plantation of vines producing grapes.
A genus of motile bacteria characterized by short, slightly sinuous filaments and an undulatory motion; also, an individual of this genus.
A group of butterflies including those known as virgins, or gossamer-winged butterflies.
A genus of Hymenoptera including the common wasps and hornets.
The process of vesicating, or of raising blisters.
The turning factor of a quaternion.
The arrangement of the leaves within the leaf bud, as regards their folding, coiling, rolling, etc.; prefoliation.
A tribe of worms including Phoronis. See Phoronis.

The ornament of woodwork upon the gable of a house, used extensively in the 15th century. It was generally suspended from the edge of the projecting roof (see Verge, n., 4), and in position parallel to the gable wall.
The use of many words without necessity, or with little sense; a superabundance of words; verbosity; wordiness. Verbiage may indicate observation, but not thinking.
A genus of herbaceous plants of which several species are extensively cultivated for the great beauty of their flowers; vervain.
A genus of coarse liliaceous herbs having very poisonous qualities.
A salt of veratric acid.
An apparatus for measuring speed, as of machinery or vessels, but especially of projectiles.
The marginal membrane of certain medusæ belonging to the Discophora.
A modified form of dentine, which is permeated by blood capillaries; vascular dentine.
A vessel; a duct. Vas deferens; pl.
A deformity in which the foot is turned inward. See Talipes.
A varicose enlargement of the veins of the spermatic cord; also, a like enlargement of the veins of the scrotum.
A genus of very large lizards native of Asia and Africa. It includes the monitors.
A machine for concentrating ore. See Frue vanner.
The hypothetical radical characteristic of vanillic alcohol.
A salt of vanillic acid.
A salt of vanadious acid, analogous to a nitrite or a phosphite.
A salt of vanadic acid. [Formerly also vanadiate.]
A ketone of valeric acid obtained as an oily liquid.

A combining form (also used adjectively) indicating derivation from, or relation to, valerian or some of its products, as valeric acid; as in valerolactone, a colorless oily liquid produced as the anhydride of an hydroxy valeric acid.
A salt of valeric acid.
The acid amide derivative of valeric acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance.
A painful spasmodic contraction of the vagina, often rendering copulation impossible.
A genus of Infusoria which form minute vaselike or tubular cases in which they dwell.
An extensive artificial group of birds including the wading, swimming, and cursorial birds.
A genus of ericaceous shrubs including the various kinds of blueberries and the true cranberries.
The posterior pigmented layer of the iris; -- sometimes applied to the whole iris together with the choroid coat.
A genus of aquatic flowering plants, in which the submersed leaves bear many little utricles, or ascidia. See Ascidium,
The act or process of whipping or stinging with nettles; -- sometimes used in the treatment of paralysis.
A genus of plants including the common nettles. See Nettle, n.
A genus of Carnivora including the common bears.
A salt of uroxanic acid.
A styliform process forming the posterior extremity of the vertebral column in some fishes and amphibians.

Any one of the abdominal appendages of a crustacean, especially one of the posterior ones, which are often larger than the rest, and different in structure, and are used chiefly in locomotion. See Illust.
A division of boring Hymenoptera, including Tremex and allied genera. See Illust.
A vessel for holding urine; especially, a bottle or tube for holding urine for inspection.
The canal by which the urine is conducted from the bladder and discharged.
The duct which conveys the urine from the kidney to the bladder or cloaca. There are two ureters, one for each kidney.
The thin-walled summer spore which is produced during the so- called Uredo stage of certain rusts. See (in the Supplement) Uredinales, Heteroecious, etc.
An extensive family of butterflies, including those known as skippers (Hesperiadæ).
A chart or catalogue of fixed stars, especially of stars visible to the naked eye.
A general term for the uranium phosphates, autunite, or lime uranite, and torbernite, or copper uranite.

An alkaline salt of fluorescein, obtained as a brownish red substance, which is used as a dye; -- so called from the peculiar yellowish green fluorescence (resembling that of uranium glass) of its solutions. See Fluorescein.
A salt of uranic acid.
The posterior half of an animal.
A cord or band of fibrous tissue extending from the bladder to the umbilicus.
A genus of birds which includes the common hoopoe.
A salt of orthosilicic acid, H4SiO4; -- so called because the ratio of the oxygen atoms united to the basic metals and silicon respectively is 1:1; for example, Mg2SiO4 or 2MgO.SiO2.
The doctrine of uniformity in the geological history of the earth; -- in part equivalent to uniformitarianism, but also used, more broadly, as opposed to catastrophism.
The current that sets seaward near the bottom when waves are breaking upon the shore.
A subterranean room of any kind; esp., one under a church (see Crypt), or one used as a chapel or for any sacred purpose.
The English name for a catboat; -- so called because Una was the name of the first boat of this kind taken to England. D.
A genus of thin papery bright green seaweeds including the kinds called sea lettuce.
A genus of owls including the great gray owl (Ulula cinerea) of Arctic America, and other similar species. See Illust.
A division of insects nearly equivalent to the true Orthoptera.
A genus of trees including the elm.
A salt of ulmic acid.
The process of forming an ulcer, or of becoming ulcerous; the state of being ulcerated; also, an ulcer.
A fluoride of the cerium metals occurring in hexagonal crystals of a pale yellow color. Cf.
A translucent mineral of a green color and pearly or vitreous luster. It is a hydrous arseniate of copper.
A fold of the wall which projects into the cavity of the intestine in bivalve mollusks, certain annelids, starfishes, and some other animals.
To write with a typewriter. [Recent]
A flatulent distention of the belly; tympany.
An intrusion of one vegetable cell into the cavity of another, sometimes forming there an irregular mass of cells. Goodale.
To plow, or fallow, a second time (land that has been once fallowed).
A plant of the genus Hypericum (H. Androsoemum), from which a healing ointment is prepared in Spain; -- called also parkleaves.
A variety of monazite.
A genus of singing birds including the true thrushes.
A division of singing birds including the thrushes and allied kinds.

A grand division of the animal kingdom, intermediate, in some respects, between the invertebrates and vertebrates, and by some writers united with the latter. They were formerly classed with acephalous mollusks.
The oxide of tungsten, a yellow mineral occurring in a pulverulent form. It is often associated with wolfram.
A salt of tungstic acid; a wolframate.
A curious vegetable production of the Southern Atlantic United States, growing under ground like a truffle and often attaining immense size. The real nature is unknown.
An extensive division of Hydroidea; the tubularians; -- called also Athecata, Gymnoblastea, and Tubulariæ.
A shell or tube formed by an annelid, as a serpula.
A division of annelids including those which construct, and habitually live in, tubes. The head or anterior segments usually bear gills and cirri.
The antecedent of trypsin, a substance which is contained in the cells of the pancreas and gives rise to the trypsin.
The thorax of an insect. See Trunk, n., 5.
The nutritive zooids of a hydroid, collectively, as distinguished from the gonosome, or reproductive zooids.

A native double salt, consisting of a combination of neutral and acid sodium carbonate, Na2CO3.2HNaCO3.2H2O, occurring as a white crystalline fibrous deposit from certain soda brine springs and lakes; -- called also urao, and by the ancients nitrum.
The second joint of the leg of an insect, -- often united with the coxa.
Anything having three valves, especially a shell.
A vessel for separating liquids of different densities. [Written also tritorium.]
A zooid of the third generation in asexual reproduction.
A genus of grasses including the various species of wheat.
A carbohydrate isomeric with dextrin, obtained from quitch grass (Agropyrum, formerly Triticum, repens) as a white amorphous substance.
A salt of trithionic acid.
A nitrate formed from three molecules of nitric acid; also, less properly, applied to certain basic nitrates; as, trisnitrate of bismuth.
A cam, wiper, or projecting piece which strikes another piece repeatedly.
Any utensil or vessel, as a stool, table, altar, caldron, etc., supported on three feet.
A collection or combination of three of a kind; three united.
The third order of the Linnæan class Polygamia.
A genus of limicoline birds including many species of sandpipers. See Dunlin, Knot, and Sandpiper.
A genus of liliaceous plants; the three-leaved nightshade; -- so called because all the parts of the plant are in threes.
A figure having three sides.
A genus of pearly bivalve shells, numerous extinct species of which are characteristic of the Mesozoic rocks. A few living species exist on the coast of Australia.
One who has been married three times; also, one who has three husbands or three wives at the same time.
A genus of leguminous herbs with densely spiked flowers and usually trifoliate leaves; trefoil. There are many species, all of which are called clover.
A genus of very large marine bivalve shells found on the coral reefs of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. One species (T.
The slender, hairlike cell which receives the fertilizing particles, or antherozoids, in red seaweeds. -- Trich`o*gyn"ic, a.
A disease of the eye, in which the eyelashes, being turned in upon the eyeball, produce constant irritation by the motion of the lids.
A white variety of amphibole, or hornblende, occurring in long, bladelike crystals, and coarsely fibrous masses.

A genus of large hymenopterous insects allied to the sawflies. The female lays her eggs in holes which she bores in the trunks of trees with her large and long ovipositor, and the larva bores in the wood.
A genus of gelatinous fungi found in moist grounds.
An extensive order of parasitic worms. They are found in the internal cavities of animals belonging to all classes.
An amorphous variety of manna obtained from the nests and cocoons of a Syrian coleopterous insect (Larinus maculatus, L. nidificans, etc.) which feeds on the foliage of a variety of thistle.
In a treble manner; with a threefold number or quantity; triply. Swift.
A white concretionary form of calcium carbonate, usually hard and semicrystalline. It is deposited from the water of springs or streams holding lime in solution.
The act of transfusing, or pouring, as liquor, out of one vessel into another. Howell.
To wash, as tin ore, with a shovel in a frame fitted for the purpose. Smart.
A wood cell with spiral or other markings and closed throughout, as in pine wood.
A division of Arachnida including those that breathe only by means of tracheæ. It includes the mites, ticks, false scorpions, and harvestmen.
A small bar, rod, bundle of fibers, or septal membrane, in the framework of an organ part.
A lover of archery; one devoted to archery.
A division of marine gastropod mollusks in which the radula are converted into poison fangs. The cone shells (Conus), Pleurotoma, and Terebra, are examples.
A building devoted to the public used of a town; a townhall.
A line used to tow vessels; a towrope.
An urchin who has soft, whitish hair. [Colloq.]
a flat heap of moist, crushed silver ore, prepared for the patio process.
A species of Turnix (Turnix sylvatica) native of Spain and Northen Africa.
The inflammable wood of certain trees (Amyris balsamifera, A. Floridana, etc.); also, the trees themselves.
A mineral occurring in emerald-green tabular crystals having a micaceous structure. It is a hydrous phosphate of uranium and copper.
The act or art of taking off the top soil of land before an excavation or embankment is begun.
The description of a particular place, town, manor, parish, or tract of land; especially, the exact and scientific delineation and description in minute detail of any place or region.
A topaz-yellow variety of garnet.
A small state, consisting of a few cities or towns; a petty country governed by a toparch; as, Judea was formerly divided into ten toparchies. Fuller.
The highest timbers on the side of a vessel, being those above the futtocks. R.
A lantern or light on the top of a vessel.
the part that supports a tool-post or a tool.
The female of the bullfinch; -- called also tonyhoop. [Prov.
The cutting edge of the bill of a bird.

The fruit of a plant of the Nightshade family (Lycopersicum esculentun); also, the plant itself. The fruit, which is called also love apple, is usually of a rounded, flattened form, but often irregular in shape.
A salt of any one of the toluic acids.
A morbid condition of the foot in which the toe is depressed and the heel elevated.
A spotted lizard native of India.
The act or process of titrating; a substance obtained by titrating.
A combining form (also used adjectively) designating certain double compounds of titanium with some other elements; as, titano- cyanide, titano-fluoride, titano-silicate, etc.
A genus of small hemipterous insects which injure trees by sucking the sap from the leaves. See Illustration in Appendix.
A division of struthious birds, including the tinamous.
A siliceous stone of a yellow color and chatoyant luster, obtained in South Africa and much used for ornament. It is an altered form of the mineral crocidolite.
The bone or cartilage of the tarsus which articulates with the tibia and corresponds to a part of the astragalus in man and most mammals.

A phenol derivative of cymene, C10H13.OH, isomeric with carvacrol, found in oil of thyme, and extracted as a white crystalline substance of a pleasant aromatic odor and strong antiseptic properties; -- called also hydroxy cymene.
A compound of thymol analogous to a salt; as, sodium thymate.
To cut or clip with a knife; to whittle. [Obs.
A shaft of lightning; a brilliant stream of electricity passing from one part of the heavens to another, or from the clouds to the earth.
The doctrine of nutrition; a treatise on nutrition.
An instrument to thrash with; a flail. [Obs.
A zeolitic mineral, occurring generally in masses of a radiated structure. It is a hydrous silicate of aluminia, lime, and soda.
A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting the presence of sulphur. See Sulpho-.
A ketone derivative of thiophene obtained as a white crystalline substance, (C4H3S)2.CO, by the action of aluminium chloride and carbonyl chloride on thiophene.

A letter of the Greek alphabet corresponding to th in English; -- sometimes called the unlucky letter, from being used by the judges on their ballots in passing condemnation on a prisoner, it being the first letter of the Greek qa`natos, death. Theta function

A picture (as of a slice of wood) obtained by first wetting the object slightly with hydrochloric or dilute sulphuric acid, then taking an impression with a press, and next strongly heating this impression.
The resolution of a compound into parts by heat; dissociation by heat.
One addicted to theosophy. The theosophist is one who gives you a theory of God, or of the works of God, which has not reason, but an inspiration of his own, for its basis.
A genus of small trees. See Cacao.
A genus of plants found in China and Japan; the tea plant.
The act or art of performing something wonderful; magic; legerdemain. T.

A rare metallic element of the aluminium group found in some minerals, as certain pyrites, and also in the lead-chamber deposit in the manufacture of sulphuric acid. It is isolated as a heavy, soft, bluish white metal, easily oxidized in moist air, but preserv
A salt of a hypothetical thallic acid.

In Old English, the article the, when the following word began with a vowel, was often written with elision as if a part of the word. Thus in Chaucer, the forms thabsence, tharray, thegle, thend, thingot, etc., are found for the absence, the array, the eagle,
A plant used as a remedy for tetter, -- in England the calendine, in America the bloodroot.
A stanza, epigram, or poem, consisting of four verses or lines. Pope.
A division of Coleoptera having, apparently, only four tarsal joints, one joint being rudimentary.
A telluride of bismuth. It is of a pale steel-gray color and metallic luster, and usually occurs in foliated masses.
A division of Tunicata including the common attached ascidians, both simple and compound. Called also Tethioidea.
An instrument from tetanizing a muscle by irritating its nerve by successive mechanical shocks.
A division of Crinoidea including numerous fossil species in which the body is covered with tessellated plates.
A division of annelids including the common earthworms and allied species.
A polymeric form of terpene, resembling terbene.
Thin iron sheets coated with an alloy of lead and tin; -- so called because made up of three metals.
The dorsal portion of an arthromere or somite of an articulate animal. See Illust.
A genus of long, slender, wormlike bivalve mollusks which bore into submerged wood, such as the piles of wharves, bottoms of ships, etc.; -- called also shipworm. See Shipworm.
