A rare element of the light platinum group, found associated with platinum ores, and isolated as a hard, brittle steel-gray metal which is very infusible. Symbol Ru.
A salt of rutic acid.
A genus of beautiful South American passerine birds, including the cock of the rock.
The channel of a stream.
A phenol derivative of anthracene obtained as a white crystalline substance, which on oxidation produces a red dyestuff related to anthraquinone.
The main part or blade of the rudder, which is connected by hinges, or the like, with the sternpost of a vessel.
A genus of rosaceous plants, including the raspberry and blackberry.
A nitrogenous base homologous with pyridine, obtained from coal tar as an oily liquid, C11H17N; also, any one of the group od metameric compounds of which rubidine is the type.
A variety of ruby of a yellowish red color, from Brazil.
A thickening, made of flour, for soups and gravies.
The beak or head of a ship.

The larva of any one of several species of lepidopterous insects which feed upon the leaves, buds, or blossoms of the rose, especially Cacæcia rosaceana, which rolls up the leaves for a nest, and devours both the leaves and buds.
A hydrous arsenite of cobalt, occuring in small red crystals, allied to erythrite.
A form of croquet modified for greater accuracy of play. The court has a wood border often faced with rubber, used as a cushion in bank shots.
To punish with a rope's end.
A mass of parenchym
To move or play in a careless, swaggering manner, with a frolicsome air; to frolic; to sport; commonly in the form rollicking. [Colloq.] He described his friends as rollicking blades.
A florid style of ornamentation which prevailed in Europe in the latter part of the eighteenth century.
A name of Allium Scorodoprasum and A. Ascalonium, two kinds of garlic, the latter of which is also called shallot.
A genus of leguminous trees including the common locust of North America (Robinia Pseudocacia).
An anchorage off shore. Same as Road, 4.
The leader of a circle of dancers; hence, the leader of a number of persons acting together; the leader of a herd of animals. A primacy of order, such an one as the ringleader hath in a dance.
A fixed star of the first magnitude in the left foot of the constellation Orion. [Written also Regel.]

A species of pine (Pinus sylvestris), and its wood, which affords a valuable timber; -- called also Scotch pine, and red or yellow deal. It grows in all parts of Europe, in the Caucasus, and in Siberia.
The timber forming the ridge of a roof, into which the rafters are secured.

A disease which affects children, and which is characterized by a bulky head, crooked spine and limbs, depressed ribs, enlarged and spongy articular epiphyses, tumid abdomen, and short stature, together with clear and often premature mental faculties. The esse
The glycerin salt of ricinoleic acid, occuring as a characteristic constituent of castor oil; -- formerly called palmin.
A salt of ricinoleic acid; -- formerly called palmate.
A species of plantain (Plantago lanceolata) with long, narrow, ribbed leaves; -- called also rib grass, ripple grass, ribwort plantain.
A genus of shrubs including gooseberries and currants of many kinds.
A quartzose trachyte, an igneous rock often showing a fluidal structure. -- Rhy`o*lit"ic, a.
A genus of shrubs and small treets. See Sumac.
A dicyemid which produces infusorialike embryos; -- opposed to nematogene. See Dicyemata.
A variety of dolomite.
A salt of rhodanic acid; a sulphocyanate. [Obsoles.]
The arrangement of the roots of plants.
A genus of trees including the mangrove. See Mangrove.
A division of marsupials. The wombat is the type.
The sheath of the upper mandible of a bird.
The examination or study of the soft palate, posterior nares, etc., by means of a laryngoscopic mirror introduced into the pharynx.
A mixture of volatile hydrocarbons intermediate between gsolene and cymogene. It is obtained in the purification of crude petroleum, and is used as a refregerant.
The class of skin disease developed by the dartrous diathesis. See under Dartrous.
An instrument which periodically or otherwise interrupts an electric current. Wheatstone.
A suborder of struthious birds including the rheas.
The continuation of the seed stalk along the side of an anatropous ovule or seed, forming a ridge or seam. [Written also raphe.] Gray.
A genus of shrubs and small trees; buckthorn. The California Rhamnus Purchianus and the European R.
A branch of inflorescence; the zigzag axis on which the florets are arranged in the spikelets of grasses.
An extinct division of Hydrozoa which includes the graptolities.
A group of spiders which spin irregular webs; -- called also Retitelariæ.
The study of the retina of the eye by means of the ophthalmoscope.

An extensive division of rhizopods in which the pseudopodia are more or less slender and coalesce at certain points, forming irregular meshes. It includes the shelled Foraminifera, together with some groups which lack a true shell.
A divisiom of gastropods; the Pectinibranchiata.
The framework of some pods, as the cress, which remains after the valves drop off. Gray.
One who has a fixed income, as from lands, stocks, or the like.
The quill feathers of the wings of a bird.
To furnish with a new mast or set of masts.
A division of Echini which includes the circular, or regular, sea urchins.

The act or process of refuting or disproving, or the state of being refuted; proof of falsehood or error; the overthrowing of an argument, opinion, testimony, doctrine, or theory, by argument or countervailing proof. Same of his blunders seem rather to deserve
The male of the European bullfinch. [Prov.
A formulary or prescription for making some combination, mixture, or preparation of materials; a receipt; especially, a prescription for medicine.

The act of retaking, as of one who has escaped after arrest; reprisal; the retaking of one's own goods, chattels, wife, or children, without force or violence, from one who has taken them and who wrongfully detains them. Blackstone.
The answer of a defendant in matter of fact to a plaintiff's surrejoinder.
The act or operation of reanimating, or the state of being reanimated; reinvigoration; revival.
A genus of plants related to the banana.
An order of birds in which the wings are small, rudimentary, or absent, and the breastbone is destitute of a keel. The ostrich, emu, and apteryx are examples.
An explanation or exposition of the principles of some opinion, action, hypothesis, phenomenon, or like; also, the principles themselves.
A New Zealand forest tree (Metrosideros robusta), also, its hard dark red wood, used by the Maoris for paddles and war clubs.
An order of birds; the Gallinæ.
The act or process of rarefying; the state of being rarefied; - - opposed to condensation; as, the rarefaction of air.
A cyst formed under the tongue by obstruction of the duct of the submaxillary gland.
A genus of anurous batrachians, including the common frogs.
A broad-leaved species of garlic (Allium ursinum), common in European gardens; -- called also buckram.
A line used to get a straight middle line, as on a spar, or from stem to stern in building a vessel.
A fluoride of alumina and soda occurring with the Greenland cryolite in octahedral crystals.
The order of elasmobranch fishes which includes the sawfishes, skates, and rays; -- called also Rajæ, and Rajii.
A genus of rays which includes the skates. See Skate.
The pungent fleshy root of a well-known cruciferous plant (Paphanus sativus); also, the whole plant. Radish fly (Zoöl.), a small two-winged fly (Anthomyia raphani) whose larvæ burrow in radishes.
The barbs of the radii of a feather; barbules.
A combining form indicating connection with, or relation to, a radius or ray; specifically (Anat.), with the radius of the forearm; as, radio-ulnar, radiomuscular, radiocarpal.
A small branch of a root; a rootlet.
Any mechanism having a rack, as a rack and pinion.
A painful affection of the spine; especially, Pott's disease; also, formerly, lead colic.
A salt of racemic acid.
A marsupial of Australia (Dasyurus macrurus), about the size of a cat.
The embryonic sac of an ovule, sometimes regarded as an innermost fifth integument. Cf.
The aspect of planets when separated the fifth part of the zodiac, or 72º. Hutton.
A radical of which quinone is the hydride, analogous to phenyl. [Written also kinoyl.]
A hypothetical radical of quinine and related alkaloids.

An alkaloid isomeric with, and resembling, quinine, found in certain species of cinchona, from which it is extracted as a bitter white crystalline substance; conchinine. It is used somewhat as a febrifuge.
A plane figure with fifteen angles, and consequently fifteen sides.

A colorless liquid of a slightly pungent odor, C9H6N.CH3, first obtained as a condensation product of aldehyde and aniline, and regarded as a derivative of quinoline; -- called also methyl quinoline. [Written also chinaldine.]
A genus of trees constituted by the oak. See Oak.
A truss framed with queen-posts; a queen-post truss.
Properly, a kind of superior olive grown in the region of Seville, Spain. It is large size and oblong shape with a small but long pit; it is cured when green, keeps well, and has a delicate flavor.
A card, die. or domino, having four spots, or pips
The bitter principle of quassia, extracted as a white crystalline substance; -- formerly called quassite. [Written also quassiin, and quassine.]
A supposed fourth integument of an ovule, counting from the outside.
A platform of a staircase where the stair turns at a right angle only. See Halfpace.
The edible drupaceous fruit of an Australian tree (Fusanus acuminatus) of the Sandalwood family; -- called also quandang.
The great extensor muscle of the knee, divided above into four parts which unite in a single tendon at the knee.
A curve made use of in the quadrature of other curves; as the quadratrix, of Dinostratus, or of Tschirnhausen.
A morbid condition in which pus is discharged in the urine.
A follower of Pyrrho; a skeptic.
A rock consisting essentially of pyroxene.
A kind of empyreumatic oil produced by the combustion of textures of hemp, linen, or cotton in a copper vessel, -- formerly used as a remedial agent. Dunglison.
A mineral, usually of a pale brown or of a gray or grayish green color, consisting chiefly of the hydrous silicate of iron and manganese; -- so called from the odor given off before the blowpipe.
A salt of pyromucic acid.
A crude acetate produced by treating pyroligneous acid with a metal or basic compound; as, pyrolignite of iron (iron liquor).
A salt of pyrogallic acid; an ether of pyrogallol.
A salt of pyroboric acid.
A variety of pyroxene; -- called also fassaite.
An albuminoid constituent of pus, related to mucin, possibly a mixture of substances rather than a single body.

The plate of bone which forms the posterior end of the vertebral column in most birds; the plowshare bone; the vomer. It is formed by the union of a number of the last caudal vertebræ, and supports the uropigium.
A division of swimming birds which includes the grebes, divers, auks, etc., in which the legs are placed far back.
The caudal plate of trilobites, crustacean, and certain insects. See Illust.
A class of marine arthropods in which the body is small and thin, and the eight legs usually very long; -- called also Pantopoda.
A massive subcolumnar variety of topaz.
The shell of a nut; the stone of a drupe fruit. See Endocarp.
A simple device, resembling a button in form, so arranged that pushing it closes an electric circuit, as of an electric bell.
A combining form signifying of a purple or purple-red color. Specif.
A strong, durable, and elastic wood of a purplish color, obtained from several tropical American leguminous trees of the genus Copaifera (C. pubiflora, bracteata, and officinalis).
A group of parasitic Hymenoptera, including the ichneumon flies, which destroy the larvæ and pupæ of insects.
A division of Diptera in which the young are born in a stage like the pupa. It includes the sheep tick, horse tick, and other parasites.
A genus of ranunculaceous herbs including the pasque flower. This genus is now merged in Anemone.

An extensive division, or sub-class, of hermaphrodite gastropods, in which the mantle cavity is modified into an air- breathing organ, as in Helix, or land snails, Limax, or garden slugs, and many pond snails, as Limnæa and Planorbis.
A genus of parasitic insects including the fleas. See Flea.
The practice of boxing, or fighting with the fist.
The external organs of generation, especially of the female; the vulva.
The external organs of generation.
The ventral and anterior of the three principal bones composing either half of the pelvis; sharebone; pubic bone.
A medicine that promotes the discharge of saliva.
An order of birds including only the penguins.
The arrangement of feathers in definite areas.
A superficial growth of vascular tissue radiating in a fanlike manner from the cornea over the surface of the eye.
A class of Mollusca in which the anterior lobes of the foot are developed in the form of broad, thin, winglike organs, with which they swim at near the surface of the sea.
The region of the skull, in the temporal fossa back of the orbit, where the great wing of the sphenoid, the temporal, the parietal, and the frontal hones approach each other.
A division of birds including the sand grouse. They are in some respects intermediate between the pigeons and true grouse.
The art of measuring the duration of mental processes, or of determining the time relations of mental phenomena. -- Psy`cho*met"ric, a.
The order of birds which comprises the parrots.
The organ in which pseudova are produced; -- called also pseudovarium.
A group of cells resembling a stoma, but without any true aperture among them.
A fictitious name assumed for the time, as by an author; a pen name. [Written also pseudonyme.]
division of insects (Zoöl.) reticulated wings, as in the Neuroptera, but having an active pupa state. It includes the dragon flies, May flies, white ants, etc.
A species of micaceous sandstone. -- Psam*mit"ic, a.
A salt of prussic acid; a cyanide. Red prussiate of potash.
A papular disease of the skin, of which intense itching is the chief symptom, the eruption scarcely differing from the healthy cuticle in color.
A genus of trees with perigynous rosaceous flowers, and a single two-ovuled carpel which usually becomes a drupe in ripening.
A sulphide of arsenic and silver of a beautiful cochineal-red color, occurring in rhombohedral crystals, and also massive; ruby silver.
The duct of a pronephros. Haeckel.
The second segment of one of the Gregarinæ.
A genus of minute unicellular algæ including the red snow plant (Protococcus nivalis).
A provisional group in which are placed a number of low microscopic organisms of doubtful nature. Some are probably plants, others animals.
The condition of being proterandrous.
The ventral plate of the prothorax of an insect.
A growing together of parts; specifically, a morbid adhesion of the eyelids to each other or to the eyeball. Dunglison.
The anterior of the body of an animal, as of a cephalopod; the thorax of an arthropod.
The entire cavity of the prosencephalon. B.
An early larval form of a trematode worm; a redia. See Redia.
The sixth joint of a typical leg of a crustacean; usually, the penultimate joint.
The bone of either the upper arm or the thing, the propodialia being the humerus and femur.
The ketone of propionic acid, obtained as a colorless fragrant liquid.
A salt of propionic acid.
The dorsal plate of the prothorax in insects. See Illust.
A muscle which produces pronation.
The porch or vestibule of a temple.
The proboscis of hemipterous insects. See Illust.
The art and science of predicting in medicine. Laycock.
A division of Crocodilia, including the true crocodiles and alligators, in which the dorsal vertebræ are concave in front.
A lateral cavity of the prosencephalon; a lateral ventricle of the brain. B.
An order of large birds; the Ratitæ; -- called also Proceri.
The kindling of a disease into action; also, the procatarctic cause. Quincy.
An order of large mammal
The wood of two small tropical American trees (Hamelia ventricosa, and Cordia gerascanthoides). It is brownish, veined with lighter color.
The genus of plants including the primrose (Primula vera).
The outermost of the two integuments of an ovule.
The office or character of a priest; the priestly function. Bk.
The first coating of plaster in work of three coats upon laths. Its surface is scratched once to form a better key for the next coat.
A hydrous borate of lime, from Oregon.

The quality or condition of being prevalent; superior strength, force, or influence; general existence, reception, or practice; wide extension; as, the prevalence of virtue, of a fashion, or of a disease; the prevalence of a rumor. The duke better knew what ki
A surmise previously formed. Shak.
The anterior segment of the sternum; the manubrium. -- Pre*ster"nal, a.
The first of the four pieces composing the dorsal part, or tergum, of a thoracic segment of an insect. It is usually small and inconspicuous.
A notice or notion which precedes something else in time; previous notion or thought; foreknowledge. Bacon.
Ignition in an internal-combustion engine while the inlet valve is open or before compression is completed.

A Roman officer who controlled or superintended a particular command, charge, department, etc.; as, the prefect of the aqueducts; the prefect of a camp, of a fleet, of the city guard, of provisions; the pretorian prefect, who was commander of the troops guardi
A leader of a choir; a directing singer. Specifically: (a) The leader of the choir in a cathedral; -- called also the chanter or master of the choir.
An inhabitant of the earth before Adam.
A variety of altered iolite of a green color and greasy luster.
A variety of cryptocrystalline of a leek-green color.

An extensive tract of level or rolling land, destitute of trees, covered with coarse grass, and usually characterized by a deep, fertile soil. They abound throughout the Mississippi valley, between the Alleghanies and the Rocky mountains.
A division of butterflies including the satyrs.
The anterior horn of each lateral ventricle of the brain. B.
A division of birds including those whose young are able to run about when first hatched.
A variety of steatite sometimes manufactured into culinary vessels.
The posterior horn of each lateral ventricle of the brain. B.
A ridge within and behind the tragus in the ear of some animals.
A kind of militia in Poland, consisting of the gentry, which, in case of invasion, was summoned to the defense of the country.
A genus of polypetalous plants; also, any plant of the genus.
A scholar at Merton College, Oxford, who has a certain academical allowance or portion; -- corrupted into postmaster. Shipley.
A grand division of the Invertebrata, including the sponges; -- called also Spongiæ, Spongida, and Spongiozoa. The principal divisions are Calcispongiæ, Keratosa or Fibrospongiæ, and Silicea.
A bird of the Western United States (Phalænoptilus Nutalli) allied to the whip-poor-will.
The compound organism of a polyzoan.
A persistently excessive flow of watery urine, with low specific gravity and without the presence of either albumin or sugar. It is generally accompanied with more or less thirst.
An African genus of ganoid fishes including the bichir.
A genus of fungi having the under surface full of minute pores; also, any fungus of this genus.
A genus of plants of the order Filices or ferns. The fructifications are in uncovered roundish points, called sori, scattered over the inferior surface of the frond or leaf.
A plant of the genus Polypodium; polypody. [Written also polypod.]
A coral, or corallum; also, one of the coral-like structure made by bryozoans and hydroids.
A receptacle which bears many ovaries.
A machine generating more than one pressure wave; a multiphaser.
A plant of the order Polygynia.
An instrument for multiplying copies of a writing; a manifold writer; a copying machine.
A genus of marine annelids, believed to be an ancient or ancestral type. It is remarkable for its simplicity of structure and want of parapodia.
A genus of plants embracing a large number of species, including bistort, knotweed, smartweed, etc.
A clinic in which diseases of many sorts are treated; especially, an institution in which clinical instruction is given in all kinds of disease.
A coherent mass of pollen, as in the milkweed and most orchids.
A genus of gamopetalous perennial herbs, including the Jacob's ladder and the Greek valerian.
The art or practice of disputation or controversy, especially on religious subjects; that branch of theological science which pertains to the history or conduct of ecclesiastical controversy.
The art or rocess of making observations with the polariscope.
The art or process of measuring the polarization of light.
The balancer of dipterous insects.
A man who has charge of railroad points or switches. [Eng.]
An irregular form of corpuscle found in the blood in cases of profound anæmia, probably a degenerated red blood corpuscle.
A group of herbivorous marsupials including the kangaroos and their allies. -- Po*eph"a*gous, a.
A variety of jade or nephrite, -- used in New Zealand for the manufacture of axes and weapons.
The scaly covering of the foot of a bird or reptile.
An order of Bryozoa of which Rhabdopleura is the type. See Rhabdopleura.
The stalk of a seed or ovule.
A stalk which bears the fructification in some lichens, as in the so-called reindeer moss.
A genus of grasses, including a great number of species, as the kinds called meadow grass, Kentucky blue grass, June grass, and spear grass (which see).
The science which treats of the lungs.
An ear tuft of feathers, as in the horned owls.
The technical name of lead. See Lead.
A switchboard in which connections are made by means of plugs.
The act or movement of forming a column from a line of troops on some designated subdivision; -- the opposite of deployment.
An old term for a river boat.
The antero-lateral piece which articulates the sternum of birds.
A group of Isectivora, including the colugo.
A painful affection of the side, simulating pleurisy, usually due to rheumatism.
A group of fresh-water turtles in which the neck can not be retracted, but is bent to one side, for protection. The matamata is an example.
An inflammation of the pleura, usually accompanied with fever, pain, difficult respiration, and cough, and with exudation into the pleural cavity. Pleurisy root.
The central column of parenchyma in a growing stem or root.
A black variety of spinel.
A maker or adapter of plays.
A piece of ground used for recreation; as, the playground of a school.
A genus of trees; the plane tree.
A substance associated with nuclein in cell nuclei, and by some considered as the fundamental substance of the nucleus.
The important living portion of protoplasm, considered a chemical substance of the highest elaboration. Germ plasm and idioplasm are forms of plasmogen.
One who, or that which, plants or sows; as, a planterof corn; a machine planter.
The art or process of producing or gauging a plane surface.
To make smooth or plane, as a metallic surface; to condense, toughen, and polish by light blows with a hammer.
A division of Turbellaria; the Dendrocoela.
An order of fishes including the sharks and rays; -- called also Plagiostomata.
A sulphide of lead and antimony, of a blackish lead-gray color and metallic luster.
A general term used of any triclinic feldspar. See the Note under Feldspar.
A stripe of color.
A division of gastropod Mollusca, including the chitons. The back is covered by eight shelly plates.
A group of fishes including the sharks and rays; the Elasmobranchii; -- called also Placoidei.

A superficial affection of the skin, characterized by irregular patches of thin scales which are shed in branlike particles. Pityriasis versicolor Etym: [NL.] (Med.), a parasitic disease of the skin, characterized by the development of reddish or brownish patc
A division of mammals including the apes and monkeys. Sometimes used in the sense of Primates.
A pitch-black mineral consisting chiefly of the oxide of uranium; uraninite. See Uraninite.
Having the arris defined by a line beyond which the rock is cut away, so as to give nearly true edges; -- said of squared stones that are otherwise quarry-faced.
The metamorphosis of other organs into pistils.

The name of a genus of trees, including the tree which bears the pistachio, the Mediterranean mastic tree (Pistacia Lentiscus), and the species (P. Terebinthus) which yields Chian or Cyprus turpentine.
The act or crime of a pirate.
A white crystalline compound of piperidine and piperic acid. It is obtained from the black pepper (Piper nigrum) and other species.
A crab of the genus pinnotheres. See Oyster crab, under Oyster.
A suborder of aquatic carnivorous mammals including the seals and walruses; -- opposed to Fissipedia.
An animal of the seal tribe, moving by short feet that serve as paddles.
A reddish fleshy herb of the genus Monotropa (M. hypopitys), formerly thought to be parasitic on the roots of pine trees, but more probably saprophytic.
A species of pine (Pinus Pinaster) growing in Southern Europe.
A West Indian name for the prickly pear (Opuntia); -- called also pimploes.
The journey of a pilgrim; a long journey; especially, a journey to a shrine or other sacred place. Fig., the journey of human life.
A cap of cells which covers the growing extremity of a root; a rootcap.
A name of several annual weeds. See Goosefoot, and Lamb's- quarters.
A small wooden pail or tub with an upright stave for a handle, -- often used as a dipper.
The hypothetical radical of picric acid, analogous to phenyl.
A fibrous variety of serpentine.
A salt of picric acid.
The powder of aloes with canella, formerly officinal, employed as a cathartic.
An instrument for picking locks. Shak.
The sauger of the St.Lawrence River.
A group of birds including the woodpeckers, toucans, barbets, colies, kingfishes, hornbills, and some other related groups.
A division of birds including the woodpeckers and wrynecks.
A division of Hymenoptera; the sawflies.
A genus of South American palm trees, the seeds of which furnish the substance called vegetable ivory.
An order of teleost in which the air bladder has no opening.
The natural constitution, or physical structure, of a person. With his white hair and splendid physique.
The tribal history of the functions, or the history of the paleontological development of vital activities, -- being a branch of phylogeny. See Morphophyly.
The science which treats of the phenomena of living organisms; the study of the processes incidental to, and characteristic of, life.
The germ history of the functions, or the history of the development of vital activities, in the individual, being one of the branches of ontogeny. See Morphogeny.
A group of simple marine organisms, usually classed as the lowest of the sponges. They have inflated hollow bodies.
An order of Siphonophora which includes Physalia.
The larva of the spiny lobsters (Palinurus and allied genera). Its body is remarkably thin, flat, and transparent; the legs are very long.
A retrograde metamorphosis of the floral organs to the condition of leaves.
The cavity of a hydrophyllium.
The hypothetical radical of phthalic acid.
A salt of phthalic acid.
An affection of the eye, in which the patient perceives luminous rays, flashes, coruscations, etc. See phosphene.
A dread or intolerance of light. Sir T.
A contraction of Photograph. [Colloq.]
A salt of phosphorous acid.
A binary compound of phosphorus.
An instrument for measuring sounds, as to their intensity, or the frequency of the vibrations.

The science or doctrine of the elementary sounds uttered by the human voice in speech, including the various distinctions, modifications, and combinations of tones; phonetics. Also, a treatise on sounds.
A group of extinct carnivorous whales. Their teeth had compressed and serrated crowns.
A genus of seals. It includes the common harbor seal and allied species.
A liquid metameric with xylenol, belonging to the class of phenols, and obtained by distilling certain salts of phloretic acid.
A genus of grasses, including the timothy (Phleum pratense), which is highly valued for hay; cat's-tail grass. Gray.
A genus of evergreen plants growing along the shores of the Mediterranean, and breading a fruit resembling that of the olive.
The science of the relations between climate and periodic biological phenomena, as the migrations and breeding of birds, the flowering and fruiting of plants, etc. -- Phe`no*log"ic*al (#), a.
A compound of phenol analogous to a salt.
The ethyl ether of phenol, obtained as an aromatic liquid, C6H5.O.C2H5.
The tissue of young cells which produces cork cells.
A layer of green parenchimatous cells formed on the inner side of the phellogen.
A genus of leguminous plants, including the Lima bean, the kidney bean, the scarlet runner, etc. See Bean.
A marsupial of the genus Phascolomys; a wombat.
The notions, doctrines, and conduct of the Pharisees, as a sect. Sharp.
An image formed by the mind, and supposed to be real or material; a shadowy or airy appearance; sometimes, an optical illusion; a phantom; a dream. They be but phantasms or apparitions.
A leucocyte which plays a part in retrogressive processes by taking up (eating), in the form of fine granules, the parts to be removed.
A colorless variety of chabazite; the original was from Leipa, in Bohemia.
A genus of fungi embracing a great number of species, some of which are remarkable for their regular cuplike form and deep colors.
A telluride of silver and gold, related to hessite.
A genus of solanaceous herbs with funnelform or salver-shaped corollas. Two species are common in cultivation, Petunia violacera, with reddish purple flowers, and P.
An ancient war engine for hurling stones.
The metamorphosis of various floral organs, usually stamens, into petals.
A delicate bar of cartilage connecting the dorsal and ventral extremities of the first pair of bronchial cartilages in the syrinx of birds.
The distal segment of the hind limb of vertebrates, including the tarsus and foot.
A term formerly given to the salts supposed to be formed respectively by neutralizing acids with certain peroxides. [Obsoles.]
An out-of-door flight of steps, as in a garden, leading to a terrace or to an upper story; -- usually applied to mediævel or later structures of some architectural pretensions.

The larva of the bean fly.
