The use of the microscope; investigation with the microscope.
A rare mineral of resinous luster and high specific gravity. It is a tantalate of calcium, and occurs in octahedral crystals usually very minute.
An instrument for executing minute writing or engraving.
A microscopic form of life; an animal or vegetable organism microscopic size.

The weight of the half hydrogen molecule, or of the hydrogen atom, taken as the standard in comparing the atomic weights of the elements; thus, an atom of oxygen weighs sixteen microcriths. See Crith.

A genus of Spherobacteria, in the form of very small globular or oval cells, forming, by transverse division, filaments, or chains of cells, or in some cases single organisms shaped like dumb-bells (Diplococcus), all without the power of motion. See Illust.
A mineral of the feldspar group, like orthoclase or common feldspar in composition, but triclinic in form.
A theoretical aggregation of molecules constituting a structural particle of protoplasm, capable of increase or diminution without change in chemical nature.
A mineral of an iron-black color, and very sectile, consisting principally of sulphur, antimony, and silver.
A unit of conductivity, being the reciprocal of the ohm.
An instrument for measuring colors.

The technical name of methyl alcohol or wood spirit; also, by extension, the class name of any of the series of alcohols of the methane series of which methol proper is the type. See Methyl alcohol, under Methyl.
A salt of methionic acid.
A binary compound of methyl with some element; as, aluminium methide, Al2(CH3)6.
A measure of energy or work done; the power exerted in raising one gram through the distance of one meter against gravitation.
The posterior division of the foot in the Gastropoda and Pteropoda.
The dorsal portion of the metaphorax of insects.
The most posterior of the three pairs of embryonic renal organs developed in many vertebrates.
A colorless liquid of an agreeable odor, C6H10O, obtained by distilling a mixture of sugar and lime; -- so called because formerly regarded as a polymeric modification of acetone.
An insect which undergoes a metamorphosis.
A group of very lowly organized, wormlike parasites, including the Dicyemata. They are found in cephalopods.
A salt of mesoxalic acid.
The fold of peritoneum connecting the ovary with the wall of the abdominal cavity.
The middle segment of the thorax in insects. See Illust.
The middle layer of the gonophore in the Hydrozoa.
A product of metabolic action.
A membrane of a seed. See Secundine.
The fold of peritoneum, or mesentery, attached to the rectum. -- Mes`o*rec"tal, a.
The fold of peritoneum which attaches the testis to the dorsal wall of the body cavity or scrotal sac.
The middle portion of the foot in the Gastropoda and Pteropoda.
The nucleus of a cell; mesoblast. Agassix.
The parenchyma of a leaf between the skin of the two surfaces. Gray.
The middle bark of a tree; the green layer of bark, usually soon covered by the outer or corky layer, and obliterated.
The dorsal portion of the mesothorax of insects.
The fold of the peritoneum supporting the oviduct.
An instrument of the ancients for finding two mean proportionals between two given lines, required in solving the problem of the duplication of the cube. Brande & C.
A fold of the peritoneum connecting the liver with the dorsal wall of the abdominal cavity.
The fold of peritoneum connecting the stomach with the dorsal wall of the abdominal cavity; the mesogastrium.
The fold of peritoneum, or mesentery, attached to the colon. -- Mes`o*col"ic, a.
The middle layer of a pericarp which consists of three distinct or dissimilar layers. Gray.
The fold of peritoneum attached to the cæcum. -- Mes`o*cæ"cal, a.
The fold of peritoneum which suspends the ovary from the dorsal wall of the body cavity.
A salt of mesaconic acid.
A bird of the Thrush family.
A class of Arthropoda, allied to the Crustacea. It includes the trilobites, Eurypteroidea, and Limuloidea.
The fourth joint of a typical appendage of Crustacea.
A tissue of growing cells, or cells capable of further division.
A permanent colony of cells or plastids which may remain isolated, like Rotifer, or may multiply by gemmation to form higher aggregates, termed zoides. Perrier.
A compound of mercaptan formed by replacing its sulphur hydrogen by a metal; as, potassium mercaptide, C2H5SK.
The details of a banquet; a bill of fare.
The front median plate of the labium in insects. See Labium.
A compound radical forming the base of menthol.
The period of natural cessation of menstruation. See Change of life, under Change.
The three membranes that envelop the brain and spinal cord; the pia mater, dura mater, and arachnoid membrane.

An American marine fish of the Herring familt (Brevoortia tyrannus), chiefly valuable for its oil and as a component of fertilizers; -- called also mossbunker, bony fish, chebog, pogy, hardhead, whitefish, etc.
The condition of being mendicant; beggary; begging. Burke.
A mineral of a honey color, found in brown coal, and partly the result of vegetable decomposition; honeystone. It is a mellitate of alumina.
A salt of mellitic acid.
A variety of sugar isomeric with sucrose, extracted from cotton seeds and from the so-called Australian manna (a secretion of certain species of Eucalyptus).
A genus of labiate herbs, including the balm, or bee balm (Melissa officinalis).
A genus of grasses (Melica) of little agricultural importance.
A variety of sugar, isomeric with sucrose, extracted from the manna of the larch (Larix). [Written also melicitose.]
A fight in which the combatants are mingled
A genus of American gallinaceous birds, including the common and the wild turkeys.
A genus of evergreen tropical shrubs; -- so called from the black berries of some species, which stain the mouth.
A dark discoloration of the skin, usually local; as, Addison's melasma, or Addison's disease. -- Me*las"mic, a.
A small fish of the Mediterranean; a gilthead. See Gilthead (a).
A hydrous sulphate of iron of a green color and vitreous luster; iron vitriol.
An alga of any kind that produces blackish spores, or seed dust. The melanosperms include the rockweeds and all kinds of kelp.
The morbid deposition of black matter, often of a malignant character, causing pigmented tumors.
A black variety of garnet.
A morbid condition in which the blood contains black pigment either floating freely or imbedded in the white blood corpuscles.
An earthy black oxide of copper, arising from the decomposition of other ores.
A member of the scapolite, group, occuring in glassy crystals on Monte Somma, near Naples.
An instrument for determining longitude by observation of the stars.
A leaf-cutting bee of the genus Megachilus. See Leaf cutter, under Leaf.
A species of gull or tern. [Prov.] Lowell.
A tree of the genus Mespilus (M. Germanica); also, the fruit of the tree.
A leguminous plant of the genus Medicago. The black medic is the Medicago lupulina; the purple medic, or lucern, is M.
A salt of meconic acid.
A genus of corals with meandering grooves and ridges, including the brain corals.
A tract of low or level land producing grass which is mown for hay; any field on which grass is grown for hay.
The edible fruit of a passion flower, especially that of the North American Passiflora incarnata, an oval yellowish berry as large as a small apple.
The seed of the opium poppy.
A fat herring with undeveloped roe. [Written also matty.] [Eng.
The doctrine of materialists; materialistic views and tenets. The irregular fears of a future state had been supplanted by the materialism of Epicurus.
The state or office of a master.
The large muscle which raises the under jaw, and assists in mastication.
A rubbing or kneading of the body, especially when performed as a hygienic or remedial measure.
A genus of plants of the Milkweed family, mostly woody climbers with fragrant flowers, several species of which furnish valuable fiber, and one species (Marsdenia tinctoria) affords indigo.
A species of small opossum (Didelphus murina) ranging from Mexico to Brazil.
The metamorphism of limestone, that is, its conversion into marble. Geikie.
A thin, laminated variety of serpentine, usually of a pale green color.
A ferruginous variety of shalerite or zinc blende, nearly black in color.
A variety of marl.
A species of civet; the zoril.
A large tree of genus Melia (M. Azadirachta) found in India.
A genus of small, polished, marine univalve shells, native of all warm seas.
The ketone of margaric acid.
A European whitefish of the genus Coregonus.
A tree of the genus Acer, including about fifty species. A.
The distal segment of the fore limb, including the carpus and fore foot or hand.
The lintel of a fireplace when of wood, as frequently in early houses.
A variety of sugar obtained by the partial oxidation of mannite, and closely resembling levulose.
The technical name of mannite. See Mannite.
A salt of mannitic acid.
The anterior segment of the thorax in insects. See Insect.
A genus of edentates, covered with large, hard, triangular scales, with sharp edges that overlap each other like tiles on a roof. They inhabit the warmest parts of Asia and Africa, and feed on ants.
A salt of manganic acid.
A genus of plants; the mandrake. See Mandrake, 1.
A salt of mandelic acid.
A fruit tree of tropical America, belonging to the genus Mammea (M. Americana); also, its fruit.
The highest class of Vertebrata. The young are nourished for a time by milk, or an analogous fluid, secreted by the mammary glands of the mother.
A genus of tropical American shrubs with opposite leaves and small white or reddish flowers. The drupes of Malpighia urens are eaten under the name of Barbadoes cherries.
The rough surface of a congealed lava stream. [Southwestern U.
A genus of small Arctic fishes. One American species, the capelin (Mallotus villosus), is extensively used as bait for cod.
An extensive group of insects which are parasitic on birds and mammals, and feed on the feathers and hair; -- called also bird lice. See Bird louse, under Bird.
A bird of Celebes (megacephalon maleo), allied to the brush turkey. It makes mounds in which to lay its eggs.
A salt of malic acid.
A salt of malamic acid.
An extensive group of Invertebrata, including the Mollusca, Brachiopoda, and Bryozoa. Called also Malacozoaria.
A peculiar disease of the bones, in consequence of which they become softened and capable of being bent without breaking.
A class of air-breathing Arthropoda; -- called also Protracheata, and Onychophora.
A variety of pyroxene.
An annual cruciferous plant with reddish purple or white flowers (Malcolmia maritima). It is called in England Virginia stock, but the plant comes from the Mediterranean.
A genus of American and Asiatic trees, with aromatic bark and large sweet-scented whitish or reddish flowers.

An oxide of iron (Fe3O4) occurring in isometric crystals, also massive, of a black color and metallic luster. It is readily attracted by a magnet and sometimes possesses polarity, being then called loadstone.
A name for daisies and camomiles of several kinds.
A genus of cruciferous plants (Alyssum) with white or yellow flowers and rounded pods. A.
A genus of reef corals abundant in tropical seas. It includes than one hundred and fifty species, most of which are elegantly branched.
A genus of composite plants, of which one species (Madia sativa) is cultivated for the oil yielded from its seeds by pressure. This oil is sometimes used instead of olive oil for the table.
A rich wine made on the Island of Madeira. A cup of Madeira, and a cold capon's leg.
A name proposed for any plant of the same natural order (Rubiaceæ) as the madder.
A division of birds; the Longipennes.
A division of birds including the swifts and humming birds. So called from the length of the distal part of the wing.
The striped mullet of California (Mugil cephalus, or Mexicanus).
A constrictor of machines and engines; one versed in the principles of machines.
One who, or that which, macerates; an apparatus for converting paper or fibrous matter into pulp.
An order of brachiopods, in which the valves of shell are not articulated by a hinge. It includes the Lingula, Discina, and allied forms.
A coarse perennial grass of several species of Elymus, esp. E.
A genus of ferns with twining or climbing fronds, bearing stalked and variously-lobed divisions in pairs.
A group of Mammalia, including the marsupials and monotremes; - - so called because the corpus callosum is rudimentary.
A plant of the genus Lycopodium.
A genus of fungi, remarkable for the great quantity of spores, forming a fine dust, which is thrown out like smoke when the plant is compressed or burst; puffball.
A weak base identical with betaine; -- so called because found in the boxthorn (Lycium barbarum). See Betaine.
A combining form signifying orange yellow or brownish yellow.
A genus of annelids, belonging to the Oligochæta, and including the common earthworms. See Earthworm.
The business of cutting or getting timber or logs from the forest for lumber. [U.S.]
A borate of iron and magnesia, occurring in fibrous masses of a blackish green color.
An American genus of sapotaceous trees bearing sweet and edible fruits.
A variety of black limestone, often polished for ornamental purposes.
A gay seducer of women; a libertine.
The golden oriole of Europe. See Oriole.
The fruit of the Japanese medlar (Photinia Japonica). It is as large as a small plum, but grows in clusters, and contains four or five large seeds.
The running together of the matter of an ore into a mass, when the ore is only heated for calcination.
The spongelike fibers of the fruit of a cucurbitaceous plant (Luffa Ægyptiaca); called also vegetable sponge.
A group of longwinged sea birds, including the gulls, petrels, etc.
Formerly, the largest boat carried by a merchant vessel, corresponding to the launch of a naval vessel.
A genus of cephalopods, including numerous species of squids, common on the coasts of America and Europe. They are much used for fish bait.
A single type, containing two or more letters; as, æ, Æ, fi, fl, ffl, etc. ; -- called also ligature.
A thin, flat piece of board in the form of a quadrant of a circle attached to the log line; -- called also log-ship. See 2d Log, n., 2.
A tin-white arsenide of iron, isomorphous with arsenopyrite.
A combination of meat with vegetables, bread, etc., usually stewed, sometimes baked; an olio.
An order of Rhizopoda, in which the pseudopodia are thick and irregular in form, as in the Amoeba.

A genus of plants, including a great number of species. Lobelia inflata, or Indian tobacco, is an annual plant of North America, whose leaves contain a poisonous white viscid juice, of an acrid taste.
A spherulitic cavity often with concentric chambers, observed in some volcanic rocks, as in rhyolitic lavas. It is supposed to be produced by expanding gas, whence the name.
The formation of stony concretions or calculi in any part of the body, especially in the bladder and urinary passages. Dunglison.
A condition in which uric (lithic) acid is present in the blood.
The systematic use of antiseptics in the performance of operations and the treatment of wounds; -- so called from Joseph Lister, an English surgeon.
A hydrated arseniate of copper, occurring in obtuse pyramidal crystals of a sky-blue or verdigris-green color.

A transparent limpid liquid, slightly blue in color, consisting of a mixture of liquefied oxygen and nitrogen. It is prepared by subjecting air to great pressure and then cooling it by its own expansion to a temperature below the boiling point of its constitue
A condition in which fat occurs in the blood.
The whelp of a lioness; a young lion.
A genus of labiate plants (Leonurus); -- so called from a fancied resemblance of its flower spikes to the tuft of a lion's tail. L.
A South European plant of the genus Leontice (L. leontopetalum), the tuberous roots of which contain so much alkali that they are sometimes used as a substitute for soap.
A genus of herbaceous plants including the flax (Linum usitatissimum).
The seeds of flax, from which linseed oil is obtained. [Written also lintseed.] Linseed cake, the solid mass or cake which remains when oil is expressed.
A salt of linoleic acid.
A peculiar genus of rotifers, remarkable for the absence of ciliated disks. By some zoölogists it is thought to be like the ancestral form of the Arthropoda.
A pin used to prevent the wheel of a vehicle from sliding off the axletree.
A hydrous sulphate of lead and copper occurring in bright blue monoclinic crystals.
The only existing genus of Merostomata. It includes only a few species from the East Indies, and one (Limulus polyphemus) from the Atlantic coast of North America.
An order of Merostomata, including among living animals the genus Limulus, with various allied fossil genera, mostly of the Carboniferous period. Called also Xiphosura.
A group of shore birds, embracing the plovers, sandpipers, snipe, curlew, etc. ; the Grallæ.
A curve of the fourth degree, invented by Pascal. Its polar equation is r = a cos + b.
A genus of small spiral pteropods, common in the Arctic and Antarctic seas. It contributes to the food of the right whales.
The capital city of Peru, in South America. Lima bean.
A genus of fresh-water air-breathing mollusks, abundant in ponds and streams; -- called also pond snail. [Written also Lymnæa.]
One belonging to a very diminutive race described in Swift's "Voyage to Lilliput."
A vessel carrying at the masthead a brilliant light, and moored off a shoal or place of dangerous navigation as a guide for mariners.
A substance isomeric with starch, extracted from several species of moss and lichen, esp. from Iceland moss.
A mineral of an olive-green color, commonly in orthorhombic crystals. It is a hydrous phosphate of copper.
The lowest of the three divisions of the Jurassic period; a name given in England and Europe to a series of marine limestones underlying the Oölite. See the Chart of Geology.
A group of birds, including the hornbills, kingfishers, and related forms.
A large antelope of North Africa (Oryx leucoryx), allied to the gemsbok.
A discharge of a white, yellowish, or greenish, viscid mucus, resulting from inflammation or irritation of the membrane lining the genital organs of the female; the whites. Dunglison.
A colorless substance isomeric with chlorophyll, contained in parts of plants capable of becoming green. Watts.
A mineral of a greenish yellow color; it is a silicate of glucina, lime, and soda with fluorine. Called also leucophanite.
A suborder of copepod Crustacea, including a large number of remarkable forms, mostly parasitic on fishes. The young, however, are active and swim freely.
An order of Crustacea, including Nebalia and allied forms.
The lowest class of Vertebrata, including only the Amphioxus. The heart is represented only by a simple pulsating vessel.
A stalked barnacle of the genus Lepas, or family Lepadidæ; a goose barnacle. Also used adjectively.
A genus of liguliflorous composite plants, including the fall dandelion (L. autumnale), and formerly the true dandelion; -- called also lion's tooth.
The Lion, the fifth sign of the zodiac, marked thus
A leguminous plant of the genus Ervum (Ervum Lens), of small size, common in the fields in Europe. Also, its seed, which is used for food on the continent.
A suborder of primates, including the lemurs, the aye-aye, and allied species. [Written also Lemuroida.]
A genus of Australian gallinaceous birds including but a single species (Leipoa ocellata), about the size of a turkey. Its color is variegated, drown, black, white, and gray.
A gift of property by will, esp. of money or personal property; a bequest.
A board, or frame of planks, lowered over the side of a vessel to lessen her leeway when closehauled, by giving her greater draught.
The sordid friar bird of Australia (Tropidorhynchus sordidus).
The stalk or petiole which supports a leaf.
A genus of maritime herbs (Plumbago). P.
A mineral of a light indigo-blue color, occurring in small masses, or in monoclinic crystals; blue spar. It is a hydrous phosphate of alumina and magnesia.

A mineral of a fine azure-blue color, usually in small rounded masses. It is essentially a silicate of alumina, lime, and soda, with some sodium sulphide, is often marked by yellow spots or veins of sulphide of iron, and is much valued for ornamental work.
The ketone of lauric acid.
A rare sulphide of osmium and ruthenium found with platinum in Borneo and Oregon.
A salt of lauric acid.
A loop or eye formed on the head rope of a bonnet, by which it is attached to the foot of a sail; -- called also latch and lasket. [Usually in pl.]

A condition of the body, or mind, when its voluntary functions are performed with difficulty, and only by a strong exertion of the will; languor; debility; weariness. The corporeal instruments of action being strained to a high pitch .
An order of Tunicata, including Appendicularia, and allied genera; -- so called because certain larval features are retained by them through life. Called also Copelata.
A small European bird of the Plover family (Vanellus cristatus, or V. vanellus).
The soft woolly hair which covers most parts of the mammal fetus, and in man is shed before or soon after birth.

A rare element of the group of the earth metals, allied to aluminium. It occurs in certain rare minerals, as cerite, gadolinite, orthite, etc., and was so named from the difficulty of separating it from cerium, didymium, and other rare elements with which it i
A curious colubriform snake of the genus Xyphorhynchus, from Madagascar. It is brownish red, and its hose is prolonged in the form of a sharp blade.
A portion of land or territory which the eye can comprehend in a single view, including all the objects it contains.
A woman having real estate which she leases to a tenant or tenants.

In Ireland, a combination of tenant farmers and other, organized, with Charles Stewart Parnell as president, in 1879 with a view to the reduction of farm rents and a reconstruction of the land laws. -- Land"*lea`guer (#), n.
A slender marine fish of the genus Ammodytes, especially Ammodytes tobianus of the English coast; -- called also sand lance.
A genus of coleopterous insects, including the glowworms.
An insect of the genus Lampyris, or family Lampyridæ. See Lampyris.

The theory that structural variations, characteristic of species and genera, are produced in animals and plants by the direct influence of physical environments, and esp., in the case of animals, by effort, or by use or disuse of certain organs.
A division of amphipod Crustacea, in which the abdomen is small or rudimentary and the legs are often reduced to five pairs. The whale louse, or Cyamus, and Caprella are examples.
A plant of the genus Briza (B. media); a variety of quaking grass.
A genus of composite herbs, several of which are cultivated foe salad; lettuce.
A salt of lactic acid.
A bundle or fascicle of muscular fibers.
An order of Reptilia, which includes the lizards.
A genus of marine fishes, including the wrasses of Europe. See Wrasse.
A region of British America on the Atlantic coast, north of Newfoundland. Labrador duck (Zoöl.), a sea duck (Camtolaimus Labradorius) allied to the eider ducks.
an East Indian name for several twining leguminous plants related to the bean, but commonly applied to the hyacinth bean (Delichos Lablab).
A small tree of the genus Citrus (C. Japonica) growing in China and Japan; also, its small acid, orange-colored fruit used for preserves.
An inert gaseous element of the argon group, occurring in air to the extent of about one volume in a million. It was discovered by Ramsay and Travers in 1898.
A genus of spreading shrubs with many stems, from one species of which (K. triandra), found in Peru, rhatany root, used as a medicine, is obtained.
A very venomous snake of India (Bungarus coeruleus), allied to the cobra. Its upper parts are bluish or brownish black, often with narrow white streaks; the belly is whitish.
A variety of cabbage, in which the edible part is a large, turnip-shaped swelling of the stem, above the surface of the ground.
The character, dignity, or condition of a knight, or of knights as a class; hence, chivalry. "O shame to knighthood." Shak.
The twisting of a rope or cable, as it is running out. [Eng.]
A mineral of a gray, red, brown, or green color, and glistening luster. It is a silicate of iron and manganese.
A unit of electromotive force equal to one thousand volts.
A species of clay; meerschaum. [Also written keffekil.]
The name of certain African species of Hibiscus, cultivated for the acid of their mucilage. [Written also ketmia.]
The operation of removing a cataract by thrusting a needle through the cornea of the eye, and breaking up the opaque mass.
The long flower stems of the ribwort plantain (Plantago Lanceolata). Dr.
The hollow stalk of an umbelliferous plant, such as the cow parsnip or the hemlock. [Written also kex, and in pl., kecks, kaxes.] Nothing teems But hateful docks, rough thistles, kecksies, burs.
A species of Macropiper (M. methysticum), the long pepper, from the root of which an intoxicating beverage is made by the Polynesians, by a process of mastication; also, the beverage itself.
A lofty coniferous tree of New Zealand Agathis, or Dammara, australis), furnishing valuable timber and yielding one kind of dammar resin. [Written also kaudi, cowdie, and cowrie.]
The reticular network of fine fibers, of which the nucleus of a cell is in part composed; -- in opposition to kytomiton, or the network in the body of the cell. W.
A West Indian plant of the Pineapple family (Nidularium Karatas).
A species of gray fox found in Russia.
The fossil resin of the kauri tree of New Zealand.
A small chevrotain of the genus Tragulus, esp. T.
A variety of mimetite or arseniate of lead in hexagonal prisms of a fine orange yellow. [Written also campylite.]
The red dusty hairs of the capsules of an East Indian tree (Mallotus Philippinensis) used for dyeing silk. It is violently emetic, and is used in the treatment of tapeworm.
The Hindoo Cupid. He is represented as a beautiful youth, with a bow of sugar cane or flowers.
A genus of North American shrubs with poisonous evergreen foliage and corymbs of showy flowers. Called also mountain laurel, ivy bush, lamb kill, calico bush, etc.
A New Zealand parrot of the genus Nestor, especially the brown parrot (Nestor meridionalis).
A compound salt consisting chiefly of potassium chloride and magnesium sulphate, occurring at the Stassfurt salt mines in Prussian Saxony.
The Arabian name of two trees of the genus Balsamodendron, which yield a gum resin and a red aromatic wood.
A Brazilian name for the lofty myrtaceous tree (Bertholetia excelsa) which produces the large seeds known as Brazil nuts.

A yellow carangoid fish of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts (Caranx chrysos), most abundant southward, where it is valued as a food fish; -- called also hardtail, horse crevallé, jack, buffalo jack, skipjack, yellow mackerel, and sometimes, improperly, horse macke
A genus of valuable trees, including the true walnut of Europe, and the America black walnut, and butternut.
A dog with large jowls, as the beagle.
An integrating wattmeter for measuring the energy in joules expended in an electric circuit or developed by a machine.
A boat of medium size belonging to a ship.

The larva of a small, hymenopterous fly (Eurytoma hordei), which is found in gall-like swellings on the stalks of wheat, usually at or just above the first joint. In some parts of America it does great damage to the crop.
A proper name of a man. John-apple, a sort of apple ripe about St.
The act or practice of jobbing.
A euphorbiaceous shrub of the genus Pedilanthus (P. tithymaloides), found in the West Indies, and possessing powerful emetic and drastic qualities.
A species of fungus (Hirneola Auricula-Judæ, or Auricula), bearing some resemblance to the human ear.
A yellowness of the parts of plants which are normally green; yellows.
A fish of the genus Leuciscus; the blue chub of the Danube.
A Mexican name for the Sisal hemp (Agave rigida, var. Sisalana); also, its fiber.
The middle division of the small intestine, between the duodenum and ileum; -- so called because usually found empty after death.
A shrubby plant of the genus Jasminum, bearing flowers of a peculiarly fragrant odor. The J.
A poisonous serpent of Brazil (Bothrops jararaca), about eighteen inches long, and of a dusky, brownish color, variegated with red and black spots.
A myrtaceous tree of the West Indies and tropical America (Calyptranthes Jambolana), with astringent bark, used for dyeing. It bears an edible fruit.

The tubers of the Mexican plant Ipomoea purga (or Exogonium purga), a climber much like the morning-glory. The abstract, extract, and powder, prepared from the tubers, are well known purgative medicines.
The keeper of a jail or prison. [Written also jailor, gaoler.]
The native name of a South American rutaceous shrub (Pilocarpus pennatifolius). The leaves are used in medicine as an diaphoretic and sialogogue.
A species of wild goat (Capra Nubiana) found in the mountains of Abyssinia, Upper Egypt, and Arabia; -- called also beden, and jaela.
A variety of the chamois found in the Pyrenees.
A tick of the genus Ixodes, or the family Ixodidæ.
A genus of parasitic Acarina, which includes various species of ticks. See Tick, the insect.
A plant of the genus Hedera (H. helix), common in Europe.
A magnificent species of palm (Mauritia flexuosa), growing near the Orinoco. The natives eat its fruit and buds, drink its sap, and make thread and cord from its fiber.
An extensive order of fishes, including the salmons, herrings, and many allied forms.
A subclass of Gastropoda, in which the body is symmetrical, the right and left sides being equal.
A genus of sapotaceous trees of India. Isonandra Gutta is the principal source of gutta-percha.
A body or compound which is isomeric with another body or compound; a member of an isomeric series.
An inhabitant of an island.
A genus of herbs, some species of which, especially the Isatis tinctoria, yield a blue dye similar to indigo; woad.
A tall weed with purplish flowers (Vernonia Noveboracensis). The name is also applied to other plants of the same genus.
An inflammation of the iris of the eye.
A proposition or device for securing peace, especially in the church. South.
The shell of a large Dentalium (D. pretiosum), formerly used as shell money, and for ornaments, by the Indians of the west coast of North America.
A genus of violaceous plants, chiefly found in tropical America, some species of which are used as substitutes for ipecacuanha.
A iodide of quinine obtained as a brown substance,. It is the base of herapathite.
A salt of iodic acid.
To surround or encompass as with a wreath. [Written also enwreathe.] Resplendent locks, inwreathed with beams.
To inclose or fortify as with a wall. Spenser.
To cover, as with a vail. W.
The property of remaining invariable under prescribed or implied conditions. J.
The act of pouring into a vessel; specif. (Med.), the operation of introducing a substance into a blood vessel; as, intrafusion of blood.
A transparent, extensible membrane of extreme tenuity, which forms the innermost coating of grains of pollen.
A rubbing or chafing of the skin; especially, an abrasion or excoriation of the skin between folds, as in fat or neglected children.
The act or ceremony of depositing a dead body in the earth; burial; sepulture; inhumation. T.
The middle pair of tail feathers, or middle rectrices.
The act or process of making whole or entire.
A gallfly which deposits its eggs in galls formed by other insects.

Not official; not having official sanction or authoriy; not according to the forms or ceremony of official business; as, inofficial intelligence. Pinckney and Marshall would not make inofficial visits to discuss official business.
To ally, or form an alliance witgh; to unite; to combine. With a willingness inleague our blood With his, for purchase of full growth in friendship.
A kind of stone containing native vitriol or subphate of iron, used in making ink.
A small vessel for holding ink, to dip the pen into; also, a device for holding ink and writing materials.
The external occipital protuberance of the skull.
The reedbuck of South Africa. [Written also ingali.]
A person dwelling in, or having charge of, an infirmary, esp. in a monastic institution.
The murder of an infant born alive; the murder or killing of a newly born or young child; child murder.
The state or period of being an infant; the first part of life; early childhood. The babe yet lies in smiling infancy.
A substance isomeric with, and resembling, indigo blue, and accompanying it as a side product, in its artificial production.
The variety of sugar (glucose) obtained from the glucoside indican. It is unfermentable, but reduces Fehling's solution.
The condition of being indigent; want of estate, or means of comfortable subsistence; penury; poverty; as, helpless, indigence. Cowper.
To pierce, as with a dart.
A tribe of bivalve mollusks, characterized by the closed state of the mantle which envelops the body. The ship borer (Teredo navalis) is an example.
The larva of any geometrid moth. See Geometrid.
To cover with a casque or as with a casque. Sherwood.
A variety of sugar, found in certain plants. It is optically inactive.
Between antæ; -- said of a portico in classical style, where columns are set between two antæ, forming the angles of the building. See Anta.
A division of Foraminifera, including those in which the shell is not porous.
An order of birds, including only the penguins, in which the wings are without quills, and not suited for flight.
The pallah deer of South Africa.
To furnish or inclose with a border; to form a border of. Milton.
To inclose or defend with a bank or banks. See Embank.
A silicate of iron and lime occurring in black prismatic crystals and columnar masses.
The quality or condition of being illegal; unlawfulness; as, the illegality of trespass or of false imprisonment; also, an illegal act.
The great flexor muscle of the hip joint, divisible into two parts, the iliac and great psoas, -- often regarded as distinct muscles.
The bitter principle of the holly.

The condition of being ignorant; the want of knowledge in general, or in relation to a particular subject; the state of being uneducated or uninformed. Ignorance is the curse of God, Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven.
An individual cell, differing greatly from its neighbours in regard to size, structure, or contents.
A disease in which the skin is thick, rough, and scaly; -- called also fishskin. -- Ich`thy*ot"ic, a.
The branch of science which treats of fossil footprints.
A genus of rodents, including the porcupine.
A division of ciliated Infusoria in which the cilia cover only the under side of the body.
A deformity of the penis, in which the urethra opens upon its under surface.
The stem of an aftershaft or hypoptilum. [Written also hyporachis.]
A salt of hyponitrous acid.
The largest genus of true mosses; feather moss.

The long, branching filaments of which the mycelium (and the greater part of the plant) of a fungus is formed. They are also found enveloping the gonidia of lichens, making up a large part of their structure.
An order of marsipobranchs including the lampreys. The suckerlike moth contains numerous teeth; the nasal opening is in the middle of the head above, but it does not connect with the mouth.
A condition of the blood, characterized by an abnormally large amount of fibrin, as in many inflammatory diseases.
A genus of plants, generally with dotted leaves and yellow flowers; -- called also St. John's-wort.
A fruit consisting in large part of a receptacle, enlarged below the calyx, as in the alycanthus, the rose hip, and the pear.
An alkaloid found with hyoscyamine (with which it is also isomeric) in henbane, and extracted as a white, amorphous, semisolid substance.
A division of ganoid fishes, including the gar pikes and bowfins. -- Hy`o*ga"noid, a.
An extensive order of insects, including the bees, ants, ichneumons, sawflies, etc.
The wild ass of Persia.
The science which treats of the fluids of the body.
An instrument for recording automatically the variations of the humidity of the atmosphere.
A constellation of the southern hemisphere, near the south pole.
A device for raising water by the direct action of steam; a pulsometer.
An accumulation of serous fluid in the cavity of the chest.
A machine for throwing water by hand power, as a garden engine, a fire extinguisher, etc.
A semitranslucent variety of opal that becomes translucent or transparent on immersion in water.
An extensive order of Hydrozoa or Acalephæ. [Written also Hydroida.]
A supposed compound of hydrofluoris acid and a base; a fluoride. [Archaic]
A collection of serous fluid in the areolar texture of the scrotum or in the coverings, especially in the serous sac, investing the testicle or the spermatic cord; dropsy of the testicle.
The hollow stem of a hydroid, either simple or branched. See Illust.
The group of hydroids to which the fresh-water hydras belong.
A compound of the binary type, in which hydrogen is united with some other element.
A genus of shrubby plants bearing opposite leaves and large heads of showy flowers, white, or of various colors. H.
An aquatic mite of the genus Hydrachna. The hydrachids, while young, are parasitic on fresh-water mussels.
An instrument for tracing designs on glass.
A pellucid variety of opal in globules looking like colorless gum or resin; -- called also Müller's glass.
A pteroid of the genus Cavolina. See Pteropoda, and Illustration in Appendix.
A back with a hunch or hump; also, a hunchbacked person.
A salt of humic acid.
The wife of a householder; the mistress of a family; the female head of a household. Shak.
The act or practice of one who is hospitable; reception and entertainment of strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality. Given to hospitality.
A vitiated condition of the body, due to long confinement in a hospital, or the morbid condition of the atmosphere of a hospital.
A convent or monastery which is also a place of refuge or entertainment for travelers on some difficult road or pass, as in the Alps; as, the Hospice of the Great St. Bernard.

The line or surface in which are situated all the points which are seen single while the point of sight, or the adjustment of the eyes, remains unchanged. The sum of all the points which are seen single, while the point of sight remains unchanged, is called th
A bryozoan of the genus Flustra.
A large nocturnal beetle of the genus Lucanus (as L. capreolus, and L.
A chain of small cells in certain algæ, by which the plant is propogated.
A hydrous phosphate of zinc in transparent prismatic crystals.
A European plant of the genus Cerinthe, whose flowers are very attractive to bees. Loudon.
The receptacle for honey in a honeybee. Shak.
A suborder of Hemiptera, in which both pairs of wings are similar in texture, and do not overlap when folded, as in the cicada. See Hemiptera.
The formation of homologous tissues.
The homology of parts arranged on transverse axes. Haeckel.
Similarity of form; resemblance in external characters, while widely different in fundamental structure; resemblance in geometric ground form. See Homophyly, Promorphology.
The condition of being homogamous.
The homology of metameres. See Metamere.
The possession of a homocercal tail.
A borosilicate of iron and lime, near datolite in form and composition.
A genus of decapod Crustacea, including the common lobsters. -- Hom"a*roid, a.
A division of phyllopod Crustacea, including those that are entirely covered by a bivalve shell.
An extensive division of ganoids, including the gar pike, bowfin, etc.; the bony ganoids. See Illustration in Appendix.
An order of elasmobranch fishes, including, among living species, only the chimæras; -- called also Holocephala. See Chimæra; also Illustration in Appendix.
an ovum composed entirely of germinal matter. See Meroblast.
An oxide of holmium.
A species of Althæa (A. rosea), bearing flowers of various colors; -- called also rose mallow.
Applied to coarse cloth made of undyed wool, formerly worn by Scotch peasants. [Scot.]
The hub of a wheel. See Hub.
A writer of history; a chronicler; an annalist. Even the historian takes great liberties with facts.
The tribal history of cells, a division of morphophyly. Haeckel.
The decay and dissolution of the organic tissues and of the blood.
A genus of birds including the swallows and martins.
A genus of leeches, including the common medicinal leech. See Leech.
An order of Annelida, including the leeches; -- called also Hirudinei.
A genus of dipterous insects including the horsefly or horse tick. -- Hip`po*bos"can, a.
The posterior of the three principal divisions of the brain, including the epencephalon and metencephalon. Sometimes restricted to the epencephalon only.
A plant of the genus Verbascum (V. Thapsus); the common mullein.
A warming cathartic medicine, made of aloes and canella bark. Dunglison.
An emerald-green variety of spodumene found in North Carolina; lithia emerald, -- used as a gem.
An American tree of the genus Carya, of which there are several species. The shagbark is the C.

A mineral of the Zeolite family, often occurring in amygdaloid, in foliated masses, and also in monoclinic crystals with pearly luster on the cleavage face. It is a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime.

Variation in arrangement from that existing in a normal form; heterogenous arrangement or structure, as, in botany, the deviation in position of the organs of a plant, from the ordinary or typical arrangement.
A suborder of Hemiptera, in which the base of the anterior wings is thickened. See Hemiptera.
That which is heteronymous; a thing having a different name or designation from some other thing; -- opposed to homonym.
An isomeric variety of terpene from orange oil.
The qualities characteristic of a hero, as courage, bravery, fortitude, unselfishness, etc.; the display of such qualities. Heroism is the self-devotion of genius manifesting itself in action.
A division of wading birds, including the herons, storks, and allied forms. Called also Herodii.
A cutting for the cure or relief of hernia; celotomy.
The habitation of a hermit; a secluded residence. Some forlorn and naked hermitage, Remote from all the pleasures of the world.
A rare fluophosphate of glucina, in small white crystals.

An extensive division of Mammalia. It formerly included the Proboscidea, Hyracoidea, Perissodactyla, and Artiodactyla, but by later writers it is generally restricted to the two latter groups (Ungulata).
The sulphate of iodoquinine, a substance crystallizing in thin plates remarkable for their effects in polarizing light.
A solid figure with seven sides.
A variety of barite emitting a fetid odor when rubbed or heated.
A plane figure of eleven sides and eleven angles. [Written also endecagon.]
A weed of the genus Lamium (L. amplexicaule) with deeply crenate leaves.
An effusion of blood into the cavity of the pleura.
A pain that affects only one side of the head.
A lateral half of the heart, either the right or left. B.
A neuropterous insect of the genus Hemerobius, and allied genera.
A disease of the eyes, in consequence of which a person can see clearly or without pain only by daylight or a strong artificial light; day sight.
A tumor filled with blood.

An important ore of iron, the sesquioxide, so called because of the red color of the powder. It occurs in splendent rhombohedral crystals, and in massive and earthy forms; -- the last called red ocher.
A vomiting of blood.
A species of agate, sprinkled with spots of red jasper.
The opening by which the two scalæ communicate at the top of the cochlea of the ear.
An instrument for drawing spiral lines on a plane.
The act or process of repairing lesions made by ulcers, especially by a plastic operation.
A common herb of the Mint family (Brunela vulgaris), destitute of active properties, but anciently thought a panacea.
The progress made by a ship in motion; hence, progress or success of any kind.
A vessel whose deck consists almost wholly of movable hatches; -- used mostly in the fisheries.
A coarse umbelliferous plant of Europe (Tordylium maximum).
An Asiatic species of Cacalia (C. Kleinia), used medicinally in India.
A genus of marine univalve shells; the harp shells; -- so called from the form of the shells, and their ornamental ribs.
A hydrous silicate of alumina and baryta, occurring usually in white cruciform crystals; cross-stone.
A species of fern (Lomaria borealis), growing in Europe and Northwestern America.
A tree of the genus Carpinus, of compact, horny texture; hornbeam.
An order of freshwater fishes, including the true pikes, cyprinodonts, and blindfishes.
A bird of the Heron family; the umber.
A genus of plants which includes the witch-hazel (Hamamelis Virginica), a preparation of which is used medicinally.
The sacred baboon of Egypt (Cynocephalus Hamadryas).
A genus of marine shells; the ear-shells. See Abalone.
A platform of a staircase where the stair turns back in exactly the reverse direction of the lower flight. See Quarterpace.
Having only the back and corners in leather, as a book.
A nematoid worm of the genus Gordius, resembling a hair. See Gordius.
A variety of native Epsom salt occurring in silky fibers.
A grass with very slender leaves or branches; as the Agrostis scabra, and several species of Aira or Deschampsia.
The history or description of the sacred writings or of sacred persons; a narrative of the lives of the saints; a catalogue of saints. J.
A plant of the genus Prunus (P. Padus); the bird cherry.
A genus of trees (Celtis) related to the elm, but bearing drupes with scanty, but often edible, pulp. C.
The pistils of a flower, taken collectively. See Illust.
A class of plants in the Linnaean system, whose stamens grow out of, or are united with, the pistil.
A plant that bears naked seeds (i. e., seeds not inclosed in an ovary), as the common pine and hemlock.
A cell or mass of protoplasm devoid of an envelope, as a white blood corpuscle.
The order of fishes which includes the Gymnotus or electrical eel. The dorsal fin is wanting.
A division of gastropods in which the odontophore is without teeth.
A cytode without either a cell wall or a nucleus. Haeckel.
A genus of leguminous plants; the Kentucky coffee tree. The leaves are cathartic, and the seeds a substitute for coffee.
A division of Hydroidea including the hydra. See Hydra.
A hydrous silicate of magnesia.
A place or building where athletic exercises are performed; a school for gymnastics.
A plant that exudes gum or resin.
A topmast arranged with metal bands so that it will readily slide up and down the lower mast.
A system of excavating by means of gullets or channels.

An association of men belonging to the same class, or engaged in kindred pursuits, formed for mutual aid and protection; a business fraternity or corporation; as, the Stationers' Guild; the Ironmongers' Guild. They were originally licensed by the government, a
The line by which a boat makes fast to the swinging boom. Ham.
A cultivated variety of a species of Viburnum (V. Opulus), bearing large bunches of white flowers; -- called also snowball tree.
A building which is occupied by the guard, and in which soldiers are confined for misconduct; hence, a lock-up.
A nocturnal bird of South America and Trinidad (Steatornis Caripensis, or S. steatornis); -- called also oilbird.
A genus of cretaceous fossil shells allied to the oyster.
A genus of insects including the common crickets.
The larva or grub of a large South American beetle (Calandra palmarum), which lives in the pith of palm trees and sugar cane. It is eaten by the natives, and esteemed a delicacy.
A West Indian name for several kinds of palm. See Macaw tree, under Macaw.
A mixture of spirit and water not sweetened; hence, any intoxicating liquor. Grog blossom, a redness on the nose or face of persons who drink ardent spirits to excess.
A cause of uneasiness and complaint; a wrong done and suffered; that which gives ground for remonstrance or resistance, as arising from injustice, tyranny, etc.; injury.
A name formerly applied rather loosely to certain dark-colored igneous rocks, including diorite, diabase, etc.
A variety of sandstone, usually imperfectly consolidated, consisting largely of glauconite, a silicate of iron and potash of a green color, mixed with sand and a trace of phosphate of lime.
A plant of the genus Genista (G. tinctoria); dyer's weed; -- called also greenweed.
The mother of one's father or mother.
The fruit of certain species of passion flower (esp. Passiflora quadrangularis) found in Brazil and the West Indies.
The name of several kinds of pasture grasses found in the Western United States, esp. the Bouteloua oligostachya.
An order of birds which formerly included all the waders. By later writers it is usually restricted to the sandpipers, plovers, and allied forms; -- called also Grallatores.
The fluke of sheep. See Fluke.
A genus of plants which yield the cotton of the arts. The species are much confused.
A large, arboreal, anthropoid ape of West Africa. It is larger than a man, and is remarkable for its massive skeleton and powerful muscles, which give it enormous strength.
The female of the gorcock.

A genus of long, slender, nematoid worms, parasitic in insects until near maturity, when they leave the insect, and live in water, in which they deposit their eggs; -- called also hair eel, hairworm, and hair snake, from the absurd, but common and widely diffu
A division of nematoid worms, including the hairworms or hair eels (Gordius and Mermis). See Gordius, and Illustration in Appendix.
A genus of herbs (Chenopodium) mostly annual weeds; pigweed.
A species of merganser (M. merganser) of Northern Europe and America; -- called also merganser, dundiver, sawbill, sawneb, shelduck, and sheldrake.
The reproductive zooids of a hydroid colony, collectively.
The bell of a sessile gonozooid.
A reproductive bud of a hydroid; a simple gonophore.
A plant of several species of the genus Chrysocoma; -- so called from the tufts of yellow flowers which terminate the stems; also, the Ranunculus auricomus, a kind of buttercup.
A fish of the genus Upeneus, inhabiting the Gulf of Mexico. It is allied to the surmullet.
A species of antelope (Procapra picticauda), inhabiting Thibet.
The aquatic larva of a gnat; -- called also, colloquially, wiggler.
The horney covering of the lower mandible of a bird.
The ramus of the lower jaw of a bird as far as it is naked; -- commonly used in the plural.
A genus of composite plants with white or colored dry and persistent involucres; a kind of everlasting.
A medicinal preparation made by mixing or dissolving a substance in glycerin.
A salt of glyceric acid.
The great muscle of the buttock in man and most mammals, and the corresponding muscle in many lower animals.
A condition in which glucose is discharged in the urine; diabetes mellitus.
The definition and explanation of terms; a glossary.
A genus of climbing plants with very showy lilylike blossoms, natives of India.
The bunch of looped capillary blood vessels in a Malpighian capsule of the kidney.
The larva or young of the mussel, formerly thought to be a parasite upon the parent's gills.
A rudimentary form of crystallite, spherical in shape.

A genus of small Foraminifera, which live abundantly at or near the surface of the sea. Their dead shells, falling to the bottom, make up a large part of the soft mud, generally found in depths below 3,000 feet, and called globigerina ooze.
A plectognath fish of the genera Diodon, Tetrodon, and allied genera. The globefishes can suck in water or air and distend the body to a more or less globular form.
An order of mammals; the Rodentia. -- Gli"rine, a.
The chambered sporogenous tissue forming the central mass of the sporophore in puff balls, stinkhorns, etc.
A genus of nudibranchiate mollusks, found in the warmer latitudes, swimming in the open sea. These mollusks are beautifully colored with blue and silvery white.
A mineral of a dark bluish color, related to amphibole. It is characteristic of certain crystalline rocks.
The green mineral characteristic of the greensand of the chalk and other formations. It is a hydrous silicate of iron and potash.

A seashore plant of the Spinach family (Salicornia herbacea), with succulent jointed stems; also, a prickly plant of the same family (Salsola Kali), both formerly burned for the sake of the ashes, which yield soda for making glass and soap.
A copious gummy secretion of the humor of the eyelids, in consequence of some disorder; blearedness; lippitude.
The median, convex lobe of the head of a trilobite. See Trilobite.
Joined work whose parts move within each other; a pair or series of interlocked rings.
A hydrate of alumina.
A pale ubspotted variety of the wrymouth.
A loose hydrated form of silica, a variety of opal, deposited in concretionary cauliflowerlike masses, around some hot springs and geysers.
A boiling spring which throws forth at frequent intervals jets of water, mud, etc., driven up by the expansive power of steam.
An organ in which the ova are developed in certain Turbellaria.
A plant of the genus Teucrium (esp. Teucrium Chamædrys or wall germander), mintlike herbs and low shrubs.
An order of marine Annelida, in which the body is imperfectly, or not at all, annulated externally, and is mostly without setæ.
The division of Mollusca which includes the land snails and slugs.
The tendency of an organism to respond, during its growth, to the force of gravitation.
A genus of plants including the common broom of Western Europe.
The edible fruit of a West Indian tree (Genipa Americana) of the order Rubiaceæ. It is oval in shape, as a large as a small orange, of a pale greenish color, and with dark purple juice.
The office of a general; the exercise of the functions of a general; -- sometimes, with the possessive pronoun, the personality of a general. Your generalship puts me in mind of Prince Eugene.
A division of birds including the true pigeons.
The process of becoming solid by cooling; a cooling and solidifying.
A land crab of the genus Gecarcinus, or of allied genera.
A species of cherry tree common in Europe (Prunus avium); also, the fruit, which is usually small and dark in color.
A Southern Asiatic species of wild cattle (Bibos frontalis).
The division of birds which includes the gulls and terns.
The intensity of a magnetic field expressed in C.G.S. units, or gausses.
An East Indian species of wild cattle (Bibos gauris), of large size and an untamable disposition. [Spelt also gour.]

A genus of ericaceous shrubs with evergreen foliage, and, often, edible berries. It includes the American winter-green (Gaultheria procumbens), and the larger-fruited salal of Northwestern America (Gaultheria Shallon).
A series of beds of clay and marl in the South of England, between the upper and lower greensand of the Cretaceous period.

A primeval larval form; a double-walled sac from which, according to the hypothesis of Haeckel, man and all other animals, that in the first stages of their individual evolution pass through a two-layered structural stage, or gastrula form, must have descended
A kind of internal-combustion engine (which see) using fixed gas; also, broadly, any internal-combustion engine.
An amorphous mineral of apple-green color; a hydrous silicate of nickel and magnesia. It is an important ore of nickel.
A water cooler or jug with a handle and spout; a gurglet. Mollett.
A genus of plants, some species of which produce beautiful and fragrant flowers; Cape jasmine; -- so called in honor of Dr. Alexander Garden.
A genus of plants, including the mangosteen tree (Garcinia Mangostana), found in the islands of the Indian Archipelago; -- so called in honor of Dr. Garcin.
An extract of madder by sulphuric acid. It consists essentially of alizarin.
The parasitic worm that causes the gapes in birds. See Illustration in Appendix.
The production of offspring by the union of parents of different sexes; sexual reproduction; -- the opposite of agamogenesis.
One who has the care of game, especially in a park or preserve. Blackstone.
A handsome breed of the common fowl, remarkable for the great courage and pugnacity of the males.

A species of grass (Tripsacum dactyloides) tall, stout, and exceedingly productive; cultivated in the West Indies, Mexico, and the Southern States of North America as a forage grass; -- called also sesame grass.
A small armed vessel, with sails and oars, -- used on the Malabar coast. A.
An order of birds, including the common domestic fowls, pheasants, grouse, quails, and allied forms; -- sometimes called Rasores.
The tread, treadle, or chalasa of an egg.
A salt of gallic acid.
A genus of African lemurs, including numerous species.
A mineral of a nearly black color and vitreous luster, and consisting principally of the silicates of yttrium, cerium, and iron.

One of the crooked timbers which are scarfed together to form the lower part of the compound rib of a vessel; one of the crooked transverse timbers passing across and over the keel. Futtock plates (Naut.), plates of iron to which the dead-eyes of the topmast r
The shaft of a column, or trunk of pilaster. Gwilt.
The wishbone or merrythought of birds, formed by the united clavicles.
A genus of simple, stony corals; -- so called because they are usually flat and circular, with radiating plates, like the gills of a mushroom. Some of them are eighteen inches in diameter.
A salt of fungic acid. [Formerly written also fungiate.]
The common uame of several species of the genus Fumaria, annual herbs of the Old World, with finely dissected leaves and small flowers in dense racemes or spikes. F.
A salt of fumaric acid.
An American species of rockrose (Helianthemum Canadense), sometimes used in medicine as an astringent or aromatic tonic.
A combining form signifying relating to the forehead or the frontal bone; as, fronto-parietal, relating to the frontal and the parietal bones; fronto-nasal, etc.
To curl or form into small curls, as hair, with a crisping pin; to crisp. With her hair frizzed short up to her ears.
A genus of liliaceous plants, of which the crown-imperial (Fritillaria imperialis) is one species, and the Guinea-hen flower (F. Meleagris) another.
A small dipterous fly of the genus Oscinis, esp. O.
A man who has been a slave, and has been set free.
The skin which a deer frays from his horns. B.
A genus of deciduous forest trees, found in the north temperate zone, and including the true ash trees.
A variety of apatite from Wheal Franco in Devonshire.
A spurred partidge of the genus Francolinus and allied genera, of Asia and Africa. The common species (F.
The chamber of a mine in which the powder is placed.
A group of hymenopterous insects including the sand wasps. They excavate cells in earth, where they deposit their eggs, with the bodies of other insects for the food of the young when hatched.
A species of civet (Viverra fossa) resembling the genet.
The Tasmanian forty-spotted diamond bird (Pardalotus quadragintus).
A small outwork of a fortification; a fortilage; -- called also fortelace.
The nest or dwelling of a swarm of ants; an ant-hill.
The female of a hawk or falcon.
A salt of formic acid. [Written also formiate.]
An aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used as a preservative in museums and as a disinfectant.
A genus of insects including the earwigs. See Earwig, 1.
A woman who is chief; a woman who has charge of the work or workers in a shop or other place; a head woman. Tatler.
An instrument formerly used at sea for taking the altitudes of heavenly bodies, now superseded by the sextant; -- called also cross- staff. Brande & C.
The fold of skin which covers the glans of the penis; the prepuce.
The forward extension of the hearth of a blast furnace under the tymp.
The anterior of the three principal divisions of the brain, including the prosencephalon and thalamencephalon. Sometimes restricted to the prosencephalon only.
A gelatin dynamite in which the dope is composed largely of sodium nitrate.
The behavior, dress, or other indication of a fop; coxcombry; affectation of show; showy folly.
A setting down of the foot; a footstep; the sound of a footstep. Shak.
A bath for the feet; also, a vessel used in bathing the feet.
A unit of energy or work, being equal to the work done in raising one ton against the force of gravity through the height of one foot.
A unit of energy, or work, being equal to the work done in raising one pound avoirdupois against the force of gravity the height of one foot.
A large copper vessel used for hot amalgamation.
A star of the first magnitude, in the constellation Piscis Australis, or Southern Fish.
A group of African edentates including the aard-vark.
The covering of an insect, esp. the elytra of beetles.
A salt of fluoboric acid; a fluoboride.
A combining form indicating fluorine as an ingredient; as in fluosilicate, fluobenzene.
A variety of aragonite, occuring in delicate white coralloidal forms; -- common in beds of iron ore.
A cultivator of, or dealer in, flowers.

A low, flat mass of floating ice. Floe rat (Zoöl.), a seal (Phoca foetida).

A flat stone used in paving, or any rock which will split into such stones. See Flag, a stone.
A division of the Carnivora, including the dogs, cats, and bears, in which the feet are not webbed; -- opposed to Pinnipedia.

A tumor consisting mainly of fibrous tissue, or of same modification of such tissue.
A variety of gelatin; the chief ingredient of raw silk, extracted as a white amorphous mass.
A vessel for conveying passengers, merchandise, etc., across streams and other narrow waters.
A ring or cap of metal put round a cane, tool, handle, or other similar object, to strengthen it, or prevent splitting and wearing.
A prefix, or combining form, indicating ferrous iron as an ingredient; as, ferrocyanide.
A combining form indicating ferric iron as an ingredient; as, ferricyanide.
A salt of ferric acid.

A group of mammals which formerly included the Carnivora, Insectivora, Marsupialia, and lemurs, but is now often restricted to the Carnivora.
One of the openings in a fenestrated structure.
a common species of fern with large decompound fronds (Asplenium Filixfæmina), growing in many countries; lady fern.
One who, or that which, fells, knocks or cuts down; a machine for felling trees.
A genus of carnivorous mammals, including the domestic cat, the lion, tiger, panther, and similar animals.

The quality or power of producing fruit; fruitfulness; especially (Biol.), the quality in female organisms of reproducing rapidly and in great numbers.

The state or condition of being faulted; the process by which a fault is produced.

A series of strata, of the Middle Tertiary period, of France, abounding in shells, and used by Lyell as the type of his Miocene subdivision.
A European species of deer (Cervus dama), much smaller than the red deer. In summer both sexes are spotted with white.
A fresh-water fish of the United States (Semotilus bullaris); - - called also silver chub, and Shiner. The name is also applied to other allied species.
A viverrine mammal of Madagascar (Eupleres Goudotii), allied to the civet; -- called also Falanouc.
A hydration of iolite.
A canine tooth of the upper jaw. See Teeth.

Having power, or intended, to make expiation; atoning; as, an expiatory sacrifice.
The outer coat of the anther.
The extreme outer wall of a spore; the epispore.
The act or process of exhaling, or sending forth in the form of steam or vapor; evaporation.
Imperfect fetation in some organ exterior to the uterus; extra- uterine fetation. Hoblyn.
An eruption of the skin; cutaneous efflorescence.
The involute of a curve. See Involute, and Evolute.
The faculty possessed by all substances capable of self- nourishment of manifesting the nutritive acts by changes of form, of volume, or of structure. Syd.

The act or process of evicting; or state of being evicted; the recovery of lands, tenements, etc., from another's possession by due course of law; dispossession by paramount title or claim of such title; ejectment; ouster.
An apparatus for condensing vegetable juices, or for drying fruit by heat.
A large division of gastropod molluske, including the Pulmonifera and Opisthobranchiata.

A genus of perennial, composite herbs including hemp agrimony, boneset, throughwort, etc.
The division of Aves which includes all the typical birds, or all living birds except the penguins and birds of ostrichlike form.
A genus of small European and American trees; the spindle tree. The bark is used as a cathartic.
A principle or mixture of principles derived from Euonymus atropurpureus, or spindle tree.
A genus of small beetles, one species of which (E. viti) is very injurious to the vines in the wine countries of Europe.
a mineral, consisting chiefly of the silicate of bismuth, found at Freiberg; -- called also culytine.

A mineral of a brownish red color and vitreous luster, consisting chiefly of the silicates of iron, zirconia, and lime.
A group which includes the typical copepods and the lerneans.
A genus of South American amaryllidaceous plants with large and beautiful white blossoms.
A myrtaceous genus of trees, mostly Australian. Many of them grow to an immense height, one or two species exceeding the height even of the California Sequoia.
A kind of small, portable, cooking apparatus for which heat is furnished by a spirit lamp. There should certainly be an etna for getting a hot cup of coffee in a hurry.
The science of causes. Same as tiology.
The operation of blanching plants, by excluding the light of the sun; the condition of a blanched plant.

A species of Spanish grass (Macrochloa tenacissima), of which cordage, shoes, baskets, etc., are made. It is also used for making paper.
A genus of fresh-water fishes, including pike and pickerel.
A genus of Bryozoa which produce delicate corals, often incrusting like lichens, but sometimes branched.
A condition of excessive redness. See Erythrochroism.

A group of chætopod annelids, including those that are not confined to tubes. See Chætopoda.
A medicine which eats away extraneous growths; a caustic.

A genus of shrubby plants, including the heaths, many of them producing beautiful flowers.
An extract made from ergot.
An instrument for measuring energy in ergs.
A genus of mammals, including the horse, ass, etc.
The uppermost member of the cornice of an entablature.
A crystallized, transparent mineral of the Zeolite family. It is a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime.
The thickish outer coat of certain spores.
The skin or coat of a seed, especially the outer coat. See Testa.
A deformity in which the urethra opens upon the top of the penis, instead of at its extremity.
The outer branch of the legs in certain Crustacea. See Maxilliped.
A structure which overlaps the mouth of certain insects.
A genus of highly ornate and brilliantly colored birds of Australia, allied to the birds of Paradise.
A cartilaginous lidlike appendage which closes the glottis while food or drink is passing while food or drink is passing through the pharynx.
The outer layer of the blastoderm; the ectoderm. See Blastoderm, Delamination.
The epithelial lining of the ventricles of the brain and the canal of the spinal cord; endyma; ependymis.
A genus of spiders, including the common garden spider (E. diadema).
The abnormal change of an irregular flower to a regular form; - - considered by evolutionists to be a reversion to an ancestral condition.

The moon's age at the beginning of the calendar year, or the number of days by which the last new moon has preceded the beginning of the year. Annual epact, the excess of the solar year over the lunar year, -- being eleven days.

A perivisceral cavity which arises as an outgrowth or outgrowths from the digestive tract; distinguished from a schizocoele, which arises by a splitting of the mesoblast of the embryo.

To defend, as with a shield; to shield. [Archaic] Shak.
A feeling of weariness and disgust; dullness and languor of spirits, arising from satiety or want of interest; tedium. T.
To surround with a halo.

A medicine that promotes the menstrual discharge.

A remedy which promotes discharges, as an emetic, or a cathartic.

An element of the rare earth-group. Symbol Dy; at.

The heartwood of an exogenous tree.

Having to duct or outlet; as, a ductless gland.

A genus of neuropterous insects. See Lacewing.
