Odd in manner or appearance; fantastic; whimsical; extravagant; grotesque. C.
That bites; sharp; cutting; sarcastic; caustic. "A biting affliction." "A biting jest." Shak.
To put in a certain situation or condition; to circumstance; to place. [Only in p.
In the condition of, or like, a beggar; suitable for a beggar; extremely indigent; poverty-stricken; mean; poor; contemptible. "A bankrupt, beggarly fellow." South.
Appropriate or fit; congruous; suitable; graceful; befitting. A low and becoming tone.
In bad taste; grotesque; odd.
Destitute of the natural or common covering on the head or top, as of hair, feathers, foliage, trees, etc.; as, a bald head; a bald oak. On the bald top of an eminence.
Slipping back; falling back into sin or error; sinning. Turn, O backsliding children, saith the Lord.
Of or pertaining to hearing, or to the sense or organs of hearing; as, the auditory nerve. See Ear.
Notoriously or preëminently bad; thorough or downright, in a bad sense; shameless; unmitigated; as, an arrant rogue or coward. I discover an arrant laziness in my soul.
Hot or burning; causing a sensation of burning; fiery; as, ardent spirits, that is, distilled liquors; an ardent fever.
Depending on will or discretion; not governed by any fixed rules; as, an arbitrary decision; an arbitrary punishment. It was wholly arbitrary in them to do so.
Capable of being seen, or easily seen; open to view; visible to the eye; within sight or view. The moon .
Gently opening the bowels; laxative. -- n.
Of or pertaining to a year; returning every year; coming or happening once in the year; yearly. The annual overflowing of the river [Nile].
Of or derived from angelica; as, angelic acid; angelic ether. Angelic acid, an acid obtained from angelica and some other plants.
Large; great in size, extent, capacity, or bulk; spacious; roomy; widely extended. All the people in that ample house Did to that image bow their humble knees.
An aliquot part of a number or quantity is one which will divide it without a remainder; thus, 5 is an aliquot part of 15. Opposed to aliquant.
Flowing to; flowing abundantly. "Affluent blood." Harvey.
Of or pertaining to the air, or atmosphere; inhabiting or frequenting the air; produced by or found in the air; performed in the air; as, aërial regions or currents. "Aërial spirits." Milton.
Operating in any way.
Acrid; corrosive; as, acrimonious gall. [Archaic] Harvey.
Wrongly used; perverted; misapplied. I am .
Loosed from any limitation or condition; uncontrolled; unrestricted; unconditional; as, absolute authority, monarchy, sovereignty, an absolute promise or command; absolute power; an absolute monarch.
Tending or intended to commemorate. "A sacrifice commemorative of Christ's offering up his body for us." Hammond.
Being a monosyllable, or composed of monosyllables; as, a monosyllabic word; a monosyllabic language. -- Mon`o*syl*lab"ic*al*ly, adv.
A word which has the acute accent on the antepenult.
A group of Mesozoic birds having the jaws armed with teeth, as in most other vertebrates. They have been divided into three orders: Odontolcæ, Odontotormæ, and Saururæ.
Having one's thoughts directed toward mean or insignificant subjects.
A genus of fossil trees of the Devonian and Carboniferous ages, having the exterior marked with scars, mostly in quincunx order, produced by the separation of the leafstalks.
A genus of very large fossil amphibians, of the Triassic period, having bony plates on the under side of the body. It is the type of the order Labyrinthodonta.
Consisting of, or having the nature of, dialogue; conversational. Interlocutory discourses in the Holy Scriptures.
An extinct order of marine reptiles, including Ichthyosaurus and allied forms; -- called also Ichthyopterygia. They have not been found later than the Cretaceous period.
A chisel, thin in proportion to its width. It has a tang to enter the handle instead of a socket for receiving it.

A substance which does not conduct, that is, convey or transmit, heat, electricity, sound, vibration, or the like, or which transmits them with difficulty; an insulator; as, wool is a nonconductor of heat; glass and dry wood are nonconductors of electricity.
One who searches diligently into a subject.
The most important tribe belonging to the Kaffir race. They inhabit a region on the southeast coast of Africa, but formerly occupied a much more extensive country.
A ring surrounding a bugle or hunting horn.
Any one of numerous species of extinct arthropods belonging to the order Trilobita. Trilobites were very common in the Silurian and Devonian periods, but became extinct at the close of the Paleozoic.
A kind of border similar to the orle, but of only half the breadth of the latter.
An extinct flying reptile; one of the Pterosauria. See Illustration in Appendix.
The property possessed by some crystals, of showing different colors when viewed in the direction of different axes.
A mark [thus ---, or ÷]; -- so called as resembling a needle. In old MSS.
A degraded Papuan race, inhabiting Luzon and some of the other east Indian Islands. They resemble negroes, but are smaller in size.
(a) A curved staff used by the augurs in quartering the heavens. (b) An instrument of martial music; a kind of trumpet of a somewhat curved form and shrill note.
Inflammation of the laminæ or fleshy plates along the coffin bone of a horse; founder. Youatt.
One of the elements which appear at the respective poles when a body is subjected to electro-chemical decomposition. Cf.

One of numerous species of slender and delicate fossils, of the genus Graptolites and allied genera, found in the Silurian rocks. They belong to an extinct group (Graptolithina) supposed to be hydroids.

A white, amorphous, tasteless substance resembling starch, soluble in water to an opalescent fluid. It is found abundantly in the liver of most animals, and in small quantity in other organs and tissues, particularly in the embryo.
An albuminous body, insoluble in water, but soluble in dilute solutions of salt. It is present in the red blood corpuscles united with hæmatin to form hæmoglobin.

A white, albuminous, fibrous substance, formed in the coagulation of the blood either by decomposition of fibrinogen, or from the union of fibrinogen and paraglobulin which exist separately in the blood. It is insoluble in water, but is readily digestible in g
A foot of three syllables, the middle one short and the others long, as in cast. Andrews.

A division of marine gastropods in which the gills are developed on both sides of the body and the renal organs are also paired. The abalone (Haliotis) and the keyhole limpet (Fissurella) are examples.
A tribe or family of dipterous flies whose larvæ live in decayed wood. Some of the tropical species are very large.
The dried twigs of a Syrian tree (Balsamodendron Gileadense). U.
A liquid hydrocarbon of the terpene series extracted from the seeds of a Japanese prickly ash (Xanthoxylum pipertium) as an aromatic oil.
A salt of xanthic acid.
A marine shell of the genus Turbo. See Turbo.
A silicate of lime of a white to gray, red, or yellow color, occurring generally in cleavable masses, rarely in tabular crystals; tabular spar.

The back of a woman's gown in which one or more very broad folds are carried from the neck to the floor without being held in at the waist, while the front and sides of the gown are shaped to the person and have a belt or its equivalent.
A species of large tupelo (Nyssa aquatica) growing in swamps in the southern of the United States. See Ogeechee lime.
An organ stop of delicate stringlike quality, having for each finger key a pair of pipes, of which one is tuned slightly sharp to give a wavy effect to their joint tone.
The act or process of vaporizing, or the state of being converted into vapor; the artificial formation of vapor; specifically, the conversion of water into steam, as in a steam boiler.
A young larval form of many annelids, mollusks, and bryozoans, in which a circle of cilia is developed around the anterior end.
A theory of the development of mammalian molar teeth. The primitive stage is that of simple cones, as in reptiles.
A glyceride formed by the replacement of three hydrogen atoms in glycerin by acid radicals.
The act or process of transuding.
One who transplants; also, a machine for transplanting trees.

A small bar of gold and silver, either pure, or alloyed in some known proportion with copper, for trying the purity of articles of gold or silver by comparison of the streaks made by the article and the bar on a touchstone.
A vessel of war carrying guns on three decks.
A fluoride of aluminium, calcium, and sodium occurring with the cryolite of Greenland.
A salt of thiosulphuric acid; -- formerly called hyposulphite.
Pert. to or designating heat rays that have undergone selective absorption and are therefore analogous to colored light rays.
An artificial alkaloid of complex composition, resembling thalline and used as an antipyretic, -- whence its name.
The cavity or ventricle of the thalamencephalon; the third ventricle.
A machine in which four pulleys act together. Brande & C.
A sulphide of antimony and copper, with small quantities of other metals. It is a very common ore of copper, and some varieties yield a considerable presentage of silver.
The production or condition of tetanus.
An extensive order of bony fishes including most of the common market species, as bass, salmon, cod, perch, etc.
An extensive division of gastropod mollusks in which the odontophore is long and narrow, and usually bears seven rows of teeth. It includes a large number of families both marine and fresh- water.
The central canal of the spinal cord. B.
The horizontal bracing of a bridge, which prevents its swaying.
The answer of a plaintiff to a defendant's rejoinder.
A species of toad native of Surinam. See Pipa.
A steel-gray mineral of metallic luster. It is a sulphide of silver and copper.
The history of the formation of stratified rocks.
The act or phenomenon of spontaneously dividing transversely, as do certain species of annelids and helminths; transverse fission. See Illust.
A horizontal band in a building, forming a part of the design, whether molded, projecting, or carved, or in any way distinguished from the rest of the work.
A genus of bacilli occurring of the form of long, smooth and apparently branched threads, either straight or twisted.
A sulphide of silver and iron, occurring in soft flexible laminæ varying in color from brown to black.
A division of swimming birds in which all four toes are united by a broad web. It includes the pelicans, cormorants, gannets, and others.
A congenital malformation in which the spinal column is cleft at its lower portion, and the membranes of the spinal cord project as an elastic swelling from the gap thus formed.
An instrument which, when applied over an artery, indicates graphically the movements or character of the pulse. See Sphygmogram.
A mass or ball of cells formed by the repeated division of a male germinal cell (spermospore), each constituent cell (spermoblast) of which is converted into a spermatozoid; a spermatogemma.
The protoplasm of the sperm cell. Haeckel.
A conceptacle of certain lichens, which contains spermatia.
The nucleus of the sperm cell.
A spectroscope fitted for measurements of the luminious spectra observed with it.
Soup made chiefly from vegetables or fish with a little butter and a few condiments.

A condition of the nervous system in which an individual during sleep performs actions approppriate to the waking state; a state of sleep in which some of the senses and voluntary powers are partially awake; noctambulism.
An order of lowly organized Mollusca belonging to the Isopleura. A narrow groove takes the place of the foot of other gastropods.
A machine the operation of which is started by dropping a coin into a slot, for delivering small articles of merchandise, showing one's weight, exhibiting pictures, throwing dice, etc.
Coverings for the legs of men or boys, consisting of trousers which reach only to the knees, -- worn with long stockings.
A naval vessel carrying seventy-four guns.
The half of a transept; as, the north semitransept of a church.
A division of ganoid fishes which includes the paddlefish, in which the mouth is armed with small teeth.
A European species of wormwood (Artemisia maritima) growing by the sea.
A division of raptorial birds composing the vultures.
The act, process, or result of salifying; the state of being salified.
A salt of saccharonic acid.
The glycerin salt of ricinelaidic acid, obtained as a white crystalline waxy substance by treating castor oil with nitrous acid.
A genus of brachiopods of which some species are still living, while many are found fossil.
A division of Pectostraca including saclike parasites of Crustacea. They adhere by rootlike extensions of the head.
The horny covering of the bill of birds.
The act or process of retrenching; as, the retrenchment of words in a writing. The retrenchment of my expenses will convince you that Walpole.
A radioactive substance apparently formed as a product from thorium.
The art of making fireworks; the manufacture and use of fireworks; pyrotechny.
A salt of pyrotartaric acid.
A salt of pyrosulphuric acid.
A mineral, usually of a white or greenish color and pearly luster, consisting chiefly of the hydrous silicate of alumina.
The characters of a mineral observed by the use of the blowpipe, as the degree of fusibility, flame coloration, etc.
A salt of pyroarsenic acid.
An extinct order of ganoid fishes. They had a compressed body, covered with dermal ribs (pleurolepida) and with enameled rhomboidal scales.
The strata of the Purbeck stone, or Purbeck limestone, belonging to the Oölitic group. See the Chart of Geology.
A class of flowerless plants, embracing ferns, horsetails, club mosses, quillworts, and other like plants. See the Note under Cryptogamia.
The surface of constant negative curvature generated by the revolution of a tractrix. This surface corresponds in non-Euclidian space to the sphere in ordinary space.
Any contractile vessel of invertebrates which is not of the nature of a real heart, especially one of those pertaining to the excretory system.
The anterior of three principal cartilages in the fins of some fishes. -- Prop`ter*yg"i*al, a.
In the universities of Germany and some other European countries, a licensed teacher or lecturer having no share in the university government and dependent upon fees for remuneration.
An old theory of the preëxistence of germs. Cf.
The production of two or more embryos in one seed, due either to the existence and fertilization of more than one embryonic sac or to the origination of embryos outside of the embryonic sac.
A division of Gregarinæ including those that have two or more internal divisions of the body.
A salt of a polychromic acid.
A condition in which air or other gas is present in the cavity of the chest; -- called also pneumatothorax.
A tracing of the respiratory movements, obtained by a pneumatograph or stethograph.
A distention of the scrotum by air; also, hernia of the lungs.
A form of dentine which shows sinuous lines of structure in a transverse section of the tooth.

A large, important class of parasitic or saprophytic fungi, the algal or algalike fungi. The plant body ranges from an undifferentiated mass of protoplasm to a well-developed and much- branched mycelium.
A tribe of neuropterous insects which includes the caddice flies; -- called also Trichoptera. See Trichoptera.
The excessive discharge of phosphates in the urine.
A hydrous arsenate of lime, usually occurring in silky fibers of a white or grayish color.
An order of Echini, including the irregular sea urchins, as the spatangoids. See Spatangoid.
A salt of permanganic acid. Potassium permanganate.
The wheel which, together with the axle, forms the axis in peritrochio, which see under Axis.
A variety of edible seaweed (Laurencia pinnatifida) distinguished for its pungency. [Scot.] Lindley.
The distinct articulation of the sounds of a patient's voice, heard on applying the ear to the chest in auscultation. It usually indicates some morbid change in the lungs or pleural cavity.
A condition in which the prepuce, after being retracted behind the glans penis, is constricted there, and can not be brought forward into place again.
A polymeric modification of cyanogen, obtained as a brown or black amorphous residue by heating mercuric cyanide.
A comprehensive division of fishes which includes the elasmobranchs and ganoids. [Written also Palæichthyes.]
The act or process of pacifying, or of making peace between parties at variance; reconciliation. "An embassy of pacification." Bacon.
A group of hoofed mammals distinguished for the thickness of their skins, including the elephant, hippopotamus, rhinoceros, tapir, horse, and hog. It is now considered an artificial group.

A poisonous nitrogenous base (C6H10N2) obtained indirectly from oxamide as a thick transparent oil which has a strong narcotic odor, and a physiological action resembling that of atropine. It is probably related to pyridine.
A suborder of fishes of which Ostracion is the type.
A disease of the bones, in which they lose their earthy material, and become soft, flexible, and distorted. Also called malacia.
An ornamental tree of the genus Maclura (M. aurantiaca), closely allied to the mulberry (Morus); also, its fruit.
An extinct order of birds. It includes only the Archæopteryx.
An evergreen species of barberry (Berberis Aquifolium), of Oregon and California; also, its roundish, blue-black berries.
A tetanic spasm in which the body is bent backwards and stiffened.

Leather made from sheep and calf skins by mechanically forcing ooze through them; esp., such leather with a soft, finely granulated finish (called sometimes velvet finish) put on the flesh side for special purposes. Ordinary ooze leather is used for shoe upper
The wood of Diospyros ebenaster, a kind of ebony found in Ceylon.
A salt of oenanthylic acid; as, potassium oenanthylate.
An inference which does not follow from the premises.
A condition of nervous debility supposed to be dependent upon impairment in the functions of the spinal cord.
The act or process of nebulizing; atomization.
A sort of steel which has been found where a burning coal seam had reduced and carbonized adjacent iron ore.
A division of Infusoria including the Noctiluca. See Noctiluca.
A suborder of Dipnoi, including the Ceratodus. [Written also monopneumonia.]
The fruit of the Adansonia digitata; also, the tree. See Adansonia.
A division of Invertebrata which includes the classes Brachiopoda and Bryozoa; -- called also Anthoid Mollusca.
A measure of electrical quantity; the millionth part of one coulomb.
A salt of metavanadic acid.
A salt of metastannic acid.
A salt of metasilicic acid.
A salt of mesitylenic acid.
An East Indian genus of large trees. Melanorrhoea usitatissima is the lignum-vitæ of Peru, and yelds a valuable black varnish.
A house used as a place of worship; a church; -- in England, applied only to a house so used by Dissenters.
A subdivision of the Niagara period in the American upper Silurian, characterized by the formations known as the Oneida conglomerate, and the Medina sandstone. See the Chart of Geology.
One who has a taste for, or is versed in, the history of the Middle Ages; one in sympathy with the spirit or forms of the Middle Ages. [Written also medievalist.]

The act or process of manipulating, or the state of being manipulated; the act of handling work by hand; use of the hands, in an artistic or skillful manner, in science or art. Manipulation is to the chemist like the external senses to the mind.
A genus of African siluroid fishes, including the electric catfishes. See Electric cat, under Electric.
A subclass of Crustacea, including Arthrostraca and Thoracostraca, or all those higher than the Entomostraca.
An extensive division of Anthozoa, including most of the species that produce stony corals. See Illust.
The art of prolonging life.
A subdivision of the British Upper Silurian lying below the Old Red Sandstone; -- so named from the Ludlow, in Western England. See the Chart of Geology.
The act or operation of making or becoming liquid; especially, the conversion of a solid into a liquid by the sole agency of heat.
A division of reptiles, including the serpents and lizards; the Plagiotremata.
A plant of the genus Cardamine (C. pratensis); cuckoo flower.
A climbing plant with fragrant blossoms (Clematis vitalba).
An order of teleostean fishes, including the Anabas, or climbing perch, and other allied fishes.
A mode of treating disease by appropriate muscular movements; - - also termed kinesitherapy, kinesipathy, lingism, and the movement cure.
Small hard yellowish aggregations found in the Caucasus region, and containing various yeasts and bacteria. They are used as a ferment in preparing kefir.
A tall composite plant of the genus Eupatorium (E. purpureum), with purplish flowers, and whorled leaves.
A variety of pyroxene of olive-green color passing into brown. It contains zinc.
An East Indian palm (Caryota urens) having leaves pinnate with wedge-shaped divisions, the petiole very stout. It is the principal source of jaggery, and is often cultivated for ornament.
The third joint of the typical appendages of Crustacea.
A comprehensive division of the animal kingdom, including all except the Vertebrata.
The act or process of swelling or enlarging; also, the state of being swollen; expansion; tumidity; especially, the swelling up of bodies under the action of heat. The intumescence of nations.
A depression, or inward sinking of parts.
The median of the three elements composing the centra of the vertebræ in some fossil batrachians.
The mixing of the food with the saliva and other secretions of the mouth in eating.
The act or practice of maliciously setting fires; arson.
A grand division of the Vertebrata, including the Amphibia and Fishes.
A transparent variety of calcite, the best of which is obtained in Iceland. It is used for the prisms of the polariscope, because of its strong double refraction.
A salt of hyposulphuric acid.
A salt of hypochlorous acid; as, a calcium hypochloride.
A condition of excessive fever; an elevation of temperature in a disease, in excess of the limit usually observed in that disease.
The act or art of riding, and of training and managing horses; manege.
A free-swimming, dimorphic, sexual form of certain species of Nereis.
A division of bivalve shells, including the marine mussels, in which the two adductor muscles are very unequal. See Dreissena, and Illust.
A lateral half of the cerebrum. Wilder.
A genus of plants, some species of which are cultivated for their beautiful flowers; day lily.
The principles of dynamics in their application to the blood; that part of science which treats of the motion of the blood.
The phenomenon of turning toward the light, seen in many leaves and flowers.
An interrupter in which contact is broken by the movement of an automatically vibrating hammer between a contact piece and an electromagnet, or of a rapidly moving piece mechanically driven.
The higher orders of Mammalia, in which the cerebrum is convoluted. -- Gyr"en*ceph"a*lous, a.
The process of invagination, in embryonic development, by which a gastrula is formed.
The use of galvanism in physiological experiments.
A unit of energy or work, equal to the work done in moving a body through one foot against the force of one poundal.
The process by which small particles of fine soils and sediments aggregate into larger lumps.
A gas burner with a device for lighting by an electric spark.
A salt of ferrocyanic acid; a ferrocyanide.
Limestone containing a large percentage of iron carbonate, and hence turning brown on exposure.
A salt of ferricyanic acid; a ferricyanide.
The female or young of the goshawk (Astur palumbarius).
The protrusion of the eyeball so that the eyelids will not cover it, in consequence of disease.
The act of excogitating; a devising in the thoughts; invention; contrivance.
An order of fishes including a vast number of freshwater species such as the carp, loach, chub, etc.
An order of insects, including the earwig. The anterior wings are short, in the form of elytra, while the posterior wings fold up beneath them.
A genus of shrubs or small trees of the Flax family, growing in tropical countries. E.
The segment of the brain next behind the midbrain, including the cerebellum and pons; the hindbrain. Sometimes abbreviated to epen.
The median plate of the plastron of turtles; -- called also entosternum.
The portion of each apodeme developed from the interepimeral membrane in certain crustaceans.
The general description of embryos.
An instrument for describing ellipses; -- called also trammel.
The modified condition of a nerve, when a constant current of electricity passes through any part of it. See Anelectrotonus, and Catelectrotonus.
An instrument for producing sound by means of electric currents.
The treatment of disease by electricity.

A parasite of man and of many domestic and wild animals, forming compound cysts or tumors (called hydatid cysts) in various organs, but especially in the liver and lungs, which often cause death. It is the larval stage of the Tænia echinococcus, a small tapewo
A fungus of the genus Geoglossum.

The doctrine of purposelessness; a term applied by Haeckel to that branch of physiology which treats of rudimentary organs, in view of their being useless to the life of the organism. To the doctrine of dysteleology, or the denial of final causes, a proof of t
A method of armature winding in which the wire is wound upon the outer surface of a cylinder or drum from end to end of the cylinder; -- distinguished from ring winding, etc.
A locomotive with pilot at each end. Knight.
The process of separation, or the condition of being separate, as of the molecules of a body.
The eliminant of the n partial differentials of any homogenous function of n variables. See Eliminant.
The condition of being diplostemonous.
The office, or the term of office, of a dictator; hence, absolute power.
The salt-marsh terrapin of the Atlantic coast (Malacoclemmys palustris).
The division of Cetacea which comprises the dolphins, porpoises, and related forms.
A machine for breaking open the kernels of wheat or other grain and removing the germs.
The scaly covering of the toes, as in birds.
The conversion of cell walls into a material which repels water, as in cork.
A group of passerine birds, including the creepers and nuthatches.
Devouring knives; swallowing, or pretending to swallow, knives; -- applied to persons who have swallowed, or have seemed to swallow, knives with impunity. Dunglison.
A tribe of wading birds including the stork, heron, crane, etc.
The act or art of writing in secret characters; also, secret characters, or cipher.
A vacuum tube in which the exhaustion is carried to a very high degree, with the production of a distinct class of effects; -- so called from W. Crookes who introduced it.
A mineral consisting principally of silicate of iron, and crystallizing in hexagonal prisms with perfect basal cleavage; -- so named from the Swedish mineralogist Cronstedt.
The qualiyu of being creative.
A conjunction or concentration of rays in one point. Bacom
The fruit of a Brazilian tree (Attalea funifera of Martius.).
The act or process of taking property or condemning it to be taken, as forfeited to the public use. The confiscations following a subdued rebellion.
An apparatus for the separation of dry comminuted ore, by exposing it to intermittent puffs of air. Knight.
A report of an officer or agent.
The act or process by which chyle is formed from food in animal bodies; chylification, -- a digestive process.
A South African mole of the genus Chrysochloris; the golden mole, the fur of which reflects brilliant metallic hues of green and gold.
The crowing noise made by children affected with spasm of the laryngeal muscles; false croup.
An order of birds, including the swans, ducks, geese, flamingoes and screamers.
The Mexican name for turquoise. See Turquoise.
An obstetrical instrument for performing cephalotripsy.
An instrument measuring the dimensions of the head of a fetus during delivery.
An instrument for drawing lines through a point, or lines converging to a center.
The cry of cats; a harsh, disagreeable noise or cry like the cry of cats. Shak.

The root of an American shrub (Chiococca racemosa), found as far north as Florida Keys, from which cahincic acid is obtained; also, the root of the South American Chiococca anguifuga, a celebrated antidote for snake poison.
A breed of dogs obtained by crossing the bulldog and the terrier.
A marine univalve shell of the genus Bulla and allied genera, belonging to the Tectibranchiata.
A large, edible, gregarious bird of Australia (Talegalla Lathami) of the family Megapodidæ. Also applied to several allied species of New Guinea.

A summer or girder extending across a building flush with, and supporting, the upper part of a front or external wall; a long lintel; a girder; -- used principally above shop windows. [Written also brestsummer and bressummer.]
The bramble, or a collection of brambles growing together. He jumped into a bramble bush And scratched out both his eyes.
A group of birds, including auks, divers, and penguins.
A mineral of a bluish gray color and metallic luster, usually in plumose masses, also compact. It is sulphide of antimony and lead.
A double fluoride of boron and hydrogen, or some other positive element, or radical; -- called also fluoboride, and formerly fluoborate.
Any vessel or canal in which blood circulates in an animal, as an artery or vein.

One of the danger signals or safety signals which guide the movement of trains in a block system. The signal is often so coupled with a switch that act of opening or closing the switch operates the signal also.
A plant of the genus Mitella; miterwort. Longfellow.
The chemistry of living organisms; the chemistry of the processes incidental to, and characteristic of, life.
To combine or treat with a bichromate, esp. with bichromate of potassium; as, bichromatized gelatine.
A strong pin in the side of a vessel, or by the mast, round which ropes are wound when they are fastened or belayed.
A leguminous shrub of southern Europe, with trifoliate leaves (Anagyris foetida).
An order of Nemertina, including the large leechlike worms (Malacobdella) often parasitic in clams.
The range within which the fire of small arms is very destructive. With the magazine rifle, this is six hundred yards.
The trichloride of gold combination with the chloride of another metal, forming a double chloride; -- called also chloraurate.
A hydrous carbonate of copper and zinc, found in pale green or blue crystalline aggregations. It yields a kind of brass on reduction.
The science treating of the physical characteristics of the stars and other heavenly bodies, their chemical constitution, light, heat, atmospheres, etc.
A genus of gigantic cephalopods, allied to the squids, found esp. in the North Atlantic and about New Zealand.
A precipitation of silver, in a beautiful arborescent form.
The introduction of water subcutaneously for the relief of pain.
The formation of an aposteme; the process of suppuration. [Written corruptly imposthumation.] Wiseman.
The suborder of primates which includes the monkeys, apes, and man.
A division of birds including the geese, ducks, and closely allied forms.
A product of gastric digestion, a mixture of hemipeptone and antipeptone.
An extensive group of fossil cephalopods often very abundant in Mesozoic rocks. See Ammonite.
The property which constitutes an allomorph; the change involved in becoming an allomorph.

The repetition of the same letter at the beginning of two or more words immediately succeeding each other, or at short intervals; as in the following lines: - Behemoth, biggest born of earth, upheaved His vastness. Milton.
An alcoholic tincture prepared with fresh plants. New Eng.
A species of Vitex (V. agnus castus); the chaste tree.
The science which treats of the air and other gaseous bodies under the action of force, and of their mechanical effects.

Too valuable to admit of being appraised; of inestimable worth; invaluable.
One who lays claim, or asserts a title (to something); a claimant. Specifically,

One who makes a request or demand; hence, a candidate.
The quality or state of being possible; the power of happening, being, or existing. "All possibility of error." Hooker.

One of several small, swift, elegantly formed species of antelope, of the genus Gazella, esp. G.
Examination of the abdomen or stomach, as with the gastroscope.

A small quantity of batter, fried in boiling lard or in a frying pan. Fritters are of various kinds, named from the substance inclosed in the batter; as, apple fritters, clam fritters, oyster fritters.

A writing paper made in sheets, ordinarily 16 x 13 inches, and folded so as to make a page 13 x 8 inches. See Paper.
A motion like that of waves; a moving in this and that direction; as, the fluctuations of the sea.

A freak; a trick; a lie. Beau.
The act of flexing or bending; a turning.

The quality or state of being flat.

The state of being flaccid.
The state or quality of being fit; as, the fitness of measures or laws; a person's fitness for office.
The state or quality of being firm.

The act by which, either in animals or plants, material prepared by the generative organs the female organism is brought in contact with matter from the organs of the male, so that a new organism results; impregnation; fertilization.

A person employed to do all kinds of work or business. B.
Easy to be done or performed: not difficult; performable or attainable with little labor. Order .
The act of fabricating, framing, or constructing; construction; manufacture; as, the fabrication of a bridge, a church, or a government. Burke.

Not belonging to, or dependent upon, a thing; without or beyond a thing; not essential or intrinsic; foreign; as, to separate gold from extraneous matter. Nothing is admitted extraneous from the indictment.
Beyond what is due, usual, expected, or necessary; additional; supernumerary; also, extraordinarily good; superior; as, extra work; extra pay. "By working extra hours." H.

The act of extirpating or rooting out, or the state of being extirpated; eradication; excision; total destruction; as, the extirpation of weeds from land, of evil from the heart, of a race of men, of heresy.
The act of expiring; as: (a)(Physiol.)
The act of expending; a laying out, as of money; disbursement. our expenditure purchased commerce and conquest.
The act of draining out or draining off; the act of emptying completely of the contents.
A written official recognition of a consul or commercial agent, issued by the government to which he is accredited, and authorizing him to exercise his powers in the place to which he is assigned.
One who executes; an executer. Bacon.
The act of exciting or putting in motion; the act of rousing up or awakening. Bacon.
One who, or that which, excavates or hollows out; a machine, as a dredging machine, or a tool, for excavating.
Raised to lofty height; elevated; extolled; refined; dignified; sublime. Wiser far than Solomon, Of more exalted mind.

In an exact manner; precisely according to a rule, standard, or fact; accurately; strictly; correctly; nicely. "Exactly wrought." Shak.
Full of, or rich in, events or incidents; as, an eventful journey; an eventful period of history; an eventful period of life.
A bringer of the glad tidings of Church and his doctrines. Specially: (a) A missionary preacher sent forth to prepare the way for a resident pastor; an itinerant missionary preacher.
Healthy nutrition; soundless as regards the nutritive functions.
The practice or employment of spies; the practice of watching the words and conduct of others, to make discoveries, as spies or secret emissaries; secret watching.
A dry slough, crust, or scab, which separates from the healthy part of the body, as that produced by a burn, or the application of caustics.

Equality of rights; natural justice or right; the giving, or desiring to give, to each man his due, according to reason, and the law of God to man; fairness in determination of conflicting claims; impartiality. Christianity secures both the private interests o
The act of equipping, or the state of being equipped, as for a voyage or expedition. Burke.
Any external topical application to the body, except ointments and plasters, as a poultice, lotion, etc.

The "falling sickness," so called because the patient falls suddenly to the ground; a disease characterized by paroxysms (or fits) occurring at interval and attended by sudden loss of consciousness, and convulsive motions of the muscles. Dunglison.
A curve traced by a point in the circumference of a circle which rolls on the convex side of a fixed circle.
The nightmare. Brande & C.
A diary; a journal. Johnson.

The act of entering or passing into or upon; entrance; ingress; hence, beginnings or first attempts; as, the entry of a person into a house or city; the entry of a river into the sea; the entry of air into the blood; an entry upon an undertaking.

Removing from one country to another; emigrating; as, an emigrant company or nation.
A large deer, of several species. The European elk (Alces machlis or Cervus alces) is closely allied to the American moose.
A mournful or plaintive poem; a funereal song; a poem of lamentation. Shak.
The act of choosing; choice; selection.
Characteristic quality of a woman, such as softness, luxuriousness, delicacy, or weakness, which is unbecoming a man; womanish delicacy or softness; -- used reproachfully of men. Milton.
A spear with barbed forks for spearing eels.
A building; a structure; an architectural fabric; -- chiefly applied to elegant houses, and other large buildings; as, a palace, a church, a statehouse.

The state of being beside one's self or rapt out of one's self; a state in which the mind is elevated above the reach of ordinary impressions, as when under the influence of overpowering emotion; an extraordinary elevation of the spirit, as when the soul, unco
The state or quality of being earnest; intentness; anxiety. An honest earnestness in the young man's manner.
The tympanum. See Illust.
A native, or one of the people, of Holland. Dutchman's breeches (Bot.), a perennial American herb (Dicentra cucullaria), with peculiar double-spurred flowers.
An audience hall; the court of a native prince; a state levee; a formal reception of native princes, given by the governor general of India. [India] [Written also darbar.]
Doubleness; a twofold state. [Archaic] Do not affect duplicities nor triplicities, nor any certain number of parts in your division of things.
The chief lady in waiting on the queen of Spain. Brande.

The quality of being droll; sportive tricks; buffoonery; droll stories; comical gestures or manners. The rich drollery of "She Stoops to Conquer." Macaulay.

A bridge of which either the whole or a part is made to be raised up, let down, or drawn or turned aside, to admit or hinder communication at pleasure, as before the gate of a town or castle, or over a navigable river or canal.
Straight down; perpendicularly.
A jet or current of water or vapor directed upon some part of the body to benefit it medicinally; a douche bath.
A child's puppet; a toy baby for a little girl.

One who dogmatizes; one who speaks dogmatically; a bold and arrogant advancer of principles. I expect but little success of all this upon the dogmatist; his opinioned assurance is paramount to argument.
One of an ancient sect of physicians who went by general principles; -- opposed to the Empiric.
The 3d pers. sing.
The act of turning aside from any course, occupation, or object; as, the diversion of a stream from its channel; diversion of the mind from business.
The act or rending asunder, or the state of being rent asunder or broken in pieces; breach; rent; dilaceration; rupture; as, the disruption of rocks in an earthquake; disruption of a state.
Things so unequal or unlike that they can not be compared with each other.
The act of displacing, or the state of being displaced. T.

An insectivorous plant. See Venus's flytrap.

Inclined to defer or put off what ought to be done at once; given the procrastination; delaying; procrastinating; loitering; as, a dilatory servant.
An authoritative statement; a dogmatic saying; an apothegm. A class of critical dicta everywhere current.

Toward the right side; dextrally.

That which locks or unlocks a movement; a catch, pawl, or dog; especially, in clockwork, the catch which locks and unlocks the wheelwork in striking.

The broken state produced by decay and the infirmities of age; infirm old age.
A duck used to lure wild ducks into a decoy; hence, a person employed to lure others into danger. Beau.

A writing acknowledging a debt; a writing or certificate signed by a public officer, as evidence of a debt due to some person; the sum thus due.
A mortal or crushing blow; a stroke or event which kills or destroys. The deathblow of my hope.

The light of day as opposed to the darkness of night; the light of the sun, as opposed to that of the moon or to artificial light.

One who cuts; as, a stone cutter; a die cutter; esp., one who cuts out garments.

A donkey. [Southern U.S.]

Of, or from, barbarian nations; foreign; -- often with reference to barbarous nations of east. "Barbaric pearl and gold." Milton.

A salt of pyroantimonic acid.
False or imaginary feeling or sense perception such as occurs in hypochondriasis, or such as is referred to an organ that has been removed, as an amputated foot.
A division of marsupials in which there are more fore incisor teeth in each jaw.
The act or process of changing to a polymeric form; the condition resulting from such change.
The eyestalk of a crustacean.
A chitinous structure which supports the gill in some invertebrates.
A species of tetanus, in which the body is curved laterally. Quain.
A class of helminthes including the cestodes, or tapeworms, the trematodes, and the turbellarians. Called also flatworms.
A double cyanide of platinum and some other metal or radical; a salt of platinocyanic acid.
A telescope adapted for taking photographs of the heavenly bodies.
The branch of chemistry which relates to the effect of light in producing chemical changes, as in photography.
A disproportionately rapid growth of the upper surface of dorsiventral organs, such as leaves, through the stimulus of exposure to light. Encyc.
A genus of birds which includes the flamingoes.
A division of fishes in which the lower pharyngeal bones are united. It includes the scaroid, labroid, and embioticoid fishes.
The operation of sewing up a ruptured perineum.

The production or absorption of heat at the junction of two metals on the passage of a current. Heat generated by the passage of the current in one direction will be absorbed if the current is reversed.
A suborder of Crinoidea found chiefly in the Paleozoic rocks.
An extinct order of sea urchins found in the Paleozoic rocks. They had more than twenty vertical rows of plates.
The condition of being obdiplostemonous.
An explosive nitro derivative of certain sugars, analogous to nitroglycerin, gun cotton, etc.
A beetle of the genus Melolontha, and allied genera. See May beetle, under May.
A family of fungi constituting the order Melanconiales. -- Mel`an*co`ni*a"ceous (#), a.
An order of fishes in which the fin rays, except the anterior ray of the pectoral and dorsal fins, are closely jointed, and not spiny. It includes the carp, pike, salmon, shad, etc.
Any apparatus for making and breaking an electric circuit; a circuit breaker.
The treatment of disease by the application of magnets to the surface of the body.
The peculiar larva of Polygordius. See Polygordius.
Cloth made of linen and wool, mixed.
The fragrant wood of several shrubs and trees, especially of species of Rhodorhiza from the Canary Islands, and of the West Indian Amyris balsamifera.

A group of birds embracing the Anseres and flamingoes, in which the bill is lamellate.
The interscapular feathers of a bird.
A division of copepod crustaceans, including numerous species parasitic on fishes.
A salt formed by the union of hydrotelluric acid and the base.
An accumulation of urine in the pelvis of the kidney, occasioned by obstruction in the urinary passages.
A hydrous carbonate of magnesia occurring in white, early, amorphous masses.
A group of birds including the trogons.
The lower group of the Wealden formation; -- so called from its development around Hastings, in Sussex, England.

The tendency of a root to place its axis in the line of a galvanic current.
A genus of perennial herbs (Iris) with swordlike leaves and large three-petaled flowers often of very gay colors, but probably white in the plant first chosen for the royal French emblem.
A process of reproduction intermediate between fission and gemmation.

The act or process of making ether; specifically, the process by which a large quantity of alcohol is transformed into ether by the agency of a small amount of sulphuric, or ethyl sulphuric, acid.
A drawing of the body forward, in consequence of the spasmodic action of some of the muscles. Gross.
An instrument for obtaining an accurate record of the time at which any observed phenomenon occurs, or of its duration. It has an electro-magnetic register connected with a clock.

A powder of ipecac and opium, compounded, in the United States, with sugar of milk, but in England (as formerly in the United States) with sulphate of potash, and in France (as in Dr. Dover's original prescription) with nitrate and sulphate of potash and licor
The loss or obliteration of division into segments; as, a desegmentation of the body.
The disorganization or disarming of troops which have previously been mobilized or called into active service; the change from a war footing to a peace footing.
An order of ganoid fishes including among living species the bichir (Polypterus). See Brachioganoidei.
The phylogeny of groups or families of individuals. Haeckel.
A subdivision of the cretaceous formation of western North America, especially developed in Colorado and the upper Missouri region.
The unoin or articulation of bones to form a joint.
The development of cartilage.
The group of seven stars, commonly called the Dipper, in the constellation Ursa Major, or Great Bear. See Ursa major, under Ursa.
An order of sponges in which the skeleton consists of horny fibers. It includes all the commercial sponges.

The act or process of centralizing, or the state of being centralized; the act or process of combining or reducing several parts into a whole; as, the centralization of power in the general government; the centralization of commerce in a city.
A remedy that purges by alvine discharges.

A system or method of connecting and operating two induction motors so that the primary circuit of one is connected to the secondary circuit of the other, the primary circuit of the latter being connected to the source of supply; also, a system of electric tra
A mineral of a white or gray color, occurring massive or crystallized. It is a compound of the carbonates of barium and calcium.
A process of extracting gold or silver by treating the ore in a revolving barrel, or drum, with mercury, chlorine, cyanide solution, or other reagent.
The quality or fact of being attractable. Sir W.
A group of Gastropoda, with limpetlike shells, including the abalone shells and keyhole limpets.
The primitive form of fin, like that of Ceratodus.
A genus of small free-swimming Tunicata, shaped somewhat like a tadpole, and remarkable for resemblances to the larvæ of other Tunicata. It is the type of the order Copelata or Larvalia.
The condition of decreased irritability of a nerve in the region of the positive electrode or anode on the passage of a current of electricity through it. Foster.
A chronic contagious affection of the skin, prevalent in the tropics.
The hardening of a gland.
The process of generation by development of blastema, or fission of cells, in which the new formation is in all respect like the individual from which it proceeds.
Of or pertaining to the pachyderms.
A very soluble crystalline body which is the chief constituent of the urine in mammals and some other animals. It is also present in small quantity in blood, serous fluids, lymph, the liver, etc.
Of or pertaining to Tasmania, or Van Diemen's Land. -- n.
To do less than is requisite or proper; -- opposed to overdo. Grew.
To go over or beyond; to cross; as, to overpass a river; to overpass limits.
In the game of pinochle, to declare or announce for a score; as, to meld a sequence.
To be lazy or idle. [Colloq.] Middleton.

A hissing or sibilant sound such as that made by a flying bullet.

A shrub (Ilex Cassine) of the Holly family, native from Virginia to Florida. The smooth elliptical leaves are used as a substitute for tea, and were formerly used in preparing the black drink of the Indians of North Carolina.
A complex nitrogenous substance related to urea and uric acid, produced as a white powder; -- so called because it forms yellow salts, and because its solution forms a blue fluorescence like quinine.
Originally, a large hound used in hunting wolves; now, any one of certain breeds of large dogs, some of which are nearly identical with the great Danes.
A North American shrub (Viburnum nudum) whose tough osierlike shoots are sometimes used for binding sheaves.
A little red flower, no doubt the pimpernel, which, when it opens in the morning, is supposed to bode a fair day. See Pimpernel.
A perennial herb (Epilobium spicatum) with narrow willowlike leaves and showy rose-purple flowers. The name is sometimes made to include other species of the same genus.
To what place; -- used interrogatively; as, whither goest thou "Whider may I flee" Chaucer. Sir Valentine, whither away so fast Shak.
A saw for dividing timber lengthwise, usually set in a frame, and worked by two persons; also, a fret saw.
The chaffinch, whose cry is thought to foretell rain. [Prov.
(a) The open space in a floor, to accommodate a staircase. (b) The open space left beyond the ends of the steps of a staircase.

Any one of numerous species of finchlike birds belonging to Estrelda and allied genera, native of Asia, Africa, and Australia. The bill is large, conical, and usually red in color, resembling sealing wax.
A vessel for holding or conveying water, or for sprinkling water on cloth, plants, etc.
One of two walls built on either side of the junction of a bridge with the bank of a river, to protect the abutment of the bridge and the bank from the action of the current.

A joint in a stone pavement where the stones are left slightly higher than elsewhere, the rest of the surface being sunken or dished. The raised surface is intended to prevent the settling of water in the joints.
A color ground with water and gum or other glutinous medium; a color the vehicle of which is water; -- so called in distinction from oil color.
One who, or that which, is face to face with another; esp., one who faces another in dancing.
To wit; namely; -- often abbreviated to viz.
The place or places adjoining or near; neighborhood; vicinity; as, a jury must be of the vicinage. "To summon the Protestant gentleman of the vicinage." Macaulay.

The quality or state of being vacuous, or not filled; emptiness; vacancy; as, vacuity of mind; vacuity of countenance. Hunger is such a state of vacuity as to require a fresh supply of aliment.
The black vulture (Catharista atrata). It ranges from the Southern United States to South America.

An apparatus for the determination of the amount of urea in urine, in which the nitrogen evolved by the action of certain reagents, on a given volume of urine, is collected and measured, and the urea calculated accordingly.

A cock for withdrawing a small quantity of liquid, as for testing.

Any one of numerous species of bright-colored American birds belonging to Icterus and allied genera, especially Icterus icterus, a native of the West Indies and South America. Many of the species are called orioles in America.
One of two strong bars of timber, fixed horizontally on the opposite sides of the masthead, to support the crosstrees and the frame of the top; -- generally used in the plural. Totten.
The fourteenth century, when applied to Italian art, literature, etc. It marks the period of Dante, Petrarch, and boccaccio in literature, and of Giotto in painting.
Labor with pain; severe toil or exertion. As everything of price, so this doth require travail.

Impeded motion of the tongue because of the shortness of the frænum, or of the adhesion of its margins to the gums. Dunglison.

One pledged to entire abstinence from all intoxicating drinks.
A machine for stirring and spreading hay, to expedite its drying.
One who teaches or instructs; one whose business or occupation is to instruct others; an instructor; a tutor.
Any of a group of meteors appearing November 20-23; -- so called because they appear to radiate from a point in Taurus.

The first day of the week, -- consecrated among Christians to rest from secular employments, and to religious worship; the Christian Sabbath; the Lord's Day. Advent Sunday, Low Sunday, Passion Sunday, etc.

A version to food; refusal to take nourishment. [Written also sitiophobia.]

That which saponifies; any reagent used to cause saponification.
One who sells anything; one whose occupation is to sell goods or merchandise.

Anciently, one who recited or composed a rhapsody; especially, one whose profession was to recite the verses of Hormer and other epic poets.

The quality or state of being reticent, or keeping silence; the state of holding one's tonque; refraining to speak of that which is suggested; uncommunicativeness. Such fine reserve and noble reticence.

Having many small branches, or ramuli.

A priest, or conjurer, among the North American Indians. Be it sagamore, sachem, or powwow.

One who pokes.

A pit deceitfully covered to entrap wild beasts or men; a trap of any kind. Sir T.
A whirling or turning on the toes in dancing.
A dynamometer for ascertaining the power required to draw carriages over roads.

A person skilled in physic, or the art of healing; one duty authorized to prescribe remedies for, and treat, diseases; a doctor of medicine.
Violent and irrational excitement; delirium. See Frenzy.
