A bird (Nyctidromus albicollis) ranging from Texas to South America. It is allied to the night hawk and goatsucker.

(Math.) A term applied to some characteristic magnitude whose value, invariable as long as one and the same function, curve, surface, etc., is considered, serves to distinguish that function, curve, surface, etc., from others of the same kind or family. Brande

A train or series of kites on one string and flying tandem, used for attaining great heights and for sending up instruments for meteorological observations or a man for military reconnoissance; also, a kite of such a train.

A name given to palms of several genera and species growing in the West Indies and the Southern United States. In the United States, the name is applied especially to the Chamærops, or Sabal, Palmetto, the cabbage tree of Florida and the Carolinas.
A camp permanently intrenched, attached to Turkish frontier fortresses.
A substance resembling gutta-percha, and used to adulterate it, obtained from the East Indian tree Isonandra acuminata.
Having an acute sound; (Gr. Gram.), having an acute accent on the last syllable.
A guard or small body of troops at a distance from the main body of an army, to watch for the approach of an enemy; hence, anything for defense placed at a distance from the thing to be defended.
An instrument for recording the height of the liquid in an endosmometer or for registering osmotic pressures.
An old instrument of the lute or cittern kind. [Spelt also orpheoreon.]
A wind instrument of music in use among the Spaniards.
An instrument for measuring the limits of distincts vision in different individuals, and thus determiming the proper focal length of a lens for correcting imperfect sight. Brande & C.
Fit or convenient time; a time or place favorable for executing a purpose; a suitable combination of conditions; suitable occasion; chance. A wise man will make more opportunities than he finds.
One of the special zooids, or cells, of Bryozoa, destined to receive and develop ova; an ovicell. See Bryozoa.
The opening of an abscess, or the removal of a tumor, with a cutting instrument. [Written also onkotomy.] Dunglison.

That quality in words or things which presents what is offensive to chasity or purity of mind; obscene or impure lanquage or acts; moral impurity; lewdness; obsceneness; as, the obscenity of a speech, or a picture. Mr.Cowley asserts plainly, that obscenity has
The act of objecting; as, to prevent agreement, or action, by objection. Johnson.

A new star, usually appearing suddenly, shining for a brief period, and then sinking into obscurity. Such appearances are supposed to result from cosmic collisions, as of a dark star with interstellar nebulosities.
A rare metallic element, of doubtful identification, said to occur in the copper-nickel of Norway.
A wooden bar, or iron pin. W.
A supposed metal alleged to have been discovered in zircon.
The act of naming or nominating; designation of a person as a candidate for office; the power of nominating; the state of being nominated. The nomination of persons to places being .
the radical NO, called also the nitroso group. The term is sometimes loosely used to designate certain nitro compounds; as, nitrosyl sulphuric acid.
Nothing; of no account; worthless; -- a term often used for canceling, in accounts or bookkeeping. A.
The special properties and functions of the nerves; that capacity for transmitting a stimulus which belongs to nerves. G.
A medicine adapted to relieve or cure disease of the kidneys.
A spot or mark on the skin of children when born; a birthmark; -- usually applied to vascular tumors, i. e., those consisting mainly of blood vessels, as dilated arteries, veins, or capillaries.

A disease producing a peculiar cretinoid appearance of the face, slow speech, and dullness of intellect, and due to failure of the functions of the thyroid gland. -- Myx`o*dem"a*tous (#), a., Myx`o*dem"ic (#), a.
A scramble, as when small objects are thrown down, to be taken by those who can seize them; a confused struggle. Shak.
A kind of monomania in which the passion for music becomes so strong as to derange the intellectual faculties. Dunglison.
A fine or penalty, esp. a pecuniary punishment or penalty.
A game of dominoes in which the object is to make the sum of the two ends of the line some multiple of five.

Applied to certain consonants having a "liquid" or softened sound; e.g., in French, l or ll and gn (like the lli in million and ni in minion); in Italian, gl and gn; in Spanish, ll and ñ; in Portuguese, lh and nh.
The walrus. See Walrus.
A kind of nearly black cherry with dark red flesh and juice, -- used chiefly for preserving.
Derangement of the mind in regard of a single subject only; also, such a concentration of interest upon one particular subject or train of ideas to show mental derangement.
One who is sent on a mission; especially, one sent to propagate religion. Swift.
Originally, a painting in colors such as those in mediæval manuscripts; in modern times, any very small painting, especially a portrait.
A leguminous herb (Astragalus glycyphyllos) of Europe and Asia, supposed to increase the secretion of milk in goats.
A substance of variable composition, but resembling a soft, dark-colored metal, used in the bearings of machines for obviating friction, and as a substitute for lubricants.
A hint, suggestion, token, or memorial, to awaken memory; that which reminds or recalls to memory; a souvenir. Seasonable mementos may be useful.

Any one of numerous species of voracious orthopterous insects of the genus Mantis, and allied genera. They are remarkable for their slender grotesque forms, and for holding their stout anterior legs in a manner suggesting hands folded in prayer.

An instrument for measuring the tension or elastic force of gases, steam, etc., constructed usually on the principle of allowing the gas to exert its elastic force in raising a column of mercury in an open tube, or in compressing a portion of air or other gas
Enmity of heart; malevolence; ill will; a spirit delighting in harm or misfortune to another; a disposition to injure another; a malignant design of evil. "Nor set down aught in malice." Shak.

A light silver-white metallic element, malleable and ductile, quite permanent in dry air but tarnishing in moist air. It burns, forming (the oxide) magnesia, with the production of a blinding light (the so-called magnesium light) which is used in signaling, in
Any species of Pedicularis, a genus of perennial herbs. It was said to make sheep that fed on it lousy.
Loo table, a round table adapted for a circle of persons playing loo.
Disposition to bear injuries patiently; forbearance; patience. Jer.
The closing of a factory or workshop by an employer, usually in order to bring the workmen to satisfactory terms by a suspension of wages.

A dyestuff extracted from certain lichens (Roccella tinctoria, Lecanora tartarea, etc.), as a blue amorphous mass which consists of a compound of the alkaline carbonates with certain coloring matters related to orcin and orcein.
of Lie. See lain.
An instrument, devised by Professor Helmholtz, for testing the color perception of the eye, or for comparing different lights, as to their constituent color or their relative whiteness.
Anything read or recited to a teacher by a pupil or learner; something, as a portion of a book, assigned to a pupil to be studied or learned at one time.
A hurt; an injury. Specifically: (a) (Civil Law) Loss sustained from failure to fulfill a bargain or contract.
One of a family (Lernæidæ) of parasitic Crustacea found attached to fishes and other marine animals. Some species penetrate the skin and flesh with the elongated head, and feed on the viscera.
Any one of various species of Lepas, a genus of pedunculated barnacles found attached to floating timber, bottoms of ships, Gulf weed, etc.; -- called also goose barnacle. See Barnacle.

One of the shooting stars which constitute the star shower that recurs near the fourteenth of November at intervals of about thirty- three years; so called because shooting stars appear on the heavens to move in lines directed from the constellation Leo.

The state or quality of being lenient; mildness of temper or disposition; gentleness of treatment; softness; tenderness; clemency; -- opposed to severity and rigor. His exceeding lenity disposes us to be somewhat too severe.
A spasmodic state of the glottis, giving rise to contraction or closure of the opening.

A mark to designate the boundary of land; any , mark or fixed object (as a marked tree, a stone, a ditch, or a heap of stones) by which the limits of a farm, a town, or other portion of territory may be known and preserved.

A small American ericaceous shrub (Kalmia angustifolia); -- called also calfkill, sheepkill, sheep laurel, etc. It is supposed to poison sheep and other animals that eat it at times when the snow is deep and they cannot find other food.
A form of capsule for inclosing a dose of medicine that is offensive, caustic, or the like.
A kind of gall produced by a gallfly on the cup of an acorn, -- used in tanning and dyeing.
A name given to earthnuts of several kinds.

A large stove or oven; a furnace of brick or stone, or a heated chamber, for the purpose of hardening, burning, or drying anything; as, a kiln for baking or hardening earthen vessels; a kiln for drying grain, meal, lumber, etc.; a kiln for calcining limestone.
Having part of the face projecting beyond the body or shank; -- said of type. "In Roman, f and j are the only kerned letters." MacKellar.
A small California food fish (Heterostichus rostratus), living among kelp. The name is also applied to species of the genus Platyglossus.
A jest book; a stale jest; a worn-out joke. [Colloq.] It is an old Joe Miller in whist circles, that there are only two reasons that can justify you in not returning trumps to your partner's lead; i.
Having jesses on, as a hawk.

An oily, volatile hydrocarbon, obtained by the distillation of caoutchouc or guttaipercha.C5H8 -- unsaturated, and used to make synthetic rubber by polymerization. In organic chemistry, viewed conceptually as the building block of the terpene series of hydroca
Pertaining to, having the nature of, or illustrating, an isocryme; as, an isocrymal line; an isocrymal chart.
A complex nitrogenous radical, C8H4NO2, regarded as the essential residue of a series of compounds, related to isatin, which easily pass by reduction to indigo blue. -- I*sat`o*gen"ic, a.
An oily liquid, Cl3.CHO, analogous to chloral and bromal.
Having a border or outline composed of semicircles with the convexity outward; -- the opposite of engrailed.
A kind of injector for forcing water by steam. See Injector, n., 2.
One who is insolvent; as insolvent debtor; -- in England, before 1861, especially applied to persons not traders. Bouvier.
The act or process to exposing to the rays of the sun fro the purpose of drying or maturing, as fruits, drugs, etc., or of rendering acid, as vinegar.
An ingrain fabric, as a carpet.

In Roman dwellings, a cistern or tank, set in the atrium or peristyle to recieve the water from the roof, by means of the compluvium; generally made ornamental with flowers and works of art around its birm.
A supposed element claimed to have been discovered by R.Harmann.
An unreal image presented to the bodily or mental vision; a deceptive appearance; a false show; mockery; hallucination. To cheat the eye with blear illusions.

A morbid condition due to intestinal obstruction. It is characterized by complete constipation, with griping pains in the abdomen, which is greatly distended, and in the later stages by vomiting of fecal matter.
The subterraneous portion of a building, as in amphitheaters, for the service of the games; also, subterranean galleries, as the catacombs.

One who plays a part; especially, one who, for the purpose of winning approbation of favor, puts on a fair outside seeming; one who feigns to be other and better than he is; a false pretender to virtue or piety; one who simulates virtue or piety. The hypocrite
Abnormal breathing, due to slightly deficient arterialization of the blood; -- in distinction from eupnoea. See Eupnoea, and Dispnoea.
A word used as a shout of joy, exultation, approbation, or encouragement.
A female servant employed to do housework, esp. to take care of the rooms.
A house kept warm to shelter tender plants and shrubs from the cold air; a place in which the plants of warmer climates may be reared, and fruits ripened.
That form of homology due to common ancestry (phylogenetic homology), in opposition to homomorphy, to which genealogic basis is wanting. Haeckel.
To this place; -- used with verbs signifying motion, and implying motion toward the speaker; correlate of hence and thither; as, to come or bring hither.

Obtained from the urine of horses; as, hippuric acid. Hippuric acid, a white crystalline substance, containing nitrogen, present in the urine of herbivorous animals, and in small quantity in human urine.
An East Indian stony coral now known to belong to the Alcyonaria; -- called also blue coral.
A slender bony or cartilaginous process developed from the heel bone of bats. It helps to support the wing membranes.

Light vapor or smoke in the air which more or less impedes vision, with little or no dampness; a lack of transparency in the air; hence, figuratively, obscurity; dimness. O'er the sky The silvery haze of summer drawn.
A fork for pitching and tedding hay. Horse hayfork, a contrivance for unloading hay from the cart and depositing it in the loft, or on a mow, by horse power.
Any wheel worked by hand; esp., one the rim of which serves as the handle by which a valve, car brake, or other part is adjusted.
One half of a shutter made in two parts for closing a porthole.
A short pike, sometimes carried by officers of infantry, sometimes used in boarding ships; a spontoon. Tatler.
A labiate plant (the Lycopus Europæus). Gypsies are said to stain their skin with its juice.
The art or the science of drawing; esp. of drawing according to mathematical rules, as in perspective, projection, and the like.
A female governor; a woman invested with authority to control and direct; especially, one intrusted with the care and instruction of children, -- usually in their homes.
A vegetable microörganism of the genus Micrococcus, occurring in the secretion in gonorrhea. It is believed by some to constitute the cause of this disease.
A mouthful; a lump; a small piece. Spenser.
A transparent mucous discharge from the membrane of the urethra, commonly an effect of gonorrhea. Hoblyn.
A gantline. Hammock girtline, a line rigged for hanging out hammocks to dry.
An organ stop with conical tin pipes.
Consisting of two iambic dimeters catalectic, the last of which lacks the final syllable; -- said of a kind of verse.
An offensive smell; a stench. [Low]

In a full manner or degree; completely; entirely; without lack or defect; adequately; satisfactorily; as, to be fully persuaded of the truth of a proposition. Fully committed (Law), committed to prison for trial, in distinction from being detained for examinat
A made-up story; stuff; nonsense; humbug; -- often an exclamation of contempt.
One of numerous species of marine gastropod shells, belonging to Ranella and allied genera.

A clutch fitted in the rear hub of a cycle, which engages the rear sprocket with the rear wheel when the pedals are rotated forwards, but permits the rear wheel to run on free from the rear sprocket when the pedals are stopped or rotated backwards. Freewheelcy
One of a special breed of hounds used for chasing foxes.
A large, strong rope, reaching from the foremast head to the bowsprit, to support the mast. See Illust.
The mast nearest the bow. Foremast hand or man (Naut.), a common sailor; also, a man stationed to attend to the gear of the foremast.
A rope applied to the fore yardarm, to change the position of the foresail.
A general name for organ stops in which the sound is caused by wind passing through a flue or fissure and striking an edge above; -- in distinction from reedwork.

In Turkey and some other Oriental countries, a decree or mandate issued by the sovereign; a royal order or grant; -- generally given for special objects, as to a traveler to insure him protection and assistance. [Written also firmaun.]
One charged with the administration of finance; an officer who administers the public revenue; a treasurer. Burke.
The feudal system; a system by which the holding of estates in land is made dependent upon an obligation to render military service to the kind or feudal superior; feudal principles and usages.
A garland or wreath hanging in a depending curve, used in decoration for festivals, etc.; anything arranged in this way.
A plant (trigonella Foenum Græcum) cultivated for its strong- smelling seeds, which are "now only used for giving false importance to horse medicine and damaged hay." J. Smith (Pop.

A system of spirit influences for good and evil believed by the Chinese to attend the natural features of landscape; also, a kind of geomancy dealing with these influences, used in determining sites for graves, houses, etc.
Any small windowlike opening or recess, esp. one to show the relics within an altar, or the like.
Puppets caused to perform evolutions or dramatic scenes by means of machinery; also, the representations in which they are used.
A privilege of setting up, and moving about, folds for sheep, in any fields within manors, in order to manure them; -- often reserved to himself by the lord of the manor. Spelman.
Anything which causes expansion esp. (Mech.) a tool for stretching open or expanding a tube, etc.
The act of practice of exhorting; the act of inciting to laudable deeds; incitement to that which is good or commendable.
To show or illustrate by example. He did but .

Related to Euclid, or to the geometry of Euclid. Euclidian space (Geom.), the kind of space to which the axioms and definitions of Euclid, relative to straight lines and parallel lines, apply; -- called also flat space, and homaloidal space.

A game at cards, that may be played by two, three, or four persons, the highest card (except when an extra card called the Joker is used) being the knave of the same suit as the trump, and called right bower, the lowest card used being the seven, or frequently
A yellow or greenish yellow gas, first prepared by Davy, evolved from potassium chlorate and hydrochloric acid. It is supposed to consist of chlorine tetroxide with some free chlorine.

An unsymmetrical, divalent, hydrocarbon radical, C2H4 metameric with ethylene but written thus, CH3.CH to distinguish it from the symmetrical ethylene, CH2.CH2. Its compounds are derived from aldehyde.
A steep descent or declivity; steep face or edge of a ridge; ground about a fortified place, cut away nearly vertically to prevent hostile approach. See Scarp.
A powerful astringent alkaloid extracted from ergot as a brown, amorphous, bitter substance. It is used to produce contraction of the uterus.
A device for measuring, or an instrument for indicating, energy expended or work done; a dynamometer. -- Er`go*met"ric (#), a.
A stage in the development of discophorous medusæ, when they first begin to swim about after being detached from the strobila. See Strobila.
A kind of scissors used for opening the intestinal canal, as in post-mortem examinations.
Tonic spasm; -- applied generically to denote any disease characterized by tonic spasms, as tetanus, trismus, etc.

An agent employed to advance, in a covert manner, the interests of his employers; one sent out by any power that is at war with another, to create dissatisfaction among the people of the latter. Buzzing emissaries fill the ears Of listening crowds with jealous
The cutting a fetus into pieces within the womb, so as to effect its removal.
Intercalation; the insertion of days, months, or years, in an account of time, to produce regularity; as, the embolism of a lunar month in the Greek year.
Effusion; loss. "Much effuse of blood." Shak.
A contrivance used to supply small quantities of sweetened liquid, water, etc., to any mixture, or to test tubes, etc.; a dropping bottle.
One of the small galleries run out in front of the glacis. They serve to annoy the enemy's miners.

A frame (commonly) of wood serving to hold a canvas upright, or nearly upright, for the painter's convenience or for exhibition. Easel picture, Easel piece, a painting of moderate size such as is made while resting on an easel, as distinguished from a painting

That branch of mechanics which treats of the motion of bodies (kinematics) and the action of forces in producing or changing their motion (kinetics). Dynamics is held by some recent writers to include statics and not kinematics.
An instrument for measuring the degree of hardness; especially, an instrument for testing the relative hardness of steel rails and the like.

The state or quality of being durable; the power of uninterrupted or long continuance in any condition; the power of resisting agents or influences which tend to cause changes, decay, or dissolution; lastingness. A Gothic cathedral raises ideas of grandeur in
A sweet-toned stop of an organ.
A genus (Lemna) of small plants, seen floating in great quantity on the surface of stagnant pools fresh water, and supposed to furnish food for ducks; -- called also duckmeat.

Bearing, or producing, on the back; -- applied to ferns which produce seeds on the back of the leaf, and to certain Batrachia, the ova of which become attached to the skin of the back of the parent, where they develop; dorsiparous.
A large European scaraboid beetle (Geotrupes stercorarius), which makes a droning noise while flying. The name is also applied to allied American species, as the June bug.
One of several shores used to hold a ship firmly and prevent her moving while the blocks are knocked away before launching.
A proving to be false or erroneous; confutation; refutation; as, to offer evidence in disproof of a statement. I need not offer anything farther in support of one, or in disproof of the other.
Inclined; minded. When he was disposed to pass into Achaia.
Dismission; discharge. Officeholders were commanded faithfully to enforce it, upon pain of immediate dismissal.

Pertaining to the scale of eight tones, the eighth of which is the octave of the first. Diatonic scale (Mus.), a scale consisting of eight sounds with seven intervals, of which two are semitones and five are whole tones; a modern major or minor scale, as disti

A basic, dark-colored, holocrystalline, igneous rock, consisting essentially of a triclinic feldspar and pyroxene with magnetic iron; -- often limited to rocks pretertiary in age. It includes part of what was early called greenstone.
A fierce, wild dog (Canis Dukhunensis), found in the mountains of India. It is remarkable for its propensity to hunt the tiger and other wild animals in packs.
Having a passive form with an active meaning, as certain latin and Greek verbs.
A substance used to prevent polarization, as upon the negative plate of a voltaic battery.
The act of deifying; exaltation to divine honors; apotheosis; excessive praise.
That which deflects, as a diaphragm in a furnace, or a come in a lamp (to deflect and mingle air and gases and help combustion).
One of a large and fleet breed of hounds used in hunting deer; a staghound.
Corruption of fidelity; seduction from virtue, duty, or allegiance. The republic of Paris will endeavor to complete the debauchery of the army.

(a) A small beetle (Anobium tessellatum and other allied species). By forcibly striking its head against woodwork it makes a ticking sound, which is a call of the sexes to each other, but has been imagined by superstitious people to presage death.
A rule for construing written instruments so as to conform as nearly to the intention of the parties as is consistent with law. Mozley & W.
A highly volatile liquid, condensed by cold and pressure from the first products of the distillation of petroleum; -- used for producing low temperatures.

Having curls; curly; sinuous; wavy; as, curled maple (maple having fibers which take a sinnuous course). Curled hair (Com.), the hair of the manes and tails of horses, prepared for upholstery purposes.
A box or perch near the top of a mast, esp. in whalers, to shelter the man on the lookout.
A colorless, volatile, pungent liquid, C4H6, produced artificially, and regarded as an unsaturated hydrocarbon of the acetylene series, and analogous to crotonic acid.
A mineral occuring in silky fibers of a lavender blue color. It is related to hornblende and is essentially a silicate of iron and soda; -- called also blue asbestus.
Reliance of the mind on evidence of facts derived from other sources than personal knowledge; belief; credit; confidence. To give credence to the Scripture miracles.
Having a cramp or square piece at the end; -- said of a cross so furnished.
Want of courage to face danger; extreme timidity; pusillanimity; base fear of danger or hurt; lack of spirit. The cowardice of doing wrong.
The act of paying court, with the intent to solicit a favor. Swift.
An adjustable gage, with double points for transferring measurements from one timber to another, as the breadth of a mortise to the place where the tenon is to be made. Knight.

The process by which miners seek to discover metallic lodes. It consist in sinking small pits through the superficial deposits to the solid rock, and then driving from one pit to another across the direction of the vein, in such manner as to cross all the vein
A substance added to a medicine to mollify or modify its action. Dunglison.
A plastic operation on the pupil, as for forming an artificial pupil. -- Cor`e*plas"tic (-plas"tik), a.
The Arabian gazelle (Gazella Arabica), found from persia to North Africa.
The highest or covering course of masonry in a wall, often with sloping edges to carry off water; -- sometimes called capping. Gwill.

The person to whom goods or other things are consigned; a factor; -- correlative to consignor. Consigner and consignee are used by merchants to express generally the shipper of merchandise, and the person to whom it is addressed, by bill of lading or otherwise
Anything which serves to compress; as: (a) (Anat.) A muscle that compresses certain parts. (b) (Surg.) An instrument for compressing an artery (esp., the femoral artery) or other part.

The act of seeking, or endevearing to gain, what another is endeavoring to gain at the same time; common strife for the same objects; strife for superiority; emulous contest; rivalry, as for approbation, for a prize, or as where two or more persons are engaged
One who writes a commentary or comments; an expositor; an annotator. The commentator's professed object is to explain, to enforce, to illustrate doctrines claimed as true.
A form of seacoast cannon; a long, chambered gun designed for throwing shot or shells with heavy charges of powder, at high angles of elevation.
Polishing rouge; a reddish brown oxide of iron, used in polishing glass, and also as a pigment; -- called also crocus Martis.

Mineral coal charred, or depriver of its bitumen, sulphur, or other volatile matter by roasting in a kiln or oven, or by distillation, as in gas works. It is lagerly used where [Written also coak.] Gas coke, the coke formed in gas retorts, as distinguished fro

Raised pieces of wood of iron around a hatchway, skylight, or other opening in the deck, to prevent water from running bellow; esp. the fore-and-aft pieces of a hatchway frame as distinguished from the transverse head ledges.
A man whose business is to drive a coach or carriage.
One of a breed of dogs trained to accompany carriages; the Dalmatian dog.

A piece of metal bent in the form of an oxbow, with the two ends perforated to receive a pin, used on the end of the tongue of a plow, wagen, etc., to attach it to a draft chain, whiffletree, etc.; -- called also clavel, clevy.
Disposition to forgive and spare, as offenders; mildness of temper; gentleness; tenderness; mercy. Great clemency and tender zeal toward their subjects.
A plant (Salvia sclarea) of the Sage family, used in flavoring soups. Clary water, a composition of clary flowers with brandy, etc., formerly used as a cardiac.
An artificial reservoir or tank for holding water, beer, or other liquids.
A fillet or band placed around the shaft of a column as if to strengthen it. [Written also cimia.]

One of the higher aromatic hydrocarbons of coal tar, allied to napthalene and anthracene. It is a white crystalline substance, C18H12, of strong blue fluorescence, but generally colored yellow by impurities.
An historical register or account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
A branching, nut-bearing tree or shrub (Castanea pumila) of North America, from six to twenty feet high, allied to the chestnut. Also, its small, sweet, edible nat.
The cudweed (Gnaphalium), used to prevent or cure chafing.
A radical, C16H33, not yet isolated, but supposed to exist in a series of compounds homologous with the ethyl compounds, and derived from spermaceti.
A rate or tax. [Obs.
A radical, C27H55 supposed to exist in several compounds obtained from Chinese wax, beeswax, etc.
Native silver chloride, a mineral of a white to pale yellow or gray color, darkening on exposure to the light. It may be cut by a knife, like lead or horn (hence called horn silver).
A hollow way, adapted to cover troops, and facilitate their aproach to a place. Farrow.
In the Corinthian capital, one of the eight stalks rising out of the lower leafage and terminating in leaves which seem to suport the volutes. See Illust.
In the Philippines, a light, two-wheeled, boxlike vehicle usually drawn by a single native pony and used to convey passengers within city limits or for traveling. It is the common public carriage.
The dead and putrefying body or flesh of an animal; flesh so corrupted as to be unfit for food. They did eat the dead carrions.
A mark [^] used by writers and proof readers to indicate that something is interlined above, or inserted in the margin, which belongs in the place marked by the caret.
A race course: the ground run over. To go back again the same career.
An extravagant or absurd report or story; a fabricated sensational report or statement; esp. one set afloat in the newspapers to hoax the public.
An open field; a large, open plain without considerable hills. SeeChampaign.
A small mine, sometimes formed in the wall or side of an enemy's gallery, to blow in the earth and cut off the retreat of the miners. Farrow.
A by-passage, for a pipe, or other channel, to divert circulation from the usual course.
A detached low mountain, or high rising abruptly from the general level of the surrounding plain; -- applied to peculiar elevations in the Rocky Mountain region. The creek .
A thin, elastic strip of metal, whalebone, wood, or other material, worn in the front of a corset. Her long slit sleeves, stiff busk, puff verdingall, Is all that makes her thus angelical.
One of the ropes toggled to the footrope of a sail, used to haul up to the yard the body of the sail when taking it in. Totten.
The bittern. [Local, Eng.]
A person employed to ascertain the bulk or size of goods, in order to fix the amount of freight or dues payable on them.
A peculiar brad-shaped spike, to be driven alongside the end of an abutting timber to prevent its slipping.

Water saturated or strongly inpregnated with salt; pickle; hence, any strong saline solution; also, the saline residue or strong mother liquor resulting from the evaporation of natural or artificial waters.
of Break. [Arhaic] Tennyson.

A rope fastened near the middle of the leech or perpendicular edge of the square sails, by subordinate ropes, called bridles, and used to keep the weather edge of the sail tight forward, when the ship is closehauled. Bowline bridles, the ropes by which the bow
A rope stitched to the edges of a sail to strengthen the sail.
A place and apparatus for boiling, as for evaporating brine in salt making.
A rope or chain to confine the bowsprit of a ship downward to the stem or cutwater; -- usually in the pl.
A small song bird (Sialia sialis), very common in the United States, and, in the north, one of the earliest to arrive in spring. The male is blue, with the breast reddish.
In certain hydroids, an imperfect zooid, whose special function is to produce medusoid buds. See Hydroidea, and Athecata.
Anything added to raise the sides of a ship. Bailey.
A molding whose section is thought to resemble a beak.
A small paper; a note; a short letter. "I got your melancholy billet." Sterne.
A trinket; a jewel; -- a word applied to anything small and of elegant workmanship.
An invitation of friends to drink ale at some poor man's house, and there to contribute in charity for his relief. [Prov.
One given to drinking alcoholic beverages too freely; a tippler; -- chiefly used in composition; as, winebibber.
A compound radical, C6H5.CH2, related to toluene and benzoic acid; -- commonly used adjectively.
A form of jack screw for lifting large bodies, and assisting in launching.

Lydian stone, or black jasper, a variety of siliceous or flinty slate, of a grayish or bluish black color. It is employed to test the purity of gold, the amount of alloy being indicated by the color left on the stone when rubbed by the metal.
An artificial bar or obstruction placed in a river or water course to increase the depth of water; as, the barrages of the Nile.
The last reef in a fore-and-aft sail, taken to steady the ship.
A commercial traveler; one employed to solicit orders for manufacturers and tradesmen. Thackeray.
A fresh-water sponge (Spongilla), common in the north of Europe, the powder of which is used to take away the livid marks of bruises.
A check; a relapse; a discouragement; a setback.
A rebate or chase in masonry left to receive a permanent slab or other filling.
An affirmative vote; one who votes in the affirmative; as, "To call for the ayes and noes;" "The ayes have it."

Turned or twisted toward one side; not in a straight or true direction, or position; out of the right course; distorted; obliquely; asquint; with oblique vision; as, to glance awry. "Your crown's awry." Shak.
A house, inclosure, large cage, or other place, for keeping birds confined; a bird house. Lincolnshire may be termed the aviary of England.

A parasitic nematoid worm, espec. the roundworm, Ascaris lumbricoides, often occurring in the human intestine and allied species found in domestic animals; also commonly applied to the pinworm (Oxyuris), often troublesome to children and aged persons.
An herbaceous grasslike plant (Triglochin palustre, and other species) with pods opening so as to suggest barbed arrowheads.
One who apples for something; one who makes request; a petitioner. The applicant for a cup of water.
The small hollow curvature given to the top or bottom of the shaft of a column where it expands to meet the edge of the fillet; -- called also the scape. Parker.

Want of feeling; privation of passion, emotion, or excitement; dispassion; -- applied either to the body or the mind. As applied to the mind, it is a calmness, indolence, or state of indifference, incapable of being ruffled or roused to active interest or exer
Any substance (but especially sodium hyposulphite) used in removing the excess of chlorine left in paper pulp or stuffs after bleaching.
A neuropterous insect, the larva of which makes in the sand a pitfall to capture ants, etc. The common American species is Myrmeleon obsoletus, the European is M.
Having the extremities terminate in the heads of eagles, lions, etc.; as, an anserated cross.

Deviation from the common rule; an irregularity; anything anomalous. We are enabled to unite into a consistent whole the various anomalies and contending principles that are found in the minds and affairs of men.
The process used to render glass, iron, etc., less brittle, performed by allowing them to cool very gradually from a high heat.
A disease due to inhaling the poisonous fumes present in the manufacture of aniline.
An earth abounding in pyrites, used by the ancients to kill insects, etc., on vines; -- applied by Brongniart to a carbonaceous alum schist.
Start modified by heat so as to become a transparent mass, like horn. It is soluble in cold water.
With might; with full force; vigorously; violently; exceedingly. They on the hill, which were not yet come to blows, perceiving the fewness of their enemies, came down amain.
The strawberry finch, a small Indian song bird (Estrelda amandava), commonly caged and kept for fighting. The female is olive brown; the male, in summer, mostly crimson; -- called also red waxbill.
Nursers, -- a term applied to those birds whose young are hatched in a very immature and helpless condition, so as to require the care of their parents for some time; -- opposed to præcoces.
An electric generator or dynamo for producing alternating currents.

A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it in its properties and circumstances. The real subject is thus kept out of view, and we are left to collect the intentions of the writer or speaker
The plant costmary, which was formerly much used for flavoring ale.
A morbid condition due to excessive increase of albuminous elements in the blood.
One prone to sound or excite alarms, especially, needless alarms. Macaulay.
With the sails furled, and the helm lashed alee; -- applied to ships in a storm. See Hull, n.
The seaman or seamen stationed on the poop or after part of the ship, to attend the after-sails. Totten.

A mode of arresting hemorrhage resulting from wounds or surgical operations, by passing under the divided vessel a needle, the ends of which are left exposed externally on the cutaneous surface. Simpson.
A simple or compound principle, whose presence is necessary to produce acidity, as oxygen, chlorine, bromine, iodine, etc.
Continued pain, as distinguished from sudden twinges, or spasmodic pain. "Such an ache in my bones." Shak.

An evergreen shrub (Hibiscus -- formerly Abelmoschus- moschatus), of the East and West Indies and Northern Africa, whose musky seeds are used in perfumery and to flavor coffee; -- sometimes called musk mallow.
Full; also, trim; neat. [Prov.
Threefold; triple. A lofty tower, and strong on every side With treble walls.

Pertaining to, or designating, one of three metameric acids, CH3.C6H4.CO2H, which are related to toluene and analogous to benzoic acids. They are white crystalline substances, and are called respectively orthotoluic acid, metatoluic acid, and paratoluic acid.
Weighed; determined; reduced to equal or standard weight; as, tared filter papers, used in weighing precipitates.
Tending to render costive, or to diminish excretions or discharges generally. -- n.
Serving to take away, diminish, or rob; esp. (Med.), serving to diminish sensibily the amount of blood in the body; as, spoliative bloodletting.
Of or pertaining to mustard oil; specifically, designating an acid of the oleic acid series said to occur in mistard oil.
Formal; precise; affectedly neat or nice; as, prim regularity; a prim person. Swift.

Capable of existing or occurring, or of being conceived or thought of; able to happen; capable of being done; not contrary to the nature of things; -- sometimes used to express extreme improbability; barely able to be, or to come to pass; as, possibly he is ho
Rising, as the sun. Moon, that now meet'st the orient sun.
Of or pertaining to sexual desire; -- mostly applied to brute animals; as, the oestrual period; oestrual influence.

Having, or imparting, the odor characteristic of the bouquet of wine; specifically used, formerly, to designate an acid whose ethereal salts were supposed to occasion the peculiar bouquet, or aroma, of old wine. Cf.
Subject to varying moods, especially to states of mind which are unamiable or depressed.

Passing or traveling about a country; going or preaching on a circuit; wandering; not settled; as, an itinerant preacher; an itinerant peddler. The king's own courts were then itinerant, being kept in the king's palace, and removing with his household in those
Not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds; irregular; excessive; immoderate; as, an inordinate love of the world. "Inordinate desires." Milton.
Exciting fear or apprehension; impressing dread; adapted to excite fear and deter from approach, encounter, or undertaking; alarming. They seemed to fear the formodable sight.
Tending to facilitate expectoration or to promote discharges of mucus, etc., from the lungs or throat. -- n.
Serving to dissolve or attenuate viscid matter, and so to remove obstructions; deobstruent. -- n.
Tending to darkness or blackness; moderately dark or black; dusky. A pathless desert, dusk with horrid shades.
Destitute of the power of speech; unable; to utter articulate sounds; as, the dumb brutes. To unloose the very tongues even of dumb creatures.
Devoted to religion or to religious feelings and duties; absorbed in religious exercises; given to devotion; pious; reverent; religious. A devout man, and one that feared God.
Expelling wind from the body; warning; antispasmodic. "Carmenative hot seeds." Dunglison.
Tending to prevent the formation of urinary calculi, or to destroy them when formed. -- n.

Contrary to reason or propriety; obviously and fiatly opposed to manifest truth; inconsistent with the plain dictates of common sense; logically contradictory; nonsensical; ridiculous; as, an absurd person, an absurd opinion; an absurd dream. This proffer is a
One who practices, or is skilled in, ventriloquism. Ventriloquist monkey (Zoöl.), the onappo; -- so called from the character of its cry.
The act of underestimating; too low an estimate.

The act of specifying or determining by a mark or limit; notation of limits. This specification or limitation of the question hinders the disputers from wandering away from the precise point of inquiry.
The act of scintillating.
Shaped like a saddle. Specifically: (a) (Bot.) Bent down at the sides so as to give the upper part a rounded form.
The act of retrograding, or going backward; retrogradation.
The act of resuscitating, or state of being resuscitated. The subject of resuscitation by his sorceries.
Reconciliation. Milton.
The act of reciprocating; interchange of acts; a mutual giving and returning; as, the reciprocation of kindness.
The action of reducing to dust or powder.
The act of prefiguring; prefiguration; also, that which is prefigured. Carlyle.
Lack of completion; failure to complete.

The act of mystifying, or the state of being mystied; also, something designed to, or that does, mystify. The reply of Pope seems very much as though he had been playing off a mystification on his Grace.
Using soft words; plausible; affectedly or timidly delicate of speech; unwilling to tell the truth in plain language. "Mealy-mouthed philanthropies." Tennyson.

The quality or state of being inflexible, or not capable of being bent or changed; unyielding stiffness; inflexibleness; rigidity; firmness of will or purpose; unbending pertinacity; steadfastness; resoluteness; unchangeableness; obstinacy. The inflexibility o
The state or quality of being immaterial or incorporeal; as, the immateriality of the soul.
A real or fancied bristling of the hair of the head or body, resulting from disease, terror, chilliness, etc.
The act of glorifyng or of giving glory to. Jer.

A tenure by which a religious corporation holds lands given to them and their successors forever, usually on condition of praying for the soul of the donor and his heirs; -- called also tenure by free alms. Burrill.
Liable to exception or objection; objectionable. -- Ex*cep"tion*a*ble*ness, n.
A kind of manstopping bullet; -- so named from Dumdum, in India, where bullets are manufactured for the Indian army.
Act of disfiguring, or state of being disfigured; deformity. Milton.
Deoxidation.
Action in opposition; hindrance resistance. [They] do not .
Affirming the contrary; implying a denial of what has been asserted; also, mutually contradicting; inconsistent. "Contradictory assertions." South.
In a conditional manner; subject to a condition or conditions; not absolutely or positively. Shak.
The act of prevailing over another by arts, address, or fraud; deception; fraud; imposture; delusion. A school in which he learns sly circumvention.
The act of searing some morbid part by the application of a cautery or caustic; also, the effect of such application.
The act of apportioning; a dividing into just proportions or shares; a division or shares; a division and assignment, to each proprietor, of his just portion of an undivided right or property. A.
An apparatus for measuring the velocity imparted by gunpowder.
Of or pertaining to sulphur; as, a sulphuric smell.
Uttered in speech; delivered by word of mouth; oral; as, a spoken narrative; the spoken word.

Being on the outside; external; farthest or farther from the interior, from a given station, or from any space or position regarded as a center or starting place; -- opposed to inner; as, the outer wall; the outer court or gate; the outer stump in cricket; the
Nine and ten; eighteen and one more; one less than twenty; as, nineteen months.
Of or pertaining to logic; used in logic; as, logical subtilties. Bacon.
Qualified for war; fit for battle. An host of fighting men.
Disk-shaped; discoid.
The development of tubercles; the condition of one who is affected with tubercles.

The zone lying between the Boreal and Sonoran zones of North America. It includes an eastern or humid subdivision and a western arid one of corresponding temperature comprising the northern Great Plains and the lower slopes of the mountains of the western Unit
A change of form or appearance; especially, the supernatural change in the personal appearance of our Savior on the mount.
The operation of sewing up a laceration of the neck of the uterus.
An instrument for determining altitudes by the boiling point of water.
An instrument for recording simultaneously the pressure and temperature of a gas; a combined thermograph and barograph.
The production of young tubers, as potatoes, from the old while still growing.
A salt of sulphotungstic acid.
A salt of sulphophosphorous acid.
A salt of sulphophosphoric acid.
A salt of sulphocarbonic acid; a thiocarbonate.
A salt of sulphantimonious acid.
A salt of sulphantimonic acid.
A division of Pulmonata in which the eyes are situated at the tips of the tentacles. It includes the common land snails and slugs.
A so-called variety of bacterium, consisting in reality of several bacteria linked together in the form of a chain.
The art of drawing up an army, or any given number of men, in any geometrical figure, or of estimating or expressing the number of men in such a figure.
Proceeding in a straight course or manner; not deviating; honest; frank. -- adv.
The development of the spermatozoids.
Repetition of one's self or of one's acts; the saying or doing what one has already said or done.
The possession of one's powers; calmness; self-command; presence of mind; composure.
The act or process of producing schiller in a mineral mass.
The middle latitudes of the southern hemisphere. So called from the boisterous and prevailing westerly winds, which are especially strong in the South Indian Ocean up to 50º S.
The act or habit of procrastinating, or putting off to a future time; delay; dilatoriness. Procrastination is the thief of time.
The study, by means of the plethysmograph, of the variations in size of a limb, and hence of its blood supply.
A double chloride of platinum and some other metal or radical; a salt of platinochloric acid.
Having a breast like a pigeon, -- the sternum being so prominent as to constitute a deformity; chicken-breasted.
The succession and variation of leaves during different seasons. R.
The dephasing of the two parts of a single alternating current in two dissimilar branches of a given circuit.
A group of invertebrates including the Tunicata and Enteropneusta. -- Pha*ryn`gop*neus"tal, a.
The equivalent of an additional circuit or wire, in reality not existing, obtained by certain arrangements of real circuits, as in some multiplex telegraph systems.
A division of Nudibranchiata, in which the mantle itself serves as a gill.
A pigment of a green color, the chief constituent of which is oxide of chromium.

A class of Vertebrata, lower than fishes, characterized by their purselike gill cavities, cartilaginous skeletons, absence of limbs, and a suckerlike mouth destitute of jaws. It includes the lampreys and hagfishes.
Cast steel containing a considerable percentage of manganese, which makes it very hard and tough. See Alloy steel, above.
The science which treats of the chemical properties, actions or relations of substances in quantity; -- distinguished from micro- chemistry.
A series of strata in the lower Silurian formations of Great Britain; -- so named from Llandeilo in Southern Wales. See Chart of Geology.
The quality or condition of being instrumental; that which is instrumental; anything used as a means; medium; agency. The instrumentality of faith in justification.
An extensive artificial division of gastropod mollusks, including those that breathe by gills, as contrasted with the Pulmonifera. -- Hy`dro*bran"chi*ate, a.
The union of the two sexes in the same individual, or the combination of some of their characteristics or organs in one individual.
A subdivision of the Devonian system of America; -- so named from Hamilton, Madison Co., New York. It includes the Marcellus, Hamilton, and Genesee epochs or groups.
The measurement of the velocity of the blood.
A group of acalephs, including the naked-eyed medusæ; the hydromedusæ. Most of them are known to be the free-swimming progeny (gonophores) of hydroids.
A division of chætopod annelids in which the branchiæ are along the back, on each side, or on the parapodia. [See Illusts.
A group of nudibranch mollusks without special gills.
A massive variety of fluor spar, found in Derbyshire, England, and wrought into vases and other ornamental work.
A large, slender, harmless snake of the southern United States (Masticophis flagelliformis).

A series of limestone strata found in Ohio and farther west, presenting bluffs along the rivers and valleys, formerly supposed to be of one formation, but now known to be partly Silurian and partly Devonian.
A group of fishes, characterized by cartilaginous fins and skeleton. It includes both ganoids (sturgeons, etc.) and selachians (sharks), but is now often restricted to the latter.
An order of ganoid fishes, including the sturgeons; -- so called on account of their cartilaginous skeleton.
The typical pentadactyloid limb of the higher vertebrates.
The closing subdivision of the Devonian age in America. The rocks of this period are well developed in the Catskill mountains, and extend south and west under the Carboniferous formation.
A prickly plant of the genus Carlina (C. vulgaris), found in Europe and Asia.
A genus of plants (Ruscus); esp. R.
A machine for cleansing wool of burs, seeds, and other substances.
An order of ganoid fishes of which the bichir of Africa is a living example. See Crossopterygii.
A custom, as in some ancient boroughs, by which lands and tenements descend to the youngest son, instead of the eldest; or, if the owner have no issue, to the youngest brother. Blackstone.
The finishing course of a wall showing above a cornice.
An infusorian of the family Vorticellidæ, common in fresh-water ponds.
A transformer in which part of the primary winding is used as a secondary winding, or vice versa; -- called also a compensator or balancing coil.
The determination of the brightness of stars, and also of the sun, moon, and planets. --As`tro*pho`to*met"ric*al (#), a.
The process of converting venous blood into arterial blood during its passage through the lungs, oxygen being absorbed and carbonic acid evolved; -- called also aëration and hematosis.
A bark beetle that feeds on ambrosia.
Furnished with fleshy cups for adhering to bodies, as cuttlefish, etc.
Having a yellowish or fair complexion; of or pertaining to the Xanthochroi.

Filled or saturated with water so as to be heavy, unmanageable, or loglike; -- said of a vessel, when, by receiving a great quantity of water into her hold, she has become so heavy as not to be manageable by the helm.
A privy; especially, a privy furnished with a contrivance for introducing a stream of water to cleanse it.

Any one of numerous species of aquatic beetles belonging to Dytiscus and allied genera of the family Dytiscidæ, and to various genera of the family Hydrophilidæ. These beetles swim with great agility, the fringed hind legs acting together like oars.
Any one of several large, thick, spiral marine shells belonging to Rapa and allied genera, somewhat turnip-shaped.
A work thrown up at the end of a bridge nearest the enemy, for covering the communications across a river; a bridgehead.
A stitch used in stem work to produce a fine line, much used in old church embroidery to work the hands and faces of figures.
a kind of block with an opening in one side to receive the bight of a rope.
Samples taken for assay from a molten metallic mass pouring a portion into water, to granulate it.
One who, or that which, serves to bring to, or keep in, mind; a memento; a memorial; a reminder. Premature consiolation is but the remembrancer of sorrow.
Of or pertaining to probation; serving for trial. To consider this life .
A table or other means for calculating the periodical functions of women. Dunglison.
A horn or flask for holding powder, as for priming. [Scot.] Sir W.

An alteration in a mineral or rock mass when involving a chemical change of the substance, as of chrysolite to serpentine; -- opposed to ordinary metamorphism, as implying simply a recrystallization. -- Met`a*so*mat"ic, a.
An instrument for measuring the intensity of magnetic forces; also, less frequently, an instrument for determining any of the terrestrial magnetic elements, as the dip and declination.
Having smooth, or nearly smooth, hair.
Absence or want of experience; lack of personal and experimental knowledge; as, the inexperience of youth. Failings which are incident to youth and inexperience.
A condition characterized by a tendency to profuse and uncontrollable hemorrhage from the slightest wounds.

One of the arms of the male of most kinds of cephalopods, which is specially modified in various ways to effect the fertilization of the eggs. In a special sense, the greatly modified arm of Argonauta and allied genera, which, after receiving the spermatophore
That stage of growth or development in an organism, in which the reproductive elements are generated and matured in preparation for propagating the species.
A composition, as in music, or in the drama, designed to produce effect by its wild irregularity; esp., a musical caricature.
A tern applied to the twelve houses, or parts, of the zodiac of the primum mobile, to distinguish them from the twelve signs; also, any one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

Common sensation or general sensibility, as distinguished from the special sensations which are located in, or ascribed to, separate organs, as the eye and ear. It is supposed to depend on the ganglionic system.
Designating or pertaining to, a process of preparing dry plates with an emulsion of bromides and silver nitrate in gelatin.
Not stratified; -- applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.

Not reputable; of bad repute; not in esteem; dishonorable; disgracing the reputation; tending to bring into disesteem; as, it is disreputable to associate familiarly with the mean, the lewd, and the profane. Why should you think that conduct disreputable in pr
Gathered into a ball or a mass; collected together; concentrated; as, conglomerate rays of light. Beams of light when they are multiplied and conglomerate.
The act of transforming, or the state of being transformed; change of form or condition. Specifically: --(a) (Biol.)
The act of tergiversating; a shifting; shift; subterfuge; evasion. Writing is to be preferred before verbal conferences, as being freer from passions and tergiversations.
An aromatic preparation of carbonate of ammonia and, often, some scent, to avoid or relieve faintness, headache, or the like.
Renewal of life; restoration of life; the act of recaling, or the state of being recalled, to life.
The state or quality of being respectable; the state or quality which deserves or commands respect.
A showing beforehand; foreshowing.
The act of predisposing, or the state of being predisposed; previous inclination, tendency, or propensity; predilection; -- applied to the mind; as, a predisposition to anger.
A wrong application. Sir T.
The act of interpelling or interrupting; interruption. "Continual interpellations." Bp.
The quality of being impressible; susceptibility.
The act of identifying, or proving to be the same; also, the state of being identified.
A vermifuge.
Sympathy; a like feeling.
False or deceitful dealing. See Double dealing, under Dealing.
The use of many words to express an idea that might be expressed by few; indirect or roundabout language; a periphrese. the plain Billingagate way of calling names .
The quality of being changeable; fickleness; inconstancy; mutability.

The act of administering; government of public affairs; the service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs; the conducting of any office or employment; direction; management. His financial administration was of a piece with his military administrat
The act or process of making or becoming white.
The doctrine of arts in general; such branches of learning as respect the arts.
The state or behavior of a parasite; the act of a parasite. "Court parasitism." Milton.
A light fabric of wool, worn on the head by women; a cloud.

The act or employment of grinding or passing through a mill; the process of fulling; the process of making a raised or intented edge upon coin, etc.; the process of dressing surfaces of various shapes with rotary cutters. See Mill.
The process of making, or of becoming malt.
The act or process of smoothing, as clothes, with hot flatirons.
A figure of St. George (the patron saint of England) on horseback, appended to the collar of the Order of the Garter.
The wood of the Rhus Cptinus or Venice sumach, a shrub of Southern Europe, which yields a fine orange color, which, however, is not durable without a mordant. Ure.
The material of which felt is made; also, felted cloth; also, the process by which it is made.
The state or condition of being easy; freedom from distress; rest.
The act or process of immersing.
The act or process of using a comb or a number of combs; as, the combing of one's hair; the combing of wool.
The act or art of one who carves.
The ancient Latin name of Scotland; -- still used in poetry.
Relating to the world; human; common; as, worldly maxims; worldly actions. "I thus neglecting worldly ends." Shak.
Of set purpose; self-determined; voluntary; as, willful murder. Foxe.
Of or pertaining to a natural order (Urticaceæ) of plants, of which the nettle is the type. The order includes also the hop, the elm, the mulberry, the fig, and many other plants.
Not avoidable; incapable of being shunned or prevented; inevitable; necessary; as, unavoidable troubles.
Of or pertaining to typhus; resembling typhus; of a low grade like typhus; as, typhoid symptoms. Typhoid fever, a disease formerly confounded with typhus, but essentially different from the latter.
Of or pertaining to the tropics; characteristic of, or incident to, the tropics; being within the tropics; as, tropical climate; tropical latitudes; tropical heat; tropical diseases.
Of or pertaining to heat; warm; hot; as, the thermal unit; thermal waters. The thermal condition of the earth.
Of, pertaining to, or designating, hydrogen sulphide, which is regarded as an acid, especially when in solution.
Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid amide derivative of succinic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance, and forming a series of salts.
Sly in design; artful; cunning; insinuating; subtile; -- applied to persons; as, a subtle foe. "A subtle traitor." Shak.
Of or pertaining to cork; specifically, designating an acid, C
Stiffened with starch.

Of or pertaining to the senses, or sensible objects; addressing the senses; suggesting pictures or images of sense. To this poetry would be made precedent, as being less subtle and fine, but more simple, sensuous, and passionate.
Showing impertinent boldness or pertness; transgressing the rules of decorum; treating superiors with contempt; impudent; insolent; as, a saucy fellow. Am I not protector, saucy priest Shak.

Of or pertaining to the country, as distinguished from a city or town; living in the country; suitable for, or resembling, the country; rustic; as, rural scenes; a rural prospect. Here is a rural fellow; .

Pertaining to, or designating, a colorless crystalline substance (called rhodizonic acid, and carboxylic acid) obtained from potassium carboxide and from certain quinones. It forms brilliant red, yellow, and purple salts.

Cloudy; hazy; misty.
Designating an acid derived from silicic acid by the removal of water; of or pertaining to such an acid.
Forming, or consisting of, a large mass; compacted; weighty; heavy; massy. "Massive armor." Dr.

Not permitted or allowed; prohibited; unlawful; as, illicit trade; illicit intercourse; illicit pleasure. One illicit .
Being in a state of health; enjoying health; hale; sound; free from disease; as, a healthy chid; a healthy plant. His mind was now in a firm and healthy state.
Relating to a genus or kind; pertaining to a whole class or order; as, a general law of animal or vegetable economy.

Pertaining to fulmination; detonating; specifically (Chem.), pertaining to, derived from, or denoting, an acid, so called; as, fulminic acid. Fulminic acid (Chem.), a complex acid, H2C2N2O2, isomeric with cyanic and cyanuric acids, and not known in the free st
Outside; extraneous; separated; alien; as, a foreign country; a foreign government. "Foreign worlds." Milton.
Contained in, or relating to, the four Gospels; as, the evangelical history.
Of or pertaining to, or derived from, a plant of the genus Croton, or from croton oil. Crotonic acid (Chem.), a white crystalline organic acid, C3H5.CO2H, of the ethylene, or acrylic acid series.
Proceeding without interruption or cesstaion; continuous; unceasing; lasting; abiding. He that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.
Pertaining to, or obtained from, cinnamon. Cinnamic acid (Chem.), a white, crystalline, odorless substance.
Of or pertaining to the ear, or to the sense of hearing; as, auricular nerves.
Relating to an appeal; appellate. "An appellant jurisdiction." Hallam.
United; joined; leagued; akin; related. See Ally.
A horse of a dark color, neither gray nor white, and having no spots. Smart.
The unit of value and account in Japan. Since Japan's adoption of the gold standard, in 1897, the value of the yen has been about 50 cents.
