A skin with the wool; a skin from which the wool has not been sheared or pulled. [Written also woolfel.]
The process of cleansing wool, cotton, or the like, with a willy, or willow. Willying machine.
A process for the recovery or regeneration of manganese dioxide in the manufacture of chlorine, by means of milk of lime and the oxygen of the air; -- so called after the inventor.
The duty of keeping watch and ward (see the Note under Watch, n., 1) with a horn to be blown upon any occasion of surprise. Burrill.

A ring-shaped mass of moving fluid which, by virtue of its motion of rotation around an axis disposed in circular form, attains a more or less distinct separation from the surrounding medium and has many of the properties of a solid.
To glide in a flying machine.
A Russian measure of length containing 3,500 English feet. [Written also werst.]
A conserve made of grapes.
A part or decoration of the breastplate of the high priest among the ancient Jews, by which Jehovah revealed his will on certain occasions. Its nature has been the subject of conflicting conjectures.

To write one's name at the foot or end of, as a letter or any legal instrument. The undersigned, the person whose name is signed, or the persons whose names are signed, at the end of a document; the subscriber or subscribers.
A pie made of umbles. See To eat humble pie, under Humble.
A word consisting of three syllables only; as, a-ven-ger.
A monument consisting of three stones; especially, such a monument forming a kind of doorway, as among the ancient Celts.
An old game of ball played with a trap. See 4th Trap, 4.
The seventh month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of September with a part of October.
A portable form of telethermometer, using a telephone in connection with a differential thermometer.
The segment of the brain next in front of the midbrain, including the thalami, pineal gland, and pituitary body; the diencephalon; the interbrain.
The tenth month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of December with a part of January. Esther ii.
A vessel with a spout, in which tea is made, and from which it is poured into teacups.
The act or occupation of driving a team, or of hauling or carrying, as logs, goods, or the like, with a team.
A defense for the front of the thigh, consisting of one or more iron plates hanging from the belt on the lower edge of the corselet.
A hen having a tuft of feathers on her head. [Scot.] Jamieson.
The parry which is connected with a riposte; also, a series of quick attacks and parries in which neither fencer gains a point.
A stout silk having satin stripes, -- used for furniture.
The flap or latchet of a shoe fastened with a string or a buckle.
To project upward, or make an angle with the horizon or with the line of a vessel's keel; -- said of the bowsprit, etc.
A bannerlike stream of snow blown into the air from a mountain peak, often having a pinkish color and extending horizontally for several miles across the sky.
A ridge of mountain and craggy rocks, with a serrated or irregular outline; as, the Sierra Nevada. The wild sierra overhead.

The office, or sphere of jurisdiction, of a sheriff; sheriffalty. It was ordained by 28 Edward I that the people shall have election of sheriff in every shire where the shrievalty is not of inheritance.
An alloy of copper, invented by the Japanese, having a very dark blue color approaching black.
A book consisting of sheets each of which is folded into six leaves.
The humbling of a person by act or words, especially by a retort or a reproof; the retort or the reproof which has such effect.
A pruning knife with a curved blade. Knight.
The ninth month of the year, containing thurty days.
A case or holder made of fire clay, in which fine pottery is inclosed while baking in the kin. [Written also saggar, sagger, and segger.] Ure.
The skin of a seal; the pelt of a seal prepared for use, esp. of the fur seal; also, a garment made of this material.
Dressing stone with a pick or pointed instrument.
A fighting with a shadow; a mock contest; an imaginary or futile combat. [Written also scimachy.] Cowley.
A lozenge having a rose flavor.
A name of several English gold coins struck in different reigns and having having different values; a rose noble.

A shaft that oscillates on its journals, instead of revolving, -- usually carrying levers by means of which it receives and communicates reciprocating motion, as in the valve gear of some steam engines; -- called also rocker, rocking shaft, and way shaft.
An engine of war used in the Middle Ages, consisting of a protected elevated staging on wheels, and armed in front with pikes. It was (after the 14th century) furnished with small cannon.
A colorless stone of high luster, made of paste. It is much used as an inexpensive ornament.
The inoculation of a cow with human vaccine virus.
The Diet, or House of Representatives, of the German empire, which is composed of members elected for a term of three years by the direct vote of the people. See Bundesrath.
A combining form signifying straight; as, rectilineal, having straight lines; rectinerved.
The act or process of using a rake; the going over a space with a rake.
A combining form meaning four, four times, fourfold; as, quadricapsular, having four capsules.
The Book of Psalms; -- often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
A comprehensive group of mankind, including those that have prognathous jaws.
A flask in which gunpowder is carried, having a charging tube at the end.
A fabric of many varieties, usually made of silk and worsted, - - used especially for women's dresses. Irish poplin, a fabric with silk warp and worsted weft, made in Ireland.
The state or practice of having several wives at the same time; marriage to several wives. H.
The flag hoisted at the fore by a vessel desiring a pilot, in the United States the union jack, in Great Britain the British union jack with a white border.

A fine material for ladies' shawls, scarfs, handkerchiefs, etc., made from the fiber of the pineapple leaf, and perhaps from other fibrous tropical leaves. It is delicate, soft, and transparent, with a slight tinge of pale yellow.
A plate or block with a printing surface (usually in relief) obtained from a photograph; also, any one of the many methods of processes by which such a printing surface is obtained.
A hydrous arsenate of iron occurring in green or yellowish green cubic crystals; cube ore.
A composition consisting of five verses.
An ornament or decoration for the person; esp., a decoration consisting of a set of ornaments to be used together; as, a parure of rubies or of embroideries.
A celebrated marble temple of Athene, on the Acropolis at Athens. It was of the pure Doric order, and has had an important influence on art.
A shoe for oxen, consisting of a flat piece of iron nailed to the hoof.
To outrun or outwalk; hence, of a vessel, to outsail. [Colloq.]
To exceed in building, or in durability of building.

A four-stroke cycle for internal-combustion engines consisting of the following operations: First stroke, suction into cylinder of explosive charge, as of gas and air; second stroke, compression, ignition, and explosion of this charge; third stroke (the workin
A fragrant variety of black tea having somewhat the flavor of green tea. [Written also oulong.]
A pot or jar having a wide mouth; a cinerary urn, especially one of baked clay.
A cake made of oatmeal.
The eleventh month of the year, containing thirty days.
A measure of surface in the metric system containing ten thousand ares, or one million square meters. It is equal to about 247.1 acres.
To eat or prey upon, as a moth eats a garment. [Rarely used except in the form moth-eaten, p.p.
A metrical composition consisting of a single strophe.
A false stroke with a billiard cue, the cue slipping from the ball struck without impelling it as desired.
The art of measuring with a micrometer.
A tribe of Lepidoptera, including a vast number of minute species, as the plume moth, clothes moth, etc.
A dish of food composed of many kings of fish.
A coat made of match-cloth.
A musical istrument of percussion, consisting of bars yielding musical tones when struck. Knight.
The act or business of stealing or kidnaping human beings, especially with a view to e

The heartwood of a tree (Hæmatoxylon Campechianum), a native of South America, It is a red, heavy wood, containing a crystalline substance called hæmatoxylin, and is used largely in dyeing. An extract from this wood is used in medicine as an astringent.
A city of France celebrated for certain manufactures. Lisle glove, a fine summer glove, made of Lisle thread.
A writing composed of words not having a certain letters; -- as in the Odyssey of Tryphiodorus there was no A in the first book, no B in the second, and so on.
The twin flower which grows in cold northern climates.
The formation of leucocytes.
To inclose, or nearly inclose, as a harbor or a vessel, with land.
The Scriptures of the Mohammedans, containing the professed revelations to Mohammed; -- called also Alcoran. [Written also Kuran or Quran.]
The seventh month of the year, containing thirty-one days.
A stone mason's tool, having a flat face and a pointed part. Knight.
A coat of defense made of small plates of metal sewed upon linen or the like; also, this kind of armor taken generally; as, a coat of jazerant.
A soldier armed with a javelin. Holland.
A salt of isosulphocyanic acid.
Anything made of iron; -- a general name of such parts or pieces of a building, vessel, carriage, etc., as consist of iron.
A suborder of marine gastropod mollusks, in which the gills are between the foot and the mantle.
The act or process of inclosing with a case, or the state of being incased.
An old game played with four dice. In signified a doublet, or two dice alike; in-and-in, either two doubles, or the four dice alike.
An Indian crested pheasant of the genus Lophophorus. Several species are known.
A cordial made of spiced wine, etc.
An abnormal formation foreign to the economy, and composed of elements different from those are found in it in its normal condition. Dunglison.
A tool used by turners in metal, having a bend forming a heel near the cutting end.
A member of any tribe or race of savages who have the custom of decapitating human beings and preserving their heads as trophies. The Dyaks of Borneo are the most noted head-hunters.
A field where grass for hay has been cut; a meadow. Cowper.
A somersault made with the assistance of the hands placed upon the ground.
A boot with a short top covering only the ankle. See Cocker, and Congress boot, under Congress.
The act or practice of hunting or shooting game with a gun. The art of gunning was but little practiced.
A heavy silk with a dull finish; as, gros de Naples; gros de Tours.
A governor who has lieutenant or deputy governors under him; as, the governor general of Canada, of India.
A male for whom one has stood sponsor in baptism. See Godfather.
A sauce made of small fish. It was prized by the ancients.
A haulage system for canal boats, in which an electric locomotive running on a monorail has its adhesion materially increased by the pull of the tow rope on a series of inclined gripping wheels.
A defensive garment formerly in use for the body, made of cloth stuffed and quilted.
A heterogenous group of fungi of which the complete life history is not known. Some undoubtedly represent the conidium stages of various Ascomycetes.
The liberty or franchise of having a chase; free chase. Burrill.
A silver coin of France, and since 1795 the unit of the French monetary system. It has been adopted by Belgium and Swizerland.
A lock for a gun or pistol, having a flint fixed in the hammer, which on stricking the steel ignites the priming.
A genus of elegant, glassy sponges, consisting of interwoven siliceous fibers, and growing in the form of a cornucopia; -- called also Venus's flower-basket.
A defense for the shoulder, composed of flexible overlapping plates of metal, used in the 15th century; -- the origin of the modern epaulette. Fairholt.
The theory that the functions of living organisms are dependent upon electricity or a kindred force.
A hardened steel plate having a hole, or a gradation of conical holes, through which wires are drawn to be reduced and elongated.
A single cut with a knife.
A village composed of Arab tents arranged in streets.
A hardy species of British grass (Cynosurus cristatus) which abounds in grass lands, and is well suited for making straw plait; -- called also goldseed.
A figure with two sides or surfaces. Buchanan.
A sirup made of poppies.
A book consisting of sheets, each of which is folded into sixteen leaves; hence, indicating, more or less definitely, a size of book; -- usually written 16mo or 16º.
A poem consisting of ten lines.
A grass with leaves having edges furnished with very minute hooked prickles, which form a cutting edge; one or more species of Leersia.
the life estate which a husband has in the lands of his deceased wife, which by the common law takes effect where he has had issue by her, born alive, and capable of inheriting the lands. Mozley & W.
A region of country having covers; a hunting country.
A piece of timber having a groove in which something glides.
An indication or symptom which forbids the method of treatment usual in such cases.
A group of artificial dyes with an affinity for vegetable fibers, so that no mordant is required. Most of them are azo compounds derived from benzidine or tolidine.

A French theory of government which holds that commune should be a kind of independent state, and the national government a confederation of such states, having only limited powers. It is advocated by advanced French republicans; but it should not be confounde
A salad made of sliced cabbage.
A material for cordage, matting, etc., consisting of the prepared fiber of the outer husk of the cocoanut. Homans.
A house of entertainment, where guests are supplied with coffee and other refreshments, and where men meet for conversation. The coffeehouse must not be dismissed with a cursory mention.
The fruit or berry of the Anamirta Cocculus, a climbing plant of the East Indies. It is a poisonous narcotic and stimulant.
A wall made of clay mixed with straw.
An andiron with a knob at the top. Bacon.
The ninth month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of November with a part of December.
A light, covered, four-wheeled pleasure carriage with two seats.
A pair of Straps, with stirrups, joined at the top and fastened to the pommel or the frame of the saddle, after they have been adjusted to the convenience of the rider. [Written also chaplet.]
A subdivision of the Quaternary age immediately following the Glacial period; -- so named from beds near Lake Champlain.
A portable bag for travelers; -- so called because originally made of carpet.
A stiff compact pasteboard of various qualities, for making cards, etc., often having a polished surface.
A division of annelids in which the gills arise from or near the head. See Tubicola.
The taking of the position of a candidate; specifically, the preaching of a clergyman with a view to settlement. [Cant, U.
An instrument with a graduated disk by means of which the angles of gems are measured in the process of cutting and polishing.
A city of Belgium, giving its name to a kind of carpet, a kind of lace, etc. Brussels carpet, a kind of carpet made of worsted yarn fixed in a foundation web of strong linen thread.

An affection of the kidneys, usually inflammatory in character, and distinguished by the occurrence of albumin and renal casts in the urine. Several varieties of Bright's disease are now recognized, differing in the part of the kidney involved, and in the inte
A member of a family which has occupied several European thrones, and whose descendants still claim the throne of France.
A cylindrical glass vessel, with a large and short neck.
The process of mixing clay in potteries with a blunger. Tomlinson.
A heart-shaped cherry with a very dark-colored skin.
A cock or faucet having a bent down nozzle. Knight.
A bolt with a barbed shank.
A method of reducing corpulence by avoiding food containing much farinaceous, saccharine, or oily matter; -- so called from William Banting of London.
A division of the Cetacea, including the right whale and all other whales having the mouth fringed with baleen. See Baleen.
A coarse woolen stuff with a long nap; -- usually dyed in plain colors. A new black baize waistcoat lined with silk.
A genus of plants found in central Europe and about the Mediterranean, having flowers on a spadix inclosed in a spathe. The cuckoopint of the English is an example.
A letter, or a combination of letters, employed in spelling a word, but in the pronunciation having no sound. -- Aph*thon"gal, a.
A shot made with the object balls in an anchor space.
A fabled serpent with a head at each end, moving either way. Milton.
A vessel, cell, duct, or tube containing or conducting air; as the air vessels of insects, birds, plants, etc.; the air vessel of a pump, engine, etc. For the latter, see Air chamber.
The grass that grows after the first crop has been mown; aftermath.

The strong tendon formed of the united tendons of the large muscles in the calf of the leg, an inserted into the bone of the heel; -- so called from the mythological account of Achilles being held by the heel when dipped in the River Styx.
The chief deity of the Greeks, and ruler of the upper world (cf. Hades).

That point in the visible celestial hemisphere which is vertical to the spectator; the point of the heavens directly overhead; -- opposed to nadir. From morn To noon he fell, from noon to dewy eve, A summer's day; and with the setting sun Dropped from the zeni
Pertaining to, or derived from, ytterbium; containing ytterbium.
Having yellow eyes. Yellow-eyed grass (Bot.), any plant of the genus Xyris.

The king of the infernal regions, corresponding to the Greek Pluto, and also the judge of departed souls. In later times he is more exclusively considered the dire judge of all, and the tormentor of the wicked.
A house for the reception of strangers. (b) In the Middle Ages, a room in a monastery for the reception and entertainment of strangers and pilgrims, and for the relief of paupers.
Consisting of wool; as, a woolly covering; a woolly fleece.
Made of wire; like wire; drawn out like wire.
Consisting of wind; accompanied or characterized by wind; exposed to wind. "The windy hill." M.
A Slavic tribe which once occupied the northern and eastern parts of Germany, of which a small remnant exists.
Fully known; generally known or acknowledged. A church well known with a well-known rite.
Having good breeding; refined in manners; polite; cultivated. I am as well-bred as the earl's granddaughter.
One of the holes in floor or other plates to permit water to flow through.
Appearing as if overlaid with a thin layer of different color; -- said of the colors of certain birds and insects.
Having little knobs on the surface; verrucose; as, a warted capsule.
The god of fire, who presided over the working of metals; -- answering to the Greek Hephæstus.
Of or pertaining to Vitruvius, an ancient Roman architect. Vitruvian scroll (Arch.), a name given to a peculiar pattern of scrollwork, consisting of convolved undulations.
Having long and slender trailing stems.
Having the form of a straight rod; wand-shaped; straight and slender.
Made of velvet, or like velvet; soft; smooth; delicate.

A fine kind of parchment, usually made from calfskin, and rendered clear and white, -- used as for writing upon, and for binding books. Vellum cloth, a fine kind of cotton fabric, made very transparent, and used as a tracing cloth.
Having a veil; veiled.
Having different shapes or forms.
Having the form or nature of vapor. Holland.

Pertaining to, or containing, vanadium; specifically, designating those compounds in which vanadium has a lower valence as contrasted with the vanadic compounds; as, vanadious acid. [Sometimes written also vanadous.]

Valerianic; specifically, designating any one of three metameric acids, of which the typical one (called also inactive valeric acid), C4H9CO2H, is obtained from valerian root and other sources, as a corrosive, mobile, oily liquid, having a strong acid taste, a
Serving to in invest, or sheathe; sheathing. Vaginant leaf (Bot.), a leaf investing the stem or branch by its base, which has the form of a tube.

One who usurps; especially, one who seizes illegally on sovereign power; as, the usurper of a throne, of power, or of the rights of a patron. A crown will not want pretenders to claim it, not usurpers, if their power serves them, to possess it.
Pertaining to, or containing, uranium; designating those compounds in which uranium has a lower valence as contrasted with the uranic compounds.
Of or pertaining to uranium; containing uranium.
Having no meaning or signification; as, unmeaning words.
Having a valence of one; capable of combining with, or of being substituted for, one atom of hydrogen; monovalent; -- said of certain atoms and radicals.
Having but one branch.
Containing but one ovule.
Having one lip only; as, a unilabiate corolla.
Having only one leaf.
Having but a single horn; -- said of certain insects. "Unicornous beetles." Sir T.
Having the surface of a uniform color.
Having a single center of growth. Unicentral development, that form of development which takes place primarily around a single central point, as in the lowest of unicellular organisms.
Nor employed in manual or other labor; having no regular work.
Having masts smaller than the usual dimension; -- said of vessels. Totten.
Having the shape of a hook; being of a curved or hooked from; hooklike. Unciform bone (Anat.), a bone of the carpus at the bases of the fourth and fifth metacarpals; the hamatum.
Not certain; not having certain knowledge; not assured in mind; distrustful. Chaucer.
Of or pertaining to an umbel; having the form of an umbel.

Capable of being turned down; specif. (Elec.), designating, or pertaining to, an incandescent lamp with a small additional filament which can be made incandescent when only a small amount of light is required.
Of or connected with nutrition; nitritional; nourishing; as, the so-called trophic nerves, which have a direct influence on nutrition.
Having a valence of three; capable of being combined with, substituted for, or compared with, three atoms of hydrogen; -- said of triad atoms or radicals; thus, nitrogen is trivalent in ammonia.
Containing three seeds; three-seeded; as, a trispermous capsule.
Having bipinnate leaflets arranged on each side of a rhachis.
Having three leaves; three-leaved.
Having the form or appearance of three petals; appearing as if furnished with three petals.
In three pairs; as, a trijugate leaf, or a pinnate leaf with three pairs of leaflets.
Having three sides or faces; thus, a trihedral angle is a solid angle bounded by three plane angles. [Written also triedral.]
Having three bellies; -- said of a muscle. Dunglison.
Three-ribbed; having three ribs from the base.
If, pertaining to, or consisting of, three colors or color sensations.

Capable of neutralizing three molecules of a monacid base, or their equivalent; having three hydrogen atoms capable of replacement by basic elements on radicals; -- said of certain acids; thus, citric acid is a tribasic acid.
Having the characteristics of a triad; as, boron is triadic.
Capable of neutralizing three molecules of a monobasic acid or the equivalent; having three hydrogen atoms which may be acid radicals; -- said of certain bases; thus, glycerin is a triacid base.
A snare; a stratagem; a trepan. See 3d Trepan.
Breathing by means of tracheæ; of or pertaining to the Tracheata.
Of or pertaining to a trabecula or trabeculæ; composed of trabeculæ.
Furnished with an entablature.
Having the appearance of a torula; in the form of a little chain; as, a torulaform string of micrococci.
Having the shape of a top; (Bot.) cone-shaped, with the apex downward; turbinate.
Having teeth; furnished with teeth. "Ruby-lipped and toothed with pearl." Herrick.
The separation of the parts of a compound word by the intervention of one or more words; as, in what place soever, for whatsoever place.

Having the anthers raised above the stigma, and visible at the throat of the corolla, as in long-stamened primroses; -- the reverse of pin-eyed.
Having three lobes. Three-lobed leaf (Bot.), a leaf divided into three parts, the sinuses extending not more than half way to the middle, and either the parts of the sinuses being rounded.
Worn to the naked thread; having the nap worn off; threadbare clothes. "A threadbare cope." Chaucer.
The god of thunder, and son of Odin.
Of or pertaining to sulphur; containing or resembling sulphur; specifically, designating certain of the thio compounds; as, the thionic acids. Cf.

Of or pertaining to thallium; derived from, or containing, thallium; specifically, designating those compounds in which the element has a lower valence as contrasted with the thallic compounds. [Written also thallious.]
Consisting of a thallus.

Of or pertaining to thallium; derived from, or containing, thallium; specifically, designating those compounds in which the element has a higher valence as contrasted with the thallous compounds; as, thallic oxide.
Having four branches diverging at right angles; -- said of certain spicules of sponges.
Having a valence of four; tetratomic; quadrivalent.
Having four columns in front; -- said of a temple, portico, or colonnade. -- n.
A Roman governor of the fourth part of a province; hence, any subordinate or dependent prince; also, a petty king or sovereign.
Of or pertaining to a tetrad; possessing or having the characteristics of a tetrad; as, a carbon is a tetradic element.
Composed of four carpels.

Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the acrylic series, obtained by the distillation of terpenylic acid, as an only substance having a peculiar cheesy odor.
Having tentacles.

Of, pertaining to, or designating, a condition assumed by the imago of certain Neuroptera, after exclusion from the pupa. In this state the insect is soft, and has not fully attained its mature coloring.
A mode or process of painting; distemper.
Having tissued composed of cells.
Having a good taste; -- applied to persons; as, a tasty woman. See Taste, n., 5.
Of, pertaining to, or designating, a certain acid composed of tartaric acid in combination with ethyl, and now called ethyltartaric acid.
Sharp to the taste; acid; sour; as, a tart apple.
A small wax candle; a small lighted wax candle; hence, a small light. Get me a taper in my study, Lucius.
Having united sepals; gamosepalous.
Having the two main flexor tendons of the toes blended together.
Having the character of a synonym; expressing the same thing; conveying the same, or approximately the same, idea. -- Syn*on"y*mous*ly, adv.

One placed to superintend others; an overseer; an inspector. Were 't not madness then, To make the fox surveyor of the fold Shak.

A white garment worn over another dress by the clergy of the Roman Catholic, Episcopal, and certain other churches, in some of their ministrations. Surplice fees (Eccl.), fees paid to the English clergy for occasional duties.
That which is to supply what is wanted. Invent suppletories to excuse an evil man.
Having a plainted and convolute arrangement in the bud, as in the morning-glory.
Having the leaves so placed that the upper part of each one is covered by the base of the next higher leaf, as in hepatic mosses of the genus Plagiochila.
Containing a third, or one part to three. Bp.
Having been subjected to the process of sublimation; hence, also, purified. "Sublimed mercurie." Chaucer.
The principal river of the lower world, which had to be crossed in passing to the regions of the dead.
Scrofulous; having struma.
Having stripes of different colors; streaked. Striped bass.
Having transverse bands of color.
Affected with a stricture; as, a strictured duct.
Having a mouth; -- applied to certain Protozoa. -- n.
Having the shape of a stalk; stalklike.
Having stipels.
A pin set on the face of a dial, to cast a shadow; a style. See Style.
Having no stem; (Bot.) acaulescent.
Of or pertaining to staurolite; resembling or containing staurolite.

A tune, air, strain, or a whole piece, played by a single person on an instrument, or sung by a single voice.
The system of arranging the scale by the names do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si, by which singing is taught; a singing exercise upon these syllables.
Having the fin rays cartilaginous or flexible; without spines; -- said of certain fishes.

Having a short, flat nose, slightly turned up; as, the snub- nosed eel. Snub-nosed cachalot (Zoöl.), the pygmy sperm whale.
A short sleep; a nap. [Colloq.]
Having a siphuncle; siphunculated.
Mud or fine earth deposited from running or standing water.
Having the form of a silique.

The act or practice of proselyting; the making of converts to a religion or a religious sect, or to any opinion, system, or party. They were possessed of a spirit of proselytism in the most fanatical degree.
A writer of prose; an unpoetical writer. "An estimable prosaist." I.
Any court or vestibule before a building or leading into any inclosure.
A declaration of something to come; a foretelling; a prediction; esp., an inspired foretelling. He hearkens after prophecies and dreams.
The book used by a prompter of a theater.
The office or dignity of a proctor; also, the term of his office. Clarendon.
Leaning forward; -- said of certain monosyllabic words which are so closely attached to the following word as not to have a separate accent.
The dating of an event before the time it happened; an antedating; -- opposed to Ant: metachronism.
The winner of a prize.
A corruption of pray thee; as, I prithee; generally used without I. Shak.
A lady superior of a priory of nuns, and next in dignity to an abbess.
The function or condition of one who presides; superintendence; control and care.

Bringing a conception or notion directly before the mind; presenting an object to the memory of imagination; -- distinguished from symbolic. How greatly the word "will" is felt to have lost presentive power in the last three centuries.
The office of the premier.
A reader of lectures or discourses; a lecturer. Sheldon.
The office or dignity of a prelate; church government by prelates. Prelacies may be termed the greater benefices.
The office, position, or jurisdiction of a prefect; also, his official residence.
To approve by preconization.
A liquid measure of four pints.

The race that proceeds from a progenitor; offspring to the furthest generation; the aggregate number of persons who are descended from an ancestor of a generation; descendants; -- contrasted with ancestry; as, the posterity of Abraham. If [the crown] should no
A system of philosophy originated by M. Auguste Comte, which deals only with positives.
The work of a porter; the occupation of a carrier or of a doorkeeper.
A food made by boiling some leguminous or farinaceous substance, or the meal of it, in water or in milk, making of broth or thin pudding; as, barley porridge, milk porridge, bean porridge, etc.
The flesh of swine, fresh or salted, used for food.
The place, office, or dignity of the pope; papal dignity. Shak.
A dwelling for a number of paupers maintained at public expense; an almshouse; a workhouse.
A game of ball of Eastern origin, resembling hockey, with the players on horseback.
A dance of Polish origin, but now common everywhere. It is performed by two persons in common time.
A member of a body of police; a constable.
The principles and rules of the art of poetry. J.
The art of composing poems; poetical skill or faculty; as, the heavenly gift of poesy. Shak.
A building used for dramatic exhibitions; a theater. Shak.
A mark or expression of applause; praise bestowed. Not in the shouts and plaudits of the throng.
A plantation of pine trees; esp., a collection of living pine trees made for ornamental or scientific purposes.
A pine forest; a grove of pines.
A conical loaf of sugar.
The tail of a pig.
The principle or practice of the Pietists.
A colorless viscous substance having a bitter-sweet taste.
A small coin of the value of six and a quarter cents. See Fippenny bit.
The dissection of plants; vegetable anatomy.
The science of plants; a description of the kinds and properties of plants; botany. Sir T.
The science of describing plants in a systematic manner; also, a description of plants.

The science of nature, or of natural objects; that branch of science which treats of the laws and properties of matter, and the forces acting upon it; especially, that department of natural science which treats of the causes (as gravitation, heat, light, magne

The tendency of the mind toward, or its preoccupation with, physical phenomena; materialism in philosophy and religion. Anthropomorphism grows into theology, while physicism (if I may so call it) develops into science.
The science of the special functions of the several parts of the brain, or of the supposed connection between the various faculties of the mind and particular organs in the brain.
A sphere of light; esp., the luminous envelope of the sun.
The doctrine or science of light, explaining its nature and phenomena; optics.
A speaking machine.
The science which treats of vocal sounds. J.
The doctrine or science of sounds; especially those of the human voice; phonology.
A kind of transparent reliquary with an ornamental top.
A house or hospital for persons who are infected with any pestilential disease.
A shed or roof sloping from the main wall or building, as over a door or window; a lean-to. Also figuratively.
The first five books of the Old Testament, collectively; -- called also the Law of Moses, Book of the Law of Moses, etc.
A solid figure having five sides.
The science or art of punishment. [Written also poenology.]
The use of the pen in writing; the art of writing; style or manner of writing; chirography; as, good or bad penmanship.
The rank or dignity of a peer. Blackstone.

The act or practice of peculating, or of defrauding the public by appropriating to one's own use the money or goods intrusted to one's care for management or disbursement; embezzlement. Every British subject .
The jurisdiction of a pasha.
An apartment or closet in which bread and other provisions are kept.
The habit or power of eating all kinds of food.
A systematic view of all branches of human knowledge; a work of universal information.
A prison so contructed that the inspector can see each of the prisoners at all times, without being seen.
One of the digestive ferments of the pancreatic juice; also, a preparation containing such a ferment, made from the pancreas of animals, and used in medicine as an aid to digestion.
A thin cake of batter fried in a pan or on a griddle; a griddlecake; a flapjack. "A pancake for Shrove Tuesday." Shak.
A remedy for all diseases; a universal medicine; a cure-all; catholicon; hence, a relief or solace for affliction.
The art or practice of divining or telling fortunes, or of judging of character, by the lines and marks in the palm of the hand; chiromancy. Ascham.
A saddle horse for the road, or for state occasions, as distinguished from a war horse. Chaucer.

The quality or condition of being pale; want of freshness or ruddiness; a sickly whiteness; lack of color or luster; wanness. The blood the virgin's cheek forsook; A livid paleness spreads o'er all her look.
To palatize.

Originally, in India, loose drawers or trousers, such as those worn, tied about the waist, by Mohammedan men and women; by extension, a similar garment adopted among Europeans, Americans, etc., for wear in the dressing room and during sleep; also, a suit consi
To expose excessively; specif. (Photog.),
To develop excessively; specif. (Photog.),
A small house or building at a little distance from the main house; an outbuilding.
The branch of science which treats of the ear and its diseases.
A practitioner of osteopathy.
The science which treats of the bones of the vertebrate skeleton.
The art of uttering words corectly; a correct pronunciation of words; also, mode of pronunciation.
The orotund mode of intonation.
The act or process of orientating; determination of the points of the compass, or the east point, in taking bearings.
The disposition of the parts of any composition with regard to one another and the whole. Their dramatic ordonnance of the parts.
The nobility or aristocracy of ancient Rome, as opposed to the populares.
The art or practice of taking advantage of opportunities or circumstances, or of seeking immediate advantage with little regard for ultimate consequences. [Recent]
A reflexive form of the indefinite pronoun one. Commonly writen as two words, one's self.
A member of an oligarchy; one of the rulers in an oligarchical government.
The fragrant gum resin of various species of Boswellia; Oriental frankincense.
The offspring of a quadroon and a white person; a mestee.
A verse containing eight feet; as, -- Deep'' in|to'' the | dark''ness | peer''ing, | long'' I | stood'' there | wond'''ring, | fear''ing. Poe.
The act or process of obtaining; attainment. Milton.
The act or operation of obscuring; the state of being obscured; as, the obscuration of the moon in an eclipse. Sir J.
A species of sorcery, probably of African origin, practiced among the negroes of the West Indies. [Written also obe and obeah.] De Quincey.
The king of the fairies, and husband of Titania or Queen Mab. Shak.
The seed of Strychnos Nuxvomica, a tree which abounds on the Malabar and Coromandel coasts of the East Indies. From this seed the deadly poisons known as strychnine and brucine are obtained.
A house in which nuns reside; a cloister or convent in which women reside for life, under religious vows. See Cloister, and Convent.
The science of coins and medals.
The act or art of numbering. Numeration is but still the adding of one unit more, and giving to the whole a new name or sign.
A shade of difference; a delicate gradation.
A book in which notes or memorandums are written.
The science of law; legislation.
The art or practice of divining the destiny of persons by the letters which form their names.
The branch of science which treats of the nervous system.
The act or process of making nets or network, or of forming meshes, as for fancywork, fishing nets, etc.
The introduction of new words, or the use of old words in a new sense. Mrs.
A kerchief for the neck; -- called also neck handkerchief.
A piece of any fabric worn around the neck.
An advocate of the doctrine of philosophical necessity; a nacessitarian.
An entertainment consisting chiefly of dancing by professional dancing (or Nautch) girls. [India]
An elementary sound which is uttered through the nose, or through both the nose and the mouth simultaneously.
A diminutive of Ann or Anne, the proper name. Nanny goat, a female goat.
The science which treats of myths; a treatise on myths.
The Dutch equivalent of Mr. or Sir; hence, a Dutchman.
A Mohammedan crier of the hour of prayer. [Written also mouezzin, mueddin, and muwazzin.]
A clump of trees in a prairie. [Local, U.S.]
The doctrine, system, and practices of the Mormons.
The bright reflection of the moon's light on an expanse of water. [Poetic]
The doctrine or belief that there is but one God.
The habit of soliloquizing, or of monopolizing conversation. It was not by an insolent usurpation that Coleridge persisted in monology through his whole life.
A species of poem of a mournful character, in which a single mourner expresses lamentation; a song for one voice.
An eyeglass for one eye. Simmonds.
The character or condition of a monk. Atterbury.
The system and influences of a monastic life; monasticism.
A dry measure, containing about a peck.
A condition in which the lower classes of a nation control public affairs without respect to law, precedents, or vested rights. It is good name that Dr.
A hater of marriage.
An incorrect union of parties or of causes of action in a procedure, criminal or civil. Wharton.
A collection or digest of Jewish traditions and explanations of Scripture, forming the text of the Talmud. [Written also Mischna.]
A hater of mankind; a misanthropist.
The arts and occupation of minstrels; the singing and playing of a minstrel.

In the Middle Ages, one of an order of men who subsisted by the arts of poetry and music, and sang verses to the accompaniment of a harp or other instrument; in modern times, a poet; a bard; a singer and harper; a musician. Chaucer.
A kind of light passenger vehicle, carrying four persons.
A painter of miniatures.
The science which treats of minerals, and teaches how to describe, distinguish, and classify them.
A writer of mimes. Sir T.
An autographic stencil copying device invented by Edison.
A certain measure of distance, being equivalent in England and the United States to 320 poles or rods, or 5,280 feet.
The popular designation of the hereditary sovereign of Japan.
A colloquial abbreviation of midshipman.
An instrument for making very thin sections for microscopical examination.
A measure of length; the thousandth part of one millimeter; the millionth part of a meter.
The description of microscopic objects.
With a medium fullness of sound.
The science of, or a system of, weights and measures; also, a treatise on the subject.
A weight of 1,000 kilograms, or 2,204.6 pounds avoirdupois.

The art of working metals, comprehending the whole process of separating them from other matters in the ore, smelting, refining, and parting them; sometimes, in a narrower sense, only the process of extracting metals from their ores.
The offspring of an Indian or a negro and a European or person of European stock. [Spanish America] Mestizo wool, wool imported from South America, and produced by mixed breeds of sheep.
The offspring of a white person and a quadroon; -- so called in the West Indies. [Written also mustee.]
The land within the boundaries of a farm; a farmstead or farm. [Archaic.] Longfellow.
The practice of begging; the life of a beggar; mendicancy. Rom.
The act or operation of meliorating, or the state of being meliorated; improvement. Bacon.
A form of mental alienation in which the patient has grandiose delusions.
A rope of hair or of maguey fiber, for tying horses, etc. [Southwestern U.

A kind of machine gun; -- named after its inventor, Hiram S. Maxim.
The process of bringing, or of coming, to maturity; hence, specifically, the process of suppurating perfectly; the formation of pus or matter.
The murder of a mother by her son or daughter.
The natural history of Mammalia.
The act or operation of masticating; chewing, as of food. Mastication is a necessary preparation of solid aliment, without which there can be no good digestion.
The seigniory, dignity, or lordship of a marquis; the territory governed by a marquis.
The worship of the Virgin Mary.
The wife of a margrave.
The last day of Carnival; Shrove Tuesday; -- in some cities a great day of carnival and merrymaking.
A rover in quest of booty or plunder; a plunderer; one who pillages. De Quincey.
The fruit of the mango tree. It is rather larger than an apple, and of an ovoid shape.
A Chinese public officer or nobleman; a civil or military official in China and Annam.
The doing of an act which a person ought not to do; evil conduct; an illegal deed. [Written also malefeasance.]
A proclaiming of evil against some one; a cursing; imprecation; a curse or execration; -- opposed to benediction. No malediction falls from his tongue.
A grotesque misuse of a word; a word so used.
A grandee or nobleman of Venice; -- so called in courtesy. Shak.
To blur; especially (Print.), to blur or double an impression from type. See Mackle.
A waterproof outer garment; -- so called from the name of the inventor.
A heap of thing confusedly mixed together; a jumble.

The act or process of one who lists (in any sense of the verb); as, the listing of a door; the listing of a stock at the Stock Exchange.

A kiln or furnace in which limestone or shells are burned and reduced to lime.

A union, or bond of union; an intimacy; especially, an illicit intimacy between a man and a woman.

The writer of a lampoon. "Libelers, lampooners, and pamphleteers." Tatler.
The first day of August; -- called also Lammas day, and Lammastide.
Loaded; freighted; burdened; as, a laden vessel; a laden heart. Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity.

A game of war, played for practice, on maps. Farrow.
A collection of huts within a stockade; a village; sometimes, a single hut. [South Africa]
A garment varying in form and use at different times, and worn doth by men and women. Wearing her Norman car, and her kirtle of blue.
The hide of a young or small beef creature, or leather made from it; kipskin. Kip leather.
The state, office, or dignity of a king; royalty. Landor.
The craft of kings; the art of governing as a sovereign; royal policy. Prescott.
The science which treats of motions considered in themselves, or apart from their causes; the comparison and relation of motions.
A tent used by the Kirghiz Tartars.
The ancient title of emperors of Germany assumed by King William of Prussia when crowned sovereign of the new German empire in 1871.
A projection in a building; also, a pier or mole; a jetty. Shak.
An old name for the judges of the higher English courts.

An outer garment worn in the 18th century; esp., a woman's riding habit, buttoned down the front. Fairholt.
A large drinking vessel; also, its contents. [Colloq.

A Scripture name of the Supreme Being, by which he was revealed to the Jews as their covenant God or Sovereign of the theocracy; the "ineffable name" of the Supreme Being, which was not pronounced by the Jews.

An officer in the Greek empire having functions corresponding to those of a justice of the peace. [Written also eirenarch.]

The ninth letter of the Greek alphabet (i) corresponding with the English i.
To separate (a compound) into ions, esp. by dissolving in water.
A sight or view of the interior of anything; a deep inspection or view; introspection; -- frequently used with into. He had an insight into almost all the secrets of state.
The condition or quality of being insecure; want of safety; danger; hazard; as, the insecurity of a building liable to fire; insecurity of a debt.

A large mass of ice, generally floating in the ocean.

The doctrine of belief that matter is God, or that there is no God except matter and the universe; pantheism. See Materialism.
The science which treats of the precipitation of rain, snow, etc. -- Hy`e*to*log"ic*al, a.
The branch of physical science which treats of the geographical distribution of rain.
The science of water, its properties, phenomena, and distribution over the earth's surface.
The act or process of stripping off husks, as from Indian corn.
The body of a ship or decked vessel of any kind; esp., the body of an old vessel laid by as unfit for service. "Some well-timbered hulk." Spenser.
The business of the mistress of a family; female management of domestic concerns.
The master or head of a family; one who occupies a house with his family. Towns in which almost every householder was an English Protestant.
A nymph of paradise; -- so called by the Mohammedans.
A Hebrew exclamation of praise to the Lord, or an invocation of blessings. "Hosanna to the Highest." Milton.
The art, practice, or method of measuring time by hours and subordinate divisions. "The horometry of antiquity." Sir T.
The killing of one human being by another.
A piece of woodland; especially, a woody hill. "Every holt and heath." Chaucer.
A cake of Indian meal, water, and salt, baked before the fire or in the ashes; -- so called because often cooked on a hoe. [Southern U.S.]
That branch of biological science, which treats of the minute (microscopic) structure of animal and vegetable tissues; -- called also histiology.
The act or practice of feeding on horseflesh.
A variant of Height.

An emphasized form of the third person feminine pronoun; -- used as a subject with she; as, she herself will bear the blame; also used alone in the predicate, either in the nominative or objective case; as, it is herself; she blames herself.
One of a party among the Jews, composed of partisans of Herod of Galilee. They joined with the Pharisees against Christ.
A collection of dried specimens of plants, systematically arranged. Gray.
A coop or cage for hens.
A dog of hell; an agent of hell. A hellhound, that doth hunt us all to death.
The state, character, or privileges of an heir; right of inheriting. Heirship movables, certain kinds of movables which the heir is entitled to take, besides the heritable estate.
A cock that strikes well with his heels or spurs.

An executioner who cuts off heads. Dryden.
A bag for oats or oatmeal. [Prov.

A diviner of ancient Rome. Same as Aruspice.
A single particle of ice falling from a cloud; a frozen raindrop; a pellet of hail.

The driver of a hack or carriage for public hire.
A cart with wooden wheels, drawn by bullocks. [Bengal] Malcom.
A garment; an article of clothing. Camden.
The adoration or worship of woman. The sentimental gyneolatry of chivalry, which was at best but skin- deep.
A loud burst of laughter, a horse laugh. "A hearty low guffaw." Carlyle.
An Anglo-Indian name for a person just arrived from Europe. H.
The offspring of a mulatto woman and a negro; also, a mulatto. [Local, U.
A color mixed of white, and red, or a gray violet. [Written also gredaline, grizelin.] Dryden.

The retiring room of actors and actresses in a theater.
A house in which tender plants are cultivated and sheltered from the weather.
A digger of graves.
The grievance complained of; the substantial cause of the action; also, in general, the ground or essence of a complaint. Bouvier.
The art of judging of a person's character, disposition, and aptitude from his handwriting.
The act or process of forming or crystallizing into grains; as, the granulation of powder and sugar.
A dictionary of prosody, designed as an aid in writing Greek or Latin poetry. He set to work .
The mistress of a house. [Archaic] Robynson (More's Utopia).
The rank or character of a god; deity; divinity; a god or goddess. O'er hills and dales their godships came.
A plate made by glyphography, or an impression taken from such a plate.

A variety of sugar occurring in nature very abundantly, as in ripe grapes, and in honey, and produced in great quantities from starch, etc., by the action of heat and acids. It is only about half as sweet as cane sugar.
The science of tongues or languages; comparative philology; glossology.

The art or practice of overlaying or covering with gold leaf; also, a thin coating or wash of gold, or of that which resembles gold.
Relating to the pressure exerted by earth or similar substance. Geostatic arch, an arch having a form adapted to sustain pressure similar to that exerted by earth.

That part of geology which treats of the materials of the earth's structure, and its general exterior and interior constitution.
A style of painting, sculpture, or other imitative art, which illustrates everyday life and manners.

A measure of length; the eighth part of a mile; forty rods; two hundred and twenty yards.
The sixth day of the week, following Thursday and preceding Saturday.
The act, process, or art of casting metals.
The quality or condition of being foul.
The mark or impression of the foot; a track; hence, visible sign of a course pursued; token; mark; as, the footsteps of divine wisdom. How on the faltering footsteps of decay Youth presses.
The impression of the foot; a trace or footmark; as, "Footprints of the Creator."
A little pocket for a watch. Fob chain, a short watch chain worn a watch carried in the fob.
A small stream of water. [Eng.]
A flying with lightness and celerity; a fluttering.
A mixture of buttermilk and boiling whey; curds. [prov.
The bite of a flea, or the red spot caused by the bite.
The business or practice of catching fish; fishing. Addison.
An estate held of a superior on condition of military service; a fee; a feud. See under Benefice, n., 2.
A peasant or cultivator of the soil among the Egyptians, Syrians, etc. W.
The quality or condition of being feeble; debility; infirmity. That shakes for age and feebleness.
The doctrine that all things are subject to fate, or that they take place by inevitable necessity.
The art of shoeing horses.
A mass ccomposed of various materials confusedly mixed; a medley; a mixture. A confounded farrago of doubts, fears, hopes, wishes, and all the flimsy furniture of a country miss's brain.
A community in which many persons unite as in one family, and are regulated by certain communistic laws and customs.
A journey in circuit of certain judges called justices in eyre (or in itinere).
To exorcise or renounce by blowing.
One who explores; also, an apparatus with which one explores, as a diving bell.
A song for the evening; the evening service or form of worship (in the Church of England including vespers and compline); also, the time of evensong. Wyclif.
A child of a European parent on the one side and an Asiatic on the other.
The science of improving stock, whether human or animal. F.
The science which treats of the division of mankind into races, their origin, distribution, and relations, and the peculiarities which characterize them.
The language of ancient Ethiopia; the language of the ancient Abyssinian empire (in Ethiopia), now used only in the Abyssinian church. It is of Semitic origin, and is also called Geez.
A piece of furniture used as a writing table, commonly with drawers, pigeonholes, and the like; a secretary or writing desk.
The doctrine of the last or final things, as death, judgment, and the events therewith connected.
The act or practice of alluring or tempting; as, the enticements of evil companions.
The state of being empty; absence of contents; void space; vacuum; as, the emptiness of a vessel; emptiness of the stomach.
The consort of an emperor. Shak.
The method or practice of an empiric; pursuit of knowledge by observation and experiment.
A flying off in small particles, as heated iron or fermenting liquors; a sparkling; scintillation. Sir T.
The act of putting or going on board of a vessel; as, the embarkation of troops.
A measure for cloth; -- now rarely used. It is of different lengths in different countries; the English ell being 45 inches, the Dutch or Flemish ell 27, the Scotch about 37.
The territory, jurisdiction, or dignity of an elector, as in the old German empire.
The science of household affairs, or of domestic management.
An official of the Eastern Church, resembling a sacrist in the Western Church.
An inhabitant of the earth; a mortal. Earthings oft her deemed a deity.
A person afflicted with dyspepsia.
The union of two men in the same office; or the office, dignity, or government of two men thus associated, as in ancient Rome.

A low hill of drifting sand usually formed on the coats, but often carried far inland by the prevailing winds. [Written also dun.] Three great rivers, the Rhine, the Meuse, and the Scheldt, had deposited their slime for ages among the dunes or sand banks heave
The quality or condition of being two or twofold; dual character or usage.
A commercial name for textile fabrics, cottons, woolens, linen, silks, laces, etc., -- in distinction from groceries. [U.S.]
A maker of gowns, or similar garments; a mantuamaker.
A coat with skirts behind only, as distinct from the frock coat, of which the skirts surround the body. It is worn on occasions of ceremony.
The occupation of a draper; cloth-making, or dealing in cloth. Bacon.
The art of dramatic composition and representation.
The author of a dramatic composition; a writer of plays.
The male of the duck kind.
A contemptuous nickname for a timid, yielding politician, or one who is easily molded. [Political cant, U.
The quality or rank of a don, gentleman, or knight. Hudibras.

A period of from four to six weeks, in the summer, variously placed by almanac makers between the early part of July and the early part of September; canicular days; -- so called in reference to the rising in ancient times of the Dog Star (Sirius) with the sun
A colloquial name for the Southern portion of the United States, esp. during the Civil War.
The act or proceeding of seizing personal property by distress. Abbott.
A word of two syllables; as, pa-per.
The act or process of dislodging, or the state of being dislodged.
The act or process of discussing by breaking up, or dispersing, as a tumor, or the like.
The science of diplomas, or the art of deciphering ancient writings, and determining their age, authenticity, etc.; paleography.

The science of the refraction of light; that part of geometrical optics which treats of the laws of the refraction of light in passing from one medium into another, or through different mediums, as air, water, or glass, and esp. through different lenses; -- di
The sound of, or as of, repeated strokes on a metallic body, as a bell; a repeated and monotonous sound.
A silver coin of the United States, of the value of ten cents; the tenth of a dollar. Dime novel, a novel, commonly sensational and trashy, which is sold for a dime, or ten cents.

The doctrine of refracted sound; diacoustics.
The governor of Algiers; -- so called before the French conquest in 1830.
The character in which Sanskrit is written.
The integument of animal; the skin.
The art or profession of a dentist; dental surgery.
The worship of demons.

The act of overthrowing, pulling down, or destroying a pile or structure; destruction by violence; utter overthrow; -- opposed to construction; as, the demolition of a house, of military works, of a town, or of hopes.
A tract of land shaped like the letter delta (as, the delta of the Ganges, of the Nile, or of the Mississippi.
To bind up; to bandage.
The doctrine or creed of a deist; the belief or system of those who acknowledge the existence of one God, but deny revelation.
The office or ministry of a deacon or deaconess.
A journal of accounts; a primary record book in which are recorded the debts and credits, or accounts of the day, in their order, and from which they are transferred to the journal.
The manners and dress of a dandy; foppishness. Byron.
A scurf which forms on the head, and comes off in small or particles. [Written also dandriff.]
A small oval plum of a blue color, the fruit of a variety of the Prunus domestica; -- called also damask plum.
The title of the feudal nobles of Japan.daimyo The daimios, or territorial nobles, resided in Yedo and were divided into four classes. Am.
The national god of the Philistines, represented with the face and hands and upper part of a man, and the tail of a fish. W.
The art of numbering or counting by the fingers.
The title of the eldest son of the czar of Russia.
The title of the empress of Russia.
The title of the wife of the czarowitz.
The act or result of curtailing or cutting off. Bancroft.
The office or employment of a curate.
A sash for the waist; a girdle. [India]
A long cannon of the 16th century, usually an 18-pounder with serpent-shaped handles. Trump, and drum, and roaring culverin.

The small, spicy berry of a species of pepper (Piper Cubeba; in med., Cubeba officinalis), native in Java and Borneo, but now cultivated in various tropical countries. The dried unripe fruit is much used in medicine as a stimulant and purgative.
The condition of being crude; rawness.

A representation in art of the figure of Christ upon the cross; esp., the sculptured figure affixed to a real cross of wood, ivory, metal, or the like, used by the Roman Catholics in their devotions. The cross, too, by degrees, become the crucifix.
The pastoral staff of a bishop (also of an archbishop, being the symbol of his office as a shepherd of the flock of God.

A king of Lydia who flourished in the 6th century b. c., and was renowned for his vast wealth; hence, a common appellation for a very rich man; as, he is veritable Croesus.
A native of Croatia, in Austria; esp., one of the native Slavic race.

A standard of judging; any approved or established rule or test, by which facts, principles opinions, and conduct are tried in forming a correct judgment respecting them. Of the diseases of the mind there is no criterion.
A game of cards, played by two or four persons, in which there is a crib. (See Crib, 11.) It is characterized by a great variety of chances.
A gambling game with dice. [Local, U.S.]
The department of science (as of ethnology or archæology) which deals with the shape, size, proportions, indications, etc., of skulls; the study of skulls.
A game in which one person gives a word, to which another finds a rhyme. I saw in one corner .
The art or practice of cozening; artifice; fraud. Shak.
A strip of red cloth notched like the comb of a cock, which licensed jesters formerly wore in their caps. (b) The cap itself.
A staff or pole on which a vessel is supported between two persons. Suckling.
The state or condition of a cousin; also, the collective body of cousins; kinsfolk.
A court of record held once a year, in a particular hundred, lordship, or manor, before the steward of the leet. Blackstone.
An inferior court of civil jurisdiction, attached to a manor, and held by the steward; a baron's court; -- now fallen into disuse.
The front compartment of a French diligence; also, the front compartment (usually for three persons) of a car or carriage on British railways.
The wife of an earl in the British peerage, or of a count in the Continental nobility; also, a lady possessed of the same dignity in her own right. See the Note under Count.
A coverlet for a bed, -- originally stitched or woven in squares or figures. On which a tissue counterpane was cast.
An unnatural retention of the fecal matter of the bowels; constipation.
The universe or universality of created things; -- so called from the order and harmony displayed in it.

An exhibition in which a series of views in various parts of the world is seen reflected by mirrors through a series of lenses, with such illumination, etc., as will make the views most closely represent reality.
A description of the world or of the universe; or the science which teaches the constitution of the whole system of worlds, or the figure, disposition, and relation of all its parts.
The waist or bodice of a lady's dress; as. a low corsage.
The chief magistrate of a Spanish town.
The horn of plenty, from which fruits and flowers are represented as issuing. It is an emblem of abundance.
A term used in the Middle Ages for Spanish leather (goatskin tanned and dressed), and hence, any leather handsomely finished, colored, gilded, or the like. Buskins he wore of costliest cordwain.
A boat made by covering a wicker frame with leather or oilcloth. It was used by the ancient Britons, and is still used by fisherman in Wales and some parts of Ireland.
The connecting crook of a harrow. [Prov.
A grove of small growth; a thicket of brushwood; a wood cut at certain times for fuel or other purposes. See Copse.
A small, flat, sweetened cake of various kinds.
The art or process of preparing food for the table, by dressing, compounding, and the application of heat.
The act or process of beating, bruising, or pounding; the state of being beaten or bruised.
The office of a consul; consulate.
The condition of a consort; fellowship; partnership. Hammond.
A member of the Congress of the United States, esp. of the House of Representatives.
A collection of particles or bodies into one mass; a heap; an aggregation.
The act or process of passing, or causing to pass, from a fluid to a solid state, as by the abstraction of heat; the act or process of freezing.
A woman who cohabits with a man without being his wife; a paramour.
The cohabiting of a man and a woman who are not legally married; the state of being a concubine.
A cutting off; a division; a schism; a faction. South.
The act or process of computing; calculation; reckoning. By just computation of the time.
A system or structure of many parts united. A regular compages of pipes and vessels.

The act or process of mixing; the state of being mingled; the blending of ingredients in one mass or compound. In the commixture of anything that is more oily or sweet, such bodies are least apt to putrefy.
The amphitheater of Vespasian in Rome. [Also written Coliseum.]
The act or art of coloring; the state of being colored. Bacon.
A member or inhabitant of a colony.

The act of collimating; the adjustment of the line of the sights, as the axial line of the telescope of an instrument, into its proper position relative to the other parts of the instrument. Error of collimation, the deviation of the line collimation of an ast
The amphitheater of Vespasian at Rome, the largest in the world. [Written also Colosseum.]

A preparation made from the seeds of the chocolate tree, and used in making, a beverage; also the beverage made from cocoa or cocoa shells. Cocoa shells, the husks which separate from the cacao seeds in preparing them for use.
An upper loft; a garret; the highest room in a building. Dryden.
A vessel employed in sailing along a coast, or engaged in the coasting trade.
The adaptation or adjustment of parts to each other, as of a broken bone or dislocated joint.
A ball of thread; a thread or other means of guidance. Same as Clew.
The science which treats of climates and investigates their phenomena and causes. Brande & C.
A large two-handed sword used formerly by the Scottish Highlanders.
A musical instrument, formerly in use, in form of a spinet; -- called also manichord and clavichord.
The backing or steaming of clams on heated stones, between layers of seaweed; hence, a picnic party, gathered on such an occasion.
The expressed juice of apples. It is used as a beverage, for making vinegar, and for other purposes.
A professed admirer of a married woman; a dangler about women.
A short, thick piece of anything. [Colloq.
The art of measuring time; the measuring of time by periods or divisions.
A writer of a chronicle; a recorder of events in the order of time; an historian. Such an honest chronicler as Griffith.
The science of colors; that part of optics which treats of the properties of colors.
the mapping or description of a region or district. The chorography of their provinces.
A loose and flowing outer garment, worn by the ancient Greeks; a kind of cloak.
The art or practice of foretelling events, or of telling the fortunes or the disposition of persons by inspecting the hand; palmistry.
The art of writing or engrossing; handwriting; as, skilled in chirography.
A chip; a piece separated by a cutting or graving instrument; a fragment.
A knot, boss, or mass of hair, natural or artificial, worn by a woman at the back of the head. A curl that had strayed from her chignon.
The presiding judge of the court of exchequer.
The Hebrew plural of Cherub.. Cf.
A deep opening made by disruption, as a breach in the earth or a rock; a yawning abyss; a cleft; a fissure. That deep, romantic chasm which slanted down the green hill.
The office of a chargé d'affaires.
The office, position, or station of a chaplain. Swift.
A thicket of low evergreen oaks.
An endowment or foundation for the chanting of masses and offering of prayers, commonly for the founder.
A maker or seller of candles. The chandler's basket, on his shoulder borne, With tallow spots thy coat.
The presiding officer of a committee, or of a public or private meeting, or of any organized body.
A cloth smeared with melted wax, or with some gummy or glutinous matter. Linen, besmeared with gums, in manner of cerecloth.
The art of making things of baked clay; as pottery, tiles, etc.
The act or process of cementing.
An East Indian Weight of 11/3 pounds.
A book in which is kept a register of money received or paid out.
A lodging for soldiers in garrison towns, usually near the rampart; barracks. Bescherelle.
The act business of forming chart's or maps.

A festival celebrated with merriment and revelry in Roman Gatholic countries during the week before Lent, esp. at Rome and Naples, during a few days (three to ten) before Lent, ending with Shrove Tuesday.
The office, rank, or dignity of a cardinal.
A member of a secret political association in Italy, organized in the early part of the nineteenth centry for the purpose of changing the government into a republic.

The weight by which precious stones and pearls are weighed.

A small basket of rushes, or wilow twigs, etc.

The light of a candle. Never went by candlelight to bed.
The lowest class of people; the rabble; the vulgar.
The principal grounds of a college or school, between the buildings or within the main inclosure; as, the college campus.
A short dressing jacket for women.
The private audience chamber of a king.
A monk of the Greek Church; a cenobite, anchoret, or recluse of the rule of St. Basil, especially, one on or near Mt.

The principle of heat, or the agent to which the phenomena of heat and combustion were formerly ascribed; -- not now used in scientific nomenclature, but sometimes used as a general term for heat. Caloric expands all bodies.
The office, dignity, or government of a caliph or of the caliphs.
A species of agalloch, or aloes wood, of a dusky or mottled color, of a light, friable texture, and less fragrant than calambac; -- used by cabinetmakers.
A cloth of exceedingly fine texture, used by the ancients. It is disputed whether it was of cotton, linen, or silk.
A court or meeting of a burgh or borough; a borough court held three times yearly.
An official of a bureau; esp. an official confirmed in a narrow and arbitrary routine.
A boat or raft used in the East Indies in the landing of passengers and goods.
A basket in which clothes are carried to the wash. Shak.
The business or employment of a broker. Burke.
The edge, margin, or border of a steep place, as of a precipice; a bank or edge, as of a river or pit; a verge; a border; as, the brink of a chasm. Also Fig.
A house of correction for the confinement of disorderly persons; -- so called from a hospital built in 1553 near St. Bride's (or Bridget's) well, in London, which was subsequently a penal workhouse.
A garment worn by men, covering the hips and thighs; smallclothes. His jacket was red, and his breeches were blue.
A fall that breaks the neck.
A thin bed of coal mixed with pyrites or carbonate of lime.
The bones which inclose the brain; the skull; the cranium.
A system of printing or writing for the blind in which the characters are represented by tangible points or dots. It was invented by Louis Braille, a French teacher of the blind.
An onomatopoetic name for a dog or its bark. -- a.
A nutritious liquid food made by boiling beef, or other meat, in water; a clear soup or broth.
An ancient species of divination by means of plants, esp. sage and fig leaves.
The rule or practices of bosses, esp. political bosses.
A growth of trees or shrubs; underwood; a thicket; thick foliage; a wooded landscape.
The height of the fashion; fashionable society.
The act or practice of rowing or sailing, esp. as an amusement; carriage in boats.
A short stick, with one end loaded, or thicker and heavier that the other, used as an offensive weapon.
A light, loose over-garment, like a smock frock, worn especially by workingmen in France; also, a loose coat of any material, as the undress uniform coat of the United States army.
The shedding or spilling of blood; slaughter; the act of shedding human blood, or taking life, as in war, riot, or murder.
A gale of piercingly cold wind, usually accompanied with fine and blinding snow; a furious blast. [U.
The supposed faculty of perceiving subterraneous springs and currents by sensation; -- so called from one Bleton, of France.
A preparation for desserts, etc., made from isinglass, sea moss, cornstarch, or other gelatinous or starchy substance, with mild, usually sweetened and flavored, and shaped in a mold.
The fruit of several species of bramble (Rubus); also, the plant itself. Rubus fruticosus is the blackberry of England; R.
A pestilence which ravaged Europe and Asia in the fourteenth century.
A cold north wind which prevails on the northern coasts of the Mediterranean and in Switzerland, etc.; -- nearly the same as the mistral.
A name applied to the amorphous or crystalline mass obtained from bile by the action of alcohol and ether. It is composed of a mixture of the sodium salts of the bile acids.
A nest of wild bees, wasps, or ants; a swarm. [Scot.] Sir W.
The offense of marrying one person when already legally married to another. Wharton.
A double form.
A lover of books.
The practice or habit of drinking too much; tippling. Blount.
A governor of a province or district in the Turkish dominions; also, in some places, a prince or nobleman; a beg; as, the bey of Tunis.
