A vocal or instrumental composition of a soft tranquil character, having a lulling effect; a cradle song.

A conical calcareous fossil, tapering to a point at the lower extremity, with a conical cavity at the other end, where it is ordinarily broken; but when perfect it contains a small chambered cone, called the phragmocone, prolonged, on one side, into a delicate
The Babylonian name of the god known among the Hebrews as Baal. See Baal.
The governor of a province of the Ottoman empire, next in dignity to the grand vizier.
The title of a heathen deity to whom the Jews ascribed the sovereignty of the evil spirits; hence, the Devil or a devil. See Baal.
An inhabitant of a madhouse; a madman. "Raving bedlamites." Beattie.

A conception or image of consummate beauty, moral or physical, formed in the mind, free from all the deformities, defects, and blemishes seen in actual existence; an ideal or faultless standard or model.
The skin of a bear.
A house of prostitution; a house of ill fame; a brothel.
The practice of procuring women for the gratification of lust.
The art or science of sounding, or measuring depths in the sea.
A warlike South African people of the Bantu stock, divided into many tribes, subject to the English. They formerly practiced cannibalism, but have now adopted many European customs.

Any instrument showing the changes in the weight of the atmosphere; also, less appropriately, any instrument that indicates - or foreshadows changes of the weather, as a deep vial of liquid holding in suspension some substance which rises and falls with atmosp
The rank or patent of a baronet.
A goblin, in the shape of a large dog, portending misfortune. [Also written barguest.]
A pleasure boat; a vessel or boat of state, elegantly furnished and decorated.
A room for balls or dancing.
The art or practice of managing balloons or voyaging in them.
The act or process of cooking in an oven, or of drying and hardening by heat or cold.
A house for baking; a bakery.
A large stick of wood, forming the of a fire on the hearth. [U.S.] There was first a backlog, from fifteen to four and twenty inches in diameter and five feet long, imbedded in the ashes.
A priestess of Bacchus.
The state or period of infancy.
A species of divination, by means of an ax or hatchet.
The pulpy fruit of Persea gratissima, a tree of tropical America. It is about the size and shape of a large pear; -- called also avocado pear, alligator pear, midshipman's butter.
The art or science of flying.
A way or opening for entrance into a place; a passage by which a place may by reached; a way of approach or of exit. "The avenues leading to the city by land." Macaulay.
A judgment of the Inquisition in Spain and Portugal condemning or acquitting persons accused of religious offenses.
A divining or taking of omens by observing birds; an omen as to an undertaking, drawn from birds; an augury; an omen or sign in general; an indication as to the future.
The practice of augury.
The office of an augur. Merivale.
A porridge or gruel of maize meal and water, milk, or the like. [Sp.
The practice of engaging in athletic games; athletism.
The felonious removal of goods from the place where they were deposited.
The condition, practice, or mode of life, of ascetics.
A soothsayer of ancient Rome. Same as Aruspex.
A public establishment for the storage, or for the manufacture and storage, of arms and all military equipments, whether for land or naval service.
The head of an arrow.
A Spanish weight used in Mexico and South America = 25.36 lbs. avoir.; also, an old Portuguese weight, used in Brazil = 32.38 lbs.
The shot of an arquebus. Ash.
A cessation of arms for a short time, by convention; a temporary suspension of hostilities by agreement; a truce.
The science of numbers; the art of computation by figures.
A prince of the imperial family of Austria.
The territory of an archduke or archduchess. Ash.
The hearing and determination of a cause between parties in controversy, by a person or persons chosen by the parties.

A style of ornamentation either painted, inlaid, or carved in low relief. It consists of a pattern in which plants, fruits, foliage, etc., as well as figures of men and animals, real or imaginary, are fantastically interlaced or put together.
The office or dignity of an apostle.
The tip, top, point, or angular summit of anything; as, the apex of a mountain, spire, or cone; the apex, or tip, of a leaf.
The state or condition of being antecedent; priority. Fothherby.
A writer of annotations; a commentator.
The state, activity, or enjoyment of animals; mere animal life without intellectual or moral qualities; sensuality.
A description of the winds.
An inversion of the natural order of words; as, echoed the hills, for, the hills echoed.
The doctrine or practice of anarchists.
A poem in which persons are represented at speaking alternately; as the third and seventh eclogues of Virgil.
A contraction of amperometer or ampèremeter.

The infliction of a penalty at the discretion of the court; also, a mulct or penalty thus imposed. It differs from a fine,in that the latter is, or was originally, a fixed and certain sum prescribed by statue for an offense; but an amercement is arbitrary.
An alteration or change for the better; correction of a fault or of faults; reformation of life by quitting vices.
A recipient of alms. Shak.
The act or art of alloying metals; also, the combination or alloy.

A vestment of white linen, reaching to the feet, an enveloping the person; -- in the Roman Catholic church, worn by those in holy orders when officiating at mass. It was formerly worn, at least by clerics, in daily life.
The bone of the rump; also, the cut of beef surrounding this bone. [Spelt also edgebone.]
A man who ascends or flies in an aircraft; a flying machine pilot.
A pipe for the passage of air; esp. a ventilating pipe.
A inferior brandy of Spain and Portugal.
The management of land; rural economy; agriculture.
To bring, or tend to bring, to a uniform grade, or slope, by addition of material; as, streams aggrade their beds by depositing sediment.
The science, doctrine, or demonstration of causes; esp., the investigation of the causes of any disease; the science of the origin and development of things.
The observation of the state and variations of the atmosphere.
A flying machine, or a small plane for experiments on flying, which floats in the air only when propelled through it.
The science of measuring the air, including the doctrine of its pressure, elasticity, rarefaction, and condensation; pneumatics.
A description of the air or atmosphere; aërology.
The nest of a bird of prey, as of an eagle or hawk; also a brood of such birds; eyrie. Shak.
A period of immeasurable duration; also, an emanation of the Deity. See Eon.

The unfaithfulness of a married person to the marriage bed; sexual intercourse by a married man with another than his wife, or voluntary sexual intercourse by a married woman with another than her husband.

A naval officer of the highest rank; a naval officer of high rank, of which there are different grades. The chief gradations in rank are admiral, vice admiral, and rear admiral.
The property of radiant energy (found chiefly in solar or electric light) by which chemical changes are produced, as in photography.
The act or posture of reclining on a couch, as practiced by the ancients at meals.
The accidents, of inflections of words; the rudiments of grammar. Milton.
The articles of dress prescribed and worn at some colleges and universities.
The butting or boundary of land, particularly at the end; a headland. Spelman.
The Patriarch, or head of the Abyssinian Church.
The state or practice of an absentee; esp. the practice of absenting one's self from the country or district where one's estate is situated.
The act or process of cutting off. "Not to be cured without the abscission of a member." Jer.
A sudden breaking off; a violent separation of bodies. Woodward.
The earliest known inhabitants of a country; native races.
The superior or head of an abbey.
The dignity, estate, or jurisdiction of an abbot.
A public slaughterhouse for cattle, sheep, etc.
Of or pertaining to xenogenesis; as, the xenogenetic origin of microzymes. Huxley.
Becoming a woman; feminine; as, womanly behavior. Arbuthnot.
Longing; wishful; desirous. Lifting up one of my sashes, I cast many a wistful, melancholy look towards the sea.
Thin and pale; weak; without strength or substance; -- originally said of liquids. Fig., weak-minded; spiritless.
prevented from sailing, by a contrary wind. See Weatherbound.
Spread to a great distance; widely extended; extending far and wide; as, widespread wings; a widespread movement.
Skillful in forecasting the changes of the weather. Hakluyt.

Causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; weariful; as, a wearisome march; a wearisome day's work; a wearisome book. These high wild hills and rough uneven ways Draws out our miles, and makes them wearisome.
Traveling; passing; being on a journey. "A wayfaring man." Judg.
Watery; damp; soft. "Washy ooze." Milton.
Absent; lacking; missing; also, deficient; destitute; needy; as, one of the twelve is wanting; I shall not be wanting in exertion.

Of or pertaining to the fox; resembling the fox; foxy; cunning; crafty; artful. Vulpine phalangist (Zoöl.), an Australian carnivorous marsupial (Phalangista, or Trichosurus, vulpina); -- called also vulpine phalanger, and vulpine opossum.
Useful in healing wounds; adapted to the cure of external injuries; as, vulnerary plants or potions. "Such vulnerary remedies." Sir W.
Of or pertaining to a volcano or volcanoes; as, volcanic heat.

Possessing vigor; full of physical or mental strength or active force; strong; lusty; robust; as, a vigorous youth; a vigorous plant. Famed for his valor, young, At sea successful, vigorous and strong.
Characterized by vice or defects; defective; faulty; imperfect. Though I perchance am vicious in my guess.
Observant of truth; habitually speaking truth; truthful; as, veracious historian. The Spirit is most perfectly and absolutely veracious.

Capable of being venerated; worthy of veneration or reverence; deserving of honor and respect; -- generally implying an advanced age; as, a venerable magistrate; a venerable parent. He was a man of eternal self-sacrifice, and that is always venerable.
Wandering; vagrant; vagabond. [Archaic] "To set upon the vague villains." Hayward.
Empty; unfilled; void; vacant. Boundless the deep, because I am who fill Infinitude; nor vacuous the space.
Making, or accompanied by, uproar, or noise and tumult; as, uproarious merriment. -- Up*roar"i*ous*ly, adv.
Not wearied; not fatigued or tired; hence, persistent; not tiring or wearying; indefatigable. -- Un*wea"ried*ly, adv.
Not warranted; being without warrant, authority, or guaranty; unwarrantable.
Not trained. Shak.
Not told; not related; not revealed; as, untold secrets.
Not thinking; not heedful; thoughtless; inconsiderate; as, unthinking youth.
Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation. -- Un*spot"ted*ness, n.
Not sparing; not parsimonious; liberal; profuse. Burke.
Not salable; unmerchantable. -- n.

Not submissive to rule; disregarding restraint; disposed to violate; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as, an unruly boy; unruly boy; unruly conduct. But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
Not reserved; not kept back; not withheld in part; unrestrained. -- Un`re*serv"ed*ly, adv.
Not remitting; incessant; continued; persevering; as, unremitting exertions. Cowper.
Not necessary; not required under the circumstances; unless; needless; as, unnecessary labor, care, or rigor. -- Un*nec"es*sa*ri*ly, adv.
Not natural; contrary, or not conforming, to the order of nature; being without natural traits; as, unnatural crimes.
Not moved; fixed; firm; unshaken; calm; apathetic. -- Un*mov"ed*ly, adv.
Not licked; hence, not properly formed; ungainly. Cf.
Being without a like or equal; unmatched; unequaled; unparalleled; single in kind or excellence; sole. -- U*nique"ly, adv.
Not ideal; real; unimaginative.

Not graceful; not marked with ease and dignity; deficient in beauty and elegance; inelegant; awkward; as, ungraceful manners; ungraceful speech. The other oak remaining a blackened and ungraceful trunk.
Not friendly; not kind or benevolent; hostile; as, an unfriendly neighbor.
Not flinching or shrinking; unyielding. -- Un*flinch"ing*ly, adv.
Not fledged; not feathered; hence, not fully developed; immature. Dryden.
Not even; not level; not uniform; rough; as, an uneven road or way; uneven ground.
Committing no mistake; incapable or error or failure certain; sure; unfailing; as, the unerring wisdom of God. Hissing in air the unerring weapon flew.
Not equivocal; not doubtful; not ambiguous; evident; sincere; plain; as, unequivocal evidence; unequivocal words. -- Un`e*quiv"o*cal*ly, adv.
Not dying; imperishable; unending; immortal; as, the undying souls of men.
Of the nature or quality of an unguent or ointment; fatty; oily; greasy. "The unctuous cheese." Longfellow.
Not broken; continuous; unsubdued; as, an unbroken colt.
Loosed from the bridle, or as from the bridle; hence, unrestrained; licentious; violent; as, unbridled passions. "Unbridled boldness." B.
Not blushing; shameless. -- Un*blush"ing*ly, adv.
Inapt; slow; dull. Bacon.
Not alloyed; not reduced by foreign admixture; unmixed; unqualified; pure; as, unalloyed metals; unalloyed happiness. I enjoyed unalloyed satisfaction in his company.

Of or pertaining to turmeric; resembling, or obtained from, turmeric; specif., designating an acid obtained by the oxidation of turmerol. Turmeric paper (Chem.), paper impregnated with turmeric and used as a test for alkaline substances, by which it is changed
Made thrice as much; threefold; tripled. Triplicate ratio (Math.), the ratio of the cubes of two quantities; thus, the triplicate ratio of a to b is a3: b3.
Being of small value or importance; trivial; paltry; as, a trifling debt; a trifling affair. -- Tri"fling*ly, adv.
Exhibiting artfulness; trickish. "My tricksy spirit!" Shak.
A traumatic medicine.
Capable of being easily led, taught, or managed; docile; manageable; governable; as, tractable children; a tractable learner. I shall find them tractable enough.
Very high; elevated; rising aloft; as, a towering height. Pope.

Bent in different directions; wreathed; twisted; winding; as, a tortuous train; a tortuous train; a tortuous leaf or corolla. The badger made his dark and tortuous hole on the side of every hill where the copsewood grew thick.
Affected with tormina; griping.
Fitted or tending to tire; exhausted; wearisome; fatiguing; tedious; as, a tiresome journey; a tiresome discourse. -- Tire"some*ly, adv.
Fearful of danger; timid; deficient in courage. Shak.
Causing a thrill; causing tremulous excitement; deeply moving; as, a thrilling romance. -- Thrill"ing*ly, adv.
Of or pertaining to heat; due to heat; thermal; as, thermic lines. Thermic balance.

Of or pertaining to a theater, or to the scenic representations; resembling the manner of dramatic performers; histrionic; hence, artificial; as, theatrical performances; theatrical gestures. -- The*at`ri*cal"i*ty, n.
Moderate; not excessive; as, temperate heat; a temperate climate.
Prolific; productive. Teeming buds and cheerful appear.
Of or pertaining to the organs, or the sense, of touch; perceiving, or perceptible, by the touch; capable of being touched; as, tactile corpuscles; tactile sensations. "Tactile sweets." Beaumont.
Of or pertaining to tabes; of the nature of tabes; affected with tabes; tabid. -- n.
Moving a great distance in a short time; moving with celerity or velocity; fleet; rapid; quick; speedy; prompt. My beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
Entreating; asking submissively. Shak.
Drawing milk from the mother or dam; hence, colloquially, young, inexperienced, as, a sucking infant; a sucking calf. I suppose you are a young barrister, sucking lawyer, or that sort of thing.
Thin; not dense or gross; rare; as, subtile air; subtile vapor; a subtile medium.
Of or pertaining to a subject.
Astonishing; wonderful; amazing; especially, astonishing in magnitude or elevation; as, a stupendous pile. "A stupendous sum." Macaulay.
Set with stiff, straight bristles; hispid; as, a strigose leaf.
Making a shrill, creaking sound. Sir T.

Eagerly pressing or urgent; zealous; ardent; earnest; bold; valiant; intrepid; as, a strenuous advocate for national rights; a strenuous reformer; a strenuous defender of his country. And spirit-stirring wine, that strenuous makes.
from Storm, v. Storming party (Mil.), a party assigned to the duty of making the first assault in storming a fortress.
from Stink, v. Stinking badger (Zoöl.), the teledu.
Done by stealth; accomplished clandestinely; unperceived; secret; furtive; sly. [Withered murder] with his stealthy pace, .
Firmly fixed or established; fast fixed; firm. "This steadfast globe of earth." Spenser.
Evincing state or dignity; lofty; majestic; grand; as, statelymanners; a stately gait. "The stately homes of England!" Mrs.
Free from stain; immaculate. Shak.
Not proceeding from the true source, or from the source pretended; not genuine; false; adulterate.
Destitute of spirit; wanting animation; wanting cheerfulness; dejected; depressed.
Flavored with, or containing, spice or spices; fragrant; aromatic; as, spicy breezes. "The spicy nut-brown ale." Milton.
Bound by, or as by, a spell.
Given to speculation; contemplative. The mind of man being by nature speculative.
Like spar; foliated or lamellar; spathose. Spathic iron (Min.), siderite.
Neither very good nor very bad; middling; passable; tolerable; indifferent. In some Irish houses, where things are so-so, One gammon of bacon hangs up for a show.
Marked by cowardly concealment; deficient in openness and courage; underhand; mean; crouching. -- Sneak"ing*ly, adv.
Easily frightened; timorous; shy; untrustworthy; as, a skittish colt. "A restiff, skittish jade." L'Estrange.
On the left hand, or the side of the left hand; left; -- opposed to dexter, or right. "Here on his sinister cheek." Shak.
Wanting sight; without sight; blind. Of all who blindly creep or sightless soar.

Arranged in a manner befitting a ship; hence, trim; tidy; orderly. Even then she expressed her scorn for the lubbery executioner's mode of tying a knot, and did it herself in a shipshape orthodox manner.
Changing in place, position, or direction; varying; variable; fickle; as, shifting winds; shifting opinions or principles.
Destitute of shape or regular form; wanting symmetry of dimensions; misshapen; -- opposed to Ant: shapely. -- Shape"less*ness, n.
Destitute of shame; wanting modesty; brazen-faced; insensible to disgrace. "Such shameless bards we have." Pope.
Shaking or trembling; as, a shaky spot in a marsh; a shaky hand. Thackeray.
Full of shade or shadows; causing shade or shadow. "Shadowy verdure." Fenton.

Of or pertaining to a servant or slave; befitting a servant or a slave; proceeding from dependence; hence, meanly submissive; slavish; mean; cringing; fawning; as, servile flattery; servile fear; servile obedience. She must bend the servile knee.
SEROW; SURROW Ser"ow, Sur"row, n. (Zoöl.)
Of the seventh degree or order. -- n.

Abounding with sentences, axioms, and maxims; full of meaning; terse and energetic in expression; pithy; as, a sententious style or discourse; sententious truth. How he apes his sire, Ambitiously sententious!

Capable of being perceived by the senses; apprehensible through the bodily organs; hence, also, perceptible to the mind; making an impression upon the sense, reason, or understanding; sensible resistance. Air is sensible to the touch by its motion.
Destitute of, deficient in, or contrary to, sense; without sensibility or feeling; unconscious; stupid; foolish; unwise; unreasonable. You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things.
More advanced than another in age; prior in age; elder; hence, more advanced in dignity, rank, or office; superior; as, senior member; senior counsel.
Shaped like a half moon. Semilunar bone (Anat.), a bone of the carpus; the lunar.
Suited to the object, occasion, purpose, or character; suitable; fit; becoming; comely; decorous. He had a seemly nose.
Of or pertaining to sediment; formed by sediment; containing matter that has subsided. Sedimentary rocks.

Suceeding next in order to the first; of second place, origin, rank, rank, etc.; not primary; subordinate; not of the first order or rate. Wheresoever there is normal right on the one hand, no secondary right can discharge it.
Using the low and indecent language of the meaner sort of people, or such as only the license of buffoons can warrant; as, a scurrilous fellow.
Resembling a boat in form; boat-shaped. -- n.
Covered or abounding with scales; as, a scaly fish. "Scaly crocodile." Milton.
Of or pertaining to, or of the nature of, the Sauria. -- n.
Conducive to health; tending to cure; healing; curative; sanative. Sanatory ordinances for the protection of public health, such as quarantine, fever hospitals, draining, etc.
Rudimentary. Addison.
Strengthening. -- n.
Involving, or engaging in, riot; wanton; unrestrained; luxurious. The younger son .

Manifesting, exercising, or favoring rigor; allowing no abatement or mitigation; scrupulously accurate; exact; strict; severe; relentless; as, a rigorous officer of justice; a rigorous execution of law; a rigorous definition or demonstration. He shall be throw
Prevailing; prevalent; abounding. Before the plague of London, inflammations of the lungs were rife and mortal.
Of or pertaining to resin; of the nature of resin; resembling or obtained from resin. Resinous electricity (Elec.), electricity which is exited by rubbing bodies of the resinous kind.
Pertaining to a residue; remaining after a part is taken. Residual air (Physiol.), that portion of air contained in the lungs which can not be expelled even by the most violent expiratory effort.
Kept for future or special use, or for an exigency; as, reserved troops; a reserved seat in a theater.
Filled again; completely filled; full; charged; abounding. "His words replete with guile." Milton.
Resisting pressure or the effect of it; acting against impluse by elastic force. "[Muscles] soft and yet renitent." Ray.
Affording a remedy; intended for a remedy, or for the removal or abatement of an evil; as, remedial treatment. Statutes are declaratory or remedial.
Directed back; attended by reflection; retroactive; introspective. The reflex act of the soul, or the turning of the intellectual eye inward upon its own actions.
Talking irrationally and wildly; as, a raving lunatic. -- Rav"ing*ly, adv.
Relating to reason; not physical; mental. Moral philosophy was his chiefest end; for the rational, the natural, and mathematics .
Of or pertaining to the Rasores, or gallinaceous birds, as the peacock, domestic fowl, patridge, and the like.
Ecstatic; transporting; ravishing; feeling, expressing, or manifesting rapture; as, rapturous joy, pleasure, or delight; rapturous applause.

Going at random or by chance; done or made at hazard, or without settled direction, aim, or purpose; hazarded without previous calculation; left to chance; haphazard; as, a random guess. Some random truths he can impart.
Of or pertaining to rachitis; affected by rachitis; rickety.
Fitted by accomplishments or endowments.
That may be sqyared, or reduced to an equivalent square; -- said of a surface when the area limited by a curve can be exactly found, and expressed in a finite number of algebraic terms.
Of or pertaining to Pythagoras (a Greek philosopher, born about 582 b. c.), or his philosophy.
Of or pertaining to the Puritans; resembling, or characteristic of, the Puritans.
Attentive to punctilio; very nice or exact in the forms of behavior, etiquette, or mutual intercourse; precise; exact in the smallest particulars. "A punctilious observance of divine laws." Rogers.
Disposed to fight; inclined to fighting; quarrelsome; fighting. --Pug*na"cious*ly, adv.
Of or pertaining to province; constituting a province; as, a provincial government; a provincial dialect.
Changeable in form; resembling a Proteus, or an amoeba.
Of or pertaining to Proteus; characteristic of Proteus. " Protean transformations." Cudworth.
Standing before; -- applied to a gland which is found in the males of most mammals, and is situated at the neck of the bladder where this joins the urethra. -- n.
Stretched out; extended; especially, elongated in the direction of a line joining the poles; as, a prolate spheroid; -- opposed to oblate. Prolate cycloid.

Preceding in the order of time; former; antecedent; anterior; previous; as, a prior discovery; prior obligation; -- used elliptically in cases like the following: he lived alone [in the time] prior to his marriage.
The first or chief female singer in an opera.
Based on presumption or probability; grounded on probable evidence; probable; as, presumptive proof.
Prior to the glacial or drift period.
Depending on the will or pleasure of another; held by courtesy; liable to be changed or lost at the pleasure of another; as, precarious privileges. Addison.
Containing, or made up, of, several languages; as, a polyglot lexicon, Bible.
Of or pertaining to polity, or civil government; political; as, the body politic. See under Body.
Progressing in a slow, toilsome manner; characterized by laborious diligence; as, a plodding peddler; a plodding student; a man of plodding habits. --Plod"ding*ly, adv.
Of, pertaining to, or characterizing, the most recent division of the Tertiary age.
Of or pertaining to the epoch, or the deposits, following the Tertiary, and immediately preceding man. -- n.
Sportive; gamboling; frolicsome; indulging a sportive fancy; humorous; merry; as, a playful child; a playful writer. -- Play"ful*ly, adv.
Consisting of, or resembling, pituite or mucus; full of mucus; discharging mucus. Pituitous fever (Med.), typhoid fever; enteric fever.
Partaking of the qualities of pitch; resembling pitch.
Of or pertaining to the voice, or its use.
Belonging or relating to the period, and also to the formation, next following the Carboniferous, and regarded as closing the Carboniferous age and Paleozoic era. -- n.

Applied to the peculiar wormlike wave motion of the intestines and other similar structures, produced by the successive contraction of the muscular fibers of their walls, forcing their contents onwards; as, peristaltic movement. -- Per`i*stal"tic*al*ly, adv.
Done merely to get rid of a duty; performed mechanically and as a thing of rote; done in a careless and superficial manner; characterized by indifference; as, perfunctory admonitions. Macaulay.
Habitually fretful; easily vexed or fretted; hard to please; apt to complain; querulous; petulant. "Her peevish babe." Wordsworth.
Of or pertaining to a patriarch or to patriarchs; possessed by, or subject to, patriarchs; as, patriarchal authority or jurisdiction; a patriarchal see; a patriarchal church.
Not active, but acted upon; suffering or receiving impressions or influences; as, they were passive spectators, not actors in the scene. The passive air Upbore their nimble tread.

Capable of being passed, traveled, navigated, traversed, penetrated, or the like; as, the roads are not passable; the stream is passablein boats. His body's a passable carcass if it be not hurt; it is a throughfare for steel.
Of or pertaining to paralysis; resembling paralysis.
Mean; vile; worthless; despicable; contemptible; pitiful; trifling; as, a paltry excuse; paltry gold. Cowper.
Bearing palms; abounding in palms; derived from palms; as, a palmy shore. Pope.
Web-footed, as a water fowl. -- n.

Of or pertaining to an era marked by early stone implements. The Paleolithic era (as proposed by Lubbock) includes the earlier half of the "Stone Age;" the remains belonging to it are for the most part of extinct animals, with relics of human beings.
Agreeable to the palate or taste; savory; hence, acceptable; pleasing; as, palatable food; palatable advice.
That stands out; undischarged; uncollected; not paid; as, outstanding obligations. Revenues .
Speaking, or spoken, freely, openly, or boldly; as, an outspoken man; an outspoken rebuke. -- Out*spo"ken*ness, n.
Being out of the common course or limits; extravagant; bizarre.
Of the nature of an outrage; exceeding the limits of right, reason, or decency; involving or doing an outrage; furious; violent; atrocious. "Outrageous weeping." Chaucer.
Of or pertaining to a division of the Silurian formation, corresponding in general to the Lower Silurian of most authors, exclusive of the Cambrian. -- n.
Unreasonably burdensome; unjustly severe, rigorous, or harsh; as, oppressive taxes; oppressive exactions of service; an oppressive game law. Macaulay.

Of, pertaining to, or in the region of, the eye; ocular; as the ophthalmic, or orbitonasal, nerve, a division of the trigeminal, which gives branches to the lachrymal gland, eyelids, nose, and forehead. Ophthalmic region (Zoöl.), the space around the eyes.
Burdensome; oppressive. "Too onerous a solicitude." I.

Of or pertaining to an omen or to omens; being or exhibiting an omen; significant; portentous; -- formerly used both in a favorable and unfavorable sense; now chiefly in the latter; foreboding or foreshowing evil; inauspicious; as, an ominous dread. He had a g
Of, pertaining to, or designating, certain strata which occupy an intermediate position between the Eocene and Miocene periods. -- n.
Nourishing; promoting growth, or preventing decay; alimental. -- Nu*tri"tious*ly, adv.
Trifling; vain; futile; insignificant.
Without sense; unmeaning; absurb; foolish; irrational; preposterous. -- Non*sen"si*cal*ly, adv.
Noxious to health; hurtful; mischievous; unwholesome; insalubrious; destructive; as, noisome effluvia. "Noisome pestilence." Ps.
Going about in the night; night-wandering.
Neither the one thing nor the other; on neither side; impartial; neutral. [Archaic] In all our undertakings God will be either our friend or our enemy; for Providence never stands neuter.
More recent than the Eocene, that is, including both the Miocene and Pliocene divisions of the Tertiary.
Of or pertaining to the world; worldly; earthly; terrestrial; as, the mundane sphere. -- Mun"dane*ly, adv.
Giving admonition; instructing by way of caution; warning. Losses, miscarriages, and disappointments, are monitory and instructive.
Capable of being moved; not fixed in place or condition; movable. "Fixed or else mobile." Skelton.
Hindmost; nearest the stern; as, the mizzen shrouds, sails, etc.
Absent from the place where it was expected to be found; lost; wanting; not present when called or looked for. Neither was there aught missing unto them.
Of or pertaining to the middle division of the Tertiary. -- n.
Belonging, or relating, to the secondary or reptilian age, or the era between the Paleozoic and Cenozoic. See Chart of Geology.
Middle; median; in, or in the region of, the mesial plane; internal; -- opposed to lateral. Mesial plane.
Worthy to be remembered; very important or remarkable. -- Mem"o*ra*ble*ness, n.
(a) Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, marrow or medulla. (b) Pertaining to the medula oblongata.
Of a middle quality; of but a moderate or low degree of excellence; indifferent; ordinary. " A very mediocre poet." Pope.

Pertaining to, governed by, or in accordance with, mechanics, or the laws of motion; pertaining to the quantitative relations of force and matter, as distinguished from mental, vital, chemical, etc.; as, mechanical principles; a mechanical theory; mechanical d
Tearful; easily moved to tears; exciting to tears; excessively sentimental; weak and silly. "Maudlin eyes." Dryden.
Advanced in years; elderly.
Possessing or exhibiting majesty; of august dignity, stateliness, or imposing grandeur; lofty; noble; grand. "The majestic world." Shak.
Of or pertaining to luxury; ministering to luxury; supplied with the conditions of luxury; as, a luxurious life; a luxurious table; luxurious ease. " Luxurious cities.
Exuberant in growth; rank; excessive; very abundant; as, a luxuriant growth of grass; luxuriant foliage. Prune the luxuriant, the uncouth refine.
Sweet; delicious; very grateful to the taste; toothsome; excessively sweet or rich. And raisins keep their luscious, native taste.
Pale yellow; ghastly pale; wan; gloomy; dismal. Fierce o'er their beauty blazed the lurid flame.
Having a form like that of the new moon; shaped like a crescent.
Faithful to law; upholding the lawful authority; faithful and true to the lawful government; faithful to the prince or sovereign to whom one is subject; unswerving in allegiance. Welcome, sir John !

Free by birth; hence, befitting a freeman or gentleman; refined; noble; independent; free; not servile or mean; as, a liberal ancestry; a liberal spirit; liberal arts or studies. " Liberal education." Macaulay.
Relaxing; emollient; softening; assuasive; -- some "Lenient of grief." Milton. Of relax the fibers, are lenient, balsamic.
Characterized by leisure; taking abundant tome; not hurried; as, a leisurely manner; a leisurely walk.
Like bricks; of the color of red bricks. Lateritious sediment (Med.), a sediment in urine resembling brick dust, observed after the crises of fevers, and at the termination of gouty paroxysms.
Coming after the time when due, or after the usual or proper time; not early; slow; tardy; long delayed; as, a late spring.
Consisting of, or resembling, lard. Lardaceous degeneration (Med.), amyloid degeneration.
Mourning; sorrowful; expressing grief; as, a lamentable countenance. "Lamentable eye." Spenser.
Uttering songs of triumph; shouting with joy; triumphant; exulting. "The jubilant age." Coleridge.
affected with jaundice. Jaundiced eyes seem to see all objects yellow.
Placed or standing alone; detached; separated from others. Isolated point of a curve.
Incapable of being recalled or revoked; unchangeable; irreversible; unalterable; as, an irrevocable promise or decree; irrevocable fate. Firm and irrevocable is my doom.
Not rational; void of reason or understanding; as, brutes are irrational animals.

Not violable; not susceptible of hurt, wound, or harm (used with respect to either physical or moral damage); not susceptible of being profaned or corrupted; sacred; holy; as, inviolable honor or chastity; an inviolable shrine. He tried a third, a tough, well-
Not tractable; not easily governed, managed, or directed; indisposed to be taught, disciplined, or tamed; violent; stubborn; obstinate; refractory; as, an intractable child.
Not enduring; not able to endure. The powers of human bodies being limited and intolerant of excesses.
Untouched, especially by anything that harms, defiles, or the like; uninjured; undefiled; left complete or entire. Buckle.
Of or pertaining to an island; of the nature, or possessing the characteristics, of an island; as, an insular climate, fauna, etc.
Careless; heedless; indifferent; unconcerned. J.
Wanting in the qualities which affect the organs of taste; without taste or savor; vapid; tasteless; as, insipid drink or food. Boyle.
Destitute of the power of feeling or perceiving; wanting bodily sensibility. Milton.
Not operative; not active; producing no effects; as, laws renderd inoperative by neglect; inoperative remedies or processes.
Harmless; producing no ill effect; innocent. A patient, innocuous, innocent man.

Not capable of being imitated, copied, or counterfeited; beyond imitation; surpassingly excellent; matchless; unrivaled; exceptional; unique; as, an inimitable style; inimitable eloquence. "Inimitable force." Dryden.
Filled, as with air or gas; blown up; distended; as, a balloon inflated with gas.
Not exact; not precisely correct or true; inaccurate.
Not efficient; not producing the effect intended or desired; inefficacious; as, inefficient means or measures.
Not producing the proper effect; without effect; inefficient; weak; useless; futile; unavailing; as, an ineffectual attempt; an ineffectual expedient. Pope.
Not effective; ineffectual; futile; inefficient; useless; as, an ineffective appeal. The word of God, without the spirit, [is] a dead and ineffective letter.
Prone to indulge; yielding to the wishes, humor, or appetites of those under one's care; compliant; not opposing or restraining; tolerant; mild; favorable; not severe; as, an indulgent parent. Shak.
Not to be subdued; untamable; invincible; as, an indomitable will, courage, animal.
That can not be removed, washed away, blotted out, or effaced; incapable of being canceled, lost, or forgotten; as, indelible characters; an indelible stain; an indelible impression on the memory.
Not capable of being cured; beyond the power of skill or medicine to remedy; as, an incurable disease. A scirrh is not absolutely incurable.
Continuing or following without interruption; unceasing; unitermitted; uninterrupted; continual; as, incessant clamors; incessant pain, etc. Against the castle gate, .
Without contents; empty; void of sense or intelligence; purposeless; pointless; characterless; useless. "Vague and inane instincts." I.
Laying as a duty; enjoining.
Rushing with force and violence; moving with impetus; furious; forcible; violent; as, an impetuous wind; an impetuous torrent. Went pouring forward with impetuous speed.
Of or pertaining to an empire, or to an emperor; as, an imperial government; imperial authority or edict. The last That wore the imperial diadem of Rome.
Not palpable; that cannot be felt; extremely fine, so that no grit can be perceived by touch. "Impalpable powder." Boyle.
Incapable of being moved; firmly fixed; fast; -- used of material things; as, an immovable foundatin. Immovable, infixed, and frozen round.
Not capable of being mitigated, softened, or appeased. Coleridge.
Immeasurable; unlimited. In commonest use: Very great; vast; huge.
Not separated in respect to place by anything intervening; proximate; close; as, immediate contact. You are the most immediate to our throne.

Inclined to imitate, copy, or follow; imitating; exhibiting some of the qualities or characteristics of a pattern or model; dependent on example; not original; as, man is an imitative being; painting is an imitative art.
Deceiving by false show; deceitful; deceptive; false; illusory; unreal. Truth from illusive falsehood to command.
Not liberal; not free or generous; close; niggardly; mean; sordid. "A thrifty and illiberal hand." Mason.
Not according to, or authorized by, law; specif., contrary to, or in violation of, human law; unlawful; illicit; hence, immoral; as, an illegal act; illegal trade; illegal love. Bp.
Totally surrounded with ice, so as to be incapable of advancing; as, an icebound vessel; also, surrounded by or fringed with ice so as to hinder easy access; as, an icebound coast.

Full of hope, or agreeable expectation; inclined to hope; expectant. Men of their own natural inclination hopeful and strongly conceited.
Worthy of honor; fit to be esteemed or regarded; estimable; illustrious. Thy name and honorable family.
Extravagant in opinions or ambition. "Highflying, arbitrary kings." Dryden.

Pertaining to, containing, derived from, or resembling, graphite. Graphitic acid (Chem.), an organic acid, so called because obtained by the oxidation of graphite; -- usually called mellitic acid.
Like gossamer; flimsy. The greatest master of gossamery affectation.
Imposing through splendid or various colors; showy; fine; magnificent. Cloud-land, gorgeous land.
Moody; silent; sullen. I frighten people by my glun face.

Transported with passion or fury; raging; violent; as, a furious animal.

Inclined to frisk; frolicsome; gay. He is too frisky for an old man.

Affectedly fine; overnice; unduly particular; fastidious. "Finical taste." Wordsworth.
Fernlike, either in form or in the nature of the method of reproduction.

Like a fiend; diabolically wicked or cruel; infernal; malignant; devilish; hellish. -- Fiend"ish*ly, adv.
Not fixed or firm; liable to change; unstable; of a changeable mind; not firm in opinion or purpose; inconstant; capricious; as, Fortune's fickle wheel. Shak.
Hot; glowing; boiling; burning; as, a fervent summer. The elements shall melt with fervent heat.
Difficult to please; delicate to fault; suited with difficulty; squeamish; as, a fastidious mind or ear; a fastidious appetite. Proud youth !

Exacting or requiring immediate aid or action; pressing; critical. "At this exigent moment." Burke.

Belonging to elegy, or written in elegiacs; plaintive; expressing sorrow or lamentation; as, an elegiac lay; elegiac strains. Elegiac griefs, and songs of love.
Possessing the quality of being effective; productive of, or powerful to produce, the effect intended; as, an efficacious law.
Pertaining to, or caused by, ecstasy or excessive emotion; of the nature, or in a state, of ecstasy; as, ecstatic gaze; ecstatic trance. This ecstatic fit of love and jealousy.
Boiling up or over; hence, manifesting exhilaration or excitement, as of feeling; effervescing. "Ebullient with subtlety." De Quincey.

At ease; free from pain, trouble, or constraint; as: (a) Free from pain, distress, toil, exertion, and the like; quiet; as, the patient is easy. (b) Free from care, responsibility, discontent, and the like; not anxious; tranquil; as, an easy mind.
